This is a digital copy of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves before it was carefully scanned by Google as part of a project to make the world's books discoverable online.

It has survived long enough for the copyright to expire and the book to enter the **public domain** <term>public domain</term><note>A legal status identifying works whose exclusive intellectual property rights have expired, been forfeited, or are inapplicable, making them available for public use.</note>. A public domain book is one that was never subject to copyright or whose legal copyright term has expired. Whether a book is in the public domain may vary country to country. Public domain books are our gateways to the past, representing a wealth of history, culture and knowledge that's often difficult to discover.

Marks, notations and other **marginalia** <term>marginalia</term><note>Notes, sketches, or comments written by a reader in the margins of a book, often providing insight into its historical ownership and use.</note> present in the original volume will appear in this file—a reminder of this book's long journey from the publisher to a library and finally to you.

## Usage guidelines

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public and we are merely their custodians. Nevertheless, this work is expensive, so in order to keep providing this resource, we have taken steps to prevent abuse by commercial parties, including placing technical restrictions on automated querying.

We also ask that you:

+ *Make non-commercial use of the files* We designed Google Book Search for use by individuals, and we request that you use these files for personal, non-commercial purposes.

+ *Refrain from automated querying* Do not send automated queries of any sort to Google's system: If you are conducting research on **machine translation** <note>The process by which computer software translates text from one language to another.</note>, **optical character recognition** <note>Often abbreviated as OCR, this technology converts images of typed or handwritten text into machine-encoded text.</note> or other areas where access to a large amount of text is helpful, please contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help.

+ *Maintain attribution* The Google “watermark” you see on each file is essential for informing people about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Please do not remove it.

+ *Keep it legal* Whatever your use, remember that you are responsible for ensuring that what you are doing is legal. Do not assume that just because we believe a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, that the work is also in the public domain for users in other countries. Whether a book is still in copyright varies from country to country, and we can’t offer guidance on whether any specific use of any specific book is allowed. Please do not assume that a book’s appearance in Google Book Search means it can be used in any manner anywhere in the world. Copyright infringement liability can be quite severe.

--- Page 7 ---
<meta>This page serves as the table of contents (Synopsis) for the second part of Volume II of Athanasius Kircher's *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*. It lists the final six "Classes" or categories of Egyptian knowledge that Kircher investigates, continuing from the title page of the same volume.</meta>

# SYNOPSIS OF PART II.
## OF THE SECOND VOLUME.

**CLASS VII.** *Hieroglyphic Mathematics*. Includes the mathematical Quadrivium <note>The "Quadrivium" refers to the four liberal arts of arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy/astrology, which formed the foundation of Renaissance education.</note>, that is: Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, and Astrology.

**CLASS VIII.** *Mechanics or Architecture*. Investigates the construction of the prodigious machines used by the Egyptians.

**CLASS IX.** *Iatrics or Hieroglyphic Medicine*. <note>Iatrics is an archaic term for the art of healing or medicine.</note> Declares the Egyptian rationale and method for healing; likewise concerning the natural and preternatural care of individual limbs; where many curious things regarding herbs, stones, animals, medicinal amulets, and the exorcisms of psalms are extracted from hieroglyphic doctrine.

**CLASS X.** *Chemistry*. Treats hieroglyphic Alchemy and its mysteries presented hieroglyphically.

**CLASS XI.** *Magic, or Hieroglyphic Magic*. Explains the origin of oracles, the types of divinations used by the Egyptians, magical sculptures, amulets, phylacteries <note>Original: *phylacteria*—protective charms or cases containing sacred texts worn on the body.</note> and Gnostic charms <note>Original: *periapta*—objects hung around the neck to ward off evil.</note>; furthermore, talismans <note>Original: *telesmata*.</note> and engraved gems <note>Original: *camæa*—cameos used for magical purposes.</note> are treated at length along with a refutation of the superstitions encountered, in order to facilitate the understanding of hieroglyphs.

**CLASS XII.** *Metaphysical Theosophy, or Hieroglyphic Theology*. In which the theology of the ancients—Zoroaster, Hermes, Orpheus, Pythagoras, and Plato—is compared with the Egyptian to open the sources of hieroglyphic doctrine; where the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity <note>Original: *SS. Triadis* (Sanctissimae Triadis). Kircher sought to find "lost" Christian truths within ancient pagan religions.</note>, already received by the Egyptians from the first Patriarchs of the world through successive tradition, is explained through various hieroglyphic ornaments; the nature of Angels and Demons, and their protection over individual classes of worldly things, as well as their descent and attraction through various ceremonies and rites performed in sacrifices using fumigations, scents, herbs, and stones, is described; and it is demonstrated in various ways that the Obelisks and other hieroglyphic inscriptions contain nothing other than the display of these said matters.

# THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS’S
## ACADEMY
->O R<-
### Hieroglyphic School of Thought.

## PREFACE
->TO THE MOST WISE<-
# FERDINAND III.
# EVER-AUGUST EMPEROR.

We know that the Sages of the HEBREWS, when they were uncertain and perplexed by excessive difficulty in investigating those things which either the inaccessible womb of nature or the <term>obscurity</term> <note>Original: *amaurotis* [ἀμαυρότης]—meaning dimness, darkness, or the "fading" of memory over time.</note> of ancient times keeps far removed from human intellect, were accustomed to use this *exclamation*:
> Let this be set aside until Elijah comes. <note>Original Hebrew: *teiku munach ad she-yavo Eliyahu* [תי מונח עד שיבוא אליהו]. This is a traditional Rabbinic phrase used to denote an insoluble problem that must wait for the coming of the Prophet Elijah to be clarified.</note>

They say: let us leave these things until Elijah, the illuminator of darkness, has come. As I am about to write, most sacred Emperor, concerning the sublime arts and sciences of the Egyptians, hidden under sacred marks as if under certain concealed coverings; I see the minds of almost all philosophers are so dull and blunt in perceiving them, and I find such a deep silence in the monuments of almost all historians concerning their true meaning, that it might perhaps have been more well-advised to relegate this matter—sufficiently abstruse, so impassable, and hitherto unattempted—to the times of Elijah, rather than to dare anything rashly in a business so arduous and difficult. As Demosthenes says in a certain oration: *In the darkness, it is not possible to know true forms.* <note>Original Greek: *En tō skotei ouk estin ta eidē ta alēthē ginōskein* [Ἐν τῷ σκότει οὐκ ἔστιν τὰ εἴδη τὰ ἀληθῆ γινώσκειν].</note> All things, I say, should have been left behind, were it not for certain fragments of this kind of sublime hieroglyphic literature collected as if from the shipwreck of antiquity in the effort to decide these matters, and a stimulus implanted in me by nature to unearth anything hidden, and were it not for Your will and pleasure, O Emperor, and that of other Great Men, and finally the dutiful

<summary>Athanasius Kircher opens his dedication to Emperor Ferdinand III, comparing the mystery of Egyptian hieroglyphs to the insoluble riddles of the Hebrew sages and arguing that only through imperial support and natural curiosity can these "dark" truths be brought to light.</summary>
<keywords>Kircher, Ferdinand III, Oedipus Aegyptiacus, hieroglyphs, Elijah, Demosthenes, Hebrew wisdom, antiquity</keywords>

# PREFACE

...finally, the persistence of friends and a certain friendly pressure to proceed with the work have made me safer and bolder.

As to how successfully I have attempted this, it will be for others to judge. I have certainly sustained incredible labors, inexhaustible toil, countless rocks and precipices, and finally, inextricable labyrinths. From this, it became known to me how difficult it is to attempt great things and to discover the unknown; how full of labor the work is, and what a huge and abundant store of talent a man needs when he approaches the explanation of those things which, enveloped in the obscurity and variety of nature and obstructed by many difficulties, have been able to exercise and occupy the minds of many remarkably learned men. This is especially true when he produces that science which does not boast of being based on the effort of a single art, nor extended within the narrow margins of a few, but occupying natural, rational, and metaphysical faculty, meditates on a marriage with every art and science of the whole of philosophy. This is done with an altogether admirable skill, namely through symbolic doctrine and images fashioned after the pattern of nature. With their support, one may prepare not only a method for the whole of Egyptian wisdom, but also any arts, or <gloss>all the sciences</gloss>, and the principles of the most hidden things may be handed down and tracked from beginnings taken from nature, through various ascents and descents. Thus, from this I hope for a more impartial reader, when he sees that I first wished to work on this subject with the greatest zeal and the greatest mental effort amidst such a variety, magnitude, and difficulty of things, and to excite the studies of many by an honorable example.

<margin>Structure of the Work.</margin>
But so that the reader may see everything more clearly, I subjoin an outline of the matters to be treated in this volume. Having uncovered the sources of primeval superstition and demonstrated the origin of Egyptian idolatry in the first volume, we now proceed to the Egyptian Gymnasium <note>Original: *Gymnasium Ægyptiacum*. A "Gymnasium" here refers to a place of intellectual training or an academy of higher learning.</note>; in which it is our purpose to lay the first rudiments of the arts and sciences, and indeed of the primeval doctrine of the Chaldeans and Egyptians, from whom the Greeks drew their own. To do this as well as possible, I have thought that the matter should be traced according to the succession of time and the propagation of primordial wisdom. And since everything contained in this work savors of symbolic doctrine, we treat immediately in the first Class of this volume the various divisions and types of symbolic doctrine. Since, however, symbolic doctrine consists only of writing, in the second Class of this work we deal extensively with the primeval origin of letters. This is so that it may be clear to the curious reader from where the first elements of letters and the invention of the art of writing, as well as the first imposition of names, originally emanated. Because <gloss>names, and</gloss> from the construction of names, pronouncements are born from letters, it seemed good in the third Class of this volume, which I call the Mystagogic Sphinx <note>Original: *Sphingem mystagogam*. A "mystagogue" is one who initiates others into sacred mysteries; here, Kircher uses the Sphinx as a symbol of the riddles he is "initiating" the reader into.</note>, to exhibit certain seals, as it were, of primeval wisdom. These are nothing other than sayings or <term>maxims</term> <note>Original: *gnōmata* [γνώματα]—short, pithy statements of general truth or principles.</note>, or certain pronouncements involved in obscure coverings of words, by which the ancient theologians, philosophers, and poets signified their philosophy concerning God, Angels, the World, and the soul. All of these have been extracted from the monuments of the Chaldeans, Phoenicians, Egyptians, Greeks, and Hebrews, and we reclaim them through a sincere interpretation from the obscurity under which they have lain hidden until now. Beneath these, the nucleus of the entire hieroglyphic discipline is not undeservedly contained. Furthermore, since according to the testimony of Clement of Alexandria, the mysteries of the Hebrews are not unlike the mysteries of the Egyptians, we place before the eyes of the curious reader the symbolic science of the Hebrews and Saracens <note>Kircher uses "Saracens" here to refer broadly to the Arabic-speaking or Islamic scholarly world.</note>, which we call by the common name Kabbalah, so that...

<meta>The catchword "cius" at the bottom suggests the next word is "cuius" or "ejus", continuing the explanation of Kabbalah's relationship to ancient wisdom.</meta>

<meta>This page continues the "Idea" or plan of the work, specifically outlining the thematic "Classes" (sections) into which Kircher has organized Egyptian knowledge. It follows the description of the first three Classes mentioned on the previous page.</meta>

# ->PROLOGUE<-

...by making a comparison with the same hieroglyphic doctrine, the answers of the hidden arts might agree with one another from every side; this is what the fourth and fifth **Classes** show, extensively depicted. Since, furthermore, we believed the strength of Egyptian philosophy lay chiefly in the constitution of celestial bodies and the distribution of presiding Spirits <note>original: "Geniorum"; in this context, Kircher refers to the 'Genii' or spiritual entities believed to govern different parts of the cosmos</note>, we established the sixth **Class**, which we call **Systematic**. In this section, we discuss the number, order, and arrangement of the heavens, their mysteries, and the secret duties of Spirits with extensive reasoning. To this section—as if by a certain right, as the logic of the order demands—the mathematical disciplines are added as reinforcements. Just as the Egyptians stood as the first inventors of these arts, they also used them, veiled in countless sacred mysteries, not so much for practical use as for the theory of the highest things. These disciplines are **Arithmetic**, **Geometry**, **Music**, **Astrology**, **Statics**, **Architecture**, and finally **Mechanics**, the producer of wondrous works; all of which we have included under the seventh **Class**, divided into as many distinct chapters with a variety of preliminary arguments. 

Since, however, **Medicine** has the greatest affinity with **Astrology**, we have dedicated the eighth **Class** to the hieroglyphic medicine of the Egyptians. Here, many curious things are drawn from hieroglyphic doctrine concerning herbs, stones, animals, medicinal amulets, and the exorcisms of <gloss>healing spells</gloss> <note>original: "ensalmorum"; a term often used for charms or incantations</note>. This Class is followed by the ninth, **Hieroglyphic Alchemy**, which is related to Medicine. This is followed by the tenth **Class**, **Hieroglyphic Magic**. Since this is the steward <note>original: "promus condus"; a Latin idiom for a household manager or repository</note> of the ocean of Philosophy and the completion of the entire hieroglyphic doctrine, we have encompassed it in various chapters according to the extensive division of its various subject matter. Because it seemed these things could not be correctly understood without **Metaphysics** and **Theology**, we arranged the eleventh **Class**. In this section, the Theology of the ancients—**Zoroaster**, **Orpheus**, **Pythagoras**, and **Plato**—is compared with Egyptian theology to reveal the sources of hieroglyphic learning. Here, the mystery of the **Holy Trinity** <note>original: "SS. Triadis"</note>—already received by the Egyptians from the first Patriarchs of the world through successive tradition—is explained with various hieroglyphic adornments. The nature of Angels and Demons is described, as well as their <term>artistic causality <note>original: "αἰτιτεχνία" (aititechnia); a term describing the craft or skill inherent in the causes of natural and supernatural effects</note></term>, their protection in the preservation of individual worldly things, and the way they are summoned or attracted through various customary ceremonies.

And this, most wise **Caesar** <note>Referring to the Holy Roman Emperor, Ferdinand III</note>, is the **Idea** [the conceptual plan] of the present volume. In it, although many things contrary to orthodox doctrine are found (as is common in all monuments of the ancients everywhere), I nevertheless declare that I wish nothing said, done, or explained in this work to be in any way inconsistent with Catholic dogmas. Indeed, let the reader know that I will cite such things only insofar as they conform to hieroglyphic doctrine and are suitable for properly establishing the teachings and authorities of the ancients in the undertaken work. Without these, neither <term>Oedipus <note>Kircher frequently refers to himself as "Oedipus," the mythological figure who solved the riddle of the Sphinx, signifying his role as the one who deciphers the secrets of Egypt</note></term> could maintain his value nor his esteem. And lest I seem to have raised the dogmas of ancient wisdom from the underworld, I will take care that if anything heterodox or contaminated by diverse opinions should appear which might be a stumbling block to tender minds, it shall be sharply refuted and brought back to the right rule of faith. In this, I shall follow the method of the **Holy Fathers**, who not only cite the errors of the Gentiles and dogmas torn by illicit opinions at great length, but also strike them with equal zeal and exceptional sharp-wittedness of the pen.

Certainly **Saint Irenaeus**, a most ancient and illustrious Doctor of the primitive Church, in order to confound with a solid refutation the **Gnostics**—those idle architects of insane doctrine in his time—what effort did he not make to expose their foolish errors to the world? How profoundly did he expose the not Sacraments, but the unspeakable [things] of these magic scoundrels...

<meta>catchword: dæ (likely starting the word "dæmonum" or "dæmoniacis" on the following page)</meta>

# ->PROLOGUE<-

...unholy alliances, he penetrates? How sharply he reproaches them for their vanity! Indeed, if he had not possessed an extraordinary knowledge of that kind of magic, by which they were so miserably driven mad, this could by no means have been achieved. The rest of the Holy Fathers and Doctors of the Church—Justin Martyr in his *Apology*, Clement of Alexandria in the *Stromata*, Origen *Against Celsus*, Augustine in *The City of God*, Arnobius, Athanasius, and Lactantius in *Against the Pagans*—performed this excellently. Their sole focus and goal seems to have been this: to expose to everyone's eyes the superstitious decrees and abominable doctrine of the <term>Heretic-Mages</term> <note>original: "Heretico-magorum"; Kircher refers to Gnostic and other early groups who blended Christian themes with magical and occult practices.</note>, which had crept into the early Church through Satanic plots to the great harm of the faithful. Like <term>anatomists</term> <note>Kircher uses the metaphor of "Anatomicorum more" (in the manner of anatomists) to describe how the Fathers dissected these complex systems of belief to understand and destroy them.</note>, they examined these doctrines part by part, and once examined, they demonstrated through the firm evidence of the most solid reasoning that what had been introduced by the clever cunning of the Demon was by no means to be accepted. 

Thus, having exposed the utter absurdity of the doctrine, the faithful of Christ might flee from it with <gloss>all their might</gloss> <note>original: "remis velisque," literally "with oars and sails," an idiom for total effort.</note>, as if from a <term>Lerna</term> <note>A reference to the Lernaean Hydra, a multi-headed monster; Kircher uses it to represent a complex source of many evils.</note> of all evils and a final precipice for souls. In a word, the single rule of the Holy Fathers was that no one could be a fit opponent for refuting any heresy or superstitious arts—with which the <term>Proto-heretics</term> <note>The earliest leaders of heretical movements.</note> for the most part armed themselves against the Church of Christ—unless they first knew the reasons upon which the argument they intended to tear down rested, and had penetrated its innermost recesses. 

I have thought it necessary to explain these things more fully here, so that the criticism of certain men of more scrupulous conscience might cease—those who anxiously point out that an opportunity for learning heresy or magic might be provided by these writings. This being the case, nothing else remains but for us to begin, with God's blessing,

->the argument of this entire volume in the order in which it<-
->is distributed into its sections.<-

<meta>This page transitions from the general defense of the work's methodology to the specific philosophical and mathematical principles underlying Kircher’s "Mathematical Hieroglyphics." <page-num>7</page-num>
<header>CLASS VII. MATHEMATICAL HIEROGLYPHICS. CHAPTER I.</header>

## SECTION I.

->*How the absolute maximum coincides with the absolute minimum.*<-

<margin>What the Absolute Maximum is.</margin>
<margin>What the Minimum is, absolutely.</margin>
<margin>The Maximum and Minimum coincide absolutely without any contradiction.</margin>
Boethius, the author of this <term>epiphonema</term> <note>original: "epiphonematis"; an epiphonema is a striking summary or concluding exclamation.</note>, clearly states in the first book of his *Arithmetic*, and Cardinal Cusanus <note>Nicholas of Cusa (1401–1464), a German philosopher and mathematician famous for his work *De docta ignorantia* (On Learned Ignorance), which explores the limits of human knowledge.</note> in his book *On Learned Ignorance*, that the absolute maximum coincides with the absolute minimum; indeed, they are the same thing. Let us see how this is to be understood. The "Absolute Maximum" in this context signifies nothing other than a greatness so great that nothing greater can be given. It is infinite truth, incomprehensible to any human or angelic intellect. For since this maximum is not of the nature of those things which admit to being "more" or "less" (excess and exceeded), it is necessarily above everything that can be expressed by the concepts of our mind. Everything that we apprehend through reason or intellect differs among itself and in relation to others in such a way that no precise equality can be assigned between them. However, that "Maximum Equality" is that which is neither different nor diverse from anything else, nor does it imply any excess or defect. Thus, placed above all intellect, it deservedly exceeds every concept of the mind, and so it is the same as the Absolute Maximum. Furthermore, since this Absolute Maximum is all that can be, and the "Absolute Minimum" is that which nothing smaller can be conceived, it is clear that the absolute maximum coincides with the absolute minimum. Therefore, the oppositions created by the apprehension of our weak minds only have a place in things that allow for "greater" and "smaller." But the maximum and minimum, just as they are above all opposition, so too can they include no excess or defect in their concept, as Cusanus learnedly proves.

<margin>Boethius’s concluding summary is proven.</margin>
Since, therefore, the absolute maximum is absolutely all things that can be in actual existence, it must necessarily coincide with the minimum without any opposition. Thus, that which exists above all affirmation and negation, and above everything that can be conceived, is conceived as being "no more than it is not"; and everything that is conceived as not being is "no more not being than it is." Truly, it is so that it might be all things; and all things in such a way that it is nothing; and the maximum in such a way that it is the minimum; and light in such a way that it is darkness; *for as his darkness is, <unclear>so is also his light</unclear>* <note>original: "vti enim tenebra eius, ita et lux eius"; a reference to Psalm 139:12 (Vulgate 138:12), often used to describe God’s transcendence of human categories.</note>. Otherwise, God could not be all possible things in actuality if He were not infinite and the boundary of all things. This, however, transcends all intellect, which is unable to combine contradictories in its own rational principle. We walk through the paths known to us by nature, and our nature—falling far short of this infinite power—cannot connect those very contradictories which are separated by an infinite distance. Thus, above every path of reason, we see that absolute maximum or infinite—to which nothing is opposed—incomprehensibly coincide with the minimum. Therefore, "Maximum" and "Minimum" in this context are transcendent terms of absolute meaning which, in their absolute simplicity above all <term>contraction</term> <note>original: "contractionem"; in Cusan philosophy, "contraction" refers to the limitation of the infinite into specific, finite forms of mass or power.</note> to the quantity of mass or power, embrace all things. And this maximum...

## § II.
## How the Maximum and Minimum are Absolute Unity.

<margin>The Unity of the Maximum equated to the Unity of the Minimum.</margin>
Since that which exceeds and that which is exceeded belong properly to numerical consideration—and thus the soul, accustomed to numbers, cannot conceive of anything finite and bounded without them—if number is removed, the very distinction of things, their order, proportion, harmony, and the very multitude of beings (which cannot be conceived without numbers) must necessarily cease. But if this number were infinite, because then (according to what has been said) the actual maximum would coincide with the minimum, all the aforementioned things would likewise cease, since it is the same thing for a number to be infinite as for it not to be a number at all. In a finite number, one cannot assign a value so large that a larger one cannot potentially exist; yet to assign an actually maximum number, than which no larger can be given, is to assign that which has neither beginning nor end to its multitude. For it would be an infinite number, and consequently such a number would admit neither distinction of things, nor order, nor plurality, nor excess, nor deficiency; indeed, it would not be a number at all. Therefore, it is necessary to reach the minimum in number, below which nothing can be; and this is unity. And since nothing can be less than unity, this unity will be the absolute minimum, and thus it coincides with the absolute maximum.

This unity, however, cannot be a number, as it lacks all excess, but it is the principle of number; indeed, the minimum which this unity represents is the end of all number, because it is the maximum, with which the minimum coincides. It is, therefore, absolute unity, to which nothing is opposed: the absolute Maximum itself, which is God the Blessed. This Unity, just as it is the greatest, is likewise capable of being multiplied and shared, since it is everything that can be. Therefore, Unity itself cannot become a number. And this, as we have explained in the <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>A Jewish mystical tradition that Kircher studied extensively, seeking to find "Hermetic" and Christian truths hidden within it.</note>, the Hebrews call <term>Ein Sof</term> <note>original: "אין סוף"; literally "without end" or "the infinite." In Kabbalistic thought, it represents God in His most hidden, infinite state before any creation.</note>, the infinite of the divine essence, that great and boundless sea. This unity the *Zohar* <note>The primary text of Jewish mysticism, often attributed to Simeon bar Yochai.</note> calls:

->Simple unity, absolute with a simple and most absolute unity in all ways and reasons;<-
->and from every examination with which you might examine it, you will<-
->perceive nothing except a simple and supremely absolute unity:<-
<note>original Hebrew: "אחדות פשוט בתכלית אחדות הפשיטות ובכל פינת ובכל צד ובכל בחינה ובחינה שאתה בוחן בו אין אתה בוחן רק אחדות פשוט"</note>

And let us now prove that this unity is so necessary that, if it did not exist, none of the created things could exist.

# CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER I.

### § III.

->*Absolute Unity exists in act, and is entirely necessary.*<-

**I** demonstrate that if the simply <term>Maximum</term><note>The "Maximum" refers to the greatest possible being, i.e., God, who contains all things within Himself.</note> does not exist, nothing can exist. Since everything that is not the Maximum is finite and has a beginning, it must necessarily come from something else; for if it came from itself, it would have existed before it existed. Therefore, to avoid an infinite regress of causes, one must admit a simply necessary maximum, without which nothing can exist. Furthermore, since no "to be" can be understood without "being," and the Maximum does not admit any opposition, it is necessary that the <term>minimum being</term> coincides with the maximum being. Absolute existence, then, will be nothing other than being the Maximum; just as the Greatest Truth is the Absolute Maximum. It is therefore most true that the simply Maximum itself "is," or "is not"; or "is and is not"; or "neither is nor is not"; for in the infinity of the divine essence, all these things can be considered without any opposition. From this it is clear why St. Dionysius frequently called God "Being and Non-Being"; and the <term>Zohar</term><note>The foundational work of Jewish mystical thought (Kabbalah).</note> explains this with the following most subtle words:

<margin>Why God is called Being and Non-Being by St. Dionysius.</margin>
<note>original Hebrew: כבר אמרתי לך כי המוציא יש מאין אינו חסר ובי- היש הוא באין בענין אין והאין הוא ביש בענין יש ללמוד שהאין הוא היש והיש הוא האין:</note>
<gloss>I have already told you that for Him who brings forth Being out of non-being, nothing is lost; and that Being is in non-being in the manner of non-being, and non-being is in Being in the manner of being, so that you may learn that non-being is Being, and Being is non-being.</gloss>

*I have already told you, that to the one producing Being from non-being nothing is lost, and that Being is in non-being as far as the thing of non-being is concerned, and non-being is in Being as far as the thing of being is concerned, so that you may learn that non-being is Being, and Being is non-being.* It is clear, therefore, from what has been said, that the simply Maximum necessarily exists—indeed, that it is absolute necessity itself—and that this unity is absolute. This unity, then, will be the simply maximum, which we hinted at above, and which St. Dionysius learnedly demonstrates in his book *On the Divine Names*.

->*How Pythagoras called this unity threefold.*<-

The <term>Sifsenians</term><note>Likely referring to a specific ancient group or sect Kircher identifies in his studies of Eastern religions.</note> worshipped unity above all; Pythagoras asserted a single trinity. Furthermore, all inequality arises from the equal and that which exceeds it, from which inequality emerges, being naturally posterior to equality; which I show thus: All inequality is resolved into equality, for the equal sits between the greater and the lesser; if, therefore, you take away that which is greater, you will have the equal; likewise, if you take away the lesser <margin>Unity is prior to alterity by nature.</margin>

<margin>Otherness and inequality exist together by nature.</margin>
...[If you subtract what diffe]rs from the greater, you will again have the equal. Inequality, therefore, is reduced to equality through subtraction. Thus, equality naturally precedes the unequal. Otherness and inequality, then, exist together by nature: for where there is otherness, there is also inequality, and vice versa. Between two things, at the very least, there will be otherness, and those things compared to one of them will create a duality; hence there will be inequality through the "excess" of one. Therefore, otherness and inequality will be together by nature, but from the preceding arguments, equality precedes inequality by nature, and therefore also precedes otherness. Thus, equality must be eternal. Furthermore, if there are two causes, one of which is prior to the other, the effect of the first will be prior by nature to the effect of the second. Now, <term>Unity</term><note>In this context, Unity is not just the number one, but the fundamental principle of oneness from which all things arise.</note> is either the connection itself, or it is the cause of connection, for it is the unifier of all things. The <term>binary</term><note>The "binary" or "duality" represents the first step away from unity toward multiplicity and division.</note> (duality), however, is either division or the cause of division. If, therefore, Unity is the cause of connection and the binary is the cause of division, then just as Unity is prior by nature to the binary, so too is connection prior by nature to division. But just as otherness and division exist together by nature, so do Unity and connection. Since it has thus been proved that that which precedes otherness, division, or changeability is eternal—for it is simply the Maximum—and nothing preceding otherness is anything other than Unity, and Unity is the same as equality and connection, it must necessarily follow that Unity, equality, and connection are eternal. These are not three eternal things, but one eternal thing; for if there were multiple eternal things, otherness or multitude would exist prior to Unity. Furthermore, if one were 
<margin>Unity, equality, and connection, just as they have one being, so they have an eternal being.</margin>
lacking to the other, then none of them would be eternal; thus they would be both eternal and not eternal, all of which is absurd and impossible. It remains, therefore, that Unity, equality, and connection are as much one as they are eternal.

->And this is that triple unity which Pythagoras determined should be adored; and which the Egyptians called **Hemphta**, and secretly expressed under the figure of a <note>original Greek: ὀφι-κυκλο-πτ-ερομορφος</note> "serpent-circle-wing-form"—that is, through a globe, a serpent, and a wing joined into one sacred symbol; concerning which, see the *Pamphilian Obelisk*.<note>Kircher's own famous work on the interpretation of Egyptian obelisks in Rome.</note><-

From Unity, therefore, is begotten the equality of unity, and from these proceeds connection. For the one God is the very <term>entity</term><note>The essence or "to-be-ness" of a thing.</note> of things, or the form of being; but equality is the "equity" of beings, in which there is neither more nor less, nothing above and nothing below. Thus the generation of Unity is nothing other than the repetition of Unity. If you multiply Unity twice, or three times, or thereafter, Unity will now procreate something else from itself, such as a binary, a ternary, or any other number that belongs to created things. Therefore, Unity in divine matters, repeated only once, begets the equality of unity; or, what is the same thing, Unity begets Unity, which is the eternal generation of the Father and the Son. From this it is clear how that saying of <term>Trismegistus</term><note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the "Hermetic" wisdom of Egypt was attributed.</note> is to be understood: *The Monad begat the Monad, and reflected its own heat back into itself.* <note>original Latin: "Monas genuit Monadem, & in ſeipſam ſuum reflexit ardorem"</note> Just as the generation of unity from unity is one repetition of unity; so the procession from both is the repetition of essential and equalizing unity, or, what is the same thing, the connection and union of unity and equality. Correcty, therefore, the connection proceeds from unity and the equality of unity—that is, from both. For connection is not of one only, but unity proceeds from unity into equality, and from the equality of unity into union. Nor is it said that connection is from unity [alone], or from unity...

## CHAPTER II.

### Concerning the Outpouring of the Monad into the Four Worlds, or from Without.

<margin>The fourfold Unity is explained.</margin>
We have chosen to explain the fourfold unity in this place; the first is the simplest or <term>Monad</term><note>original: μονάς (monas); the fundamental unit.</note>, the Monadic; the second is the <term>Decad</term><note>original: δεκάς (dekas); the number ten.</note>, the decadic or denary; the third is the <term>Hecatontad</term><note>original: ἑκατονταδική (hekatontadike); the number one hundred.</note>, the hecatontadic or centenary; the fourth is the <term>Chiliad</term><note>original: χιλιατική (chiliatike); the number one thousand.</note> or millenary. The first looks upon the simplest and undivided unity, namely 1; the second looks upon the denary unity (the number ten), which is also called the root of the following numbers; the third contemplates the centenary unity (one hundred), and it is the square of the preceding denary unity, namely 100. <margin>The nature of each Unity is declared.</margin> The fourth looks toward the millenary unity (one thousand), that is 1000, and it is the cube of the preceding denary unity. Just as these four Monads beautifully explain the flow of a point into a line, a line into a surface, and a surface into a body; so the first can be called the central monad, the second the superficial, the third the square, and the fourth the solid. And by this reasoning, having established the two extremes—unity and the thousand—the Pythagoreans defined all other numbers by their movement toward or away from them; and this is that varied and mysterious <term>Tetractys</term><note>original: τετρακτύς. A sacred Pythagorean symbol of ten points arranged in a triangle, representing the harmony of the universe.</note> of Pythagoras. Indeed, between these two extremes they established two means, namely 10 and 100; and they called the denary the "root," the centenary the "square," and the millenary the "cube." Unity is without division, and is like a point; the denary is the root of the millenary with a single division, for it is <term>evenly-odd</term><note>original: pariter impar. In ancient arithmetic, an even number that becomes odd when divided once (like 10, which becomes 5), suggesting a single step from unity toward complexity.</note> and is like a line; the centenary has a double division and is like a surface, for it is divided into 50 and 50, and then 50 into 25 and 25; the millenary truly has a triple division and is like a body, for 1000 is first divided into 500 and 500, then 500 into 250 and 250, and again 250 into 125 and 125, and there the division ceases. Therefore, just as the monad is free from all division, so the number 10, admitting only one division, is aptly applied to the **Intelligences** (Angels); the number 100, with its double division, to the **Soul**; and the number 1000, with its triple division, aptly shows the **Corporeal World**. But let us explain each one individually.

<margin>The four Unities are explained.</margin>
In the monadic unity, we contemplate the simplest Mind, the producer of all things, the Divine essence; in the second "root" unity (10), we see the Angelic intelligence; in the "square" (100), the soul; and finally, in the "cube" (1000), we behold the body. Thus, in these four distinct unities, we find distinct ratios of properties in each. For in God, all things are God;

## CHAPTER II.

In the intellect, all things are intellect; in the soul, all things are soul; in the body, all things are body. This is nothing other than saying that the Mind encompasses all things either divinely, or intellectually, or through the soul, or corporally. It does so divinely insofar as the thing is the ultimate truth; intellectually, that is, where the thing is not the truth itself, but is perceived truly; through the soul, that is, as the thing exists as a likeness of truth; and finally corporally, that is, as it leaves the likeness behind and enters into a state of confusion.

<margin>The first prerogative of Unity.</margin>
The first unity is like the archetype of all things, preceding all multiplicity and, consequently, all "otherness," opposition, inequality, and division. Even though this kind of unity is not the number two, nor three, nor four, it is nevertheless all those things which make up the two, the three, the four, and so on. If the species of things are distinguished by numbers, then absolute unity itself belongs to no specific species, has no name, and possesses no figure; rather, it is all things in all things. For this unity is the measure of every multitude of genera, species, substances, accidents, and of all created things. It is the one measure of all measures, the one equality of all things equal and unequal, and the connection of all things joined or separated. Just as unity, by its own simplicity, enfolds, unfolds, and connects every number—both even and odd—it is a unity of infinite power and an ineffable unity. If you were to separate all things from it, and if you understood that nothing else ever was, is, or could be; if you cast away all multiplicity and entered only into that most simple unity itself—so that you could not prove it to be multiple rather than simple, nor one rather than "not one"—then you would know that you have penetrated all secrets. For you will see its life, which is not at all subject to decay, in its absolute unity in which all things exist. Furthermore, there is a most precise certainty in this absolute unity, such that the mind acts upon all things in it and through it. There can be no question that does not presuppose it, for it is the <term>entitas</term><note>The "being-ness" or essence of a thing.</note> of all beings, the <term>quidditas</term><note>original: "quidditas." A philosophical term meaning the "what-ness" or the very nature of an object.</note> of all essences, the cause of all causes, and the end of all things. We have seen the miracles of the Omnipotent Unity; now let us proceed to the other unities.

<margin>The power and nature of the second Ten-fold Unity.</margin>
The second <term>decadic</term><note>From the Greek "dekas," referring to the number ten.</note> unity regards Angelic intelligence. Since this unity is the first to recede from that infinite unity, it is necessarily forced to enter the mixture of intellectual composition. This composition is made of "one thing and another"—that is, of opposites. These opposites do not come before the unity, but arise simultaneously with it, and are joined in its radical simplicity in an undivided and inseparable way. For this ten-fold unity is "without a root," because no unity precedes it except the first, and it cannot arise from the multiplication of any other, since it is the very first to take its origin. And although it stands at an infinite distance from the first unity in terms of its essence, it is nevertheless the simplest expression of the divine work, the <note>original: "promus condus." A Latin idiom for a steward or manager who stores and brings forth supplies.</note>steward of the divine archetypes. For the Creative Unity, exerting itself into action, first produced the <term>dyad</term><note>The number two, representing the first movement away from the singular "One."</note>, which is the decadic <term>monad</term><note>A single unit.</note>, or the Intellectual World—the absolute image of God and the immediate model of the number ten, which represents its final completion.

<margin>The power and nature of the third hundred-fold Unity.</margin>
The third hundred-fold unity, which pertains to the soul, is the number of intelligence, which it explains "squarely" <note>In Kircher's mathematical mysticism, 100 is the square of 10.</note>. Intelligence is the number of absolute unity (the first monad), for the unity of intelligence is numbered within the soul while it multiplies...

CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS 13 CH. II.

<note>The text begins mid-word, continuing from the previous page.</note> ...is simply contracted. God is the light of intelligence because He is its unity; intelligence, in turn, is the light of the soul because it is the soul's unity; and the corporal <term>corporal: relating to the physical body</term> form exists as the number of the soul’s unity. We do not perceive the unity of the soul in itself, but rather through a sensory investigation of its body; in the same way, we perceive intelligence not in itself, but in the soul. Nor do we perceive the first, simplest, and most absolute unity <note>meaning God</note> in itself, but rather we perceive it within intelligence, as if in a number or a <term>signaculo: a seal or imprint made by a signet ring</term>. God, therefore, is the "form" or blueprint of intelligence, intelligence is the form of the soul, and the soul is the form of the body.

Thus, Reason should be considered not as the "root" of the cubic body <note>the physical 3D world</note>, but as the medium through which the intellectual root descends into the body. Reason is the instrument of the intellect, and thus the instrumental principle or "root" of all bodily things. The <term>centenaria monas: the number 100</term> represents the soul, while the <term>millenaria: the number 1,000</term> represents the body. This thousand arises from leading the ten into the hundred—that is, from the multiplication of intelligence by the soul. For every number is perfected in the ten; the number of the simplest unity proceeds through the simplest number into the ten. Therefore, those things which in the First Unity are the simplest unity itself, are found to be divided and distinguishable when they are "unfolded" into numbers. 

In this way, the "intelligences" <note>angelic or divine minds</note>, which are the number of the simplest and absolute union, likewise participate intellectually in the nature of number in relation to the First Unity. Intellectual difference, opposition, and "otherness"—and similar qualities that belong to number—are in fact the absolute unity itself. "Squared" otherness and opposition exist in Reason as intellectual unity. Finally, "cubic" oppositions and the otherness of the senses and the body exist as unity within Reason.

<margin>The Power and nature of the Fourth Millenary Unity.</margin>

Finally, the fourth "millenary" unity <note>the number 1,000</note> is the final and sensory unfolding of these unions. Just as the number one thousand is composed of many parts, so too is this unity. The First Unity, therefore, behaves like a **point**; the second like a **line**; the third like a **surface**; and the fourth like a **body** or a **cube**. The unity of the point is the simplest version of everything found in the linear, superficial, and corporal unities; and the superficial unity unfolds everything that is within the corporal unity. 

These first three unities are not sensible <note>perceivable by the five senses</note> and cannot be distinguished except by the mind itself, which alone considers the point, line, and surface in isolation. The senses, however, can only reach that which is "corporal" (physical). If anyone, therefore, tried to measure mental things by using sensory things, he would be doing the same thing as someone trying to measure a point or a line with a solid 3D block; he would be acting imprudently, if not foolishly. 

Everything sensible must therefore be elevated to Reason, or to Intelligence, or to the Absolute Unity. If, in this way, you reduce a thing from all sensory, rational, or intellectual multiplicity back to its infinite simplicity, nothing more can be affirmed about it. At that point, it is no more a "stone" than it is a "non-stone"; rather, it is *all things*—namely, the simplest Unity, God, who is blessed forever. Thus, just as the absolute unity of that sensory and rational stone is God, so its intellectual unity is "Intelligence." You see from these unities how the senses return into reason, reason into intelligence, and intelligence into God, where there is a beginning and a completion in a perfect circulation—as <note>Nicholas of</note> Cusa and Francesco Patricius <note>Patrizi</note> beautifully prove from the *Hermetica* <note>ancient philosophical texts attributed to Hermes Trismegistus</note>.

# THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>CHAPTER II.</margin>

### A Schematic Explanation of the Four Aforementioned Monads

<margin>An example of mystical arithmetic in the numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4.</margin>

**F**rom the preceding points, it is clear that a certain supreme World is established from the <term>Theophanies: divine appearances or manifestations of God</term> of the first <term>monad: a single, indivisible unit representing the source of all things</term> in its descent into the <term>denarius: the number ten</term>; a second World is established from the second monad’s descent into the third; and a third World is established through the descent of the third monad into the fourth, through which a return into unity is made. The center of the first World is God; of the second, Intelligence; of the third, Reason; and of the fourth, Sensation. The first center possesses an indivisible entity—all things in all things, centrally present everywhere. All things exist in the first World through absolute unity; all in the second through intellectual unity; all in the third through rational unity; and all in the fourth through sensation. But let us see how this Pythagorean <term>tetractys: a triangular figure consisting of ten points arranged in four rows, which the Pythagoreans used to explain the nature of the universe</term> or "four-fold" exists within God, Angel, Soul, and Body, repeating some points from our work *Musurgia*, Volume 2, page 144 and Volume 2, page 451.

It is well established that one, two, three, and four joined together produce ten, which is the Symbol of the entire Universe, the goal and boundary of all things, and the natural power of simple unity when unfolded. From this very ten—which is itself a second kind of unity—one reaches the explanation of the square root by a similar four-step progression: for 10, 20, 30, and 40 joined together constitute 100, which is the square of the root ten. Likewise, the hundred-fold unity exerts itself into the thousand-fold; for 100, 200, 300, and 400 joined together constitute 1,000, which is the <term>cube: in sacred geometry, the cube represents the three-dimensional physical world</term> of the second unity (that is, of the root ten). Therefore, by natural influence, there are no more than 10 numbers, which are confined by this four-fold progression; nor is there any further variation of repetition beyond the thousandth of the root ten (the cube), since the number four, having repeated its progression three times, 
<margin><unclear>... inv ...</unclear></margin>
arises from the ten in order. You have here, therefore, the four-fold nature of unity, containing the potential explanation of every number. For the general Unity is distinguished by four unities, which are arranged here in a fitting order: the first is the most simple; the second is distant from the first by the addition of a <term>zyphra: a zero or "cipher," from the Arabic *sifr*</term> and constitutes the root of ten; the third, denoting the hundred, constitutes the square; and the fourth, denoting the thousand, constitutes the cube. Thus, the mind contemplates its own entire being as distinct in these four unities: in the simplest unity it considers God as the Creator of all; in the root or unity of ten, it considers Intelligence; in the square of intelligence, it considers its contraction or the Soul; and finally, in the cubic number which enfolds nothing further, it considers the Body. Moreover, all things in God are God; in intelligence, they are intellect; in the Soul, they are soul; and in the body, they are body. In the first unity, you will behold all the remaining unities <note>original: "indivisim, indifferenter, indistinctè complicatas"</note> enfolded without division, without difference, and without distinction. 
<margin>One skilled in mystical arithmetic can penetrate all secrets.</margin>
Certainly, if anyone penetrates this most simple unity alone, having cast aside all multiplicity—so that he proves it to be no more simple than non-simple, no more one than non-one—let him know that he has penetrated all secrets. For through this unity, he will see the unity of the mind, stripped of all multiplicity, and he will find that its life is not corruptible in its absolute unity, in which it is all things. Of this absolute unity there is the most perfect certainty, so that the Mind acts all things in it and through it; for it is the entity of all entities, the essence of all essences, the cause of all causes, and the end of all ends.

### CHAPTER II. 16 THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: HIEROGLYPHIC EXERCISE

<meta>Catchword: twice</meta>

<margin>All numbers are contained within the ten.</margin>
Therefore, by the ten <note>Latin: *denario*, the decad</note>, as we have shown at length above and also in our work *Musurgia*, volume 2, page 451, every number is contained; but by the four <note>Latin: *quaternario*, the quaternary</note>, every progression of numbers is completed, for four times ten makes 40. For this reason, we distributed the whole harmonic scheme into 40 circles in the cited passage of the *Musurgia*. In that distribution, we used the numbers 1, 3, 9, and 27. This is a most mystical number, established by Plato in the *Timaeus* as the symbol of the soul, as will be discussed shortly. For these numbers, when collected together, constitute 40—a number most suited to our purpose.

<margin>Explanation of the mystical numbers.</margin>
For just as 1, 2, 3, and 4 represent the most orderly progression of the universal number (for if you multiply two by itself, you produce 4; and if you add 1 to 3, that same four will result), so toward the decad of the quaternary—namely 40—no progression is more orderly than 1, 3, 9, and 27. For just as the first simple numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4, taken together, constitute 10, and this multiplied by 4 constitutes 40; so 1, 3, 9, and 27, joined together, constitute 40.

<margin>Explanation of the figure.</margin>
It is according to these principles that we shape the preceding <term>Schema</term><note>The diagram on page 15</note>, in which the simple unity—by which we denote God—touches four circles: specifically, the greatest circle of all nature, the highest of the World, the highest of the Order, and finally the highest circle of the Choir. From this unity, they participate in light and being by degrees: first the Universe, after this the highest Order, and in the fourth and last place, the highest Choir. Consequently, you see Choir communicating light to Choir down to the very last. You also observe how that which is found in the Universe and in any World is also found in the Order. For the decimal unit signifying <term>intelligence</term><note>Latin: *intelligentia*; in this context, it refers to angelic or higher spiritual intellect</note>, the hundredfold unit signifying the soul, and the thousandfold unit—as has been said—signifying the body, exists in one way in the highest World (according to that World’s sublime, simple, and noble nature), in another way in the middle, and in another way in the lowest, shadowy World. For you will observe that the lowest point of a superior realm coincides with the highest point of the inferior realm in all things; for the perception of the superior World is simpler than the intelligence of the Middle World, and the perception of the superior Order is more perfect than the intellect of the one following it.

<margin>All things in all things.</margin>
You see, therefore, how aptly the whole Universe is distributed with its triple series of Worlds—nine tens, nine hundreds, and just as many thousands—all contained within the smallest circles. If you add to these nine triads the three units indicated by the three larger circles, you will finally find the thousandfold signified in the simple unity through the greatest circle that encompasses and enfolds all things. You will see how anything exists within any World, and how the same law and constitution of progressions exists in each series of the Worlds. For if the first ten of the superior World was as two, the second as three, and the third as four, you would have a perfect progression. The second World, marked by the decimal series, will keep the same law of progression, as follows: 200, 300, 400; for if you join these correctly, a mixture of the decad emerges in each.

<margin>Further explanation of the figure.</margin>
From these things, it is clearly evident how the unity of intelligence of the lower World, even if it is not of the nature of the superior or middle World (being more remote from their simplicity), nevertheless touches their nature in a wonderful way according to a certain analogy, as appears in the levels of being of the three Worlds. <margin>Orders of Angels. Seraphim.</margin>

<margin>Cherubim.</margin>

<margin>Thrones.</margin>

There are, therefore, three primary duties of this [Angelic] Order: first, to purge lower beings of their impurities through a certain divine heat; second, to illuminate them with the knowledge proper to each; and finally, to perfect them in both respects. For all beings naturally long for the Highest Good <note>Latin: *summum bonum*, referring to God</note> from which they flowed, and they strive with all their might to turn back toward it, so that they may be joined to it as much as possible, enjoy it, and inflame others to achieve the same. Since these beings are closest to the Highest Good in essence, power, and action, and are its most immediate participants, they are themselves necessarily made good. They bear no envy toward any being, and it is necessary for them to cooperate with all things in goodness through their own benevolence. This is done, as we have said, through a triple action: by illuminating, purging, and attracting. Through these same actions, the minds of the first triad themselves are also immediately and continually illustrated by God and inflamed by divine fire, and they are both helped and impelled by a certain sweet force toward these works, becoming the primary ministers of divine providence.

The second Order also performs this same duty, but according to its own nature; as it is more remote from the Creator, it performs it more moderately than the first, having been brought to its own perfection by God through the higher Order. 

<margin>Dominations.</margin>
This perfection consists in the **Dominations** exercising a certain free mastery over lower things; compelled by no force, they bestow their graces upon them, and they illuminate, purge, and perfect them, leading them to the highest good. 

<margin>Virtues & Powers.</margin>
The **Virtues** do the same with a certain characteristic stability and fortitude, while the **Powers** maintain order in these activities, keeping all confusion far away.

The third Order provides most closely for the human race. 

<margin>Principalities. Archangels, Angels.</margin>
The **Principalities** appear to take care of Princes <note>Rulers and leaders</note>; the **Archangels** care for the peoples subject to those Princes; and finally, the **Angels** care for individual men. Through them, the whole human race is illuminated in its understanding, purged in its will, and perfected in both. For it was not fitting for that Goodness which transcends all things to create all beings and then leave them to chance, or to permit them to remain alienated and discordant from Himself. Rather, if they were to remain whole, as Goodness itself is, it was necessary that He join the universe together and cause it to depend continually upon Himself.

### CHAPTER II. 38 OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS: HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

...to lead [all things] back, to connect them to Himself, and to return them to the first source, He brought it about that they were made fit; but this could in no way happen unless the highest, middle, and lowest beings were bound together by certain chains. This was achieved as fittingly as possible through the love and ministry of these Minds <note>The "Minds" refers to the Angelic orders described previously</note>. 

<margin>The Heracleotic Chain.</margin>
And this is that **Heracleotic Chain** <note>Also known as the "Golden Chain" or "Great Chain of Being," a concept from Neoplatonic philosophy where every part of the universe is connected to God</note> connecting all things; this is that **ten-stringed instrument** <note>Latin: *decachordon*. A musical metaphor for the ten levels of the universe</note> of the nature of the Universe, adapting all things into one and the same most beautiful harmony. Thus, just as God flows into all things, He flows most especially into the Angelic World, this into the Celestial, and the Celestial into the Elemental World in an admirable way. And again, the triple Choir of the Angelic World, the triple Choir of the Celestial World, and the individual Choirs of this lower World respond to one another. Indeed, there is no "string" of the lower World that does not have corresponding strings in both the Celestial and Angelic Worlds, according to that famous pronouncement of the secret Kabbalists:

> *There is no herb below that does not have a planet above saying to it: grow.*

<margin>Harmony of the Angelic Choirs with the World.</margin>
Therefore, when a "string" is struck in any series of the World, the remaining corresponding strings are immediately brought into harmony by a certain hidden force and consensus. Beneath the perfect knowledge of these things lies hidden the greatest secret <note>Latin: *sacramentum*. Here meaning a sacred mystery or hidden principle</note> of the whole mystery of nature: that whoever knows how to produce marvelous effects in the nature of things will know how to do so by adapting like to like <note>literally "consonants to consonants," continuing the musical metaphor</note>.

<margin>Explanation of the figure.</margin>
But you will understand these things better from the **Diagram** placed above, in which you see the circle surrounding all things signifies the eternal, immutable, and immobile unity. The three circles [signify] the three Worlds: Elemental, Celestial, and Angelic; each of which is seen divided again into three other circles, as if into three Choirs. Moreover, the individual Choirs of each World are divided into three small circles, ending in the degrees of beings and things of the Universe. 

The first Worldly circle represents, through 9 small circles, the 9 Choirs of Angels. The second represents the nine Orbits of the heavens, which are the **Primum Mobile** <note>the "first moved" sphere that drives all other celestial spheres</note>, the **Firmament**, and the spheres of **Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon**. The third circle signifies nine beings of the Elemental World, which are **man, beast, zoophyte** <note>An organism sharing characteristics of both plants and animals, like coral or sea anemones</note>, **tree, shrub, herb, minerals, mixed bodies, and elements**. 

And these are the 27 degrees of beings of the three Worlds; if you join the remaining larger circles to these, 40 circles will emerge—exactly as many as the aforementioned numbers 1, 3, 9, and 27 constitute when added together <note>1 + 3 + 9 + 27 = 40</note>. Of these, the first term, 1, constitutes absolute unity; the second, 3, the superficial or radical unity; the third, 9, namely the square of three; and finally the fourth, 27, the cube of three. These, as I said, joined together give 40. By these, the Pythagoreans indicated numbers as absolute (or radical), plane, and solid. The Hebrews, however, as we said in the Kabbalah, differing with wonderful skill concerning the triple World, make their letters correspond to the numbers. You see also how aptly these things agree with what we said in the preceding pages regarding the 9 decads of the four Worlds.

<margin>Demonstration through a double pyramid, light and dark.</margin>
All these circles are linked by a double pyramid. The first is a **light pyramid**, having its base at the summit of the Angelic or luminous heaven, and its apex at the level of the lower World. The other is a **dark pyramid**, having its base at the level of the lower World—that is, in prime matter, deprived of all light—with its apex ending at the summit of the Angelic heaven. Hence, just as the supreme World abounds in light, so [the lower world abounds] in a bounty of darkness— <note>The page ends mid-sentence; the catchword "dat" indicates the word "abundat" (abounds) is completed on the next page.</note>

You will find the opposite process in the inferior World. If you investigate these things with a keen mind, you will perceive the greatest and most obscure matters with the clearest light, reaching even to the most hidden secrets of nature. 

It is necessary, however, that you conceive the unity of any particular thing in its perfection, and imagine the quality of darkness according to that intensity of light. Among the gradations of unities, you should consider that one lesser which possesses more darkness, more multiplicity, more potentiality, and more divisibility; but that one greater which has more light, more unity, more act, and indivisibility. For the less a unity is in act and the more it is in potentiality, the more changeable it is. For a "unifying unity" is more perfect than a "unifiable unity," just as the unity of the Soul is more perfect than the unity of the body, because the end of the body’s unity is the unity of the soul, upon which the bodily unity depends, as if from its own principle.

At this point, a wondrous property of the Monad <note>Monad: A term derived from Greek meaning "Unit" or "the One." In Kircher's philosophy, it represents God as the source of all numbers and existence.</note> and its offspring meets us, which demonstrates the middle state in the three aforementioned Worlds produced by God, and opens other remarkable mysteries (as will be said) of that almighty union, and it is as follows: If any number of odd numbers are arranged in their natural order starting from unity <margin>A wondrous property of arithmetic progression.</margin>; then for any two numbers equally distant from the middle of the progression, the half of their sum will equal the middle term of the progression. Let the following arrangement of numbers be given in a numerical series:

-> 1 — 2 — 3 — 4 — **5** — 6 — 7 — 8 — 9 <-
-> ( 1 + 9 = 10 ) <-
-> ( 2 + 8 = 10 ) <-
-> ( 3 + 7 = 10 ) <-
-> ( 4 + 6 = 10 ) <-

In this series, the middle term is 5; therefore, if you join any numbers equally distant from five into one sum, they will produce 10, of which the half is 5. Likewise, 3 and 7, 2 and 8, 1 and 9 joined together will constitute 10, whose half is similarly 5. From this property, therefore, it is clearly perceived how Unity is the principle of numbers, which I demonstrate thus: <margin>Demonstration of the proposed question.</margin> If Unity had something prior to itself—for instance, some other number or any other distinguishing thing—that thing would be placed alongside the number 2 with Unity [in the middle]. Therefore, according to the given proposition, Unity would be the middle of this aggregate; but Unity itself is the half of 2. Thus, by a common notion of the mind, such an aggregate and the number 2 would be equal, since things that are equal multiples of one and the same thing must necessarily be equal. Such an aggregate and the pair <term>binarius: the number two, representing the first step away from unity into multiplicity</term> would be equal multiples of Unity—namely, double—especially since Unity is [the principle] of them...

# CHAPTER II. 20 THE HIEROGLYPHIC SCHOOL OF OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS

...indeed a half; therefore they would be equal, and so the whole would be made equal to the part. Since this is absurd and impossible, it necessarily follows that Unity is the beginning of all numbers, and does not admit any number before itself. To express the mysterious offspring of these sacred truths <note>original: "sacramentorum foeturam"</note> more deeply from this proposition, the Ancients established two opposing pyramids—which were also mentioned a little earlier—of which one is the pyramid of light and the other the black pyramid of darkness. These they divided into nine spaces by parallel lines;

<margin>Demonstration of the proposition in the pyramid of light and darkness.</margin>

you see, therefore, that the more the pyramid of light is immersed into the material pyramid, the more light it loses and the more matter it acquires; conversely, the more the material pyramid is immersed into the pyramid of light, the more light it acquires and the more matter it loses, so that the number five <note>original: "quinarius"</note>, placed in the middle position, always possesses an equality of light and darkness. 

Truly, since there is a triple World—the supercelestial, the celestial, and the sublunary—the middle celestial world possesses a certain nature shared by both extremes. For the supercelestial World is one of light, the sublunary is one of darkness, and the celestial is tempered by both light and darkness. Since its power reaches the sublunary World, it is rightly placed to be governed by the supercelestial; indeed, in power and resistance, in action and passion, it is the middle. In the sublunary world, there is the change of life and death; in the supercelestial, there is perfect life and the perpetual stability of functions; but in the celestial, there is a certain middle nature, composed of stability and change. Therefore, if you compare the said pyramids more exactly to one another, you will find an abundance of perfection in the superior World, a lack of the same in the sublunary world, and in the middle of both, a mixture of perfect equality. These things are not only true in the mentioned Worlds, but in any of the particular levels of said Worlds.

<margin>This is evident in the combination of the Elements.</margin>

For an Element which mediates between two neighboring ones, being placed between them, obtains a middle disposition, participating equally from those surrounding it; and thus there is a certain middle point of the aggregate in its disposition. In this way, between water and fire, the intermediate air participates in heat from the fire and moisture from the water; therefore, it is the nature and property of the hot-and-moist air to participate from each of the elements pressing upon it. In the same way, water, being intermediate between air and earth, participates in the moisture from the former and the cold from the latter, obtaining a moist-and-cold nature.

<margin>In mixed beings.</margin>

This also appears clearly in mixed beings; for shrubs <note>Kircher uses "frutices" to mean woody plants smaller than trees.</note> mediate between herbs and trees; among mineral liquids and terrestrial substances, there are metals; between humans and <term>zoophyta</term> <note>Kircher refers here to "animal-plants" like sponges or coral, which were thought to bridge the gap between the plant and animal kingdoms.</note>, there are the brute animals; between human and divine nature, the mediator is Christ our Savior.

<margin>In the Heavens.</margin>

In the celestial World, Mercury is intermediate between Venus and the Moon; not unlike a certain celestial water, it participates equally in moisture from Venus and cold from the Moon. Between the three superior planets—Saturn ♄, Jupiter ♃, and Mars ♂—and the inferior ones—Venus ♀, Mercury ☿, and the Moon ☽—the Sun is the intermediate, giving and receiving from each. Between Saturn ♄ and Mars ♂, Jupiter is the middle, tempering the malignity <note>In traditional astrology, Saturn and Mars were considered "malefic" or harmful; Jupiter was the "great benefic" that balanced them.</note> of those surrounding him on both sides with his own virtue. Furthermore, in the supercelestial World, it belongs to the first hierarchy to perfect, illuminate, and purge; to the lowest, on the contrary, to be perfected, illuminated, and purged; but to the middle hierarchy, the said operations belong both actively and passively with a certain reciprocity. Therefore, the mystery of the mentioned proposition is clear from what has been said.

<header>CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER III.</header>

# CHAPTER III.

->*On the hieroglyphic expression of numbers used chiefly by the Egyptians.*<-

**I** find that the Egyptians expressed their numbers through hieroglyphs in two ways: either through the "hierogrammatic" <note>sacred writing</note> or the "kyriological" <note>literal or proper naming</note> method. In the former way, they expressed their mysteries through numbers by means of the hidden symbols of the most profound things; in the latter way, they repeated the object they wished to express numerically as many times as that number had units. We must deal with the latter method first, and then the former.

---

## § I.

->*On the Kyriological method of representing numbers used by the Egyptians.*<-

<margin>How the Egyptians express numbers by a multitude of things.</margin>
<image-desc>A vertical column of symbols on the right margin illustrating numerical representation:
- A single circle next to '1'.
- Two circles next to '2'.
- Three circles next to '3'.
- Two vertical columns of circles (two and three).
- A single square.
- Two squares stacked vertically.
- Three squares stacked vertically.
- Roman numerals I, II, III.
- Four small triangles arranged in a triangular cluster.</image-desc>
**W**e say, therefore, first, that hieroglyphic <term>Kyriology</term> <note>original: Κυριολογία; the use of symbols in their literal or primary sense</note> was nothing other than placing the thing signified, which they wished to express by a number, as many times as the number contained units. Thus, for example, a globe or circle placed by itself signified the eternal, superior World; two globes or circles signified two superior Worlds, three globes three superior Worlds, and four globes or circles four superior Worlds. They used circles for the Worlds to indicate the eternity of the Spirits <note>original: Geniorum</note> presiding over them, for it is a figure lacking beginning and end. However, they displayed the material <note>original: hylacos</note> or elementary worlds sometimes through squares and quadrangles, and sometimes through right-angled triangles; and they used squares specifically when they suggested the successive propagation of generation in the Worlds of mixed things; for which reason they also called them "genetic triangles"; concerning all and each of these I have written more extensively in our *Hieroglyphic Geometry*. In like manner, by placing one scepter, they expressed one particular dominion; by two, a double dominion; by three, triple; by four, quadruple; or even by the number of knots carved into the scepters, they expressed the empires and dominions of some Spirit. In a word, every hieroglyph placed once, twice, thrice, four times, and so on for the rest, denoted the multiplication of the meaning. This custom has been accepted by posterity even to this day.

<margin>The ancients used small lines for numbers.</margin>
For it is well established that the ancients, since they had not yet discovered certain figures for numbers, expressed them with as many small lines as the number signified; hence, to indicate one, two, three, four, etc., they placed one, two, three, or four lines up to ten, in this manner: I, II, III, IIII. Some traces of this still seem to exist among the ancient Romans, when they expressed the <term>Duumviri</term> <note>a board of two men</note>, <term>Triumviri</term> <note>a board of three men</note>, and <term>Septemviri</term> <note>a board of seven men</note> thus: II-man, III-man, VII-man.

<margin>How the Egyptians expressed five and ten.</margin>
They seem to have expressed five by the inclination of one line toward another, as is evident here: V; and ten by a cross <note>original: decussim</note>, which appears to consist of these two figures joined.

Concerning this, Horapollo <note>A 5th-century author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs</note> writes in Book 2, Chapter 28: <note>original Greek: Γραμμή ὀρθή μιᾷ ἅμα γραμμῆ ἐπικαμμένη... δίχα γραμμὰς δέκα σημαίνει</note> *A straight line, which is similarly cut by another line in the manner of a 10, in this fashion, X, (either as a cross-mark or <unclear>☩</unclear>) signifies 10 flat lines.* Consequently, this cross-mark was found everywhere among hieroglyphic inscriptions as a symbol of the number Ten or of perfection; about which more is written extensively in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, page 386, and in the following sections in its proper place.
