->§ II.<-

->*On the hierogrammatic <note>The sacred system of writing used by Egyptian priests</note> method of numbering, and first concerning Unity, the Dyad, and the Triad.*<-

<margin>The Phoenix represented by Unity.</margin> **T**he hierogrammatic method of numbering consisted in this: they signified numbers through hidden metaphors and the figures of animals. In this way, when they intended to signify the number 1, they placed a phoenix, because this bird is said to have no companion of its own species; concerning this, see Horapollo, Book 2.
<margin>How the Egyptians expressed the Binary.</margin> Also, when they intended to signify absolute Unity through a center, they would draw a circle, because just as the center is the beginning of all lines and of figures composed of lines, so supreme Unity is the cause of all things existing in the world; about which more is found in *Hieroglyphic Geometry*.
<margin>Λ</margin> They first indicated Binary numbers through any angle of a binary <note>an angle formed by two lines</note>, because the supreme unity, diffused from its center, first creates the Dyad <note>the number two</note>, that is, the intellectual World; for the flow of the monad <note>the number one</note> into "otherness" necessarily creates an angle through the extension of two surrounding lines, whose vertex is a point, as will be declared more fully later.
<margin>Two Crows signify the Dyad</margin> Furthermore, when they intend to signify the Dyad or the principle of generation, they paint two crows; for these animals, according to Horapollo, are accustomed to always lay two eggs, from which come a male and a female—that is, the active and passive principle—from which all things have the beginning of their generation. Thus, in the pyramid, the Dyad is indicated by the flow of any two latent lines, which, since it is the principle of diversity, inequality, and dissimilarity, and the distinction of unity, and the first fall from the "one"; it is not undeservedly considered in every discipline as the number of division. By this number, the Egyptians represented the distribution of opposites among themselves, and the Magicians of the Persians represented the vicissitudes of clashing qualities in nature under the allegory of Ahriman and Ormazd <note>The Zoroastrian spirits of evil and good</note>, or the Egyptians under the story of Osiris and Typhon <note>Set</note>.
<margin>Different names for Good and Evil.</margin> Hence the Pythagoreans, according to Plutarch, affect both principles with different names: such as "Good" for unity, the finite, the resting, the straight, the odd, the square, the equal, the right-handed, and the splendid; but they designate "Evil" by the name of the binary, the infinite, that which is in motion, the curved, the even, the oblong, the unequal, the left-handed, and the dark; and they establish these to be the principles of the origin of things.
<margin>Synesius</margin> Hence Osiris is said to be all that which, as said above, is beneficent, according to Synesius in Book 1 of *On Providence*. Typhon, however, is the principle of all [evils], as with Syne-

# CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. 23 CHAPTER III.

<margin>Names of Typhon.</margin>
<margin>The bones of Horus are Magnet; of Typhon, iron.</margin>
...I shall speak of that workshop of evils, whom the Egyptians also call Seth, Bebon, and Smy; by which words they indicate a certain violent inhibition, contrariety, and overthrow, without which Horus—or that sensible World—can by no means be preserved. And therefore the Egyptians rightly said (as is read in Manetho <note>An Egyptian priest and historian, c. 3rd century BCE</note> according to Plutarch), that the **bones of Horus were Magnet**, and the **bones of Typhon, iron**. For just as iron experiences diverse movements of attraction and repulsion in the presence of a Magnet, so the healthy, good, and rationally constant movement of the World somehow turns, draws to itself, and renders more soft and obedient that harsh and Typhonian force. Hence they fable that Mercury <note>The Roman name for Hermes/Thoth</note>, as Plutarch witnesses, cut out the sinews of Typhon and used them for lyre strings; by arranging the universe, he rendered it harmonious out of dissonance, and meanwhile did not abolish the power of the World, but fulfilled it. Whence it happens that this force, weak and languid, clings to bodies in this World of changes and various affections; in the earth it contrives concussions and tremors; in the air, heats and untimely winds, as well as fiery whirlwinds and lightning bolts; it infects the waters and the spirits with the blight of pestilence, and even rushes up to the Moon, raising itself up and darkening the splendid air. And these two principles of things are well denoted in a pyramid by the flow of two lines from a single point; although others twist this "binary" <note>The number two or duality</note> toward the production of forms. For just as the binary arises from the one, so (preserving the ratio of similarity) form is first drawn out from the potentiality of matter; and for that reason, it was named by Homer not *aidos* <note>shame/reverence</note> but *aidoia* <note>generative parts</note>, that is, the Goddess of forms.

<margin>In ancient times they referred all things from the one to the one.</margin>
This, therefore, was the consideration of the ancients, who deduced all things from the One by a certain perpetual and continuous chain through all grades of things, and by the same steps referred them back to the One. Because, therefore, matter is the last in resolution <note>the process of breaking things down to their elements</note>, it will necessarily be the first in the composition of bodies; which is clearly shown through the apex of the pyramid, which, while it returns into lines, surfaces, the body, and from these into itself, beautifully teaches this process. For that reason, matter is deservedly called "Proteus" in physics, just as the One was called "Proteus" in the First Wisdom <note>Metaphysics</note>. And because form is the second-to-last in resolution, it is the second in composition, and thus undergoes the ratio of the binary, whose nature is feminine to the Pythagoreans. Therefore those ancient ones—whether Sages, Magi, or even Priests—following the order of nature in composing and resolving things, called matter "Protean" and established God as the second form, and consequently his daughter, just as duality is of the one. <margin>Matter called Prothea.</margin> This the Egyptians also hinted at through Oceanus the Father and Tethys the Mother. But enough of such things here.

<margin>The excellence of the Triad.</margin>
The **Triad, first in a threefold way**, as Boethius witnesses, **is the Leader and Prince of odd numbers**; perfect, first, entire, consummate, universal, whole. For just as the Monad <note>The number one/unity</note> is simple without extremity, and the Dyad <note>The number two/duality</note> is a divided and gaping extremity without the unity of a middle; so the Triad, by a wondrous embrace, seizes both that preceded it. For it surrounds and walls in the Monad by the aid of the Dyad, and joins and knits the extremes of the Dyad with unity. And just as an act implanted in a divided power is by its nature odd, it fashions and fills the substance of the whole: so also the Monad, having progressed into the Dyad and being received by its boundaries,

# CHAPTER III. OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM.

It completes the triad and perfects the number; hence, not without merit, it is called the Prince of numbers, the image of divine emanation, and the foundation of all contemplation and wisdom. And if the primary existence of things occurs in the Monad <note>The number one or the point</note> or point, and the knowledge and appearance of existing things occurs in the Dyad <note>The number two</note> or line; then the supreme love and festive pursuit of known and supreme substances shall be the triad. It is no wonder, therefore, that the ancient Philosophers brooded upon the mysteries of the triad with such great zeal. But let us return to our purpose.

<margin>The equilateral triangle is the hieroglyphic Image of the Triad.</margin>
The hieroglyphic Triad is the equilateral triangle; and among the Egyptians, it denotes the diffusion of God the Creator <note>original: Δημιουργου (Demiourgou)</note> into the World, as was explained in the Pamphilian Obelisk. For Plato relates that Horus flowed forth from the Archetypal triangle. By Horus, he indicates this sensible World; by the Triangle, he indicates the Divine Creator, who—having been moved from the Monad into the Dyad, and from there into the Triad—founded the World. From this, a sufficiently beautiful speculation on this matter is conceived

<margin>What the hieroglyphic Diagram of the Bembin Table denotes.</margin>

->SYMBOLS OF HORUS<-

in that hieroglyphic Diagram, which is found twice in the Bembin Table <note>A famous bronze tablet from antiquity, also known as the Mensa Isiaca, depicting Egyptian mysteries</note>; a Boy bound with fillets, wrapped in a netted garment, from whose back hangs a triangle to which a globe is attached; furthermore, he is equipped with a staff in the shape of a hoopoe’s head <note>original: cucuphomorpho</note> joined together with a curved augur's staff and a sundial's pointer <note>original: gnomone</note>. The Boy bound with fillets signifies nothing other than Horus—that is, the World equipped with an innumerable variety of things and proceeding from the archetypal triangle—which the triangle with the globe attached to the neck of Horus also beautifully indicates. The netted garment signifies the unknown and involved operations and effects of the World; the hoopoe-headed scepter signifies the variety, order, and series of things; the augur's staff signifies harmony; the pointer signifies the exact order of distribution and measurement of every single thing within the whole. The triangle, however, signifies the triple-formed Deity, who is Hemphta, or the supramundane Osiris; Isis, his Wisdom; and Amun, the All-Nourishing Spirit <note>original: παντοτροφος (pantotrophos)</note> animating all things by his power. Although these are distinguished by three divine names, they are nevertheless one in reality; for by these three powers, as the Egyptians say, the World is founded, animated, and sustained. Therefore, it is not incongruously said to have flowed forth from the archetypal triangle. See more on these matters in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, page 212.

<margin>The Genesis of the number Three.</margin>
Just as the Dyad is born from the Monad by the addition of unity, so by the addition of the Monad to the Dyad, the Triad is born—a triune number reduced from one into one. Because just as unity is the beginning of numbers, so the triangle is the first of all rectilinear figures; it is born from the binary and unity, and in hieroglyphic pyramids it is signified by the letter Δ <note>The Greek letter Delta</note>. This takes its beginning from the point or Monad of the pyramid, and is extended through any two sides into the base, by which the Δ is constituted—that sacred figure celebrated in so many writings of the ancients...

# CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER III.

<margin>Praise of the number three.</margin>
The celebrated triad, that Archetype of Horus, the true Platonic model and idea of the triple World; the true balance of Pythagorean justice brought back to the center between two vices on either side: the principle of all numbers, the triangle of divine nature, the mistress of all imperfection <note>original: "imperfectionis Magistra" - likely referring to the triad's role in resolving the instability of the dyad</note>, and the fulfillment of the nature of matter; the sole center of the appetite for forms flourishing in Proteus, the foundation of the mystical pyramid, the fountain and origin of bodies—nothing is more fertile than this for mythical meanings and hidden explanations of things. For just as the first part, namely duality, is division and the first diversity; so also, as we have said, the triad is the first odd number from the one, acting as a return to unity and the principle. It is more perfect than the even number, since it encompasses the even and is not encompassed by it. Hence it is the most fitting number for justice; for in even numbers, justice is as if dissolved without a center, as <margin>Plato, Book 1 of the Laws.</margin> Plato rightly warns in Book 1 of the *Laws*, nor does it have any hinge upon which to lean. But in the odd number itself, above the one, there is a middle point like a center and a Divine Power <note>original: "Numen"</note>, by which there is an equal distribution, and toward which, as if to a goal, everything is directed. The odd number also, because of the middle being its own bond—as <margin>Plotinus. The number three is most perfect because it contains a beginning, middle, and end.</margin> Plotinus rightly says—possesses its own bond within itself; it exists because of the circular center, and because of the comparison of the extremes to the middle, it is the principle of the universal order. For in the triad there is a beginning, a middle, and an end; hence "The All" <note>original: "Τὰ πάντα" (Ta panta)</note>, and the ancient Theologians also, to designate that the beginning, middle, and end are to be referred back to God, offered three things in their sacrifices.

<margin>The Oracle of Apollo.</margin>
> Indeed, a triple victim to the heavenly Gods, and she
> White, must be slain; and triple to the earthly, black.

Likewise Statius:

> The ancient form of a perfect sacrifice
> Commands the offering of three loaves.

And in Theocritus, Idyll 2:

> I pour libations thrice, and thrice, O Lady, I speak these words.
> <note>original: "Ες τρὶς ἀποσπένδω καὶ τρὶς τάδε πότνια φωνῶ."</note>
> Thrice I pour, and thrice I pronounce these mystical words.

<margin>Rites performed with the number three.</margin>
Hence the Egyptians also, according to Plutarch, established their fumigations three times: in the morning, at midday, and in the evening. And certainly, that this number full of mysteries was always held in the highest veneration is witnessed by so many triangular types and forms of things—so many pyramids, tripods, and triangles; likewise the various figures which occur everywhere both on Obelisks and especially in the *Bembine Tablet* <note>The Bembine Tablet, or Mensa Isiaca, is an elaborate bronze tablet with Egyptian-style motifs, famous in the Renaissance as a key to hieroglyphs.</note>, which we shall interpret at length in their proper place. Most especially, however, through the triangles represented in the pyramid, they wished to insinuate nothing else, <margin>Plutarch.</margin> according to Plutarch, but the nature of the Universe, and a certain Idea of Osiris, Isis, and Horus, represented through three operations and effects. For that cruel Typhon, whom we previously represented by the number two, by tearing apart the body of Osiris and scattering it into many parts—proceeding from the one to the many, from the perfect to the imperfect, from the whole to the parts, from the good (which consists of an integral cause) to the evil (which consists of any defect)—[created] many [things] in nature...

...sowed discord among kings and dangerous enmities signified by the number two <note>original: "binarium"</note>; desiring to prevent these, the provident parent of nature, Isis, diligently searched for the scattered parts of Osiris. It must be understood that the line standing at a right angle represents the male, the base the female, and the subtending line the offspring of both; and that Osiris is the principle, Isis the receptacle, and Horus the result: for the number three is the first odd and perfect number.* **Thus says Plutarch.**

<margin>The Pythagorean problem seems to have been taken from the Egyptians.</margin> From these words it is surely clear that nothing else is being described to us here than that most celebrated Pythagorean Hecatomb <note>A "sacrifice of a hundred," referring to the legend that Pythagoras sacrificed 100 oxen upon discovering his theorem</note>, famous for so many mysteries and of such infinite use in Mathematical business; so that I strongly doubt whether perhaps Pythagoras first received such a great geometric secret from the Egyptians, and then made it his own discovery. For if you multiply the line of the triangle subtending the angle (5 units) by itself, it produces a square of 25; and the lines of the surrounding sides of 4 and 3 units produce squares of 16 and 9. By these they surely hinted at the greatest mysteries in nature. But of these things elsewhere. From this it is clear with what genius and what great mysteries they displayed through a triangle of this kind.

# CHAPTER III. THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

It remains to be shown how they joined both the celestial and the sublunary <term>tetrad</term><note>A group or set of four.</note> into one. Since that spirit of the <margin>The Ancients explained all things through numbers.</margin> World, the celestial Mercury, has filled all things with numbers, proportions, and harmony, these things certainly cannot be understood without numbers. For as Pythagoras testifies, the nature of numbers has passed through all things, and the knowledge of it is that true divine and incorruptible Wisdom, concerning which the most ancient <margin>Artephius.</margin> Artephius <note>A legendary medieval alchemist often cited by Kircher as an ancient authority.</note> says in his *Book of Secrets*: *Once the number is known, you shall know how the knowledge of all things is possessed through it.* And elsewhere: *From the calculations of the first man, the science of all arts and all knowledge is found;* for all things that exist in the World, as Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher who wrote on the quadrivium (arithmetic, music, geometry, astronomy).</note> testifies, consist of numbers. Since these things are so, it seems the Ancients represented all the mysteries of numbers under that <term>caduceus</term><note>The staff carried by Hermes/Mercury, typically entwined with two snakes.</note>, or Mercurial character, not without reason. For if you unfold it into its parts, as has been said—that is, into <note>Symbolic decomposition of the Caduceus: O (Circle), ☽ (Crescent/Moon), + (Cross), Υ (Upsilon/Forked line)</note> O, ☽, +, Υ—you will soon have that wonderful Pythagorean **tetraktys** <note>original: "τετρακτὺν" - a triangular figure of ten points arranged in four rows, sacred to the Pythagoreans.</note>, which he used to call the fountain of perpetual nature, the idea of all created things, and the forum of knowledge operating rationally in the divine <margin>Iamblichus.</margin> mind. Hence the <term>tetras</term> was also called "mystical" according to Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on Pythagoreanism.</note>, by which the four parts of the World were represented <margin>A figure expressing the Idea of the entire speculation represented in the Tautic character.</margin> by the Egyptians, as we shall say in the progress of this Work. Likewise, it clearly appears by what reasoning all things are governed and comprehended by that *tetraktys*; a fact which did not escape the Hebrews, since under the <term>Tetragrammaton</term><note>The four-letter unpronounceable name of God in Hebrew (YHWH).</note> name of God they comprehend the things of the entire Universe, as we have said elsewhere. But let us now set forth the explanation of the Mercurial sacrament.

# OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>And it contains all things.</margin>
Furthermore, it is not without reason that the <term>Tetractys</term> <note>A mystical triangular figure consisting of ten points arranged in four rows; a central symbol for Pythagoreans representing the organization of the universe.</note> is said to contain all things, since the number four—as we have shown elsewhere—is potentially the number ten, the most perfect and absolute of all numbers, and is the "idea" of all things. Beyond this, no other number is found, as demonstrated in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, Book 2, Chapter 10. 
<margin>The Kabbalists reduce all things to 10.</margin>
The <term>Kabbalists</term> <note>Followers of Jewish mysticism.</note> of the Hebrews also reduced this to the ten <term>Sephiroth</term>, which are divine attributes and measures by which they were accustomed to describe God, divine providence, and the immensity of things. However, so that what has been said thus far may be contracted into a compendium, I have decided to further explain the preceding figure, in which we place before the eyes of the curious reader the "idea" of this entire speculation as considered in the 
<margin>Explanation of the Tautic character.</margin>
<term>Tautic character</term> <note>A complex symbol associated with Thoth/Hermes/Mercury, often resembling a cross or a staff.</note>. The figure consists of a circle, a segment of the Moon, and a Cross. The circle denotes the Sidereal World divided into its planetary orbits; the Moon, intersecting this, forms the character of Mercury, composed of the Sun and Moon. The Cross, however, denotes the Elemental World, upon which the Sidereal World exerts its power through the "Soul of the World" <note>original: *anima Mundi*</note> which pervades all things. The four extremities of the Cross contain four statues presiding over the four Elements indicated by the four quarters of the world. The topmost statue is hawk-shaped <note>original: *accipitriformis*</note> and denotes fire, situated in a <term>ypsilomorph</term> <note>shaped like the Greek letter Upsilon (Y).</note> position, the mystery of which we shall reveal elsewhere. The second statue is dog-shaped <note>original: *caniformis*</note>, representing air; the third is ibis-shaped <note>original: *Ibiformis*</note>, representing water; and finally the fourth is <gloss>human-shaped</gloss> <note>original: *ἀνθρωπόμορφος* (anthropomorphos)</note>, representing the domain of earth. From this earth breaks forth a serpent, a sign of fertility, by which the earth is impregnated by the diffusion of the Mundane Spirit. All are positioned in the form of a "Y" <note>the letter Upsilon</note>, the mystery of which will be opened elsewhere; all are equipped with <term>handled crosses</term> <note>original: *crucibus ansatis*; the Ankh symbol.</note> to indicate the power they draw from the Spirit of the World. The entire Cross is filled with these handled crosses to indicate the "ideas" of the Divine Mind, of which that entire character is a symbol. Attached are the horn of a Ram with a small Moon, and the heads of a Bull and a Scarab, from which—as if from elements—the Tautic character is constituted. Thus, the whole figure expresses the character of Mercury <note>Astrological symbol for Mercury</note>, as it was invented by him. He who desires more should consult the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, page 375 and following, where we have explained the secrets of this character professionally; here, however, let this expanded exhibition of this truly most mysterious character, gathered as if into a summary, suffice.

# CHAPTER IV. 31 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: HIEROGLYPHIC SCHOOL

<margin>The number five is a circular number.</margin>From these things it is clearly evident how the soul—participating partly in an individual and immutable nature, and partly in a divisible and mutable bodily nature—holds a certain middle place. Furthermore, according to the observation of the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, who believed numbers were the fundamental reality of the universe.</note>, the number five is called a circular or spherical number, and it designates Nature. Just as Nature always returns into itself through its own multiplication, so too does the number five. <margin>The numbers five and six look back upon themselves.</margin> Indeed, while other numbers, when multiplied by themselves, end in various different digits as they increase, only the numbers five and six, when led into themselves (as was shown in the first Part of the second Volume regarding the Hebrew Kabbalah <note>Kircher refers to his earlier analysis of Jewish mystical traditions where numbers hold divine secrets.</note>), always show, look back upon, and follow themselves. For if you increase five by itself, it becomes two times itself <note>original: "fiet duo in seipsum" - Kircher likely means the squaring process</note>, and you will have 25, a square whose side is 5. Let 5 be led again into its square 25, and you will produce the cube 125, whose side is likewise 5. Furthermore, let 5 be led once more into the cube 125, and 625 will come forth; and so on for the rest, which is also to be understood regarding the number six, as is evident.

<margin>The prerogative of the number five.</margin>You see, therefore, that the multiplication of five and six, even if carried out to infinity, will always return the roots from which they were produced; hence, they deservedly hold the sovereignty in the entire economy of numbers. They are, consequently, an absolute symbol of the revolution of the soul, by which the soul, having been agitated through all the orders of beings, is finally restored to itself through a reflected act once each stage has been weighed. In this circle, it is entirely equal, where every end is a beginning, and <margin>A sphere representing the soul of the world, returning into itself after a fivefold revolution is completed.</margin> every last thing is the first—that is, it is always the same. This was also observed by the Ancients, not without praise for its subtlety: that a sphere rolled forward in a straight line within a parallelogram <note>A four-sided figure with opposite sides parallel; here used to describe the geometric path of a rolling object.</note> through five spaces is restored to the place from which it departed, and measures out five parallelograms equal to itself. So that you may see this, I have decided the matter should be demonstrated. Let there be a sphere *abcd*, whose center is *e*; let there also be a line *afghi* of indeterminate length. Let the sphere *abcd* be placed at point *a*, and let it be moved forward in a straight rotation in this manner: so that the arc *ad* of the sphere is fitted to the straight line *af* (that is, point *d* of the sphere coincides with point *f* of the line *af*); and arc *dc* is fitted to line *fg* (that is, point *c* of the sphere coincides with point *g* of line *fg*); and arc *cb* is fitted to line *gh* (that is, point *b* of the sphere coincides with point *h* of line *gh*); and finally arc *ba* is fitted to line *hi* (that is, point *a* of the arc coincides with point *i* of the line *hi*). It is clear that this sphere, rolled between equidistant lines so that if the line is equal to arc *ad*, line *fg* to arc *dc*, line *gh* to arc *cb*, and finally line *hi* to arc *ba*, then the whole line *ai* to the whole cir- <note>The text cuts off mid-word "circumference" as it moves to the next page.</note>

And indeed, by these means, the motion of the **World Soul** <note>original: "anima Mundi"</note>, driven through the series of Worlds, finally returns into itself once a quintuple circumvolution is completed. This was beautifully indicated by the famous five-rayed star (as will be seen in its proper place), <margin>The totality of sensible things is signified by the pentad.</margin> when they mark the totality of sensible things with the <term>pentad</term> <note>The number five.</note>. Thus, the first consistency of sensible things is matter itself; neighboring to matter is the act of being; neighboring to this in the third place is the vital act; that which is numbered in the fourth place from matter is the sensitive act; and finally, the fifth and last place of sensible things is claimed by the rational act, which is capable of perceiving the sensible World. For just as a circular motion is completed at the fifth point, and the Sun, having departed from the East, returns to the place of the East in the fifth position; so also the totality of sensible things is consumed <note>In the sense of being brought to fulfillment or completion.</note> in the fourth act, but in the fifth place from matter—that is, by reason.

---

### § V.

### *The Hieroglyphic Senarius.*

<margin>The senarius is the leader of the perfect numbers.</margin> **J**ust as the <term>quinarius</term> <note>The number five.</note> discerns and numbers the outermost knowledge of the senses, so the <term>senarius</term> <note>The number six.</note>—the leader of the perfect numbers, constituted from the <term>dyad</term> <note>The number two.</note> led into the <term>triad</term> <note>The number three; i.e., 2 x 3 = 6.</note>—takes up the task of distributing and numbering all material knowledge. And just as the quinarius designates the revolution of the World Soul through the five orders of sensible things, <margin>The number six represents the revolution of four units into absolute Unity.</margin> restored at last to itself at the point from which it flowed; so the senarius marks the revolution of four units into absolute Unity; for a progression returning into itself in a circle is numbered by the six. Therefore, absolute Unity coincides with absolute infinity: intellectual with intellectual, rational with rational, and sensible unity with sensible infinity. Every unity is unparticipatable, indivisible, and incorruptible; whence it follows that unity is not absolute unless it is participatable in intellectual "otherness"; nor intellectual, except in rational otherness; nor rational, except with the sensible itself. God, therefore, who is absolute unity, is not reached except

intellectually; nor is intelligence reached, except rationally; nor reason, except sensibly. Thus, absolute unity descends into intellectual infinity, the intellectual into the rational, and the rational into the sensible; truly, sensible unity, having flowed back <note>original: "refluxa"</note>, ascends into the rational, the rational into the intellectual, and finally the intellectual into the supramundane and infinite unity. These stages are aptly indicated by the number six <term>senarium; the number six, considered by Pythagoreans to be a "perfect" number because it is the sum of its parts (1+2+3)</term>; for the beginning of the flowing unity and the end of the returning unity coincide in absolute unity. Likewise, the end of the flowing and the beginning of the returning unity coincide in the sensible realm, and the middle stages are doubled, so that the four terms of the flow and return, together with the two middle points, exactly constitute the number six. But let us demonstrate the matter in a figure.

-> *A figure indicating how the measure of eternity is ascribed to the number six; and how the most specific can return into the most universal, and vice versa.* <-

<note>Diagram: A circle with an inscribed hexagon representing the 'senarium'. Labels around the vertices indicate the cycle of emanation. Top center (point a) is the 'Beginning of the flow' (Initium fluxus). The left side descends through 'intellectual' (b) and 'rational' (c). The bottom (d) is labeled 'Point of return' (Punctum refluxus) and 'sensible' (sensibilis). The right side ascends back through 'rational' (e) and 'intellectual' (f) to absolute unity.</note>

Let *a* be absolute unity, *b* intellectual, *c* rational, and *d* sensible; in which the flow of unity ends, and the return of sensible unity begins, ascending from the sensible *d* into the rational *c*, and from *c* into the intellectual *b*, and finally into absolute unity. Let it be that just as six diametrical chords <note>The radius of a circle, which when marked six times around the circumference, creates a perfect hexagon.</note> subtended by the circumference perfectly measure and complete the circuit of the circle, in no different a way does the end knit together the beginnings by the number six through the ascent and descent of the revolved unity. From this it is clear that the descent of light is nothing other than the ascent of darkness; for it is no different for God to be in the World than for the World to be in God; nor is it different for act to proceed into potency than for potency to proceed into act; nor is it different for darkness to raise itself into light than for light to descend into darkness; nor finally is it different for the potency of matter to proceed toward the act of form, than for actual form to descend into potential matter.

You see, therefore, how the measure of eternity is ascribed to the number six, and how the most universal returns into the most specific, and the most specific into the most universal. Whence it is no wonder that the Egyptians held this number in such great veneration that they marked the throne of the supreme Multiform Deity <note>original: "Numen Polymorphus," referring to a god who takes many shapes, likely Osiris or Serapis in Kircher's view</note> with it, as <margin>The Egyptians decorated the throne of God with the number six.</margin> will be made clear in the explanation of the Bembine Tablet <note>The Mensa Isiaca or Bembine Tablet is an elaborate bronze tablet with Egyptian-style motifs that Kircher believed held the key to hieroglyphics.</note>: all of which things look toward the theories of the matters discussed.

# § VI.

->*The Hieroglyphic Septenary.*<-
<note>The "Septenary" refers to the number seven and its mystical properties.</note>

<margin>The number seven contains hidden mysteries.</margin>
**T**he Septenary is a most sacred number in the Oracles, and most full of mysteries; it holds such a sacred and venerable dignity that among those numbers included within the decad <note>The numbers 1 through 10</note>, it possesses a singular and extraordinary logic above the others. For some of them beget but are not begotten; others are begotten but do not beget; others do both; the septenary alone neither begets any of them, nor is it begotten by any. For Unity, as the principle of all number, begets all following numbers, while being itself begotten by none. Thus 2, 3, and 5 beget 4, 6, 9, and 10, yet they are not begotten <note>In this Pythagorean context, "begotten" refers to being a product of multiplication or addition of other numbers within the decad</note>; whereas 4, 6, 8, <margin>The number seven within the decad neither begets nor is begotten.</margin> 9, and 10 do not beget, but are begotten; but the septenary neither begets nor is begotten, since it has no number below it from which it may be begotten, nor is there any within the decad which it might beget. Hence, it was aptly used by the ancient followers of Pythagoras as a Symbol of the Leader and Ruler of all things, as one who, since he is immobile, is said neither to be begotten nor to beget; which Plutarch describes in these words: *He is the Leader and Prince of all things, God always one, stable, lacking motion, free from motion, like unto himself, unlike others, surrounded by a sevenfold Choir of beings.* For that reason, the Pythagoreans established this number as a symbol of Minerva <note>The Roman goddess of wisdom, associated with the Greek Athena</note>, who was born from the head of Jupiter, a perpetual Virgin, born without a mother. The Egyptians held this number in the highest veneration above all others, establishing it as the seal of all things: for in the Universe, it denotes seven kinds of beings; <margin>The Universe is shaped by the number seven.</margin> in the higher World, the seven Prince Spirits; in the Zodiac of the firmament, the seven configurations or aspects of the signs to one another; in the planetary heaven, the seven wanderers <note>The seven classical planets: Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn</note>; in the elementary world, as many kinds of metals; in the Microcosm <note>The human body as a reflection of the universe</note>, as many principal members; in the Moon, seven phases, and a period of four times seven, that is, 28 days; in the growth of man, seven ages; in the perfection of the fetus, seven stages; and innumerable other things which consist of the septenary measure, which for the sake of brevity I include in the following table.

<margin>The various ways the Egyptians expressed the septenary <note>the number seven</note> of the Universe.</margin>
Since the Egyptians saw the whole universe of things marked by this number seven, they judged it impossible that some distinguished and hidden mystery did not lie concealed beneath it. Hence, they exhibited it in various ways through hieroglyphs: the celestial septenary thus, III ⊕ <note>Symbol: Circle divided by a cross</note>; and the sublunary <note>earthly</note> septenary thus, III ☩ <note>Symbol: Cross</note>. They represented the celestial through three lines and a four-part circle; the sublunary through three lines and a cross ☩; by which they secretly denoted that the sevenfold or universal power of the supreme Divinity is exerted when it moves from the triad <note>three</note> into the tetrad <note>four</note>—first into the celestial, then into the sublunary—and, the revolution having been completed, it is restored to itself. ### CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER III.

### But let us proceed to the hieroglyphic novenary <note>The number nine</note>, which, although <margin>Mysteries of the hieroglyphic novenary.</margin>
we have followed it copiously in the preceding sections, it nevertheless seemed appropriate to repeat its mysteries briefly in this place. To the Egyptians, the Novenary was a symbol of Generative Nature derived from the supreme Deity—that is, falling short of the decad <note>The number ten</note>—as Pherecydes <note>A 6th-century BCE Greek thinker</note> left in his writings; and it was called the leader of the troop falling away from God, and according to Eusebius, *Ophoneus*, that is, the Serpentine Demon. Perhaps they were alluding to the fall of Lucifer. They strove to appease this figure in various ways, along with the rest of his followers, who are the False Gods, spirits of lying, vessels of iniquity, avengers of crimes, deceivers, powers of the air, furies, accusers, and tempters, as will be said in its proper place; although later thinkers consecrated the number nine not only to Demons, but also to the Muses, who are (as the Platonists believe) the souls of the stars, and to the intellectual Ennead <note>A group of nine</note> of the World. But since these kinds of Enneads have been treated abundantly in the preceding pages, we refer the reader there.

There remains the number ten, which at all times the ancient Pytha- <margin>The hieroglyphic denarius.</margin> goreans extolled with the highest praise, because it obtains its origin from the *tetractys* <note>The mystical triangular figure of four rows (1+2+3+4) totaling ten</note>; for these four numbers 1, 2, 3, 4 joined together constitute 10, <margin>The number ten is the completion of all numbers.</margin> the end and completion of all numbers, beyond which there is no number, but only a repetition of numbers. It contains the mystery of the four unities, which were discussed previously, namely 1, 10, 100, 1000: in which the first Monad <note>Unity/One</note> corresponds to the absolute Monad; the second to the <term>Dyad</term> <note>The number two; duality</note>; the third (100) to the <term>Triad</term> <note>The number three; trinity</note>; the fourth (1000) to the <term>Tetrad</term> <note>The number four; quaternary</note>: so much so, indeed, that the Monad exactly fits the point, the decad the line, the *hecatontas* <note>The hundred</note> the surface, and the *chilias* <note>The thousand</note> the body <note>Kircher is mapping numbers to geometric dimensions: 1D point, 2D line, 3D plane, 4D solid</note>. The Monad is the root, the square, and the cube of itself; the hundred is the square of ten; while the thousand fulfills the cubic nature of the decad. The simple and odd Monad is etched with a single small line; the decad is carved with two figures, just as the dyad is composed of two units; the hundred is written with as many figures as the triad has units, and the thousand consists of as many figures as the quaternary has units. If anyone, therefore, joins these seats of numbers, he will elicit from them the number one thousand one hundred and eleven, thus: 1111, the supreme and ultimate of all numbers, finished by every reason, the expanded mystery of the four monads; for this number will be at once a point, a line, a surface, and a body, explaining the ratio of all things that are and that fall under sight—the epitome and summary of the Universe. But see what we have brought forth above concerning the four Monads, which is most worthy of consideration. And the Egyptians, as has been said, exhibited this ten through a decussis <note>The Roman numeral X</note> or <margin>The Egyptians represent the Denarius by a decussate cross.</margin> cross thus, X, or thus <note>original: a six-pointed asterisk-like mark</note>, which they composed from two fives; for by a line inclined toward another, yet not cutting it, as is evident here, V, or thus, Λ, they noted the number five. This Λ they placed as a symbol of the influence of the upper five into the lower, while that V was the symbol of the lower five as it stood subject to the heavenly influence; both signs were discovered from the spread feet of the Ibis, which, joined into one, constitute the symbol of the ten, as we have deduced amply in the construction of the Hieroglyphic Alphabet in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, and in Volume III.

X, or <note>Hieroglyphic symbol: A six-pointed star-like cross</note> expresses the number ten <note>original: "denarium"</note>, and it is composed of two fives, V and Λ.

<note>Hieroglyphic/Numeric symbol: I over X or X over I</note> is the sign for eleven <note>original: "vndenarij"</note>; and it continues in this way always up to 15 by means of linear units, following the order of numbers for the increase of the number beyond ten.

<note>Hieroglyphic symbol: A six-pointed star-cross with a horizontal bar across the bottom stem</note> Signifies the number fifteen <note>original: "quindenarium"</note>, from the cross <note>six-pointed star</note> and the Λ; if you join a small line to this sign below, or above <note>Hieroglyphic symbol: the star-cross with a line and a '1' below it</note>, you make 16; if two lines, seventeen; if 3, eighteen; if four, nineteen.

<note>Hieroglyphic symbol: An X inside a circle</note> The symbol for twenty <note>original: "vigenarij"</note> is composed of a cross-mark <note>original: "decussi"</note> and a circle.

<note>Hieroglyphic symbol: A circle with a small vertical stroke or hook on the top</note> is the mark for one hundred <note>original: "centenarij"</note>.

<note>Hieroglyphic symbol: Same as 100, but with two strokes/hooks</note> Two hundred.

<note>Hieroglyphic symbol: Same as 100, but with three strokes/hooks</note> Signifies three hundred.

<note>Hieroglyphic symbol: Same as 100, but with four strokes/hooks</note> Four hundred.

<note>Hieroglyphic symbol: A circle containing a V-shape</note> Five hundred.

<note>Hieroglyphic symbol: A circle containing an eight-pointed star</note> One thousand.

<note>Closing bracket for the list above</note> } They also expressed all these numbers in other ways, concerning which a more copious opportunity for discussion will be given in the explanation of the Obelisks themselves.

->And these are the literal <note>original: "κυριολογικὰ" (kyriologika) - meaning direct or proper terms</note> numbers used by the Egyptians; all of which it seemed best to set forth in this place, extracted partly from the Obelisks, partly from the Bembine Tablet <note>The Mensa Isiaca, a famous bronze tablet depicting Egyptian deities</note> where they occur very frequently here and there, and finally partly from the Great Egyptian Scale <note>Kircher's own dictionary/thesaurus of Coptic and Egyptian terms</note>.<-

### Hierogrammatic Numbers:
<note>Hierogrammatic refers to "sacred writing" or symbolic priestly script.</note>

<note>Hieroglyphic symbol: A circle with a distinct point in the center</note> This denotes the central Unity <note>original: "Vnitatem centralem"</note>, that is, they placed the center for "one"; and because the center is imperceptible except by the positioning of a point, they considered that it should be signaled by no better method than a circle; for where there is a circle, it is necessary that there also be a center: Moreover, they noted through the circle the evolution of the center, or the Divine Monad <note>The "Monad" refers to the ultimate, indivisible source of all being in Neoplatonic philosophy</note>, into the nature of things, concerning which we have discussed at length above; they also hinted at this through the Phoenix.

# CLASS VII. MATHEMATICAL HIEROGLYPHS. CHAPTER IV.
<sig>F 2</sig>

<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: Two crows or ravens facing each other. Kircher identifies them as representing the number two (Dyad) and the principles of action and passion.</note> By two Crows, according to the testimony of Horus <note>referring to Horapollo, a 5th-century author of a treatise on hieroglyphs</note>, they denoted the **Dyad** <note>the number two</note> of the principles of nature, or what is the same thing, the active and passive principle; concerning which, see the exposition on the **Dyad**.

<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: An equilateral triangle. Kircher identifies it as the number three and the triform Numen or the ideal world.</note> By an equilateral triangle, they denoted the triform **Divinity**, as was shown above, or the Ideal World.

<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: A square or rectangle. Kircher identifies it as the number four and the four seasons.</note> By a square, they denoted the four seasons of the year, about which more will be said in the following sections.

<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: A dove (Columba). Kircher identifies it as the number five, noting it only lays two eggs at a time (though his text says quinarium/five, possibly referring to a different symbolic logic).</note> By a Dove, they denoted the **quinary** <note>the number five</note>, because it is always accustomed to bring forth only five eggs <note>Kircher's natural history here is idiosyncratic; doves usually lay two eggs</note>.

<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: A rooster (Gallus). Kircher identifies it as the number seven, claiming it salutes the Sun seven times a day.</note> By a Rooster, they denoted the **septenary** <note>the number seven</note>, for the reason that it salutes the Sun by crowing at seven individual intervals of the day.

<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: A Cynocephalus (baboon) in a seated posture, appearing to urinate. Kircher identifies it as the number twelve, representing the twelve hours of the day and night.</note> By a Baboon, they signified 12, because by urinating twelve times on the day of the equinox, it marks the equinoctial day of twelve hours.

And these are the things concerning hierogrammatic numbers that have come to my notice; they expressed the species of the remaining numbers here and there through the <term>Kyriological</term> <note>from Greek 'kyrios' (proper/literal); here referring to numbers used in their primary sense</note> numbers placed a little before, and for the most part inserted into Obelisks and Egyptian fragments.

# CHAPTER IV.
->*On the wondrous effects of numbers.*<-

It has been made clear from the preceding that the Egyptians possessed certain most secret numbers dedicated to the seven principal Gods; however, what these numbers were, to which Gods they were dedicated, or what uses they had, remains to be explained, lest it be said that anything of hidden matters escaped the notice of "Oedipus" <note>Kircher refers to himself as Oedipus, the solver of the Sphinx's riddles</note>. Concerning these, Abenuaschia <note>Ibn Wahshiyya, a 9th/10th-century polymath</note> writes thus on the worship of the Egyptians:

<note>original Arabic: "The philosophers of Egypt mentioned that they had seven types of numbers held in great honor, and they assigned them to the gods who are the seven: Saturn, Jupiter, Rephan (Mars), Sun, Venus, Mercury, and Moon..."</note>

<margin>Which were the seven numbers that the Egyptians venerated, and to which gods they consecrated them.</margin> *That is: The Egyptian Philosophers remember that there were seven numbers held by them in great veneration, which they consecrated to their seven Gods; namely to Saturn, Jupiter, Rephan or Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon. To Saturn they dedicated these numbers: 3, 9, 15, and 45. To Jupiter these: 4, 16, 34, and 136. To Mars these: 5, 25, 65, and 325. To the Sun these: 6, 36, 111, 666. To Venus these: 7, 49, 175, and 1225. To Mercury these: 8, 64, 260, 2080. Finally, to the Moon: 9, 81, 369, and 3321.* We have the numbers; now let us see what mystery lies hidden beneath them, and from where they derive their origin.

# CHAPTER IV. THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

<margin>
The Pythagoreans demonstrated all things that exist in the nature of things through certain arrangements of numbers.
</margin>

It must be noted, therefore, that the genuine disciples of the Egyptians, the Pythagoreans, learned certain secret arrangements of numbers, to which they attributed so much that they believed there was nothing in the nature of things they could not demonstrate through them. And indeed, they did not lightly call Unity itself—the parent of all numbers, similar only to itself and to no other besides, which when multiplied by itself (a thing that happens to no other number) is always the same—the soul most like unto itself, the King of the whole body, the Lord of all actions, and the very <term>ousia</term> <note>original: "οὐσίαν"; essence or true being</note> of all things. But the first number born from doubled unity, that is, 2, they called both "opinion" (subject to change) and "motion" (never standing still); likewise calling all other things by the names of other numbers. They especially observed square numbers, as if explaining the rationale for the generation of all things in the sevenfold World. Now, a square number is that which is produced from a root multiplied by itself. And to begin from unity: just as it is indivisible, so it is 

<margin>
Unity is invariable.

It indicates the Divine nature.
</margin>

unmultipliable; yet it is not so barren that it fails to provide what the rest of the numbers offer, since it is the mother and principle of all numbers. Others, when multiplied by themselves, always produce something divided; unity alone, when multiplied by itself, always restores itself into unity—always the same, subject to no variation, being its own root, its own square, and its own cube. This proves more than sufficiently the one essence and immortal nature of God, the Best and Greatest, which is free from all diversity and alteration, while diversity exists only in the numbers following unity. Therefore, just as all things emanated from the one supreme architectonic <term>Monad</term> <note>The primary unit or "The One" in Pythagorean philosophy</note> of the World, so the order of numbers proceeding from that unity had to be aptly established—not here, but there where that which it represents exists. But to approach more closely the mysteries of square numbers:

<margin>
The mysteries of square numbers.
</margin>

It should be known that just as two squares always have one proportional mean between them, so two cubes have two proportional mean numbers between them. For example: if 2 is multiplied by itself, the square 4 is produced; if 2 is multiplied by four, the cube 8 is produced. Likewise, if 3 is multiplied by itself, 9 is born; and again, if 3 is multiplied by 9, the cube 27 is born. If then 2 is multiplied by 3, the result is 6, the proportional mean between the squares 4 and 9, created in this arrangement: 4, 6, 9, which are in a <term>Sesquialtera</term> <note>A ratio of 1.5 to 1, or 3:2</note> proportion; for as 4 is to 6, so 6 is to 9. Furthermore, if you multiply the root 2 by the proportional mean 6, and multiply the root 3 by this same 6, there will be born 12 and 18, the two proportional means between the two cubes 8 and 27; for 8, 12, 18, 27 are in the same continuous sesquialtera proportion. You will find this exact same thing in unity, which shares the same power with numbers; for although unity, when multiplied by itself, is always entirely the same, yet when compared with the numbers it has generated, it is considered by the same logic. Thus, if 1 (having the power of a side/root) is multiplied by itself, a 1 (having the power of a square) is produced; if again 1 (as a root) is multiplied by 1 (as a square), it will obtain the power of a cube. If afterwards 1 (having the power of a root) is multiplied by the root 2, the proportional mean 2 is produced between the 1 (having the power of a square) and the 4 (having the power of a square), for 1, 2, 4 are in a double proportion. If again, first the power of the root...

# CLASS VII. MATHEMATICAL HIEROGLYPHS
## CHAPTER IV.

...having 1 as the starting point, then the side <note>The "side" refers to the root of a square or cube.</note> 2; if 2 is multiplied as the mean proportional of the squares, then 2 and 4 (which hold the power of the mean between the unit cube and the cube of 8) are generated as proportionals; for they are: 1, 2, 4, 8 in a continuous double proportion. If again 2 behaves as the side or root, and this is then multiplied into the mean proportional 2, 4 will be produced: therefore 2 and 4 will be the mean proportionals between 1, which behaves as a cube, and 8, the other cube, as follows: 1, 2, 4, 8.

<margin>Unity enfolds all things.</margin> Therefore, the Pythagoreans applied this Unity—which enfolds all units, roots, squares, and cubes—to the eternal and immense God; it was, as it were, the first square and cube of the divine nature, in which all things are one. <margin>To which Gods the squares were dedicated.</margin> The second square was the number four, produced from the dyad <note>The number 2</note> multiplied by itself, which they likened to imperfect matter, submerged in the abyss of potentiality. The third square, 9, produced from the triad <note>The number 3</note> multiplied by itself, they dedicated to Saturn. The fourth square, 16, produced from the quaternary <note>The number 4</note> multiplied by itself, they assigned to Jupiter. The fifth square, 25, produced from the pentad <note>The number 5</note> multiplied by itself, to Mars. <margin>The production of squares.</margin> The sixth square, 36, produced from the hexad <note>The number 6</note> multiplied by itself, to the Sun. The seventh square, 49, emanating from the heptad <note>The number 7</note> multiplied by itself, to Venus. The eighth square, 64, proceeding from the ogdoad <note>The number 8</note> multiplied by itself, to Mercury. Finally, the ninth square, 81, proceeding from the ennead <note>The number 9</note> multiplied by itself, they dedicated to the Moon. Indeed, they assigned the cubes to the Elementary Spirits in the same order as they assigned the squares to the celestial Gods, as will be discussed later. And from these nine squares reviewed here, they set aside the first two squares emanating from the Monad <note>The number 1</note> and the Dyad; the square of the Monad because it is far removed beyond all boundaries of human intellectual sublimity; and the square of the Dyad, 4, because of the imperfection of the matter which it involved. The remaining seven squares they dedicated individually to the individual Planets, as we have said. The first square after the number two—that is, 9, emanating from three multiplied by itself—they assigned to Saturn, led by this reasoning: that the closer the Gods were to the supreme Leader <note>original: "Antesignano"</note> of all Gods and to the highest or supramundane Monad, the simpler they would be, and the less they would be merged into the multitude of material things; but the further they were removed from the Monad, the more they would participate in the material mixture. Thus, not without reason, they thought that 81—the largest among those squares emerging from roots established within the first ten numbers—should be dedicated to the Moon.

Therefore, having assigned these seven squares, and noting a certain wonderful property in the various arrangements of each, they believed it could not be otherwise than that God, the highest and uncomprehended, wished to exhibit under them the greatest mysteries to the human intellect, and even to indicate the order, administration, and economy of the seven Worlds under them. I clarify the matter with an example. If someone considers the confused typographic forms of letters, even though they contain within themselves all imaginable knowledge, he nevertheless does not know which one he desires, or under what combination it lies hidden; yet a skilled person soon knows how to combine the forms so aptly that at last he can produce whatever he wishes—indeed, all the mysteries of the sciences—from them...

## CHAPTER IV

...eliciting the same through the appropriate senses. In a not dissimilar manner, certain most mysterious squares are given; but since they lie hidden under certain forms of numbers, it is necessary that the mysteries remain confused as long as they are concealed. However, they will soon become clear once some skilled <term>Arithmantes</term><note>A practitioner of Arithmancy, the divination or mystical study of numbers.</note> has aptly and ingeniously arranged the individual numbers in order within as many small cells as the square contains units. But first, let us reveal the mysteries of the individual squares, and then the method and reasoning for arranging them within the cells of the square.

<margin>The method of arranging the square.</margin> Thus, the Wise Men of old used to arrange the said squares in such an order that, in whatever way the numbers placed within the areas were added together, one and the same number would always emerge; the sum of all of these would then also have its own mystery. These were called the "seals of the immortal Gods," because their dominion was expressed through them in a certain wonderful manner.

->**The Seal of Saturn.**<-

<margin>The arrangement of the Square of Saturn.</margin> Therefore, when they wished to depict the number 9, the first square of Saturn—whom they called the Mind of the entire Universe, as we explained in the *Sphinx Mystagoga*—they arranged its numbers within nine small squares with such skill that the individual rows of numbers (vertical, horizontal, and diagonal), when joined together, restored one and the same number, as follows:

You see, therefore, how the numbers, however they are taken, always restore 15. Moreover, all the numbers taken together contain 45. And this is <margin>Abennaſchia. The numbers 3, 9, 15, 45 dedicated to Saturn. Abuhali.</margin> what Abennaſchia <note>Likely a reference to an Arabic or Hebrew source, possibly Ibn Ezra or a similar commentator.</note> hinted at a little earlier when he said that 3, 9, 15, and 45 were dedicated to Saturn: for 3 constitutes the root or side of the square, 9 the square itself, 15 the numbers of the individual rows added up, and the sum of all constitutes 45. And from this it is clear why the Arab Abuhali <note>Abu Ma'shar, a famous Persian astrologer.</note> said in his *Astronomy* that Saturn is surrounded by three greatest royal powers, and each of these by 9 other principals, and these by 15 others, and that the sum of all constitutes the Saturnian Choir of principal <term>Genii</term><note>Guardian spirits or celestial intelligences.</note> presiding over the whole Universe. I cite his words:

> <note>original Arabic: "Saturn had three kings, and each one of them had nine kings under him, and each one of them had fifteen spirits, and all of them are forty-five; and this is what the name Zahal [Saturn] means, which itself comprises forty-five."</note>
> <note>Arabic script followed by astrological symbols for Saturn and a celestial motif.</note>

<margin>زحل Zahel, Saturn. <br> 7 <br> 8 <br> 30 <br> 45</margin> Saturn has three Kings, and each of these has nine other Kings, and each of these has 15 others; the sum of all is 45; as the name زحل *Zahel*, that is, Saturn, demonstrates, which when resolved into numbers, exhibits the same number; namely, the sum of the Saturnian Monarchy distributed into 3, 9, and 15 classes is 45. <note>Kircher is using Gematria here: in the Arabic alphabet, Z (ز) = 7, H (ح) = 8, and L (ل) = 30, totaling 45.</note>

->### The Seal of Jupiter.<-

But let us proceed to the arrangement of the second square, or the Seal of Jupiter, which emerges from the number four multiplied by itself, which is 16. Its arrangement is such that each of the rows of numbers—whether normal or perpendicular, transverse, diagonal or diametrical—as well as the numbers of the small squares surrounding the center when joined together, always restore the same number, namely 34; the sum of all of them, however, becomes 136. # CHAPTER V.
## Concerning the Mathematical reasoning for the manufacture and construction of the said seals.

**T**he more hidden and worthy of admiration this business is, the more its clarification must rightly be considered difficult, perplexed, and intricate. For the nature of numbers is so arduous and recondite <note>hidden or obscure</note> that it seems to escape the sharpest edge of almost all human intellect. But since I am so constituted by nature that I think nothing more worthy of a man than to apply industry to these kinds of tortuous labyrinths of hidden things—and the said secret arrangement of numbers holds a significant place among things hitherto inaccessible and unknown—I have applied myself with the greatest diligence to penetrate this secret arrangement and its logic, as far as the powers of my intellect would permit. Having penetrated it, I have brought it forth, and having brought it forth, I communicate it in this place to the reader eager for curious matters. There are, however, two things to be considered in this business: first, the arrangement of odd-numbered squares <note>original: "imparium quadratorum" — squares with an odd number of cells per side, like 3x3 or 9x9</note>, and then the even-numbered ones. Just as the former is easier, so the latter suffers from greater and almost inexhaustible difficulties. We shall reason first about squares, and then about cubes, with equal pace.

# § I.

### The construction of the square, which is formed from the number three multiplied by itself, and is the Seal of Saturn.

<margin>The square emerging from the number two is imperfect.</margin>
We omit here the first square, emerging from the number two <note>original: "binarius"</note> multiplied by itself—namely, the number four <note>original: "quaternarius"</note>—because it departs so far from the nature and properties of the remaining squares. It is an imperfect number and can hardly be called a square in the proper and absolute sense. This is because it emerges not only from the multiplication of two by two, but also from the addition of two to two (which happens to no other square). Thus, it represents a potential mixture of matter <note>Kircher suggests that because 2+2 and 2x2 both equal 4, the number lacks the distinct mathematical "purity" required for celestial seals</note>. For this reason, it was deservedly rejected and eliminated by the ancient Philosophers, who dedicated nothing but the perfect to the Gods.

It must first be noted that in every odd-numbered square, as can be seen in this square of three, three types of terms are given: the greater, the lesser, and the middle. The **greater terms** are those which are counted after the middle term until the end of the numbers of the nine-fold square. The **lesser terms** are those which are computed from unity <note>The number 1</note> up to the middle term. The **middle term** is that which stands in the middle between the four lesser and four greater terms; it arises from half of the aggregate sum resulting from the addition of the smallest and largest terms. For example, 1 (the smallest term) joined to 9 (the largest term) gives 10, the half of which is 5—the middle term in the progression, which always occupies the middle place among the cells of the square, as is evident from the figure and in this following progression:

So in the numbers 2, 7, 6: if the middle term communicates one unit to each extreme 2 and 6, it will remain 5; while 2 and 6, increased by a unit, become 3 and 7, which joined together constitute 10, another two fives. In these numbers 4, 9, 2, if you subtract 4 from 9, 5 will remain; while the 4 added to 2 gives 6, which [with the remaining units] give 10, two other fives. Finally, in these numbers 8, 1, 6, if you add 2 subtracted from 8 and the same from 6 to the 1, they become 5; while the two terms diminished by two, 6 and 4, added together make 10, constituting another two fives. You see, therefore, by what a wonderful reason, through exceeding and falling short, the numbers—beautifully balanced—aspire to one sum. And from these things, unless I am mistaken, the reason is clearer than light why the <term>novenarius</term> <note>the number nine / the 3x3 square</note>, according to the number of its side, when aptly arranged within the three cells of the square in all directions, always infallibly produces the same number. This is to be understood not only regarding this odd square, but also regarding all other odd squares produced to infinity, as we shall say in what follows.

A wonderful property of the numbers in this square. In which the numbers, however they are taken, always produce the same sum.
</margin>

And from this arises 그 wonderful property, by which the numbers contained and added in the individual four-fold rows of the said square, however they are taken, always produce the same sum, namely 34. For since all numbers in a natural progression <note>A sequence of consecutive numbers starting from 1</note> of 16 terms equidistant from the extremes make 17, as has been proven; and since 8 and 9, the middle terms of the whole progression, likewise make 17 when added; 17 joined to 17 necessarily constitutes 34. Hence, if you join the four terms 1, 8, 9, 16 into one—namely the extremes with the means 8 and 9—you will again have 34. If, however, you join 2, 8, 9, 15—namely two from the extremes with the two means—you will again have 34. If you join 3, 8, 9, 14—the third terms from the extremes with the two means—you will have 34 once more. And so with the rest; for the same number 34 will always result from the addition of two numbers equidistant from the extremes to the two means. It is no wonder, therefore, if the said numbers are arranged within the square skillfully—that is, with the diligence previously described—that in every four-fold row (straight, transverse, or diagonal) and in every group of four smaller squares joined together however they are taken, the same sum always emerges; for the entire foundation of this arrangement lies hidden beneath the natural progression of 16 numbers. In this progression, as many combinations of four numbers making 34 can be established as there are combinations found in the square producing the same sum.

# § III.

## ->The Mathematical construction of the third square, which is also called the Seal of Mars.<-

**T**he third square of odd numbers arises from five multiplied by itself <note>5x5, resulting in 25</note>; the construction of which does not differ from the construction of the first square <note>The 3x3 square of Saturn</note>. But let us explain the matter in a few words.

Let a rhomboid quadrangle <note>A diamond-shaped grid</note> be made, in whose rows of five small squares arranged diagonally the 25 numbers are written in natural order. This is done in the manner you see in the following figure, and there will remain within the square *a. b. c. d* as many empty spaces as you see numbers separated outside the square. These you shall transfer into the empty spaces corresponding to each by this industrious method: Since we previously instructed that in odd squares, the individual terms of numbers facing each other should be transferred into the opposite empty places in the same column, you will complete the business with the greatest ease according to the tenor of this rule. Proceed thus: in column *g h*, 1 is to be transferred into the opposite empty place within the same column, namely in the area already above 19; while 25, the lowest number in the same column *g h*, shall be placed in the opposite place within the same column below 7.

# CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. 67 CHAPTER V.

The construction of the Seal of the Moon is made from 9 multiplied by 9, the sum of which is 81; this provides the square for which we seek the structure of the Seal of the Moon. Therefore, proceed as follows. Let a diagram be made in the shape of a Rhomboid <note>a diamond or slanted parallelogram</note>, in which you arrange 9 sets of nine in rows through cells arranged <term>diagonally <note>original Greek: πλαγίως (plagios)</note></term>, as appears from what was said before. Once this is finished, nothing will be easier than to insert the individual numbers written in the four corners into their respective empty spaces. As the method involves absolutely no difficulty, I shall indicate it in only a few words. Since each corner has seven numbers, which are the heads of columns—partly vertical and partly transverse—the numbers of the highest and lowest corners occupy the same columns, of which the upper ones occupy the head of the columns and the lower ones the base of the same. Thus, column D H displays 1 at the head and 81 at the base. However, the numbers in the right and left corners occupy the same transverse columns. From this, the transfer of numbers into the square a b c d must be established crosswise. 

With these things explained, you will insert the numbers of the highest corner a D b into the square with no trouble if you count ten cells downward from the first cell of each column; for the tenth cell will necessarily be that empty one into which the number displayed at the front of the column must be relocated. For example: if you count ten cells downward from 1 within column D H, the tenth will be that cell within which 1 must be placed. You shall proceed in like manner with the rest of the numbers. Indeed, the numbers of the lower corner, by likewise counting upward, will have every tenth cell within the appropriate columns ready for the number which the base of the appropriate column displays. In like manner, the numbers in the left corner a G c will always find the tenth cell in the appropriate transverse columns, capable of relocating the number which any part of the left column displays. Also, the individual numbers in the right corner b E d will find the tenth cell prepared within their transverse columns for receiving the number which the right part of the column displays. For example: 73 will be located in the tenth cell of the transverse column G E, and 9 will find a place within the same column toward the left in which it may be placed. And in this way, you will have the whole square filled with its numbers with absolutely no trouble, in which the numbers of the individual columns—whether vertical, transverse, or diagonal—when added will always produce 369; these, multiplied by 9 (the side of the square), give the sum of all the numbers: 3321.

It now remains to speak of **cubic squares** <note>Kircher uses "cubic" here to mean multiplicative squares, where the product of the lines is constant, rather than the sum</note>, especially since neither the Ancients nor the Moderns have (to my knowledge) sensed the secret method of this progression. If they had known it, they would undoubtedly have dedicated these cubic squares to the seven classes of the elemental World and their presiding Spirits <note>original: "Genijs"</note>, just as they dedicated the seven [additive] squares to the seven bodies of the starry World and their Spirits. But let us perform the duty of Oedipus <note>A reference to Kircher's role as the "riddle-solver" of Egyptian and hermetic mysteries</note> in bringing to light this artifice, which has perhaps remained unknown until now.

<margin>What a cubic square is.</margin> A cubic square is nothing other than a series of numbers in a **geometric progression** <term>Geometric progression: A sequence of numbers where each term after the first is found by multiplying the previous one by a fixed, non-zero number (here, doubling)</term> continued from unity in a double proportion, having as many terms as a given square number has units. For example: if someone desires to construct a cubic square that corresponds to the square of 9 produced from itself <note>a 3x3 square</note>, let him work as follows. Let 9 terms be placed in a geometric progression starting from unity, as follows:

-> **T** 1 2 4 8 16 32 64 128 256 **V** <-

<margin>An example with an odd number.</margin> You will insert these terms into the square *a b c d* by the exact same method that we taught above in the first paragraph regarding the square of nine for Saturn. But let us give an example. Let a **Rhomboid diagram** <note>A diamond-shaped grid used to organize numbers before shifting them into a square</note> be drawn, as you see.

In this diagram, you will place the given geometric progression *T V* in order, as the figure indicates. Then, you will transpose these numbers into the empty cells of the square *a b c d* by the same law used in the square of 9: namely, you transpose 1 into the opposite fourth cell from the first; 256 upwards into the opposite fourth cell; 4 into the fourth cell to the left; and 64 by moving into the fourth cell to the right. As you see, you will then have a cubic square in which the individual rows—transverse, vertical, and diagonal—will give the same number. However, there is this difference: whereas the numbers in the preceding squares produced the same sum when **added**, here they are not to be added, but **multiplied** by one another to obtain the same number. # ## CHAPTER VI.

## ->Concerning the use, effects, and mysteries—or rather the superstitions—which the Ancients believed to lie hidden beneath the said Seals, together with a refutation of them.<-

<margin>The opinion of the Ancients, who thought that all things in the World were produced according to numbers hidden in the mind of God.</margin> It was the common sentiment of the Ancient Philosophers that the species of things behave like numbers, and that the World, and all things that are in the World, were produced according to numbers hidden in the mind of the Creator <note>original: "Opificis," referring to the Divine Architect or Demiurge</note>. For just as certain wonderful properties and powers lie hidden under fixed limits of numbers, although they may be confused and undefined; so it is certain that they have a wonderful and incredible connection to one another, which only he knows who rightly understands the nature of numbers, and who has acquired a singular skill in connecting them through ingenious arrangement, translocation, digestion, and combination. In like manner, in the nature of things, countless species of things occur, which although they may seem confused and undefined, nevertheless all breathe together into one harmony by a certain wonderful concatenation. This will be found only by him who knows how to fitly and skillfully arrange the species of things according to the ideal disposition of the said numbers, and how to adapt these to those and others through analogous combinations. Throughout this entire work, it is shown that the Egyptians were endowed with a certain wonderful industry in rightly arranging these worldly things above all others, since they knew how to associate the individual grades of natural things so aptly both to the grades of the Celestial and the <term>Genial World</term> <note>The "Genial World" refers to the realm of Genii or guiding spirits/intelligences</note>, so that given any species of the sublunary World, they immediately assigned both a corresponding star and an Intelligence. Having investigated these, they persuaded themselves that it was impossible not to produce admirable and prodigious effects in the congruent application of things. <margin>The power of numbers corresponding to one another according to the Egyptians.</margin> For they thought that individual numbers had corresponding <term>Genii</term> <note>Guardian spirits or presiding intelligences</note> in the worldly economy; when they beheld these coordinated into phalanxes by a certain ineffable artifice, they studied how to arrange those numbers naturally implanted in them—and toward which they inclined with a certain wonderful vehemence—by a similar artifice. They persuaded themselves that nothing was more efficacious or more powerful for attracting them than these things, as if they were genuine matters committed to their guardianship. But truly, since no treatment of the hidden mysteries of nature can be rightly transacted without blemish and the commission of demonic commerce if the light of the true faith be lacking—
