->### The Seal of Saturn.<-

<margin>The ravings of the Arabs concerning the Seal of Saturn.</margin> The Arabs cited in the *Saracenic Kabbalah* say that if anyone engraves this Seal of Saturn on a leaden plate while Saturn is dominant, it brings aid to those in labor, renders a man powerful and safe from enemies, and bestows such favor that one asking anything of Princes shall never suffer a refusal. If, however, the engraving is made while Saturn is weak, it acts as an impediment to the buildings of mortals, the planting of trees, and all machines; it drags one down from the highest rank of dignity to abject fortune, and prepares and nourishes quarrels and disturbances whenever desired, so that it can even split and put to flight unconquered armies. These are the words of <margin>Abenpharagi.</margin> Abenpharagi <note>Likely Bar Hebraeus, also known as Abu'l-Faraj, a 13th-century scholar</note>. Behold how nothing is accomplished in these trifles without astrological vanity and madness.

<margin>Abenmorgun.</margin> Abenmorgun the Arab <note>Likely the Moroccan scholar Ibn al-Banna al-Marrakushi</note> describes its use in other words in his treatise *On the Seals of the Seven Planets*, where he has these things, translated from the Arabic idiom into Latin <note>original: "in Arabicum idioma in Latinum translata"</note>: "If this figure is written on virgin parchment on the day and hour of Saturn <note>original: ♄</note>, with Saturn positioned in the houses of Libra or Aquarius, and it is smoked with alum and asafoetida <note>A pungent resin used in folk medicine and magic</note>, and tied to the neck of a woman in labor, then she shall give birth most happily. But if it is engraved on a leaden plate while Saturn is retrograde and the Moon is waning, and one places that figure in a newly begun building, then that building shall never be completed; and wherever this figure is placed on the day and hour of Saturn, there the most unhappy spirits of Saturn will stir up all quarrels and disturbances. Saturn has 45 in its numbers, and they are placed three by three, so that in all directions they result in 15; nevertheless, it is necessary that all things be performed with the right hand, and one must add the name of the day and hour, and the Angel of Venus <note>Kircher may be noting a contradiction or specific ritual requirement here</note>, and the character of the planet." But how so many observances and so many foolish machinations contribute to the matter, I cannot perceive. It is manifest, therefore, that a pact lies hidden here with him who, being the Author of all wickedness, is accustomed to grant the things requested to such makers of machinations, in order to make them deluded followers of his will. <margin>The fabulous use of the Sigil of Mars.</margin> The Arabs describe the third Sigil, that of Mars, and its fabulous and most superstitious use in this way. If anyone, while Mars is ascending, carves the figure into an iron plate or onto the sword itself, they say that person is rendered robust and strong in battle, and terrible to his adversaries, and a victor in war; moreover, in judgments and petitions, he is made to obtain his wish. If, however, while it is descending...

# THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

They report that if this is engraved upon a plate of red copper while Mars is ascending, it can delay new buildings and cast down whomever one wishes from the highest rank of honors, riches, and dignities. It is said to insatiably create discords, seditions, and hatreds among both men and beasts, to drive away bees, pigeons, and fish, and to frustrate the hopes of hunters and warriors. Furthermore, it supposedly renders both brute animals and humans of either sex unfruitful and sterile, strikes terror into approaching enemies, compels them to yield honor, and produces six hundred other monstrous effects. O, the blindness of men entangling themselves in so many and such great insanities! For if a plate of Mars truly possessed these powers, woe to Monarchs, woe to those divided by enmities, woe to those enduring envy, and woe to those exercising rigorous justice. Certainly, against such plotters, neither Kings, nor Princes, nor Republics, nor any state of the human race would ever be secure again; indeed, it would be certain that the World would have perished long ago.

They adorn the figure of the Seal of Mars in this way: within a circle, they describe a pentagon to indicate the side of the square of Mars, which is 5; and inside the pentagon, they place the square of Mars consisting of 25, arranged by its numbers. ->### The Seal of the Sun.<-

<margin>The method of preparing the Seal of the Sun and its most vain effects. From Abenpharagi.</margin> This Seal of the Sun was prepared with great craftsmanship by the Arabs; (I quote the words of <term>Abenpharagi</term> <note>Likely referring to Bar Hebraeus, a 13th-century scholar often cited by Kircher</note>): *Take six drachms of pure gold, and make from it a round plate, in which you shall engrave the table of the Seal on the day and hour of the Sun being in its exaltation, or in its own degree of Aries, or the nineteenth degree of Aries, namely at the end of the month of Nisan <note>The first month of the Hebrew calendar, corresponding to March–April</note>.*

->**The Seal of the Sun**<-

They fashion this Seal of the Sun in this manner: In a circle they first describe a hexagon, and within the hexagon (which is the indicator of the side or root of the <term>square of the Sun</term><note>A mathematical grid where every row and column adds up to the same number; for the Sun, this is 111</note>) they place the numerical square. In the segments of the circle, they place the characters of the <term>Zodiac signs</term> under which the operation is to be established; in the first, second, and third segments, the characters indicate <note>Aries symbol: ♈</note>; in the fourth, fifth, and sixth segments, the characters for <note>Leo symbol: ♌</note> Leo are placed. Within the angles are placed the names of the Solar Angels: Eaphahal, Tharahel, Hegeagfigete, and Raphael, whom they believe to be most inclined toward all humanity and mutual love. The names of Iebion indicate the day and hour of the Sun in which the metal plate must be fashioned. And these are the vanities to be observed in this Seal—things more suited for the fire than for the light of the Sun. <note>Kircher often includes these magical instructions while simultaneously dismissing them as "vanities" or superstitions to avoid trouble with Church censors.</note>

### The Seal of Venus

<margin>The method for fashioning the Seal of Venus.</margin> They fashion the Seal of Venus in this way, according to the testimony of the cited Arabic Author (I quote his words): On the day and hour of Venus, take three <term>drachmas</term><note>An ancient unit of weight</note> of the best silver, or white copper, while Venus is in <note>Pisces symbol: ♓</note>, or <note>Taurus symbol: ♉</note>, or <note>Libra symbol: ♎</note> Libra (her own houses), and let her be without any evil <term>aspect</term><note>The geometric relationship between planets that astrologers believe influences their power</note> or interference, direct and increasing in light; and make a plate, upon which you shall engrave the figure of Venus. Once this is done, you shall perfume it with wood of aloes, ambergris, and mastic; and wrap it in a white silk cloth, and carry it with you.

# CHAPTER VI. THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

And having first performed the adjuration <note>A formal command or solemn oath used in ritual magic to summon or control spirits.</note> (without which you will achieve nothing), they foolishly believe they can win the friendship of all people, remove discords, settle seditions, take away sterility, dissolve evil spells, make flocks and herds fertile, and recall men from "black bile" <note>original: "bili atra" - Melancholy, according to the ancient theory of the four humors.</note> to the joy of life. However, they say that when Venus is descending, she provides the opposite effects. We have seen these trifles; now let us consider the logic of the Sigil.

<note>
Sigil of Venus: A large circular diagram containing a heptagon (a seven-sided shape). At the center is a 7x7 magic square (the Kamea of Venus) containing numbers from 1 to 49. Around the central square are inscribed the names of planetary spirits or angels: Requiel (top), Hamabel (right), Anahel (bottom right), Lebionn (bottom), Kalacttin (bottom left), and Sequyel (left). The heptagon is enclosed within a circle divided into seven numbered segments (1-7). These segments contain "gymnosophistic" <note>A term Kircher uses for "naked philosophers" or ancient mystical characters.</note> characters and astrological signs. Segments 1-4 contain magical characters associated with Libra; segment 5 contains a character for Pisces; segments 6-7 contain characters for Taurus.

Within the circle, they first describe a heptagon, and within the heptagon, the figure of the square of Venus; within the segments of the circle, they write gymnosophistic characters, indicators of the signs of the Zodiac, by which the operation must be opportunely established. In the first, second, third, and fourth segments are placed the Magic characters indicating the sign of Libra; the character in the fifth indicates <note>astrological sign for Pisces</note> Pisces; in the sixth and seventh, they place <note>astrological sign for Taurus</note> Taurus, the sign of the exaltation of Venus. Within the heptagon, however, they place the names of the Venerean Angels, who are *Requiel*, *Sequiel*, *Anabel*, *Hamabel*, and *Kalactin*; whom they foolishly assert are most inclined toward pleasing unions, pleasures, and loves. The name *Iebion* indicates the first day and the first hour of Venus, under which the fanatical practice is to be inaugurated. On the back, they place a Sigil which the author cited above calls a "great secret," known only to visionary philosophers; he says its meaning is the same as "Sweet Sower, provoker of union, joy, love, and true affection"—if it pleases the Gods to believe it.

They place this in the location of some estate, and they think that all—

# CLASS VII. MATHEMATICAL HIEROGLYPHS <note>original: "MATHEMATICA HIEROGLYPH."</note> <note>Mercury symbol: ☿</note> CHAPTER VI.

...all those goods will be multiplied. And if they fashion this in a ring, or a glass vial, on the day and hour of Mercury, during the first seven lunations <note>cycles of the moon</note>, and in the square of the Moon, and preserve the figures afterwards washed with clean water, and carried for three days, during which they eat nothing but bread with honey and raisins; and then engrave the said figure in gray Agate, and fumigate it with aloe wood; they say the one carrying it becomes pleasing to all, increases their riches, recovers the power of lost memory, illuminates the sharpness of the mind, and acquires full knowledge of divination; in a word, they put forward innumerable other delusions <note>original: "deliramenta"</note> concerning the powers of this amulet, which it would be better to suppress in eternal darkness than to bring to light. But let us explain its figure.

<note>
Hieroglyphic inscription: A complex talismanic diagram consisting of a central 8x8 magic square (the Square of Mercury). The square is enclosed within an octagon, which is further enclosed within a circle. 

Inside the segments between the octagon and the circle are various characters:
- At the top: The Hebrew word Star <note>original: "כוכב" (Kokab), meaning "Star" or "Mercury"</note> and the planetary sigil of Mercury.

    - Right: Michael / מיכאל
    - Left: Sarypiel / סריפיאל
    - Bottom: Hanunel / חנוניאל
    - Top (within the square area): Ischion (Latin)
- Astrological symbols for Gemini (♊) and Virgo (♍) are placed in the corners of the octagon.
- The magic square contains numbers 1 through 64 arranged so that each row, column, and diagonal sums to 260.
</note>

First, they inscribe within a circle an octagon of the side, or root, of the numerical square of Mercury, which they describe within the octagon. Then, around the octagon, they place magic characters which signify the operation in <note>Gemini symbol: ♊</note> Gemini and <note>Virgo symbol: ♍</note> Virgo, which constitute the houses of Mercury. Afterward, within the octagon, they place the names of four Mercurial Angels, whose nature they believe to be benign, ingenious, and willingly condescending to others, as you see. *Ischion* indicates the first day and hour for performing the work: to this, they add another great thing from behind, as they imagine to themselves, of virtues, whose character in this sense is: The Evoker; a rational and wise voice, sharp, and prophesying all things.

Within the sides of the enneagon they place the names of the Lunar Angels, as you see; and *Iebion*, which word always indicates the day and hour of the Moon in which the operation must be completed. On the back they place another Seal of great virtue (as they believe), whose characters represent these words: *The Ruler, the kind one, the defender, and the guardian*.

However, so that the curious reader may be able to recognize immediately what such exotic characters mean and signify—lest the anxious reader hesitate in the following pages (for they will occur very frequently)—it seemed best to set down here their complete nomenclature and interpretation. These characters are common to both the Eastern and Western peoples, secretly formed from segments of a circle and the drawing of lines; they emerged partly from the hieroglyphics of the Egyptians and partly from the School of the <term>Gymnosophists</term> <note>Ancient Indian philosophers known to the Greeks as "naked wise men," whom Kircher believed shared a common wisdom with the Egyptians</note>, as we shall show more extensively in its proper time and place. ## PREFACE

->“Let no one ignorant of Geometry enter,” <note>original: Οὐδεὶς ἀγεωμέτρητος εἰσίτω</note> was inscribed upon the gates of Plato’s Academy; let us explain what Plato intended by this epigraph.<-

---

<margin>The science of Geometry leads to the recognition of invisible things.</margin>
The philosophers of ancient ages, led by nature, noted certain wondrous properties within geometrical quantity. Observing a certain natural order in the production of things, they seem to have labored for this one goal: that, relying on the knowledge of these shapes, they might arrive at an understanding of sublime matters. And since they saw that everything exposed to the senses appeared to consist of its own points, lines, surfaces, and bodies, they persuaded themselves it was impossible that the <term>Artisan of all things</term> <note>A reference to the Creator or Demiurge.</note> had not used these as an idea and model in the first founding of the world. A line is made from the motion of a point; a surface from a line moved in breadth; a body from a surface moved in height. What 
<margin>The triple dimension signifies the unfolding of the supreme Unity into this world.</margin>
else do these denote, if not the unfolding of the first and supra-mundane <term>Unity</term> <note>The "Monad," representing the singular divine source.</note> into this sensible world? The great Plato perceived this when he cried out, <term>God always geometrizes</term> <note>original: Ὁ Θεὸς ἀεὶ γεωμετρεῖ</note>; <term>Trismegistus</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the origins of Egyptian wisdom.</note> marveled at it when he pronounced <term>God to be a Circle, whose center is everywhere, and whose circumference is nowhere</term>; <term>Pythagoras</term> looked up to it when he asserted God to be now an Arithmetician, now a Musician, now a Geometer. All 
<margin>The ardor of the ancient philosophers in learning Mathematics.</margin>
later philosophers, followers of their doctrine, followed these men, constantly asserting that the entire doctrine of truth is contained in nothing other than magnitude and multitude. Hence arose that flaming ardor and intense study of the said philosophers in embracing Mathematics, so that they thought no one would ever be great in Philosophy who had approached the investigation of difficult matters by any way other than the Mathematical one. And indeed, it is so: for since all invisible things, as the Apostle Paul testifies, are perceived through those things which have been made, it must necessarily be admitted that all those things presented to the senses are like certain images, sketches, and <term>catoptric reflections</term> <note>Reflections as seen in a mirror.</note> of invisible things, which place before our eyes and explain the likeness of the primordial light from which all things come. But since we take the first foundations of our investigation from the phantasms of sensible appearances, the way to the uncertain can only be through the presupposed and certain. The images—from whose metaphorical proportion we track down things unknown and abstract—ought to be doubted by no one, unlike most sensible objects which are tossed about in a certain continual inconstancy and mutability because of the potential mixture of matter abounding in them. Hence, they adhered with singular zeal to those sensible things which are abstracted from matter and are firm by their nature, having the most evident certainty—such as Geometrical things. Upon these, as if upon a <term>Lydian stone</term> <note>A touchstone used to test the purity of gold.</note>, they attempted to test the power of their contemplations. That the Egyptians were such people will be demonstrated more than sufficiently by the <term>hierogrammatisms</term> <note>Sacred symbolic writings or engravings.</note> composed of Geometrical figures which we shall cite throughout; for just as they were the first inventors of letters and Mathematics, so too, relying on that knowledge, they indicated the greatest mysteries and sacraments of the higher beings, as will be seen shortly.

# CHAPTER I.

### Concerning the Circle, or the Hieroglyphic Sphere, as it is the Image of God unfolding Himself from the Monad into the circumference of all things.

<margin>The wonders of the Circle according to Aristotle in his Mechanical Questions.</margin>
**A**RISTOTLE, when he was more deeply investigating the cause of the wonderful and prodigious effects which occur everywhere in mechanics regarding the lever and the scale—to the great admiration of all—found at last no other cause than that most astonishing of astonishing things: the circle. And not without merit: for it is most agreeable to reason that wonderful effects should proceed from a wonderful cause. <margin>Definition of the Circle.</margin> Now, a circle is a plane figure contained by a single line, which is called the circumference, to which all straight lines proceeding from one point, which they call the center, are equal. In this figure, therefore, there occurs a most wonderful existence of opposites. For every circle is made from that which moves and that which remains still: one foot of the compass standing fixed, while the other is driven around into a periphery. <margin>A wonderful property of the Circle.</margin> Furthermore, it is most marvelous that the line which embraces the orb of the circle, called <term>periphery</term> <note>original Greek: περιφέρειαν</note> by the Greeks, although it is entirely devoid of width, also admits a certain agreement of opposites, namely the concave and the convex <note>The text uses "curvum" (curved/convex) to contrast with "concavum" (hollow/concave)</note>; which are indeed contrary in the same way as the great and the small. For the medium of the latter is the "equal," but of the former it is the "straight." Indeed, everything that is great, in order to become small, or small to become great, must necessarily arrive at the "equal" before it reaches either extreme: so a curved line, before it becomes concave, must become as if straight; and a concave line, to pass over to the convex and circular, must similarly first be in some way straight.

---

# § I.

-> The Circle was held in great admiration and honor among the Egyptians. <-

**T**he Egyptians seem by no means to have been ignorant of these wonderful qualities and virtues of the circle. For when they beheld certain cyclic <term>ideas</term> <note>original Greek: ἰδέας; here referring to the Platonic archetypes or forms</note> shining forth, as it were, in the circumference of all things contained in this world; and when they contemplated with the highest admiration the spiral ideas of that supreme Architect, who affects something spherical both in Himself and in His works (which, according to the testimony of Plutarch, are made only according to the model of the circle); <margin>The ancients thought something divine was in the Circle.</margin> they judged that something divine was present in the circle. So much so, indeed, that whenever they wished to indicate something great, wonderful, or excellent, in which some traces of divinity appeared, they demonstrated it by applying a circle or a sphere. <margin>Trismegistus.</margin> Hence that Hermes, truly called <term>Trismegistus</term> <note>Thrice-Greatest; the legendary Hellenistic figure representing a syncretism of Hermes and Thoth</note>, when defining the divine nature, assumed the circle as his medium. For when asked what GOD was, he replied: <term>God is a circle, or an intelligible sphere, whose center is everywhere, and whose circumference is nowhere.</term> <note>This famous paradox is a cornerstone of Hermetic mysticism, suggesting God's omnipresence and infinity.</note> For since God...

# CHAPTER I

<margin>God is a circle, and how this is to be understood.</margin> Since God is not a body, nor can He even be one, for the reason that He is supremely simple—because everything most perfect must be most simple—He is devoid of all composition, because every composite thing is secondary to its components. Therefore, to distinguish Him from a physical sphere, He is said to be an **intelligible sphere** <note>original: "sphæra intelligibilis"; a sphere understood by the mind rather than the senses</note>. Hence, through the **center**, which is the smallest and simplest thing compared to the circumference, you should understand the **Divine Simplicity**; but through the **circumference**, which is the greatest, you should perceive the **Divine Immensity**. The meaning of the aforementioned description is therefore this: God is a circle, or a sphere—that is, lacking beginning and end, much more so than a material circle or sphere—so that His **eternity** may be noted. He is "intelligible" so that His **immateriality** may be noted; His center—that is, His indivisible essence—is everywhere in its entirety; but His circumference—that is, His immensity—is nowhere, because He cannot be contained by any place.

<margin>God is compared to the center of a circle.</margin> We also compare God to the center of a circle, around which all things exist, and from which the universe proceeds in a certain order into an Orb, until the complete totality of things is finished. For just as the center is neither a magnitude, nor a circle, nor an orb, but is the principle <note>the source or starting point</note> of all circles and orbs; by equal measure, God is none of those things which are in the World, nor is He the whole World, but He is nevertheless the principle of the whole World. Therefore, the summit of every creature terminates at this center, just as in a circle all portions are bounded from the circumference to the center in the form of a pyramid. And from this doctrine of **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom and magic</note>, our **Pythagoras** received that ceremony which he later handed down: namely, that God is to be worshiped by a circular motion of the body, or <greek>reverence for the Divine through turning</greek> <note>original: "θεοσέβειαν περιφερομένων"</note>.

<margin>The saying of Pythagoras, that God is to be worshiped by a circular motion of the body; how it is understood.</margin>
<margin>Pierius Valerianus.</margin>
<margin>Pliny.</margin> **Pierius Valerianus** (in Book 39) is the authority that this was also an institution of **Numa Pompilius** <note>The legendary second king of Rome</note>; for he instructed that before anyone worshiped God, he should turn himself in an Orb, and having made a circle, offer worship to God, because they venerated Him who was to be signified through the circle, the perfect figure. **Pliny**, cited in Pierius, says: *In adoring, we bring the right hand to the mouth, and we turn the whole body in a circle.*

<margin>The Circle held in honor among the Egyptians.</margin> But let us return to the point from which we digressed. The **Egyptians**, therefore, always held the circle in the greatest veneration among other geometric figures, both for the reasons mentioned and because they saw this mass of the Universe marked with a circular shape.

<margin>The spherical figure is suited to the Heaven.</margin> For it escapes no one that this figure, out of all others, is most suited to the heaven; because just as it ought to be the most capacious, simplest, and most perfect, so the most wise **Architect** chose the most capacious, simplest, and most perfect figure in its construction. For it is most perfect when it possesses all its own parts, nor can it happen that it suffers even the slightest loss.

<margin>The Platonists.</margin> It is most simple because, as the **Platonists** feel, there is nothing from which it may be made, or into which it may be resolved; otherwise, it would undergo generation and corruption. It is most capacious because it leaves nothing outside of itself, but embraces all things within.

<margin>The property of the Circle and the sphere.</margin> That the sphere is of this kind is indicated by the fact that it has the same relationship to other solids as the circle has to its own planes. First, indeed, the figure of the circle is the most capacious of all **isoperimeters** <note><term>Isoperimetra</term>: shapes having the same perimeter or boundary length</note>; furthermore, it is most perfect because it undergoes no increase or decrease; and it is most simple because it is contained by only one line. So also the sphere is a solid figure, [contained] by a single sur-

# CLASS VII. MATHEMATICAL HIEROGLYPHS. CHAPTER I.

...contained by a surface, to which all straight lines drawn from a single central point are equal. Therefore, the sphere is also the most capacious shape, because it has the circle as its limit; it is the most perfect, since, unlike an angular body, it neither increases nor decreases anywhere; indeed, it is the simplest, for it is enclosed by a single surface. To this cause is added another reason for such great veneration: that <margin>Another reason why the Circle was held in honor among the Egyptians.</margin> through the straight line and the circle, there was the first and simplest production and representation of things into the light—both of those not yet existing and those lying hidden in the coverings of nature. But a circle can be made neither correctly nor skillfully without a point; therefore, by the logic of the point and the <term>monad</term> <note>The "monad" refers to the number one or a single unit, representing the indivisible source of all things in Pythagorean and Neoplatonic philosophy.</note>, things both first began to exist and, having been shaped into a periphery, no matter how large they become, they can in no way lack the service of the central point.

These things having been demonstrated, it remains for us to say why the Egyptians placed the circle and the sphere upon the heads of their statues, as can be seen from many images on the <term>Obelisks</term> <note>Tall, four-sided stone pillars tapering to a pyramid top, covered in hieroglyphs.</note>. For one hardly encounters a hieroglyphic image where something spherical or circular does not occur; these, however, have different meanings according to the nature of the things added to them. A globe or circle placed upon the heads of images always figures something divine, eternal, and infinite; but placed separately, it indicates either God, or the World, or the Heavens, as has been shown at length in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* <note>A reference to Kircher's own earlier work on the Agonalis obelisk in Rome</note>, in the "Hierogrammaticism of the sphere or circle," and will be shown copiously in Volume III. But so that all these things may be made more clearly manifest, it seemed best to begin a little deeper, repeating some points from the *Pamphilian Obelisk*.

<margin>Why the Egyptians placed circular crowns or orbs on the heads of the Gods.</margin> Antiquity was accustomed to studiously venerate things considered religious and august in the opinion of men. Among these, the most noble is the circle or a certain orb sometimes circumscribed around the head, an index of veneration and of a Majesty that exceeds the human. This is noted everywhere as being placed around Emperors (whom the Ancients looked up to as raised above the height of mortality), the Provinces of the Roman World, primary Cities, and even the animals of the Gods. And as pertains to the Augusti, there exist bronze coins of Antoninus Pius and Constantius, <margin>Lorenzo Pignoria.</margin> which <term>Lorenzo Pignoria</term> <note>1571–1631, an Italian antiquarian and scholar</note>, a man most skilled in antiquity, mentions in his exposition of the *Isiac Table*. "This orb," he says, "the Egyptians located at the very top of the head of their images; which may be noted both here and elsewhere: one may suspect the Romans took it from them, and varied the habit for the sake of beauty, because a crown was fitted in that position to the head, in which they thought something divine resided; which ornament, however, in the moderation of subsequent Princes and by the silent consent of all, passed entirely to God and His Saints, as most things did, and retained the ancient name of 'diadem' to this day."

Thus far <term>Pignoria</term>, who is supported by those things which <term>Pierius</term> <note>Pierio Valeriano, author of the famous 16th-century work 'Hieroglyphica'</note> says on page 4, book 29. <margin>Pierius. What the Circle denotes among various nations.</margin> "A single circle, drawn either simply or around some other sign of a picture, signified to the Egyptians sometimes 'always,' sometimes 'perpetual and eternal,' and sometimes 'all things'—namely <term>The All</term> <note>original: "τὸ πᾶν" (to pan). A Greek philosophical term for the totality of the universe.</note>—precisely because in that figure one can find neither beginning nor end; which is the property of eternity." And a little later: "By reason of this principle and end nowhere appearing, the Egyptians understood God from the hieroglyphic of the circle." <margin>Porphyry.</margin> <term>Porphyry</term> <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 234–305 AD)</note> in <term>Eusebius</term>, chapter 3 *On the Preparation [for the Gospel]*: "The ball, and all round things, are attributed to the World, and especially to the Sun and Moon: altars and temples [are made] in the figure of a circle..."

Surrounding a head with a circular wrapping, and
<margin>A Diadem composed of arrows.</margin> fixing arrows into it in a ring, they turn the winged parts toward the head, but extend the points outward in the likeness of rays. By which they wished to indicate nothing else, according to the mind of the Egyptians, but the signs of a hidden divinity. Hence you will find scarcely any image of a man, bird, quadruped, or insect, or a composite of these, among the hieroglyphic inscriptions, to which this circle is not attached; a manifest sign of hidden divinity: and therefore a proper invention of the Egyptians, as will be said in the course of the Work. These things having now been set forth, let us look more closely at the secrets of the hieroglyphic circle.

<margin>
In what sense it is true that God is a Circle, square, triangle, point, and line.

It is asked, therefore, how God can be a circle, how a square, and a triangle, how a line and a point; and how things so disparate and contrary can be one in God, or fall within any comprehension of the human intellect regarding the simplicity of the divine nature? I respond that the Ancients learned all these things from the nature of the circle considered abstractly. For it must not be thought that they considered the circle under its physical properties, but according to a certain analogy of the Mathematical circle to that Circle whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere. For since all things affected by quantity in any way consist of boundaries, it is necessary that we conceive of them as finite. But if we wish to raise these things to the logic of an infinite essence, it is impossible for us to imagine them except insofar as they are affected by infinite logic and powers, as <term>Cusanus</term> <note>Nicholas of Cusa (1401–1464), a German philosopher and mathematician who used geometry to explain the relationship between the finite world and the infinite God</note> rightly teaches. However, so that this may become clear, I have decided to explain the following three propositions.

<margin>
The circle considered abstractly, and elevated to the logic of the infinite, is both a line, a triangle, a square, and a point.
</margin>

***If circles, ever larger and larger, each of which touches a straight line at the same point, are drawn into infinity; the greatest and ultimate of circles, than which none can be larger, will necessarily be infinite, and the same as an infinite straight line.***

# THE HIEROGLYPHIC SCHOOL OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>CHAPTER I.</margin>

Given a straight line $ST$, let circles $avo, bun, cum, dul, euk, fut, gu, \& bs$ be drawn from various centers to its midpoint $V$. It is certain that the smaller the angle the circles form with the line $ST$ at point $V$, the larger they will be; and the larger the angle, the smaller they will be, as is gathered from the demonstrations of Clavius <note>Christoph Clavius (1538–1612), a Jesuit mathematician and astronomer who commented on Euclid.</note> in the *Elements of Euclid*, Book 3, Proposition 16. Now, if a circle were described so large that it no longer formed an angle of contact, but coincided with the straight line $ST$ itself; I say that this circle would necessarily be infinite, and one than which no greater can be given. For since the centers of the said circles are more remote from point $V$ as the circles become more obtuse and closer to the straight line $ST$, the center must necessarily be infinitely remote from point $V$ at the moment the circle coincides with the straight line. Since an infinite radius necessarily implies an infinite circumference, it follows that a circle coinciding with the line $ST$ will necessarily be infinite; which was to be proved; even though human industry cannot reach this result by working for any amount of time.

---

->Corollary.<-

<margin>This explained method admits contradictions.</margin>

From this it is clear how not only the Ancients, but also modern theologians, following Saint Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian philosopher who used "negative theology" to describe God by what He is not.</note>, have seemed to posit contradictions in God, while they repeatedly called Him being and non-being, light and darkness, understanding and non-understanding, and so on. For a maximum circle, than which no greater can be given, considered in this way is both a circle and not a circle; it is equally a straight line and a curve; its circumference is simultaneously infinite and a straight infinite line. Therefore, it necessarily involves what appear to be contradictions; all of which belong to God alone. All these things will be declared more fully once we have first explained other matters pertaining to this.

## PROPOSITION II.

IF in a finite circle a line fixed at the center travels from any point on the circumference to the opposite point, the angle which the said line describes with the diameter at the center will increase continuously toward infinity; so that the angle of the diameter with which the moving line coincides is utterly infinite; but in an infinite circle, it is necessary that the quantity, the circumference, the radius, and the angle are all exactly the same.

...to become infinite. For since an infinite angle is that than which no greater can be given, and before a rotating line falls upon the diameter, ever greater and greater angles can be given unto infinity through continuous section; it follows that the diameter $ac$ <note>Referring to a line segment in a circle</note> obtains the power of a straight line of an infinite angle, since it enfolds all possible angles imaginable within a semicircle; which was the first point. Now let *a g c* be an infinite circle, than which no greater can be given; I say that the diameter, the circumference, and the angle coincide into one, and thus all are infinite. For although the diameter may be, in our way of conceiving (by which we are accustomed to conceiving only finite and bounded things), a straight line, and the circumference a curved line, and the angle the quantity of two lines inclining toward each other; nevertheless, it is necessary that these distinctions cease entirely in non-quantitative and infinite things. For since the circumference in infinite things is the highest rectitude <note>i.e., perfect straightness</note>; it necessarily follows that both the circumference and the diameter are exactly the same. Again, if *b* remains immobile and *a* is drawn around until it reaches the opposite place *c*, a semicircle will necessarily emerge; and if the diameter *a c* remains immobile and the semicircle is drawn around it, a sphere will be born. This sphere is the ultimate potential of the line, existing totally in act, since a sphere is not in potential toward any further figure. If, therefore, these figures are in the potential of a finite line, and an infinite line is all things in act to which a finite line is in potential, it follows that an infinite circle is a triangle, and a sphere, and a diameter, and an angle, and all things are likewise one; which was the second point. And just as all these things differ in quantities—inasmuch as they have no proportion to one another—so too the imagination, which does not transcend the genus of sensible things, is least able to conceive these matters; rather, this is the work of the abstracting intellect alone, as will be clear from what follows.

Moreover, let us show that this line is both a triangle and, at the same time, a circle. Let there be, therefore, a triangle $abc$ which is infinite by supposition; and let the line $ba$ run from point $b$ toward $c$ and back to point $b$; from this there will necessarily be produced an infinite "great circle," of which $bc$ is a portion. And since that portion is an arc of an infinite circle, it must necessarily be a straight line according to what was demonstrated before, as is $bc$. And since every part of an infinite circumference is infinite, that portion $bc$ will therefore be no smaller than the entire infinite circumference; and thus, that portion will be equal to the infinite circuit of that circumference. It also necessarily follows that the triangle $abc$ is a "great circle" or an infinite circle. And because its circumference (as was explained in the preceding sections) is a straight line, the arc or portion of the infinite circle $bc$ will also be a straight line; and the circumference will not be larger than the infinite line $bc$, since one infinite thing cannot be larger than another. Nor are they two separate lines, because it is impossible for there to be two infinites. Therefore, the infinite line, which is a triangle, is simultaneously a circle. And this is what Pherecides <note>An early Greek philosopher (c. 6th century BCE) often cited by Kircher as a source of ancient wisdom</note> said long ago: that God is a circle, and a line, and a triangle, and the "all of all things." Let us now see how this is to be applied to God.

### § III.

->How it can be gathered from what has been said that God is all things in all, and all things are in Him.<-

<margin>
The "Simply Maximum" is actually all things that exist in potential.
</margin>
From this fact—that an infinite line "enfolds" <term>complicat: a term from Nicholas of Cusa meaning to contain many things within a single unified source</term> all things in actuality which a finite line contains only in potential—we gather how the "Simply Maximum" <note>Kircher's term for God as the greatest possible reality</note> is actually all those things which exist in the potentiality of absolute simplicity. For whatever is possible, this very thing is the Maximum, absolutely and simply—not as it exists as a mere possibility, but as it exists in its highest state. Just as a triangle is drawn out from an infinite line, yet the infinite line is not a triangle in the way it is constructed from a finite line, but is actually an infinite triangle because it is identical with the line; for absolute potentiality in the Maximum is nothing other than the Maximum in actuality, just as an infinite line is actually a circle. But the matter stands differently in things that are not the Maximum; for there, potential is not the same as act, just as a finite line is not a triangle. Since, therefore, all things are "enfolded" in that Maximum in actuality, contradictions and oppositions necessarily result from this; such as that in God...

# CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER I.

### In God, the maximum and the minimum coincide.

For as that great <margin>Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-century Christian theologian and philosopher whose "Mystical Theology" heavily influenced medieval thought.</note></margin> Dionysius rightly asserts in his *Mystical Theology*: In God (who is this very "maximum" or greatest thing) it is not that one thing exists and another does not; nor is He in one place and not in another; for He is made into all things, yet is none of them. For He is the perfect and singular cause of all things, standing above every position, and His excellence is above the removal of all things, as He is simply absolute from all, and beyond all. Hence the theologians of the Hebrews, as was explained in the Cabala <note>The Jewish mystical tradition; the author frequently links Egyptian and Hebrew wisdom.</note>, call God "Being" and "Non-Being," agreeing with Dionysius. Hence the Egyptians defined God equally through light and through darkness or gloom.

<margin>God is all in all.</margin> Therefore, just as infinite curvature is infinite straightness; so the essence of God is simultaneously the circumference and the straight line, enclosed by no boundaries, for it is the simplest essence of all essences. And just as all the essences of things—which ever were, will be, or are—are always and from eternity actually in that very essence; so all essences are that essence itself: and as He is the essence of all, so is He the essence of any individual thing as much as of all things together. Parmenides undoubtedly alluded to this when he said, "anything is in anything"; although, lacking the light of faith, he could not extricate himself from such a deep mystery. Finally, just as <margin>The infinite line is the most adequate figure of all.</margin> the infinite line is the most adequate measure of all things; so the maximum essence of all essences is that in which the maximum and the minimum adequately coincide, so that it is neither larger than the minimum nor smaller than the maximum. For since one foot in an infinite line is not larger than two feet—indeed, any part of the infinite is infinite—it is necessary that one foot coincides with many. Furthermore, just as a finite line is divisible, so an infinite line is indivisible, since the infinite admits no parts into which it can be cut, nor does the maximum fall away from the minimum within it. But since a finite line is infinitely divisible, and no part can be assigned so small that a smaller cannot be given, it is impossible for it to be divided into a "non-line"; for this property falls only to the infinite line, which is why it is the "reason" <term>ratio: here meaning the underlying principle or mathematical proportion</term> of the finite line. In the same way, the maximum of all is the reason of all; and reason, according to <margin>Aristotle.</margin> Aristotle, is measure. Therefore, just as the infinite line is the perpetual and immutable reason of the finite line; so also the reason of all things, which is God the Blessed, is eternal, and subject to no change or instability.

And from this it is clear why the Ancients perceived an eternal reason in things; <margin>God in all and all in Him.</margin> for there is, according to Plato (as cited by Chalcidius in the *Phaedo*), one absolute exemplar and idea of things, which, diffused into a multitude, brings forth many exemplars. Since, therefore, the infinite line is the reason for all finite lines, it follows that it is in each one in such a way that it is in none, and every finite line is in it; not otherwise than God is in all things, and in nothing, yet all things are in Him.

In this way, you proceed to the remaining properties of the infinite line, which we do not call "one" in such a way that it is not equally "threefold." For we said above that the greatest line is a triangle; and because the line is most simple, that which is considered threefold within it will also be most simple: and since the whole triangle is a line, every angle in it will also be a line. Therefore, the infinite line is threefold. However, since it is impossible for there to be multiple infinites; this trinity, in the one—

For since every polygonal figure has the triangle as its simplest element, and this is thus the smallest of all polygons—than which no smaller can be given—and since the minimum coincides with the maximum, it follows that it relates to <margin>The maximum triangle, than which no greater can be given, enfolds all polygonal figures.</margin> the remaining figures just as unity relates to numbers; it happens that just as every number is resolved into unity, so are polygons into the triangle. Therefore the maximum triangle, with which the minimum coincides, encompasses all polygonal figures. A quadrangular <note>four-sided</note> figure is truly not the minimum, as is evident, but exceeds the triangular by one line: hence it implies a contradiction for there to be a "maximum quadrangle": for since it always exceeds triangular figures, no most-adequate figure of them can be conceived by any reason. Since, however, there cannot be several maximums or infinites, hence the single maximum itself is the simplest and most absolute measure of all quantities. # CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. 95 CHAPTER I.

...knowledge, object, and act, subsisting as a trinity; similarly visions, understandings, volitions, similarities, dissimilarities, beauties, proportions, correlations, natural appetites, and all other things whose unity of being consists in plurality; of which kind are the being and operation of nature consisting in the correlation of the agent and the patient.

->### § IV.<-

->*The circle demonstrates how all things are identified in God; and the sphere demonstrates His actual existence in all things.*<-

**S**ince it is established from what has been said that the triangle is the circle, and the trinity is unity, this unity will undoubtedly be infinite, just as the circle is infinite. Since, however, there cannot be multiple infinites, the unity in which the triangle and circle are identified will be more "one" than any unity comprehensible to any intellect in infinity. Its identity will be so great that it precedes even all relative oppositions; for there, "otherness" and "diversity" are not opposed to identity. Therefore, since it is an infinite unity, consequently all things that can in any way belong to it are the thing itself without diversity <margin>In infinite unity, all the attributes of God are not diverse.</margin> or alterity. Thus, His goodness is not one thing and His wisdom another; His mercy is not one thing and His justice another; but in this infinite unity they are altogether one and the same, since every diversity apprehended by us is identity in Him. So, in the unity of divine duration, past and future do not differ, and the future is not different from the present, but they are one duration and eternity, in which the beginning is the end, and the end is the beginning. All these things shine forth beautifully in that infinite circle; for since a circle of this kind is the greatest, its diameter will also be the greatest. And since there cannot be multiple "greatest" things, that circle will be "one" to the extent that its diameter is the circumference itself. Since, however, an infinite diameter has an infinite middle, and the middle is the center, it necessarily follows that the diameter, circumference, and center are the same. And this is that Hermetic Circle <margin>What the Hermetic Circle is like.</margin> <note>A reference to the famous Hermetic definition: "God is an infinite sphere whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere."</note> about which we have frequently discussed in this entire Work, whose center is everywhere, and whose circumference is nowhere. Therefore, the Greatest is most perfectly within every simple <margin>The Greatest is all things.</margin> and indivisible thing, because the center is infinite and everywhere; likewise it is outside all things and encompasses all things, because the circumference is infinite; equally it penetrates all things, because the diameter is infinite. It is the beginning of all things because it is the center; the end of all things because it is the circumference; the middle of all things because it is the diameter. It is, moreover, the efficient cause because it is the center; the formal cause because it is the diameter; the final cause because it is the circumference. Again, it gives being to all things because it is the center; it governs all things because it is the diameter; it preserves all things because it is the circumference. You see, therefore, how the Greatest is identical with nothing, nor diverse from anything; and how all things are in Him, from Him, and through Him, because He is the center, diameter, and circumference. It is also clear how all the attributes of God are identified in God in perfect unity: likewise how God is [the cause] of all...

->con-<- <note>Catchword for the next page, likely "continuing" or "concluding".</note>

</margin>

...is a folding together <note>original: "complicatio"; a term used by Nicholas of Cusa to describe how all things are "folded" within God's unity</note> of contradictions. Finally, it is gathered how all things—whether future or not future, whether possible or impossible—lie hidden in the abyss of divine providence. For what God knows, He does not know with a distinction of times; He does not know the future as future, nor the past as past,

<margin>
What Fate is, and of what kind it is.
</margin>

but as eternal; and He knows changeable things unchangeably. And this is that Fate which has tormented every single one of the Philosophers; for all things, when referred back to Providence itself, are said to possess necessity. This is rightly so, because all things in God *are* God, who is absolute necessity. For example: I am able to travel tomorrow, or not to travel; whichever I do, I shall not escape Providence, since Providence folds together those opposites. Thus, whatever I do, I shall have done according to

<margin>
In the "Maximum" simply, all things are one.
</margin>

the providence of God. Furthermore, just as in an infinite sphere (from what has been said previously) the center, the circumference, and the solid volume are one; so in the "Maximum" <note>The "Maximum" refers to the Infinite or God as the greatest possible reality</note> simply, all things are one. For He is the center or beginning, the middle, and the end of all things. And just as the sphere is the "act" <note>The realized state or perfection</note> of the triangle and the circle, so the Maximum is the act of all things. Therefore, every actual existence possesses from Him whatever actuality exists; and every existence exists in "act" only insofar as it is from that infinite Act. Hence, the Maximum is the "Form of forms" and the "Form of being," or the greatest actual entity. This did not escape Parmenides <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher</note>, who, defining God, said: *God is He for whom to be anything that is, is to be all that which is.* <note>original Latin: "Deum esse, cui esse quodlibet, quod est, esse omne id quod est."</note> Then, just as the greatest sphere is the perfection of all figures, so the Maximum is the most perfect of all most perfect things; in Him, curvature is straightness, composition is simplicity, diversity is identity, and "otherness" is unity. In Him, imperfection is infinite perfection, and possibility is infinite act—the single and simplest measure of all things existing in the Universe. (For in Him, the whole is not greater than the part, just as an infinite sphere is not greater than an infinite line). He is the most absolute reason, measure, and meter of all rotations, motions, and the entire Universe; whence, not without merit, God is defined by

<margin>
Trismegistus.
</margin>

Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the origin of Egyptian wisdom</note> as the "universality of things." And since He is the entity of the "being" of all things, and every motion is toward "being," it follows that the rest of motion is He Himself, who is the end of motion; therefore, all things tend from Him and toward Him. All these

<margin>

secrets of the divine essence the Egyptians aptly displayed through a winged globe teeming with a serpent, and a straight-lined scepter distinguished by three nodes, as can be seen in the Bembine Tablet <note>A famous bronze tablet of Egyptian style, likely Roman in origin, which Kircher used as a primary source for his decipherment</note>, and is evident here.

<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: An emblem featuring a central globe or sun-disk with wide-spread avian wings. A serpent is depicted either emerging from or coiled around the globe. Behind or through the globe passes a vertical scepter marked with three distinct, rounded joints or nodes.</note>

Through the globe, they signified the infinite, the eternal, and the immense; through the wings, the motion by which He penetrates all things; through the serpent, the life of all things; through the straight scepter, that all things in Him—the curved, the straight, the great, the small, etc.—are one; and through the three nodes, they hinted at unity, equality, and connection; likewise the beginning, middle, and end of all things.

<meta>This page begins Chapter II of Class VII (Mathematical Hieroglyphs) in Athanasius Kircher's Oedipus Aegyptiacus. # CHAPTER II.

### ->Concerning the Circle, the Decussis <note>The 'decussis' refers to the Roman numeral X or a cross-shaped intersection, often symbolizing the fourfold division of the world.</note>, and other angular figures; how the Egyptians employed them to indicate the secrets of the perceptible World.<-

---

**IN** the preceding sections, we considered the circle and the triangle as infinite things and as symbols of immense divinity; now let us contemplate these same things as finite, and let us indicate how they expressed the secrets of the perceptible World through them.

<margin>The analogy of the infinite ideal circle with the Mathematical circle.</margin> If anyone wishes to depict a circle, he first designates a center, then by the opening of a compass he establishes a line or radius, and finally from the straight line he describes a curved line, which is the circle. In the ideal circle, we find the same thing occurs. For that ineffable circle, which can be named by the names of all things, is constituted such that it contains a center, from which a line arises, and from both of these the circumference exists. But since a circle of this kind is infinite, it is necessary that the center, the line, and the circumference itself be equal, as we have said above. Since these things are infinite, and are nothing other than eternity and supreme equality, it is certain that the point cannot exist before the line, nor the line before the circumference; rather, from eternity, the center, line, and circumference existed together. Thus, the line, point, and circumference are the unfolding <note>original: "explicatio" — a key Neoplatonic term meaning the 'unfolding' or manifestation of a singular unity into complexity.</note> of the point and line. Furthermore, this point in eternity relates as a generator, or as one unfolding from its own enfolding <note>original: "complicante" — the opposite of unfolding; the state where all things are contained as one in God.</note> power a generated, consubstantial line; and the center with the line relates as that which from eternity unfolds the bond or circumference. Thus, the paternal principle in divine matters relates as the center, the line as the principle from a principle (which is called equality), and the circumference as the union or bond. 

But if you truly understand how a circle revolved upon an infinite straight line (which is eternity) does not touch it in a single point, you will grasp how in one "now" or instant of eternity, all revolutions of time—whether great or small—subsist; and how eternity is the very subsistence of time, and also the meter and measure of all duration. You will also see that it is false to claim the revolutions of the spheres have been from eternity, since infinity can by no means be compatible with a number of periodic revolutions. For if we could count ten past revolutions, or a hundred, or a thousand, or indeed all of them; and if someone were to say that not all are countable, but that infinite ones preceded, and then says one future revolution will follow next year, it necessarily follows that they are "infinite plus one"—and who does not see how absurd that is? 

Furthermore, the Creator seems to have made two things: namely, "nearly nothing" and the "point"; for between the point and nothing there is no middle ground. Indeed, the point is so nearly nothing that if you added more than a point to it, no more would result than if you joined nothing to nothing. Then He made "One," and joined the point with the One, so that it is "One Point"; and in this one point lies the enfolding <note>original: "complicatio"</note> of the entire Universe. The Universe, therefore, having been brought forth in this way, is conceived from that one point, just as from one point a single line might be drawn out, so that from it a triangle or a quadran-
<note>The text continues on the next page with the completion of the word "quadrangle" (tetragonus).</note>

He argues against the idea of an eternal universe, positing instead that the cosmos was "unfolded" by the Creator from a single mathematical point.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Chapter III of the Gymnasium Hieroglyphicum, focusing on the transition from the point to the circle and subsequently to angular figures like the cross (decussis) as symbols of divine creation and influence.</meta>

# CHAPTER III.

The final form, and indeed the most perfect, simplest, and most similar to the Creator, is the circle. In the triangle, which is made of three angles, the form, the unity of the triangle, and the trinity coincide; that is, the unity of essence and the trinity of angles. In the circle, however, unity and infinity coincide; namely, the unity of essence and the infinity of angles. For a circle is nothing other than a polygon consisting of infinite sides, the actualization of all possible angles formed from a line. It is clear, therefore, how God, the Creator of all things, produced the entire Universe from a single point which He created, specifically through the unfolding of that point into angles, and finally into a circumference.

-><-

Hence, when the Egyptians noted the circular property of all things in God as if in the Archetype <note>The original divine blueprint or pattern.</note>, they rightly chose that same circle as the symbol of the sensible World, so that it might perfectly correspond in every way to the Idea of its own Ideas. Indeed, beholding the traces of all things and their circular actions, they called the World and the things in the World "sensible circles," but the incorporeal Intelligences "invisible circles." Proclus explains this with his usual subtle wit: <margin>Proclus, Commentary on the 1st book of Euclid.</margin> *All mathematical things,* he says, *are first in the soul itself; and before numbers, there are numbers that move by themselves; and before apparent figures, there are Vital figures; and before those which harmonize above, there are harmonic ratios; and before the bodies that move in a circuit, invisible circles were produced.* For when they recognized that the stars, resting upon their rays and their poles, described circles in their rotation, they considered this the proper work of a divine faculty. When they wished to indicate either divinity, or the World, or the Heavens with a symbol, they expressed it with a circle, or a sphere, or some other symbol assumed from inferior things that was not dissimilar. From this, I believe, arose the practice that the basins, altars, and instruments with which they administered sacred rites were all fashioned with a circular apparatus; and likewise, the ceremonies, gestures, and movements were performed in a circle. Since we discuss these matters dispersedly throughout this entire Work and in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, we wished only to indicate them briefly here.

-><-

From the circle, therefore, let us proceed to the remaining angular figures. Since the Ancients—as we have also said previously regarding the entire *Pamphilian Obelisk*—imagined a line sent from the point of the center, of which one end remained unmoved while the other was led around to describe a line they called a circle; progressing a little deeper from this contemplation, they imagined something angular even in the center itself. For an angle is established therein as a symbol of pyramidal influence. Then, any other line cutting the diameter at the center constitutes a decussis <note>original: "decussim." An X-shape or cross-shaped intersection.</note> <note>Symbol: A circle containing a cross (decussis) similar to ⊕</note>. If this were done at right angles, it constituted a perfect cross <margin>What is a *chiasma*? And its figures here.</margin>, a symbol of influence into the four quarters of the World; if at acute angles, it properly performed the function of a <term>chiasma</term> <note>A Greek term for a cross-shaped mark or intersection, like the letter Chi (X).</note>. Hence the decussis is the symbol of the pyramidal influence of the Deities. Justin Martyr proves the former, saying that the World was founded by God, who *placed a cross-mark upon the universe.* <note>original: "ἐχίασεν ἐν τῷ παντὶ" (echiasen en tō panti)</note> He "decussated" it in its entirety, alluding to that pronouncement, just as he shows in his *Second Apology*, about three leaves before the end: <note>original Greek: "ὅτι δὲ καὶ ἐν τῷ παρὰ Πλάτωνι Τιμαίῳ φυσιολογούμενον περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ Θεοῦ, ὅτε λέγει, Ἐχίασεν αὐτὸν ἐν τῷ παντὶ, παρὰ Μωϋσέως λαβὼν εἶπεν."</note> *And as for what is discussed physiologically in Plato's Timaeus concerning the Son of God, when he says, "He placed Him like a cross in the universe," he said this having taken it from Moses.*

<summary>Kircher explains the transition from the divine unity of the point to the perfection of the circle and the symbolic "decussis" or cross. He links these geometric forms to Egyptian theology and Platonic philosophy, citing Justin Martyr's claim that Plato's concept of the cosmic cross was derived from Moses.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Class VII, Chapter II, focusing on the mathematical and geometric symbolism of the Egyptians. Kircher is connecting Platonic philosophy regarding the "X" shape of the world-soul with Egyptian hieroglyphic concepts of divine emanation and return.</meta>

->CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER II.<-

Thus Plato granted and acknowledged—not knowing with certainty that it was a type of the cross, but only recognizing the principle of the *decussis* <note>The Roman numeral X, or a cross-shape formed by two lines intersecting diagonally</note>—that the power from the first God was made in the form of a *decussis* throughout the Universe. He had explained the mystery of the bronze serpent concerning Christ, toward which he draws this Platonic idea. Sylburgius, in his notes on Justin, adds Plato’s own words: <note>original Greek: ταύτην τὴν οὖν σύστασιν πᾶσαν διπλῆν, κατὰ μῆκος σχίσας μέσην πρὸς μέσην, ἑκατέραν ἀλλήλαις, οἷον Χ προσβαλὼν κατέκαμψεν εἰς κύκλον.</note> "Dividing this entire double composition lengthwise, and joining the centers to one another, he crossed them like the letter X and bent them into a circle." <margin>Plato</margin> This mystery of the *chiasma* <note>A crossing or X-shape</note> or *decussis* he had undoubtedly drawn from the Egyptians, who also gladly adopted the *decussis* into their number of letters because of the extraordinary mysteries hidden beneath it, as we stated in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*. From this character, indeed, countless others found their origin, and among others the *crux ansata* <note>The Ankh, or "handled cross," a symbol of life</note> (the mysteries of which we declared in the same *Obelisk*) and various other species of the *decussis* emerged, which occur everywhere on the Obelisks and which we shall explain in their proper place.

For first, through the <note>Hieroglyphic/Geometric sign: Λ-shape</note>—found from the gait of the Ibis—they denoted the influx of the Divine Power into the lower material worlds; through the <note>Hieroglyphic/Geometric sign: V-shape</note>, the open beak of the Ibis, they denoted the return of the Divine Power from the lower to the higher regions. When these vertices were joined into one, the famous and mysterious *decussis* <note>Hieroglyphic/Geometric sign: X-shape</note> emerged, by which they aptly hinted at the process of the Spirit of the World "upward and downward" <note>original Greek: ἄνω κᾲ κάτω</note>. Regarding this, Horus <note>Horapollo, author of a treatise on hieroglyphs</note> most clearly teaches that the number ten is a symbol of the universality of things in these words: <note>original Greek: Γραμμὴ ὀρθὴ μιᾷ ἅμα γραμμῇ ἐπικεκαμμένῃ δίχα γραμμὰς ἑκατοντάδας σημαίνουσι.</note> "A straight line together with another bent above signifies ten flat lines." <margin>Horus book 2, chapter 30.</margin> See the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, page 386, where we also cited this passage from Horus.

---

Furthermore, the Egyptians expressed this *decussis*, or angular figure, under the figure of a double pyramid expressed in this manner: <note>Diagram of the letter 'N' formed by two triangles/pyramids meeting at a point, with vertices labeled b, d, a, and c</note>. By this sign they likewise marked that process of the Divine Power "upward and downward"; they also referred this to the number of letters, <margin>Mysteries under the letter N.</margin> as was shown on page 126 of the *Pamphilian Obelisk*. The first pyramid A-B-C denotes the gliding of the supreme Monad <note>The ultimate, indivisible divine unity</note> into the multitude; the other pyramid B-C-D denotes the return of that same Monad from the lower or material world into the world of light. Or, what is the same thing: they indicated the active influx of the Divine Power through the pyramid A-B-C (which arises from point B and is propagated into the multitude or width of A and C), and the passive influx (or the reception of the active influx in the lower realm) through the inverted pyramid B-C-D. See what we have discussed more extensively regarding these matters on page 175 of the *Pamphilian Obelisk*.

Since the genius of the Egyptians was such that they related the process of other sensible things appearing in generation and corruption according to a certain analogy fitting the archetype, they quite aptly displayed through this figure the progression of the "spermatic power" <note>The creative, formative force in nature</note> by which all things contained in the material worlds—and which are indicated by the fourfold, the sevenfold, and the *decussis* of the number ten—are exhibited. But I explain the mystery in a few words, using the example of vegetables. Since a tree proceeds from a seed, and from the tree a seed is made again, the latter is indeed later and the former earlier; the end does not coincide in number with the beginning, but the end of the outflow coincides with the beginning of the reflux; thus the sevenfold rightly arises, and from there...

He links these "hieroglyphic" mathematics to the writings of Plato and Horapollo to prove a universal ancient wisdom.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Egyptian symbolic philosophy, specifically focusing on the cyclical nature of life and death as represented by geometric and mythological allegories. It follows the previous page's introduction to the "trigramma" or triangular letter-symbol.</meta>

# CHAPTER II. 100 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>
The hieroglyphic of the generation and corruption of things.
</margin>

<note>
Hieroglyphic diagram (Trigramma): A complex geometric figure composed of two overlapping triangles and a central diamond shape, forming a multifaceted star or rhombus. 
- The top apex is labeled **K**. 
- A downward-pointing triangle has its apex at **A** (bottom) and its base labeled with **B** and **H**.
- An upward-pointing triangle has its apex at **D** (top) and its base labeled with **C** and **I**.
- Inside the central diamond, the point **F** is marked. Above it is the Greek word **ἄνω** <note>original: "ánō", meaning "up" or "above"</note> and below it is **κάτω** <note>original: "kátō", meaning "down" or "below"</note>.
- Labels: "**Inverted pyramid**" <note>original: "Pyramis invers."</note> is written near the top; "**Upright pyramid**" <note>original: "Pyramis recta."</note> is written near the bottom.
- The diagram is used to illustrate the <term>denarius</term> <note>The number ten, considered a symbol of perfection and completion in Pythagorean thought</note> progression of a seed into a tree.
</note>

**K** represents the <term>denarius</term>. For if **A** is like the seed, **D** like the tree, **G** like another seed, and **K** indeed like another tree; then **A** proceeds through **B** and **C** into **D**, while **D** proceeds into **G** through **E** and **F**, and the <term>septenarius</term> <note>The number seven, representing a complete cycle or week of creation</note> is closed; then **G** ascends into **K** through **H** and **I**, and thus the <term>denarius</term> is completed. Therefore, the individual contraction of the species (as the Schools <note>Refers to Scholastic philosophers of the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note> say) in the seed **A** is corruptible in itself, but in its species it is incorruptible. Striving to preserve itself by the power of the contracted species existing within it, and resolving itself into that species, it sheds the "individuation" of the seed so that it may draw out something like itself through the medium of the species. Thus, by a fourfold progression, it ascends into the tree; for without this medium, it cannot multiply itself in specific likeness. Therefore, **A** intends to produce **G**; and because it cannot accomplish this without ascending into **D**, it ascends into **D** to reach its goal. But **D**, being the tree, seeing that it cannot preserve itself except in a similar tree, intends **K**; yet it cannot reach **K** without **G**; therefore it descends into **G**, so that by its medium, it may reach **K**. Thus in **A** a double appetite is joined: the natural, which ends in **G**, and the accidental, which ends in **K**. In **D**, likewise, a double appetite is joined: the natural, which finds its end in **K**, and the accidental, which ends in **G**. Therefore, the <term>quaternarius</term> <note>The number four, representing the material world and the four elements</note> moves the appetite, with one appetite stimulating the other, so that there is a continuous succession of generation and corruption.

But this discourse, which we have proposed in the Scholastic manner, the Egyptians explain allegorically thus: **Osiris** is moisture, **Isis** is the earth with which Osiris is mixed, from which **Horus**—the spirit that nourishes and fertilizes all things—is born from the seed. Isis resuscitates Horus from the underworld when the seed committed to the earth bursts forth into a plant, tree, leaves, flowers, and fruits. But with the scorching power and dryness of **Typhon** <note>The Egyptian god Set, associated with storms, desert, and chaos</note> lying in wait for Horus, which happens in the Autumn season, Horus is slain by Typhon; that is, the falling fruit provides a new sowing, which, hidden in the earth, is once again restored by Isis through the industry of **Anubis**, that is, the <term>Mercurial</term> <note>Referring to the god Mercury/Hermes, symbolizing the cleverness and skill of the farmer</note> skill of the Husbandman. By this likeness, they reasoned symbolically not only about the change of generation and corruption of things exerting itself in the vegetable seed, but also in the sensible, and indeed in the rational and intellectual realms. For from the "seed of wonder," the "rational tree" arises, which bears fruits similar to wonder; for through the wonder drawn out, it raises a similar tree of reason. So from the seminal principle of demonstration, the "intellectual tree" proceeds, exerting seminal principles from itself, through which the intellectual tree rises again. From all these things—narrated perhaps more diffusely than was necessary—it is clear by how subtle a reasoning they indicated the change of generable things even under this most humble "trigramma" letter; and how that mundane spirit, lurking in the seeds of the things of the Universe, gradually ascends and descends, so that it may ascend again, instilling generative principles into each and every thing, so that the World may be preserved in its being; which without this alternation would not happen at all.

<margin>
What is the rational tree?
</margin>

# SECTION I.

->How the World is understood by the Egyptians to have flowed forth from the archetypal triangle.<-

**T**o understand this, it must be known that by this archetypal triangle, nothing else is understood than the triform, triune Deity, which the Egyptians express through three names: *Hemphta* (or Osiris), Isis (or *Phta*), and *Amun*. To these, the three <term>Middoth</term> <note>Hebrew: "measures" or "attributes"</note> in the Hebrew Tree of the <term>Sephiroth</term> <note>The ten emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite is revealed</note> perfectly correspond. Therefore, what the Hebrews call the Crown or <term>En Soph</term> <note>original: "אין סוף"; the Infinite or Boundless</note>, the Egyptians call *Hemphta* or *Emepht*: the first craftsman-intellect, whom they also prefigure in the second series of sensible causes as Osiris or the Sun. Again, just as the Hebrews speak of <term>Chokmah</term> <note>original: "חכמה"; Wisdom</note> as the creator of the World, so the Egyptians call the Wisdom of the first intellect *Phta*. By this name they call Mercury, the Counselor of Isis, and even Isis herself, who is the full image and pattern of Osiris, the first intellect. For this reason, Orpheus not inappropriately called her Pallas <note>Athena</note>, and for the stated cause the Ancients feigned her to have been born from the brain of Jove. <margin>Pallas born from the brain of Jove.</margin> *Amun*, however, responding to the <term>Binah</term> <note>original: "בינה"; Understanding</note> or Intelligence of the Hebrews, is the active power of both from without, by which the World—Horus—is produced. Hence arises that various equipment of hieroglyphic things with which the Priests everywhere expressed Horus: namely, the <term>Cynocephalus</term> staff <note>original: "κυνοκέφαλος"; literally "dog-headed," though Kircher here identifies it with the Hoopoe</note>, that is, marked with the head of a Hoopoe; also the <term>lituus</term> <note>a curved ritual wand</note> and the <term>gnomon</term> <note>an L-shaped tool for measuring angles or shadows</note>; and from the back, a triangle to which a circle is attached. These indicate nothing other <margin>Note that in this figure, a globe is attached to the triangle.</margin> than that the World, produced by God through His Wisdom, shines forth with an admirable variety of things (signified by the Hoopoe's head), with the highest harmony (indicated by the lituus), and finally with a fitting order (indicated by the gnomon). Thus Plato, a diligent disciple of the Egyptians, sufficiently demonstrates that this sensible World flowed forth from that archetypal triangle when he asserts it; which that triangle with the attached globe among the other symbols of Horus clearly indicates, and is expressed quite beautifully and elegantly in the following diagram.

And from these things it appears, and becomes manifest to all, that the Sacrosanct and thrice-blessed Triad—the greatest as well as the most sublime mystery of the Christian faith—was at all times shadowed forth even under the obscure fictions of fables.

### Concerning the Triangle, Square, and other angular figures exhibited hieroglyphically.

It must be known that the Egyptian Priests, as has been proven elsewhere, exhibited their secret mysteries not only under the ingenious architecture of sacred animals, but also under various Geometric figures. For they were, as the inventors of Geometry, more skilled in it than other mortals, and well aware of its secrets, whence they were called <term>Arpenedaptae</term> <note>original Greek: "αρπενεδαπται" - literally "rope-stretchers," referring to ancient Egyptian surveyors or geometers</note>; so much so, that this kind of science, which among other nations was held in the highest honor and price and fell to the lot of few skilled men, was in Egypt almost common, as <margin>Clement.</margin> Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria, a Christian theologian</note> suggests in the first book of the *Stromata*, which we cited in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* on page 422, which place you may consult.
