Indeed, searching more deeply into the reasons for secret things, when they discovered that God affects numbers, geometric figures (such as triangles, squares, and circles), and harmonic proportions in His operations, they judged that they could not show these same things in a better or more comprehensible way than through the said forms. Following them, Pythagoras <margin>Pythagoras. Plato.</margin> and Plato—the wise disciples of wise masters—expressed all the greatest mysteries under these same forms.

And so, just as the Egyptians cleverly indicated the genesis of things through lines, angles, and figures, they also noted the process of the World Spirit <note>original: "Spiritus Mundani"</note> according to the genesis of figures and bodies resulting from points, lines, and surfaces. This Spirit, having unfolded from the point or center of its unity into circles, first forms something angular in the lower world; returning from here, while it permeates all the bodies of the world, it describes innumerable rectilinear figures below, but above, according to the condition of the measures, it describes its own revolutions <note>original: "pericyclases," a Greek-derived term for circular orbits or cycles</note>. Horus <note>original: "Horus"; referring to Horapollo, the supposed author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs</note> does not differ here in his words: <note>original Greek: Ἐν' ᾧ δ' α'ν ε'νιαυτο'ν θἐλωσι γρα'φειν, Ἴβιν ζωγραφοῦσι</note> *When they wish to write a year, they paint an Ibis;* <gloss>Signifying the coming year, they write this part of the field as far as the eye can see;</gloss> (for among them, a "field" is a measure of land comprising one hundred cubits;) and this is because from one rising of Sothis <note>The star Sirius, whose rising marked the Egyptian New Year</note> to the next, a fourth part of a day is cast between. For since the solar year is completed in 365 days, the Egyptians, every fourth year, would calculate and intercalate an extra day, which they call <note>original Greek: ἐπαγόμενον</note> *epagomenon* <note>An "added" or "intercalary" day</note>, since four quarters of a day complete a full day. You see, therefore, how that supramundane, triform *Agathodæmon* <note>A "Good Spirit" or protective deity</note>—from that incorruptible, eternal triad of intellectual Worlds indicated by circles—is moved into the tetradic or fourfold triad of the three elementary Worlds. That is to say, it is carried from the simple and immutable into the angular, various face of material mixture, subject to corruption, which the quadrangular figure aptly represents. Let these matters be clarified a little more deeply.

It must be known that the Egyptians, to signify the powers of God, made great use of geometric figures (which Laërtius and Malchus <note>Porphyry</note> show in their *Lives* that Pythagoras and Plato followed them in doing). Among others, however, they especially observed the triangle, and within it, three conditions. For a triangle either consists of three equal sides, and is called **Isopleuron** <note>Equilateral</note>; or only two, and is called **Isosceles**; or three unequal sides, and is called **Scalenus**.

# CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS 105 CHAPTER II.

The **Scalene** triangle <note>A triangle with three unequal sides</note> is the element of the pyramid <note>the tetrahedron, representing Fire</note>, the Octahedron <note>representing Air</note>, and the Icosahedron <note>representing Water</note>. This is because the pyramid is composed of four triangles, all having equal sides, each of which may be distributed into six scalene triangles of the kind just mentioned. The Octahedron is composed of eight, which are similarly divided into six scalenes each; as is the Icosahedron from twenty. The other triangle (I mean the **Isosceles**) is suited for constructing the cube <note>representing Earth</note>, since four triangles of this species joined together complete a square; just as six squares complete a cube.

However, God used the **Dodecahedron** <note>the 12-sided solid representing the Aether or the Universe</note> for the Universe; because the twelve signs are seen in the heavens in the Zodiac, each of which is cut into thirty parts. In the same way, in the Dodecahedron composed of twelve pentagons, with each of these divided into five triangles, there are six triangles <note>Kircher is likely referring to the further subdivision of the pentagonal faces into 30-60-90 triangles to match the 360 degrees of the circle</note>; and thus in the whole Dodecahedron, three hundred and sixty triangles are found, as many as there are sections of the Zodiac itself. By these figures, therefore, matter expressed by God was moved: at first indeed in rough traces without order, then brought into order by Him, according to the proportion which all things obtain among themselves in that "coagulation" <note>The process of forming solid matter from chaos</note>. Yet these do not remain discrete in one place, but are in perpetual agitation, and bring the same to matter; since they are driven, constricted by the circuit of the World, and are carried by alternating pulses; those which are of thinner parts into the region of the thicker. Wherefore nothing at all is left empty or void of body: and in them, a permanent inequality brings about a shaking, since matter is agitated by them, and they by it.

How Plato, following the mind of the Egyptians, composed the four regular figures from Scalenes—of which one angle is a right angle, the second is two-thirds of a right angle, and the remaining is a third part of the same (that is, one angle of 90, another of 60, and a third of 30 degrees)—is something we have judged to be our duty to demonstrate in this place by geometric reasoning, since it has remained hidden from his commentators until now. First, therefore, they described an equilateral triangle **A B C**, from whose angles **A B C** they drew as many perpendiculars **A D**, **C F**, and **B E**. The equilateral triangle was thus divided into six scalene triangles, all equal and similar, as the numbers show. Each of these constitutes one right angle, and the remaining two are partly 60 and partly 30 degrees: those which stand at the center point **S** are 60; those which terminate at the points **A B C** of the triangle are 30; and finally, those which stand at the midpoints of the sides at points **F D E** are 90 degrees.

<note>Hieroglyphic/Geometric Diagram: An equilateral triangle ABC with internal altitudes AD, BE, CF intersecting at center point S. This subdivision creates 6 numbered scalene triangles (1-6) demonstrating how regular shapes are composed of basic geometric units.</note>

And the sides are allotted according to that proportion which the numbers 3, 4, and 5 have, the mystery of which will be explained hereafter. This kind of triangle they called sometimes "genetic" <note>generating</note>, and sometimes <term>γαμήλιον</term> <note>original: "gamēlion", meaning "nuptial" or "pertaining to marriage"</note>, <margin>The genetic triangle which [is] from...</margin> or the "nuptial figure," because it was the principle of the generation of all sublunary things, in this manner:

<note>Geometric Diagram: A right-angled scalene triangle with vertices A, B, C and the letter P in the center. The sides are labeled with numbers 3, 4, and 5, representing the Pythagorean triple.</note>

# CHAPTER II. 106 OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS: HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

From the Scalene triangle, as if from first principles, the four regular figures—and consequently the four Elements of which they are symbols—are produced. They constructed the symbol of Earth, the **cube**, in this manner: they quadrupled the Isosceles triangle <note>original: "Isoscelem"; in diagram: a b c</note> and a square resulted <note>in diagram: a b e d</note>; this, multiplied by 6, constituted the cube <note>in diagram: a b e d i f g</note>. Thus, according to the testimony of Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on Euclid's geometry</note>, the Isosceles triangle was the first principle of earth, while the square was the proximate principle.

Furthermore, they constructed the symbol of fire, the pyramid or **Tetrahedron**, in this way. Since the Tetrahedron consists of four equilateral triangles, each of which (as was shown a little earlier) is again composed of six Scalenes, 4 multiplied by 6 produced 24 "genetic Scalenes" <note>Kircher uses the term "genetic" to mean "generative" or "form-giving"</note>; (for so we shall hereafter call a triangle of this kind). Thus, the four-sided pyramid denoted in this way not only fire, but also the entire Universe, into which the fiery force secretly diffused itself; and in this manner they derived it into that body. Subdividing the Equilateral triangle <note>original: "Isopleurum"; in diagram: A C D</note> into two parts, they created two Scalenes <note>in diagram: B A C, B A D</note>; by which they indeed noted the procession of the Divinity from the archetypal World into the World exposed to alterations and changes. Cutting these Scalenes in half again, they produced Isosceles triangles <note>in diagram: B F A, B E A</note>, which are indicators of the procession of the Divinity through the influence of the stars. They cut these Isosceles triangles in half again through the line $F E$, and produced four Equilateral triangles $A F E, F E B, E B D, F C B$; by folding these, they formed the first of all solid bodies, the Tetrahedron. Here the triad passes into the tetrad—that is, from the figure of the triangle there arose a figure of four planes, or a three-sided pyramid—and from three angles were born twelve angles, so that in this single figure they held the entire series of the whole World, both the starry and the elementary.

<margin>
How the Tetrahedron, the symbol of fire, is composed of triangles.
</margin>

Mystical philosophy in the Tetrahedron.

For the triangle, by its triad, expressed the generation of things, as will be shown later; the four-fold nature of the sides expressed the Elements; three and four joined together gave the seven-fold nature of the starry World, visible in the circles of the seven planets; the twelve angles denoted the <term>Aplanes</term> <note>The sphere of the fixed stars, which does not "wander" like the planets</note>, or the twelve dimensions of the Zodiac. The figure was sharp and pyramidal, by which they hinted at fire or heat—the active principle of the generation of things—which permeates the elements, the planets, the Fixed Stars, and in a word, everything. Again, since the **Octahedron** is composed of eight Equilaterals or triangles of equal sides, each of which is again made of six genetic Scalenes, 8 multiplied by 6 gave 48 Scalenes, by which the Octahedron, the symbol of air, is constituted. Finally, since the **Icosahedron** consists of 20 equilateral triangles, and each of them of six Scalenes, these multiplied by 20 will give 120 Scalenes, from which, as if from principles, the Icosahedron is constituted, and therefore it was adopted as the symbol of water.

# CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER IX.

[Iso]sceles <note>original: "Isoscelem"</note>; he concluded that all these things could by no means be dissolved into one another or exchanged—I mean the Earth with the remaining three—but that the three, namely Air, Water, and Fire, because of a genetic principle common to each, are in fact dissolved and exchanged into one another. He also indicated that the proportion existing in the numbers of triangles (from which, as if from first principles, the three elements consist) between 24, 48, and 120, is the same proportion in the density and rarity of substance between Fire, Air, and Water. Specifically, Fire is twice as rare as Air, and four times as rare as Water; and they relate to each other just as the 24 scalene triangles of the Tetrahedron <note>A four-sided solid representing fire.</note> relate to the 48 scalenes of the Octahedron <note>An eight-sided solid representing air.</note> and the 120 scalenes of the Icosahedron <note>A twenty-sided solid representing water.</note>. The Cube, however, is the symbol of Earth; just as it is composed of a heterogeneous part, namely the isosceles triangle, so too he judged it could not be exchanged with the other three elements from this same source. Nevertheless, he recognized from its parts that there lies beneath the Cube (the symbol of Earth) a certain harmony that moderates the entire harmony of the World—namely from its six planes, twelve lines, eight solid angles, and twenty-four planes <note>Likely referring to the 24 right triangles that can compose the surface of a cube.</note> from which the cube consists. That is, it contains the harmonic proportions <margin>The Cube contains the harmony of the entire Universe.</margin> of 6 to 12 (the double, or octave <note>original: "diapason"</note>); 6 to 9 (the sesquialter, or fifth <note>original: "diapente"</note>); 12 to 8 (the sesquitertial, or fourth <note>original: "diatessaron"</note>); 8 to 24 (the triple, or octave-plus-fifth <note>original: "diapason diapente"</note>); and finally 6 to 24 (the quadruple, or double octave <note>original: "disdiapason"</note>).

But besides these four regular solid figures, they saw that a fifth could also be established from pentagons, three of which, joined into one, <margin>How the Dodecahedron is made</margin> would form a solid angle, and thus complete a figure of twelve bases, or a Dodecahedron. In this way, the bodies that exist in nature would correspond entirely to the Mathematical ones, which the Pythagoreans, following the Egyptians, therefore called the first principles of natural things. And they ascribed this Dodecahedron to the Universe—not, as some think, to a superlunary "fifth essence" <note>The "ether" or quintessence believed to make up the heavens.</note>, but to the fifth great body of the Universe, composed of the four primary simple bodies. In this manner, therefore, since they saw that twelve equilateral pentagons <margin>The Dodecahedron denotes the Universe.</margin> (each of which was divided into five isosceles triangles) could be fitted together into one so that no vacuum remained between the joints of the sides, and moreover, that these joined at the center of a circle constitute twelve pentagonal pyramids; sensing the mystery of the Universe, they first related the twelve sides of the dodecahedron to the twelve seats of the Zodiac, which they called the boundary of the entire Universe. For these seats, joined as if by the radiant influence of the stars in the center of the earth, constituted as many five-sided pyramids—a symbol of the twelve inner shrines through which the Divinities might flow into the lower World. Regarding the mystical reasoning of these, since I have already dealt with them in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, the reader may consult that work. Therefore, just as these twelve pentagonal pyramids are connected by their vertices at the center of the earth and are so aptly joined that they leave no intervening vacuum; so the life of the World is diffused through all things by the Divinities who preside over the dodecahedrons of the Zodiac, so that there is nothing that does not participate in it. # CHAPTER II. THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

...from which all things were said to be born. For just as from the bisection of the Isosceles <note>A triangle with two equal sides.</note> and the pentagons in the dodecahedron <note>A twelve-sided solid; Kircher associates this with the structure of the universe.</note> the Scalenes are born, so from the earth as a passive principle, and from the motion of the planets under the 12 signs of the Firmament (which are like a certain active principle) and the influence made upon the earth, the genetic Scalenes are born—that is, all the diverse kinds of beings in the sensible World.

You see, therefore, how they proceeded from the first and simplest lines and figures to the generation of bodies and the secret of all corporeal nature. Moreover, just as they noted the triune divinity through the circle—triple in its center, radius, and circumference— <margin>The equilateral triangle denotes God as Creator.</margin> so they noted the triune divinity manifesting itself in the works of creation through the equilateral triangle, as was said above. And indeed, the circle begets nothing from itself, being the fulfillment and the greatest of all polygons consisting of infinite sides; it further signifies the solitary threefold unity. But the triangle is the principle of all generation, the father of all remaining things, whether polygonal figures or bodies, as was <margin>What the Scalene triangle denotes.</margin> shown a little earlier. This is followed closely by the Isosceles, the symbol of the earth and the firmament; what follows is the right-angled Scalene <note>A triangle where all three sides are of different lengths.</note>, to indicate the highest mysteries of genetic nature.

The right-angled Scalene consists, as said above, of three unequal sides and as many angles: one right angle and two acute. Through the right angle, they indicated the constant and immutable law of nature in its operation; through the remaining two—one larger (sub-double), the motion of increase; through the third (sub-sesquialter), the ratio of decrease and division. Furthermore, through the lower line which constitutes the base of the triangle, they signified (according to the testimony of Plutarch <note>A Greek philosopher whose work 'On Isis and Osiris' is Kircher's primary source here.</note>) the passive principle of things, especially the Earth or Isis; through the perpendicular line standing straight upon it, the active principle of things, the Form, Osiris, or the Sun; finally, through the hypotenuse or the line stretching under and joining both lines, they acutely indicated the "Composite," Horus, the son born from both, as we also said a little before.

# CHAPTER III.
## On the hieroglyphic mysteries of the pyramid.

**A** pyramid is a solid figure whose sides, drawn from one of the planes, converge at a single summit vertex. It is to solids what the triangle is to planes; both are the primary figures of planes and solids respectively, so that just as all conceivable plane figures may be reduced to a single triangle, so may solids be reduced to a single pyramid and resolved into it. And although there can be many species of pyramids, such as triangular, quadrangular, pentagonal, etc., the Egyptians seem to have primarily adopted the four-sided pyramid to indicate their mysteries. They established this as twofold: the complete and the truncated. Just as they applied the former to souls bound to bodies, they applied the latter to the whole Universe, calling it an Obelisk or the "finger of the Sun." It did not end in a point by the straight path of its sides, but terminated in a small pyramid just before the apex. What they intended by this mystical construction, I have decided to indicate formally in this place; and first we shall treat the pyramid properly so called, then the mysteries of the Obelisk, tasting some portions from the Pamphylian Obelisk.

<margin>Among the Egyptians, all things are full of mysteries.</margin> Since, as Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria, a 2nd-century Christian theologian</note> testifies in Book 6 of the *Stromata* <note>original: "Stromat." - Clement's work 'Miscellanies'</note>, nothing was done among the Egyptians that was not filled with mystery—so much so, indeed, that even the houses themselves, the temples, instruments, clothing which they wore in solemn pomp either in the worship of the Gods or in performing sacrifices, and even the very nods and gestures they made, were a certain mystical representation of the highest things signified through such means <note>original: "τὰ αὐτῶν" - their things/their ways</note>. Certainly, we shall by no means think that they used Obelisks to represent their hieroglyphic wisdom to posterity rashly, or without reason, or only for the sake of ornament (as many wrongly feel). Rather, with the greatest zeal and a certain remarkable investigation of the mind, they wished to acquire for themselves that figure <margin>The mysterious figure of the Obelisk.</margin> which, being itself filled with mysteries, would correspond in every way to the mystical context of the symbols. That the four-sided pyramid is such a figure will be copiously demonstrated in what follows; for whatever the Hierophants <note>term: Hierophant - a priest who interprets sacred mysteries or ceremonies</note> connoted in the description of particular things expressed under symbols, they represented all of this <unclear>universally</unclear> on the exterior face of the Obelisk or pyramid, as if in a certain synopsis or in the outline of a certain stone inscription; so much so, that nothing in the inner recesses of nature is so hidden that it does not seem prefigured here. ...in which Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on Egyptian mysteries.</note> says that, as if hidden under a certain Silenus-figure <note>A reference to Alcibiades' speech in Plato's *Symposium*, where ugly statues of Silenus contained beautiful images of gods inside; here meaning "outwardly simple but inwardly profound."</note> of Astrology, Geometry, Music, Arithmetic, Theology, and the more recondite Philosophy, the greatest mysteries of every kind lie hidden. <margin>Primordial matter indicated by the figure of the Obelisk.</margin>
We say first, that through the pyramid or Obelisk, the Egyptians wished to represent the nature of things and that formless matter which has a certain innate appetite for receiving forms. For this is what Abenephius <note>Ibn Wahshiyya, an Arabic author whom Kircher believed had decoded hieroglyphs.</note> thinks; his words are:

<margin>Abenephius.</margin>

*That is: By the very figure of the pyramids they used to signify primordial matter.*

<margin>Artephius.</margin>
With whom the Arab Artephius <note>An Alchemical author, often identified with Al-Tughrai or a legendary figure.</note> agrees in the chapter where he proves: *From a point, all things*; and after him, a certain anonymous author cited in Pierio <note>Pierio Valeriano, author of a famous Renaissance book on hieroglyphs.</note> beautifully deduces the same. For just as a pyramid, beginning from its highest peak as if from a point, proceeding through lines into surfaces and a body, gradually dilates in all directions; so the nature of all things, proceeding from a single principle and source which cannot be divided—namely, from God the Supreme Architect—subsequently takes on various forms, and is spread out into various genera and species, and joins all things to that apex and point from which all things flow and emanate. By this, indeed, that primordial origin of the World seems best represented, by which all parts of the World were shaped and produced that appearance which we now see. 

<margin>The World as a rough, undigested mass.</margin>
For formerly the World was formless and muddy, not yet having attained the integrity of its form through the distinct marks of things; for neither had the earth established its center as the foundation of all things, nor was the perpetual motion of the heavens rolled in a fixed seat, but all things lay stagnant, motionless without the use of the Sun, and weighed down by a gloomy silence. Nothing else existed but the sluggishness of formless, diffused matter, before that principle from which all things were produced and constituted, drawing forth the health-giving motion of life, gave the World back to the World, and distinguished the heaven from the earth, and the sea from the Continent. At which time the four first Elements of things—from which, as if from a root and principle of birth, everything is begotten—represented by the square base of the pyramid, received their order and proper form.

# CLASS VII. MATHEMATICAL HIEROGLYPHS. CHAPTER III.

...or that the cause of growth is the approach and retreat of the Sun in that oblique circle, which, because the life of living creatures depends upon it, Astronomers have called the Zodiac. Therefore, this circle—to which alone among the celestial circles latitude is attributed—is divided by the Egyptians into twelve parts, or <gloss>twelve divisions <note>original: δώδεκα μόρια (dodekamoria)</note></gloss>, which they call mansions. Over each of these they place individual Angels or Spirits, whom they call lesser Gods, and they say that with them <margin>The distribution of the Zodiac and the Gods presiding over its individual parts.</margin> all lower things are also divided, so much so that whatever is contained under one of them, down to the very center of the earth, is said to be subject to that twelfth-part and to its presiding Angel. This sign or twelfth-part they intended to be like a certain pyramid, whose base is in the Zodiac and whose apex is in the center of the earth. Concerning these things, Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on Egyptian mysteries.</note> writes thus in his book *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians*: <margin>Iamblichus.</margin> *Dividing, he says, the heaven into two parts, or four, or twelve, or thirty-six, or doubles of these, or in whatever other way; they also place over these divisions rulers, either fewer or more. Again, they place one Leader over them, and thus this Egyptian treatise on principles is like a pyramid, which, proceeding from the base—that is, from the multitude—into one, descends from the one into the multitude. It is clearly governed by the One; by God, a nature undefined on all sides is imperiously encompassed under a certain defined limit, especially by the unity which is the sublime cause of all things. Indeed, God produced matter through materiality—namely, derived from essentiality—which the Creator, assuming Unity, made into simple and impassive spheres; but he finally received matter itself for the purpose of fashioning generable and corruptible bodies.*

Since, therefore, all things occur within these pyramids of the Zodiac, and the approach of the Sun causes the birth of things, while its retreat from them causes their destruction; they certainly represented the nature of all things through the pyramid in a way that was not at all incongruous. Indeed, Mercury <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the god Thoth.</note> is the authority in Chapter 8 *To Aesculapius*—which begins thus: <note>original Greek: Καὶ τὸ δαιμόνων χορόν (And the choir of demons)</note> and so forth—that they placed twelve Horoscopes and Decan-Rulers <note>term: Vsiarchos/Ousiarchs; spiritual entities or "essence-rulers" in Hermetic cosmology.</note> over each of these twelve pyramids of the twelfth-parts. <margin>Trismegistus.</margin> This means: *Around it are many companies of Spirits, to be gathered in various forces; and these familiars, existing not far from the immortals, having been allotted this region, act as Overseers of human affairs. They proceed to execute what is commanded by the Gods, presiding over whirlwinds, storms, flashes of fire, and earthquakes; moreover, they avenge impiety with the fury of wars.* And a little later: *The Sun is the preserver and nourisher of every kind.* and the rest that follows, by which words he suggests nothing other than the diversity of effects produced from the mixture of different stars existing in different twelfth-parts.

And these are those twelve Horoscopic Gods, over whom he says <term>Pantamorphus <note>Literally "the All-Formed" or "Multiform One," a symbolic name for the universal creative force or the Sun.</note></term> presides with seven Rulers of Essence, about whom Trismegistus says much in the cited chapter. <margin>The 12 signs of the Zodiac with their Gods. Who is Pantamorphus?</margin> These are indeed nothing other than the twelve signs of the Zodiac, which they called the twelve lesser Gods; and the seven planets, which they called the Rulers of Essence or the greater Gods and Spirits. Whence Artephius <note>An Alchemical author, often identified with various historical figures, here cited for his Arabic wisdom.</note> in the place cited above <margin>Artephius.</margin> speaks thus:

*And there was in Heliopolis <note>The "City of the Sun" in ancient Egypt.</note> the Temple of the Sun, and in it were twelve columns representing the twelve signs of the Zodiac and the mysteries of the elements.* <note>Arabic text: Describes the twelve columns in the Temple of the Sun at Heliopolis representing the signs of the Zodiac and the mysteries of the elements.</note>

*There was, moreover, in Heliopolis a Temple of the Sun, and in it twelve columns, signifying <margin>12 Obelisks at Heliopolis.</margin> the twelve signs of the Zodiac, and the secrets of the Elements: that is, the twelve Horoscopes.*

immersed in bodily pleasures and filthy delights, they called heavy, sluggish, and dark; but that soul which followed the guidance of right reason and raised itself to the contemplation of incorruptible and heavenly things, they called lucid, celestial, and Angelic. By these numbers, he certainly signifies nothing other than that expansion of lines which, drawn from a point to the base, create an angle; and through the intervals, the surfaces themselves which are enclosed by the lines. # EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

### CHAPTER III.

...marked with the character of divinity, is diffused through the four sides of the fourfold World, a protection distributed into the twelve strongholds of the World. This is aptly denoted by each of the three numbers of the 4 triangular surfaces; for 3 multiplied by 4 makes 12. Again, just as 3 joined to 4 constitutes 7, so they indicate the Sacrament of the entire natural perfection of the Procreative World. Furthermore, the four triangular sides joined to the four quadrangular sides <note>Referring to the base and faces of a pyramid or the sections of an obelisk</note> constitute 8, a most fitting symbol of the influence of the Angelic nature upon the corporeal World. If the base of the pyramid is added to these, they then beautifully indicated the mystical <term>ennead</term> <note>The number nine</note>, a symbol of the Angelic and corporeal World; which the 9 solid angles, considered in any Obelisk, also noted. Finally, if the apex of the pyramid were added to these, 10 were then constituted, by which they hinted at the completion of all nature and of the three Worlds: the Archetypal, the Angelic, and the corporeal World. This number was implicitly contained in that <term>tetractys</term> <note>original: "tetractys"; the Pythagorean "four-foldness" where 1+2+3+4=10</note> or quaternary number; for if you join 1, 2, 3, 4 placed in order to one another, that mystical <term>decad</term> <note>The number ten</note> will come forth, or the <term>tetractys</term>, celebrated with such silence by the Pythagoreans and enveloped in such great mysteries. They beautifully indicated these through two groups of five, in the first of which they aptly suggested the influx of the divine nature into the Angelic World, and in the other the womb of creatures or the corporeal World—noted by the quadrangular base with a continuous diminishing of the sides upward toward the center. Moreover, if you join the formal unity <margin>The formal Unity of God indicated by the apex.</margin> latent in the womb of divinity (indicated by the apex) to any order of things, you will always constitute 10: the completion of all things, the type and exemplar of divine perfection.

...type and exemplar of perfection. For if you join the tripartite triad of the Angelic World to 1 and 9, you will constitute 10, a number exhausting all things, a type of divinity embracing all. If you join 8 to 2, in which the doubled unity resides, you will have the influx of the Angelic through the formal unity into the lower World—namely, into the sensible World, aptly suggested by the cubic number 8. If again you add 3 (that is, that Triad which is the exemplar of all perfection) to 7 (the symbol of worldly perfection), you will again have 10. If you add the quaternary, or that <term>tetractys</term> so greatly celebrated by Pythagoras, to 6 (the "senary" number, a symbol of worldly operations), 10 will once more result. Finally, if you double 5—that is, join two groups of five together—the same number ten will emanate. You see, therefore, how the orders of the worldly constitutions joined to one another always produce 10; that is, the formal unity implied in each Class, joined to the remaining numbers that are symbols of creatures, always constitutes 10: a fitting hieroglyphic of the entire Universe with its Author. Furthermore, 1 joined to 2 gives the triad again; this joined to the triad generates the tetrad; and this again joined to the tetrad, the pentad; and thus each...

And from here, there is a return again through nature to the presiding authority of nature, namely that Monad <note>The ultimate unit or "The One"</note> which is the very apex of the mundane pyramid. Similarly, the ascent to the peripheries of the vastest heavens through the intermediate spaces of the World from the center of the Universe is not absurdly indicated by a radiant or inverted pyramidal letter <note>Inverted Lambda or V-shape symbol</note>. What else does this signify but that magical chain of love connecting the higher things to the lower, fixed in the reciprocal harmony of individual parts? 

<margin>What Love properly is according to Dionysius.</margin> Whence the greatest philosopher, the Areopagite <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist</note>, defines love not poorly as being a *Circle perpetually revolved from good to good*. For as it begins from God and entices, it offers the reason of perfect beauty; but as it passes into the World, it is chiefly called love; and finally pleasure, insofar as it returns to the Author, converting the beautiful image back to the beautiful exemplar by a beautiful revolution. In this circuit, penetrating through all things, it causes the same things to be rolled continually upward with itself and downward; not otherwise than a simple ray of the Sun, uniform in itself, creates light in the heaven, splendor in the ether, illumination in the elements, and bright color in mixed bodies. It is clear, therefore, that the amatory order is the cause of conversion in all things toward divine beauty and the primary form; 

<margin>The amatory order is the cause of things.</margin> and (to use the words of Proclus <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher</note>) it leads all following things back to that beauty, joining them to it, confirming those joined, and presently filling the following things from there, distributing the gifts of divine light gushing forth from that source through the universe. This was indeed nothing else to the Egyptians than the <term>Anima Mundi</term> <note>World Soul</note>, or the <term>Triform Deity</term>, the cause and origin of all things in the World. They expressed this most aptly in the Hieroglyphic Schema placed below, of a winged globe surrounded by serpents leaping out from both sides, a figure placed above the mundane System. And the globe indeed designates nothing other than first the Archetypal World, and then the Universe, as has been proven in the preceding pages.

# CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER IV.

# THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

### CHAPTER IV.

...the point or apex is the first progression in God through the triple World, distributed in a threefold manner; the end, however, is in matter itself. Finally, there is a certain infinity around the summit, an infinity of pure power around matter, and an infinite power of connection through all the intermediate levels of nature.

<margin>The force of Love in the Universe.</margin>
Now let us return to Love, the primary effect of which is the Universe. For Love, <margin>Dionysius the Areopagite</margin> according to the testimony of Dionysius <note>original: "Dionys. Areop." refers to the 5th-century Christian theologian and philosopher</note>, did not permit the King of all things to remain without offspring. This same zeal for propagation flowed down from the first Author into all His images. For through this Love, the Intelligences <note>Celestial beings or angels</note> move the heavens and bestow all their gifts upon those that follow. Through this, the stars diffuse their light into the Elements; fire communicates its power to the air, air to the water, water to the earth; the simple elements bestow themselves upon all mixed or composite things; and plants and animals, out of a desire to multiply their own species, give of themselves, according to that passage in the *Georgics*, Book 3:

> *So every race on earth, of men and beasts...*
> *And the sea-brood, the cattle, and painted birds...*
> *Rush into fires and madness; Love is the same for all.* <note>original: Virgil, Georgics 3.242-244</note>

By the impulse of this same Love, lower things obey the higher ones in the greatest degree. Thus the tractable earth is resolved into water, and this into air, then air into fire; and then, digested through imperceptible pores into the ether, small portions of the firmer sublunary substance—partaking of a gradual thickening and coagulation—are snatched higher into the hidden fibers of heaven. There, just as is customary in living creatures, having been more and more refined, it is first applied, then glued together, and finally thoroughly assimilated and transmuted into a celestial nature. Who, then, does not now see how aptly that monogram of the word $\Phi\Upsilon\Lambda\mathrm{O}$ <note>original: "PHYLO", likely related to the Greek *philo* (love/affinity)</note> is adapted to the Universe? Certainly, when I scrutinized this a little more deeply, I then recognized that saying of Iamblichus to be true: <margin>Iamblichus.</margin> <term>The characters of the Egyptians</term> <note>Kircher argues that Egyptian symbols are not random but are scientific diagrams of nature</note> *were by no means fabricated by chance or rashly, but with great genius according to the model of nature*. This shines forth most clearly in this very thing; in which, under two pyramids entwined in a contrary process within a spherical character <note>Symbol: A circle bisected by a vertical line, resembling the Greek letter Phi ($\Phi$)</note>, suddenly the colures, meridians, tropics, and the equator, the paths of the Love of the World—that is, the Sun (for in the Sun, worldly love flourishes most greatly)—and finally the whole sphere of love shines forth. Thus, from this it may be understood that Love, diffused through the Universe, is in all things. But since there is a great diversity of things in this World, it is necessary that it often be born from contraries; for no part of the World hates another, except out of love for itself, as <margin>Marsilio</margin> Marsilio Ficino <note>The famous Renaissance Neoplatonist</note> beautifully teaches in his explanation of the *Symposium*; and again, that Love is the primary effective cause of contraries; whence that passage of Plautus is exceedingly elegant: <margin>Plautus.</margin>

> *Divine Astarte, the force, life, and salvation of men and Gods, yet she is also*
> *Destruction, death, ruin, the sea, the earth, the sky, and the stars.*
> *Whatever temples of Jove we inhabit, they are led by her nod and obey.*

Hence Orpheus, in the *Argonautica*, not without cause praises this Love as the genius of the World, and as great and most ancient. For although you place Chaos before the World, and Saturn, Jupiter, and the other Gods before it; he certainly established Love in the bosom of Chaos itself, defining it as the principle by which an unformed thing desires ornament, or <term>kosmon</term> <note>original: "κόσμον", meaning order, beauty, or the world-system</note>, and perfection.

# CHAPTER I.

### On the invention and etymology of Music.

<margin>God used harmonic proportions in the creation of the World.</margin>
It was the opinion of Pythagoras—accepted by later philosophers in unanimous agreement—that God, when about to establish the World, made use of harmonic proportions. As the Sacred Text <note>A reference to Wisdom of Solomon 11:20: "Thou hast ordered all things in measure and number and weight."</note> also bears witness, we know that God produced all things in number, weight, and measure. Since, therefore, the ideas of all things are proven to consist of harmonic numbers, it is necessary that the supreme idea of all things <note>The "Divine Mind" or the blueprint of creation.</note> cannot, and indeed must not, lack them. Hence Music, divinely implanted in human breasts, exerted its vigor immediately from the very cradle of the World; how this happened, I have seen fit to explain in this place, repeating certain points from our *Musurgia* <note>original: "Musurgia Universalis," Kircher's massive 10-volume work on music theory and acoustics published in 1650.</note>.

<margin>The first principles and origin of Music.</margin>
In this worldly theater of things, nothing is more common than sound. Yet, just as it does now, it gave the earliest race of mortals various occasions and opportunities for its discovery. And first of all, the whistling of the winds, as well as that of certain animals, which those first mortals—dispersed here and there through the fields—perceived repeatedly, gave the first occasion for the construction of pipes. These they fashioned in imitation of nature from oat stalks, reeds, the leg-bones of cranes, and other hollow stalks <term>thyrsis</term> <note>Kircher uses the Greek term 'thyrsos' to refer to the hollow, pithy stems of plants.</note> of plants.
<margin>The first rudiments of pipes came from reeds.</margin>
Indeed, the sound and noise of hollow bodies gave birth to a diverse supply of percussion instruments. For since the earliest mortals for the most part devoted their efforts to a rustic and pastoral life, and fixed their dwelling tents there where rich pastures occurred and places watered by streams—and consequently abounded in rushes, reeds, papyrus, and similar sprouts of a tubular nature—it could not happen that a people, mostly idle all day, would remain without some relaxation of the mind. It is likely, therefore, that these men first fashioned various trumpets for themselves from the said tubular stalks, and indeed with no less skill than we see shepherds and others who lead a rustic life doing at this time; and perhaps even with greater skill, inasmuch as they then possessed a more vigorous intellect. Since, moreover, those same first mortals were for the most part skilled in the craft of smithing (as without it the society of the human race would perish), it could certainly not happen but that they would occasionally excite various sounds and noises from the accidental collision of different bodies while working. From this, it is very probable that they arrived at the knowledge of various percussion instruments on this occasion, in exactly the same manner as happens to us from time to time today.
<margin>The origin of Musical instruments.</margin>
Music, therefore, had the first origin of its invention not from the Greeks, or Egyptians, or Chaldeans, but from the first men before the Flood; indeed, if all men were removed from the World except for a few children ignorant of things, I would not doubt that these—driven by necessity, and in time through chance and experience—could fall upon various inventions necessary to the human race. For the inventions of things are innate to man, and not found in books <gloss>alone</gloss> <note>The gloss corrects the OCR 'folùm' to 'solùm'.</note>.
<margin>All inventions seem to have been accidental.</margin>

<summary>Kircher argues that music is a divine science based on the harmonic proportions God used to create the universe, but its practical invention arose naturally from early humans imitating wind and animal sounds using reeds and bones.</summary>
<keywords>Pythagoras, Music, Musurgia Universalis, pipes, percussion instruments, antediluvian history, harmonic proportions, creation, pastoral life</keywords>

-> CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER I. <-

...are not only learned, but are brought forth by some remarkable intellect, either through compelling necessity, chance, experience, or the suggestion of genius. That Music, therefore, existed from the very beginning—besides the fact that the Holy Scriptures testify to this clearly—reason itself dictates, as I have said. Certainly, in Genesis chapter 4, verse 21, the invention of musical instruments is openly ascribed to Jubal in these words:

<margin>Jubal, the Author of Music.</margin>
> <note>original Hebrew: "And his brother's name was Jubal; he was the father of all those who handle the lyre and pipe."</note>
> **And his brother's name was Jubal; he was the father of all those who handle the lyre and pipe.**

*And his brother's name was Jubal; he was the father of those handling, or striking, the Lyre and the Organ:* where the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> have, **this was the one who showed the psaltery and the lyre**; *this was he who demonstrated the Psaltery and the Lyre*. Truly, what sort of instruments were invented by them is contained in our *Musurgia* <note>Kircher's own massive work on music theory, "Musurgia Universalis" (1650)</note> in the chapter on the Music of the Hebrews. But indeed, after the flood, the Egyptians were the first restorers of skilled Music. <margin>Music invented in Egypt.</margin> For these people, instructed by Ham and his son Mizraim, brought Music to such a high state of renown that the etymology of "Music" itself is taken from the Egyptian word <term>Moys</term> <note>Kircher links "Music" to the Coptic word for water, "Moys" or "Mu"</note>, because it was invented and restored near the stagnant marshes of the Nile, on the occasion of the growth of reeds and papyrus (from which they fashioned their pipes) sprouting there in great abundance.

Thus, Music was undoubtedly derived from the Egyptian word **moys**, which signifies water, and so it seems to openly indicate the very beginnings of the invention of Music. <margin>The etymology of Moses.</margin> Indeed, that Moses drew the etymology of his name from the waters from which he was drawn out needs no other testimony than the Sacred Text; its words are:

> <note>original Hebrew: "And the child grew, and she brought him to Pharaoh's daughter, and he became her son. And she named him Moses, and said, 'Because I drew him out of the water.'"</note>
> **And the child grew, and she brought him to Pharaoh's daughter, and he became her son. And she named him Moses, and said, 'Because I drew him out of the water.'**

*And when he was grown, she delivered him to Pharaoh's daughter; whom she adopted in place of a son, and called his name Moses, because I drew him out of the waters.* From which words it is clearly evident that this name <term>Moses</term> was bestowed neither by his parents, nor by anyone else from the Hebrew Nation, but by Pharaoh's daughter herself; since she had no other familiar language besides her native Egyptian, it is an admitted fact that she called the found child by the Egyptian name <term>Moses</term>, as if she were saying, "saved from the waters." Furthermore, the most ancient writers, Philo and Flavius Josephus, clearly show this, the former of whom discusses it in his *Life of Moses* thus: **Then she gives him a name, calling him Moses according to the etymology, because of his being taken up out of the water. For the Egyptians call water 'Moys'.** After these things, a name is given to him taken from the fact itself, because he had been lifted out of the water: for in the language of the Egyptians, <term>Mos</term> is called water. But the latter <note>Josephus</note> in Book 2 of the *Antiquities of the Jews* says thus: **And she gave him this name, and placed it upon him because of the accident of his falling into the river. For the Egyptians call water 'Mo', and 'uses' those saved from water; therefore, composing the name from both, they bestowed this title upon him.** And because he had been cast into the river, he obtained his name from this event. For the Egyptians call water <term>mō</term>, and <term>uses</term> saved. Therefore, the name of Moses was bestowed as a word composed of both. <margin>Rabbi Abenezra.</margin> Rabbi Abenezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a medieval Jewish scholar</note> agrees with these, even if he reports that he was called <term>Monios</term> in Egyptian (a word, as I believe, that is corrupted). His words are:

> <note>original Hebrew: "The name Moses is translated from the Egyptian language into the Holy Tongue; and his name in the Egyptian language was Monios. And it is written in the book 'The Service of the Earth' that it was translated from the Egyptian language into the ancient language; also it is so in the books of the Greek sages; perhaps Pharaoh's daughter learned our language."</note>

### CHAPTER II. 122 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

The name of Moses, he says, was translated from the Egyptian language into the Holy language <note>Hebrew</note>, and his name in the Egyptian language had been *Monios*. So it is written in the book *On the Cultivation or Servitude of the Earth*, translated from the Egyptian language into the Ethiopic language. CLASS VII. MATHEMATICAL HIEROGLYPHS. CHAPTER II.

By the account of almost all mythologists, the invention of the many-formed lyre <margin>The many-formed Lyre is the invention of Trismegistus.</margin> is attributed to the same man <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note>. And although he was a singular lover of artistic music, he nevertheless left behind that common and vulgar sort. He turned all his labor and industry toward penetrating that music which consists primarily in the wondrous distribution of the supreme minds and the harmony of worldly things, and which regards the order and connection of individual parts. He used the portions of harmonic measures as if they were a magnetic compass guiding his journey toward the scrutiny of more hidden things. It is now time for us to discuss these matters.

---

### CHAPTER II.

-> **That Hieroglyphic Music was nothing other than the science of the order of things in the Universe.** <-

Rightly and wisely <margin>Psellus</margin> Psellus says in his *Music*: <term>Music, they say, holds all things together</term> <note>original Greek: Τὴν Μουσικὴν εἴπασι τὰ πάντα συνέχειν.</note>. The ancients said that Music contains everything. For when <margin>The order of the universe is music.</margin> they cast their eyes more attentively upon the circuit of the entire Universe, and recognized the entire order, connection, variety, and diversity of things, they called it Music itself, in which the consonant responds to the dissonant, the lowest to the highest, the highest to the middle, and the middle to the lowest and highest, by a certain wondrous proportion. And it is of this Music that <margin>Trismegistus</margin> Trismegistus speaks when he says in the <term>Asclepius</term> <note>A famous Hermetic dialogue between Hermes and his disciple Asclepius.</note>: *To know music is nothing else than to know the order of all things, and what divine reason has allotted to them; for the order of individual things, gathered into one by the masterly reason of all, produces a certain most sweet and true harmony of divine melody.* But what this harmony is, and in what it consists, it seemed fit to discuss in this place.

Just as music, or vocal harmony, consists in a fit distribution of intervals, by which the highest tones respond to the lowest and middle tones in exact proportion; so also the intervals of the Tones depend on one another in such a way that if you scatter their order, you would rightly seem to have confused and disturbed the entire harmony. Dissonant things are also so beautifully applied to consonant ones that if you separate them from each other, you destroy all the sweetness of harmonic symphony. The Egyptians were by no means ignorant of this musical secret; hence, weighing the order of things and their wondrous connection a little more deeply, they said the order of things was nothing other than a Music most perfect in all its numbers, in which the middle things harmonize with the lowest and highest, just as with the bass and treble, not without a certain proportion of intervals. There are <term>neti</term> <note>The highest note in the ancient Greek musical system.</note>, or superior sounds, in the inferior ones; the inferior or <term>hypati</term> <note>The lowest note in the ancient Greek musical system.</note> exist in the neti or superior ones; and finally, the middle ones exist in the extremes. He who sounds the <term>diapason</term> <note>The interval of an octave.</note> or eighth, immediately has the base spread beneath him. For just as the number ten is unity replicated, so also the octave is rightly a replication of the base, since according to the musical <term>epiphonema</term> <note>A technical exclamation or rule: "The same judgment is made of octaves."</note> *the same judgment applies to octaves*. Again, he who sounds the base soon obtains the <term>diapente</term> <note>The interval of a perfect fifth.</note>, the <term>diatessaron</term> <note>The interval of a perfect fourth.</note>, and the remaining harmonic intervals, and vice versa. So that, by the testimony of <margin>Aristotle</margin> Aristotle himself, Music is a thing entirely celestial and divine, and it displays the logic of the entire worldly workmanship—

For when they diligently turned their minds to exploring the powers of the celestial bodies, and their harmony, the alliance entered into, and the sympathy with the things of lower nature—namely, in what way and by what knot all things were bound together, clung, and agreed—and further, in what manner that moving force and nourisher of all things was derived from heaven into the whole Circle of the lands, first from the Sun, then from the Moon, and the rest of the Choir of celestial lights; philosophizing a little more deeply, they discovered that all things lie hidden in all things.

# CHAPTER II. THE GYMNASIUM OF EGYPTIAN HIEROGLYPHICS FROM THE OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS

According to Proclus <note>A Greek Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 412–485 AD) who heavily influenced later mystical and scientific thought.</note>, animals, plants, and minerals—by reason of their specific or individual constitution—are imbued with a certain power from heaven. This power is sometimes so familiar and friendly to certain things that it joins with them of its own accord, producing and obeying them; yet to other things, it is so contrary and hostile that it halts and binds their operations. And from here, as I judge, is the **origin of natural magic**, <margin>The origin of natural magic.</margin> which was always kept hidden by the Sages of the Egyptians behind hieroglyphic letters and symbols, like the greatest secret in natural things. This was done lest it be dragged into abuse by the unskilled, as we (alas!) are forced to groan in our own century, when we behold this most sublime science—the very peak of all philosophical discipline—so miserably corrupted by the writings of ignorant men and filled with old wives' superstitions.

However, before we pass from this sublime Philosophy of the Egyptians to other matters, it seemed fitting to add here the words of Proclus, by which the things said above are so confirmed that they alone could suffice in place of an explanation; for he says thus in his book *On Sacrifice and Magic*: <margin>Proclus on sacrifice and Magic.</margin>

>*Just as lovers proceed by reason from the beauty that appears to the senses toward divine beauty little by little; so also the ancient Priests of the Egyptians, when they considered a certain kinship in natural things, and a sympathy of some for others, and of manifest things for occult powers, and found all things in all things, they established their sacred science. For they recognized the highest things in the lowest, and the lowest in the highest; in heaven indeed are earthly things according to their cause, but in a heavenly manner; and on earth are heavenly things, but in an earthly manner. For from where do we think those plants, which they name Heliotropes <note>literally "Sun-turners"</note>, move toward the movement of the Sun, and Selinotrope <note>literally "Moon-turners"</note> toward the Moon? Truly all things pray, and sing hymns to the Leaders of their Order. Some indeed in an intellectual way, others in a rational way, others in a natural way, and others in a sensory way. Therefore, the Sun-follower moves toward the Sun in whatever way it can; and if anyone could hear the pulsation made by it in the circuit of the air, he would surely perceive through such a sound a certain harmony toward its King, such as a plant is able to produce. For this reason, one may behold the Sun and Moon on earth, but according to an earthly quality; and in heaven all plants, and stones, and animals, having an intellectual life according to their heavenly nature. Having contemplated these things, the Ancients brought down divine powers into this lower place from among the heavenly and earthly things through a certain similarity.* <margin>How much similarity is worth.</margin> *Truly, similarity itself is a sufficient cause for binding individual things to one another. For if someone heats hemp or papyrus, and then brings it near a lamp, even if he does not touch it, he will see the hemp suddenly ignited, although it did not touch the fire, and the ignition descending from above to the lower parts. Let us therefore compare the heated hemp or papyrus to a certain kinship of lower things to higher; its approach to the lamp to the opportune use of things according to time, place, and matter; the process of the fire into the hemp to the presence of divine light to that which is able to receive it; and finally the ignition of the hemp to a certain participation in the divine seed. But what shall I say of the Lotus?* <margin>Wonders of the Egyptian lotus.</margin> *The Lotus indeed folds its leaves into itself before the rising of the Sun, but as the Sun rises it gradually unfolds them, and as far as the Sun ascends to the middle region of heaven, so far does it spread its leaves; but as it seeks the setting from the middle, it gradually contracts its leaves: it seems to honor the Sun by the expansion and contraction of its leaves no less than men do by the gesture of the body and the movement of their labors. And a little later he says: Not only indeed in...*

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Class VII, "Mathematical Hieroglyphs," specifically exploring the "Music of the Spheres" and the chain of sympathies connecting the celestial and terrestrial realms. It builds on the concept that earthly objects act as mirrors for divine powers.</meta>

# CLASS VII. MATHEMATICAL HIEROGLYPHICS. CHAPTER II

In plants, which possess a trace of life, but also in stones, one may observe an imitation and a certain participation in the higher lights; just as the <term>Helites</term> <note>original: "Helites lapis"; likely the Sun-stone or Heliolite</note> stone imitates the solar rays with its golden beams; and the stone called the <term>eye of heaven</term> <note>original: "caeli oculus"; possibly a variety of opal or tiger's eye</note> has a shape similar to the pupil of the eye, and a ray stands out from the middle of the pupil. Thus all things are full of divine beings—earthly things full of celestial ones, and celestial things full of those above the heavens. Every order of things proceeds down to the very last, as if to say: those things which are gathered into one above the order of things are subsequently spread out as they descend, where different souls are arranged under different Divinities. <margin>Lions and Roosters are solar animals.</margin> Furthermore, there are many solar animals, such as Lions and Roosters, which by their nature participate in a certain Solar Divinity. Hence it is marvelous how much the lower things in the same order yield to the superior ones, even if they do not yield in size or power. For this reason, they say the Rooster is greatly feared by the Lion, and almost revered; the cause of which we cannot assign to matter or the senses, but only to the contemplation of the higher order—namely, because the presence of Solar virtue is more fitting to the Rooster than to the Lion. <margin>Solar Angels.</margin> He confirms this through various <term>Metamorphoses</term> <note>Transformations or changes in form</note>, in which he says that at times certain Solar Angels have appeared endowed with such forms. Solar demons have also been seen with the face of a lion, who, when a Rooster was placed before them, vanished instantly. Indeed, <term>Proclus</term> <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 412–485 AD) who wrote extensively on divine chains of being</note> says this proceeds from the fact that lower things established in the same order always revere the superior ones, just as many people, when looking upon images of divine men, are accustomed by that very sight to fear committing any offense. Having said and explained these things, he nevertheless concludes with these words:

> *To speak briefly, some things revolve along with the revolutions of the Sun, such as the plants we mentioned; others imitate the shape of Solar rays in some way, such as the Palm and the Date; others the fiery nature of the Sun, such as the Laurel; others something else. One may clearly see the properties which are gathered in the Sun distributed far and wide among the following things established in the Solar order: namely, Angels, Demons, souls, animals, plants, and stones.*

Therefore, the authors of the ancient Priesthood discovered the worship of higher Powers from apparent things, while they mixed some things and balanced others, etc., as follows.

Behold, Reader, the Music of the ancient Egyptians, covered by a hieroglyphic veil through the words above; which I have declared to you more at length so that you might see and better understand that in which they thought the greatest philosophy resided. For once the connection of higher things with lower things was known and investigated, they produced wonders through the application of active things to passive things by art. ->*How, and by which hieroglyphics, the Egyptians expressed Mundane Music.*<-

When the Egyptian Priests of the Sacred Rites <term>Hieromantæ; those who interpret sacred things</term> wished to express "Mundane Music" or the harmony of the world, they depicted a boy wrapped in a netted garment. In his hands was a <term>cucuphomorphon</term> scepter—that is, one adorned with the head of a <term>Hoopoe</term>—as well as a curved staff <note>original: "lituus"</note> and a carpenter’s square <note>original: "gnomon"</note>. From his back hung a triangle <note>original: "trigonus"</note> which resolved into a globe, as is made clear from the figure placed here, taken from the Isiac Table, which we call the Bembine Tablet.

<margin>Note that the globe must be attached to the triangle in this figure.</margin> <note>Hieroglyphic inscription: A circular emblem containing a profile of a youth (Harpocrates/Horus) wearing a patterned (netted) garment. He holds a scepter topped with the head of a hoopoe (cucupha) and another staff. Behind his shoulder is a triangle/trigon with a small circular attachment. The text inside the circle reads "SYMBOLS OF HORUS".</note>

By the boy, the Sensible World <note>The physical world perceived by the senses</note> was indicated, flourishing daily as if in a perpetual succession of generation. He is wrapped in a netted garment because the World, involved in the hidden complexities of the things it contains, is difficult to perceive. Through the hoopoe-headed scepter, the great variety of things in this sensible World is shown; through the square, their fit connection and exact rectitude; and finally, through the curved staff, a harmony most perfect in all its proportions <note>original: "numeris," literally "numbers"</note> is expressed. The triangle with the attached circle denotes that this World flowed forth from the Archetypal World, being as similar as possible to its Father and Maker. However, since we have treated these matters extensively both elsewhere in this book and in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, we refer the Reader there. Furthermore, the Egyptians used another kind of musical instrument, which they called a Sistrum, and they prepared it in various forms. Moreover, what the seven strings mean is clear from Macrobius, *Saturnalia* Book I. The Lyre of Apollo, he says, has seven strings: it provides an understanding of as many motions of the celestial spheres, over which he established the Sun as the moderator of nature. Sidonius also, in the *Epithalamium of Polemius and Araneola*, says that the <term>septenary number</term> <note>The number seven, considered sacred and perfect in antiquity.</note> was preserved according to the same model in the Lyre, the Cithara, and the Pipe. Thus in Euripides' *Iphigenia in Tauris*, the Chorus, speaking of Apollo, names the **seven-toned cithara**. Callimachus follows the myth in his *Hymn to Delos*; he says this number was chosen by Apollo because, while his mother was giving birth to him, singing swans had circled the island seven times in flight. 

Because a certain harmony, the searcher of the Universe, seems to flow forth from the equally vibrated succession of the four parts of the year, or the proportioned mixture of the elements, we see the lyre sculpted in the middle of the Obelisk as a fitting indicator of that matter. For just as the power of Music is situated in it so that various tensions and relaxations of voices, and sounds both high and low, arranged in a congruent measure of time, may merge into a sweet concord; so Osiris, or the celestial Apollo, that <term>Citharode</term> <note>A professional performer/singer who plays the cithara or lyre.</note> of the World, striking all parts of the Universe from the <term>nete</term> to the <term>hypate</term> <note>The highest and lowest strings/notes in the ancient Greek musical system.</note>, and proceeding from these to the <term>mese</term> <note>The middle string/note.</note> and the other intermediate strings, preserving a symmetry as if by the count of time, associating hot things with cold and moist with dry, produces a most beautiful temperament. 

For as Pliny well says in Book II, Chapter 49: *The nature of the Sun is understood for the tempering of things*, so that what we read concerning Orpheus in Cassiodorus (*Variae*, Book I) fits him more truly: *Contrary desires were collected into one assembly, and while the Lyre spoke its song, all things believed their adversities were gone.* Furthermore, Orpheus seems to have adapted this Lyre to the three seasons of the year, when he says:

# THE EGYPTIAN GYMNASIUM OF HIEROGLYPHICS

<margin>
The seasons of the year.
</margin>

<margin>
The Egyptians divided the year into only three parts, omitting Autumn.
</margin>

<margin>
Diodorus, Book 1, Chapter 2. Hieronymus Aleander, *On the Tablet of the Sun*.
</margin>

<margin>
Minerva Tritogeneia
</margin>

<note>original Greek: "ἤτοι μὲν γὰρ Ἀπόλλων [...] Ἄδειν ἀξίας..." — This refers to Apollo judging the seasons through music.</note>

That is, *In the lowest notes (hypate) he judges the winter; in the highest (nete), the summer; and in the Dorian mode, the spring.* The reason he omitted Autumn is that the ancient Egyptians, according to Diodorus (Book 1, Chapter 2), established only a threefold division of the year. For this reason, they devised three "Hours" <note>The Horae, or personified seasons</note> in number, as Hieronymus Aleander well notes in his explanation of the *Solar Tablet*. Diodorus also writes that Minerva—by whom they signified the ether—was called <term>Tritogeneia</term> <note>Literally "thrice-born" or "third-born," here linked to the three seasons</note> because she changes her nature in the same way during Spring, Summer, and Winter. The same author asserts that the Egyptians believed Osiris and Isis (namely the Sun and Moon) <gloss>govern the entire world by spirit and fire, and by the favorable opportunities of nature through the three seasons</gloss>, perfecting the circuit of all things with nourishment and growth through the invisible motion of the three-part times: Spring, Summer, and Winter. The Latin translators who named "Autumn" here in place of "Winter" seem to have read <term>opora</term> <note>harvest/autumn</note> in their manuscript instead of <term>cheimoni</term> <note>winter</note>, unless it was a slip of negligence.

Therefore, in imitation of the ancient three seasons, the Lyre was equipped with three strings. If to these we add the four-stringed instrument (tetrachord) of Terpander and Orpheus—or, as Boethius prefers, of Mercury—which was harmonized to the four elements of the universe, we arrive at the <term>heptachord</term> <note>seven-stringed lyre</note> indicated in our inscription. As we said above, this is a type of the Universe and a symbol of the most orderly worldly concord, by which all members of the World harmonize with one another. Indeed, Mercury Trismegistus, contemplating this "dissonant harmony" and the "discordant consonance" of all things, dared to say that the entire World with all its parts lies hidden within a single piece of Music. His sayings agree so closely with these two inscriptions we have explained thus far, that I believe Mercury himself to be their sole author. He provides the most abundant and indubitable witness in his books when he asserts everywhere that "whatever is below is also above," or "that which is inferior is also superior," along with many other things he says concerning the Sun and Moon as the parents of all things.

<margin>
Trismegistus
</margin>

<margin>
On the comparison of the three Worlds to one another.
</margin>

Elsewhere, however, he transfers these ideas to the archetypal World when he says: *In the Angelic or intellectual World, there are the same beings that exist in this visible machine, but spiritually and invisibly. In the supreme Ideal World, which is <term>aktisto</term> (uncreated), infinite, incomprehensible, and the Archetype, both the Angels and the World are one and together, in a most perfect divine manner.*

From this long discourse, it appears by what reasoning—through this sublime wisdom of the Egyptians—the lowest things show the highest, and corporeal things declare intellectual things. Through the natures and properties of inferior and earthly things, we see those of the superior and celestial. For these inferior, external, and visible things are the marks of superior patterns and symbols of invisible internal realities, by which we are led by the hand from seductive temporal things to those that are eternal and spiritual. The whole of creation and this vast machine of the World, in which the invisible Creator exhibits himself to us to be seen and touched, is nothing other than the shadow of God and a figure of the internal paradise—namely, that intuition by which creatures are clearly seen and understood, which are the "back parts" and effects of the Creator...

<margin>
This visible world is a shadow and figure of the future state of the Blessed.
</margin>

...and effects, through the knowledge of which the Creator-Artisan is known, the first cause who acts upon all things. For every creature, as Saint Augustine well said, was created by God so that it might stand as a witness to the Word of the Creator, through which it was made. Moreover, that all things are contained in the Archetypes in an invisible and spiritual manner—things which appear bodily in this visible world—and that all things flow from within toward the composite whole, and nothing is taken from the outside; this the very light of Nature proves and demonstrates by ascending and descending, by entering and exiting. <margin>Three Worlds are represented by Osiris, Isis, and Horus.</margin> Three Worlds are numbered, as we have proved above, as much according to the Hebrews as the Egyptians: the Archetypal World is represented by Osiris, the Angelic by Isis, and this sensible machine of the World by Horus. These are indicated above by the three spirits: the lower, the superior, and the medium composed of these, or harmony. Furthermore, each of these Worlds is governed by the one above it, and receives the influence of its powers, so that the Archetype itself and the supreme Artisan—through the Angels, heavens, stars, elements, animals, plants, metals, and stones—pours forth the virtues of His omnipotence into us, for whose service He founded all these things. Now, the "entrance" or ascent occurs when I am raised from the lowest to the highest by <note>A biblical reference to a ladder reaching to heaven, symbolizing the stages of spiritual ascent.</note> Jacob’s ladder: ascending from sensible things to intellectual things, from the creatures to the Creator Himself. <margin>50 Gates of Light.</margin> The Hebrews call this the <term>Key <note>original: מפתח (Maphteach)</note></term> through the 50 gates of intelligence; these are the steps or boundaries of all things collected from the first chapter of Genesis, by which, as if by symbols and marks, we are led to the highest knowledge of all things. The "exit" or descent, however, occurs where we are rolled down from God to the creatures, from intellectual things to external forms, from the center to the circumference. For example, I behold with the eye of the senses this apple seed; but leaving behind its corporeality, I withdraw from the external form to the interior invisible seed, and with the eye of the mind I contemplate the entire tree—with its root, trunk, branches, shoots, leaves, flowers, and fruits—to be <term>folded <note>The concept of "complicatio" (folding) suggests that the potential of the whole tree is folded into the simplicity of the seed.</note></term> within it, to be manifested in its own time through separation. That seed does not take those bodily parts from the outside or from elsewhere, but emits each one from itself and from its own inner recesses. Since such a seed is an image or shadow of Angelic substance, and folds the entire bodily mass of the tree within its inner recesses without quantity or quality; certainly a single Angel will fold the seeds of all things within himself much more easily, as he is of a more excellent, superior, and distinguished nature. <margin>On the Angelic nature.</margin> For the simpler a thing is (according to <note>St. Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologica, Part 1.</note> Saint Thomas, part 1), the more perfect, absolute, and powerful it is; and whatever an inferior power can do, a superior power can do much more perfectly and excellently. Therefore, when an Angel produces wonders, he does not take them from outside himself, but from within, from the inner recesses of his virtues (because he is a perfect image of God); he produces and bestows them when he wills, and as often as he wills, without any diminishing of himself. For an Angel carries and possesses all things with him in an Angelic and spiritual way; indeed, he folds the entire machine of the World within himself, and all these lower things with it. Since, therefore, an Angel can do these things, it must not be denied that the first and supreme cause—existing from itself, independent—folds all things within Himself invisibly and spiritually in His abyss; indeed, all things exist in a foundational unity in the simplest manner. <margin>On the Divine nature.</margin> For God is the center and the circle of Himself, dwelling within Himself, that is, in the abyss—
