# CHAPTER III. THE HIEROGLYPHIC SCHOOL OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

From the abyss of infinity (which the Hebrews call <term>Ein Sof<note>original: "אין סוף"; literally "without end," referring to God in His essence before manifestation.</note></term>), not out of any necessity of a needy nature, but by His own most free will alone, and out of pure goodness for His infinite glory; emitting all things from His own bosom as if from the deepest concept and retreat of divinity (Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the wisdom of Thoth.</note> says: *from the bowels of darkness*), He first produced Light through His Word—that is, the Angelic substances. Following that Angelic light came the stars, and then these bodies, or the machine of the visible World, fashioned from the seven spheres and the four elements. Thus, all things are in all things in their own way, and one remains in the other, just as the seed is in the tree, and the tree is in the seed. All visible bodies or elements are in the stars as invisible powers or spiritual elements; and the stars or powers are in the bodies. The stars are in the Angels, and the Angels are in the stars. The Angels are in God, and God is in the Angels, so that the higher can always exist without the lower, but not the reverse.

<margin>How all things are in all things.</margin> Therefore, by knowing God, the Angels are known; by knowing these, the stars are known—that is, the invisible powers of things; and once these are known, all created things, or the visible World, will be understood. Once the visible World is known, finally man will be known as the <term>microcosm<note>original: "μικρόκοσμος"; the "little world," the idea that man reflects the entire universe within himself.</note></term>, the son of the World; for such is the son as the father is in all things. Thus, from visible things, we grasp the invisible. Just as all things exist divinely in God and angelically in the Angels, so in the World all things exist corporally. Whatever exists sensibly in the elements of the visible World exists spiritually in the invisible powers of things; and whatever exists spiritually in these exists angelically in the Angels, and divinely in God.

And this is that chain indicated by the Egyptians in the preceding inscription—truly a golden chain, let down from heaven to our earthly fragility. By its help, through the order of creatures, we ascend from the lowest to the middle, and through these beyond the World to the Maker of things Himself, rising toward the One, the First, and the Highest. Toward this goal, as toward a longed-for end, all creatures strive with their own effort and voluntary groaning. All things, therefore, are in all things: heaven above, heaven below; stars above, stars below. And as Mercury <note>Another name for Hermes Trismegistus.</note> well said: the seed is the tree folded up, and the tree is the seed unfolded and explained. Unity is number folded up according to Plato, and number is unity unfolded. An Angel is the stars folded up, and the stars are an Angel unfolded. God is He in whom, as the <term>Archetype<note>The original model or "blueprint" in the mind of God.</note></term>, the World is folded in a divine manner; the World is God (if one may say so) unfolded. So also in the microcosm, the five senses are in the imagination, the imagination in reason, reason in the mind, and the mind in God; but God is in nothing except Himself.

Thus, lower things are seen in their superiors, the last in the second-to-last, and again the prior things similarly in those before them, one thing always in another, until the summit is reached. This was not poorly suggested by the Egyptians through the seven-stringed Lyre; for from the <term>Hypate<note>The lowest-sounding string in ancient Greek music.</note></term> to the <term>Nete<note>The highest-sounding string.</note></term>, through the intermediate strings and proceeding in reverse, we see all things contained in all things, tone by tone, in a certain wonderful harmony and concord. But enough on these matters, which we have explained at length so that the admirable wisdom of the Egyptians and its agreement with our own way of philosophizing might more easily shine forth. For they called that man "blessed" who was skilled in this Philosophy; the reason they gave, according to the testimony of Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on Egyptian and Chaldean wisdom.</note>, was because they perceived the celestial Sun and the other planets to be hidden within all lower things.

He uses the metaphor of a seed and a tree, as well as a seven-stringed lyre, to illustrate how the divine essence permeates every level of reality from God to man.</summary>

### CHAPTER IV.

->**That all the hymns of the Ancients alluded to World Music, which they believed whoever understood would perform admirable effects by its power.**<-

**T**he ancients did not only hold the symphony of <term>world music</term><note>original: "Musicæ mundanæ"; the "Music of the Spheres," a theory that the movements of celestial bodies create a divine harmony</note> as a goal for contemplation, but also through practical operation. By its aid, they sought out the orders, classes, agreements, and disagreements of individual things with the greatest zeal; they believed they would achieve their intent by no easier means than this. Hence, in their sacrifices, they arranged everything according to the rule of harmonic consonances. And just as a touched string moves a string similar to itself, so by adapting active things to passive things according to a certain harmonic analogy, they believed they would move the strings of the harmonic and mundane instrument in equal measure to produce prodigious effects in the nature of things. They thought this could not be done by any better method unless they first solicited the supreme presidents of the World and the players of the world's <term>many-stringed instrument</term><note>original: "polychordi mundani"; a metaphor for the universe as a giant harp or lyre</note> through sacrifices and hymns, using analogous things—especially those most acceptable to them. Once these were solicited, they believed that through a continuous provocation of the strings, as it were, propagated down to the lowest orders of things, the many-stringed instrument of the soul would be moved above all others. Thus, the soul, seized outside of itself by a certain frenzy, would soon be invaded by the harmony of the divine breeze, and from there reveal hidden things, <margin>The Egyptians established divination in hymns.</margin> predict the future, avert and guard against unfortunate outcomes of events, and finally obtain by the necessity of infallible fate those things which pertained to the public or private prosperity of anyone. And such were the hymns presented by the Egyptians through the patterns of <term>hieroglyphics</term><note>Kircher viewed hieroglyphs not just as writing, but as symbolic keys to cosmic forces</note>, by which they enticed the <term>Spirit</term><note>original: "Genium"; a guardian spirit or presiding deity of a specific natural order</note> set over a certain order of natural things through hymns, sacrifices, and the supplications of incantations; these have been dealt with in various preceding places and will be discussed amply in the following. Such were those mystic hymns of Orpheus, inscribed to the presidents of the world's parts, <margin>The mystic hymns of Orpheus.</margin> to the Spirits, to Pan, Pluto, Jupiter, Saturn, Apollo, Hercules, Mercury, Rhea, Minerva, Pallas, Hecate, Proserpina, and similar Gods and Goddesses. To the <term>Lyre</term><note>original: "Cytharam"</note> of these, the Priest-Prophet adapted his own with the greatest genius; and indeed, the sound analogous to celestial harmony moved the celestial lyre by a certain fatal necessity, while the words solicited the Spirits to respond. Hence they believed it impossible that the Spirits, attracted by the vows of the Prophets, would not satisfy them in every way; so that not without reason <margin>The origin of the fabled song of Orpheus.</margin> the Ancients presented Orpheus as a Musician and Magician, drawing animals, woods, and even the very rocks by the magical sound of his Lyre, concerning which Claudian speaks quite elegantly in the preface to the second book of *The Abduction of Proserpina*, in these words:

<margin>What the attraction of rocks performed by Orpheus signifies.</margin> Indeed, this prodigious attraction of animals, forests, and rocks is to be understood partly tropologically <note>In a moral or figurative sense</note> and partly allegorically. For the Ancients noted that the power of Music over the soul is greatest, and that the soul is changed according to its various sounds and harmonies, following them like wax, wherever you might mold it. Therefore, they called it the <term>beginning of all things</term> <note>original Greek: ἀρχὴν πάντων</note>, or the principle of all, as Psellus says in his *Music*: <term>The ancients said that the Muses hold the universe together.</term> <note>original Greek: Τῶν Μουσῶν οἱ πάλαι συνέχειν εἶπον τὸ πᾶν.</note> Furthermore, they saw that this same Music was able to compose and vary moral character; for nothing flows so easily into tender and soft minds as the various sounds of singing. It can hardly be expressed how great its power is in either direction: for they both incite the listless and make the excited languish; they now relax the mind, and then contract it, as will be said more extensively a little later. Therefore, the rocks, forests, and animals—that is, men who were utterly senseless, beast-like, and monstrous in their cruelty—he drew toward humanity and a civilized way of living, attracted by the divine sound of his Lyre. Others, however, understand the said attraction allegorically. For since, they say, Orpheus was a distinguished Astrologer and Musician, most perfectly skilled in both arts, he so opportunely tempered and mixed sounds that <margin>The power of Music in the souls of mortals.</margin> he imitated the harmony of the celestial stars (which he himself understood best of all), and drew into himself and called down all their influence and power. Relying on this, he could stir or soothe whatever he wished by his playing. Some also add that since he knew best by what proportion and by what concord each thing was constituted and composed by nature, and which star it obeyed and was subject to, he adapted musical ratios to these things and their stars. By this movement, he enticed inanimate things through the power of the stars, which he brought forth (as it were) from where it lay hidden within them by his own external harmony; not unlike how iron strikes hidden fire from flint, or the blast of a bellows brings forth a concealed flame. For there are in all things certain latent sparks, as it were, and seeds of harmony or sensation, so much so that the Ancients even called God himself the <term>harmony of all things</term> <note>original Greek: ἁρμονίαν πάντων</note>.

### CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER IV

I truly do not know what hidden and hitherto unpenetrated force of nature resides in motion, by which we see that one person can effect in another that which they do themselves. This happens not only in the external movement of the body, but most especially in that movement which occurs through the office of the tongue, breaking forth into words and songs. For we see that even a single person singing can, by a certain hidden force, rouse others to do the same (whether this happens through fear, as in those struck by a panic, or by an instinct of joy, as occurs in those dancing). While this occurs in other movements, it certainly holds the greatest place in human voices. <margin>The human voice provokes imitation.</margin> For since the human voice is nothing other than a certain skillful movement of the tongue, formed according to a person's intention to signify something, we see it produce exactly that in others which the speaker themselves performs. Experience has taught us that one person humming, or wailing, or whistling, or even yawning, excites others to do the same. Since this is true in sounds and voices that are raw and unpolished, it will certainly be verified much more so in a harmonious arrangement of words and voices. The Masters of primeval wisdom noted this hidden force of nature from the beginning; hence they did not compose the praises of the immortal Gods with just any haphazard arrangement of words, but by casting "chains" upon them, they constrained their Orations with a certain harmonic measure, so that the very measure of the words would correspond precisely to the internal affections of the soul. From this, you may recognize the first rudiments of sacred Poetry, which just as it did then, has at all times maintained a certain divine quality in the minds of posterity. For they believed that by this means, they could not only bring the Spirits and Gods close to them through a certain sympathetic alteration, but could also change the minds of men into whatever state they wished. All these things that <term>highly learned</term> <note>original Greek: polyidanta</note> Horace teaches so excellently, that it seems nothing else can be added to his words:

### CHAPTER IV. 238 THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

We have declared more extensively elsewhere that [human expression] has no origin other than from harmonic motion; especially if it responds in a measured way to the internal passions of the soul. Moreover, it will correspond in a measured way if the Speech is drawn together through the brevity or length of syllables into fit and harmonious periods—or, what is the same thing, if a quick and swift measure follows the quick movements of the soul, and a slow measure follows the slow ones. And although this possesses a wonderful power in the Metric or Rhythmic art, it is certainly found to have a much greater energy in Musical Poetry or Rhythmics. For the infinite monuments of historians testify that the latter, when joined to the former as if completed in every part, obtains altogether prodigious effects in the souls of men. For there is, as I also said a little while ago, some kind of sympathy between our soul and harmonic and rhythmic movements, so that as soon as metric harmony is presented to the ears, the mind—stirred by various passions—may now show signs of joy, now of love, now of sorrow, compassion, anger, groaning, and other <term>pathematum</term> <note>original: "pathematum" (Greek: παθημάτων); refers to the "passions" or "suffering" of the soul, specifically how it is affected by external stimuli</note>; which sometimes increases so much that the mind, unable to be contained within the internal cloisters of the soul, also rouses the external limbs to actions responding to the passion. But since we have shown these things at length in our <term>Magnetic Art</term> <note>Kircher's work *Ars Magnetica* (1641), where he explores universal attraction</note>, Book III, concerning the <term>Magnetism of Music</term> and <term>Tarantism</term> <note>The phenomenon of "dancing mania" attributed to spider bites, which Kircher believed could be cured by specific musical rhythms</note>, we refer the Reader there.

<note>Decorative initial C: Historiated woodcut featuring a scene with figures and foliage</note> When I deeply ponder those gifts with which **God, the Best and Greatest**, has most liberally seen fit to honor the human race, I am led to the opinion that no greater gift can be found than a burning zeal for letters and the exquisite cultivation of learning and wisdom; it is surely the most excellent protection, whether you look to the refining of morals or the good and blessed administration of the Republic. I remember, Most Exalted Prince, that you not only felt this same way once in Rome, but as soon as you were restored to your Fatherland for the good of the Empire, you produced such a reputation for your name through that supreme and innate vigor of counsel and prudence, as well as through your education in the most refined arts, that you have proven yourself to have made great progress toward the principles of a right life by relying on their help. Furthermore, you have opened those paths for yourself from which all hope that joyful and most abundant fruits will one day overflow for the benefit of the Empire. Indeed, a desired success of fortune has abundantly confirmed and increased this hope and expectation (since not long ago you were raised to the rank of Prince of the Holy Roman Empire by the Great Emperor **FERDINAND III** <note>Ferdinand III (1608–1657) was the Holy Roman Emperor; his son Ferdinand IV was King of the Romans but predeceased him.</note> amidst the greatest applause and congratulation of all); so that we now confess we shall attain far greater advantages than we ever expected from your great fortune and high rank. Therefore, since I am not only a sharer in this public joy, but also privately well aware of your kindness and well-disposed mind toward me, I might appear altogether ungrateful if I did not prove my respect toward you by some notable testimony. For this reason, I have seen fit to inscribe this present argument concerning the Astrology of the Egyptians to the glorious splendor of your name. I trust that, in accordance with your accustomed kindness, you will receive it as mine, yet owed to you; and defend it as yours, yet proceeding from me. Farewell, ornament of the Holy Roman Empire, and as you once favored me, do not cease to favor me hereafter.

# SECTION IV.

## PREFACE

In this Section, we shall set forth the twofold science of celestial matters used by the Egyptians; the first of these will be **Astronomy**, the investigator of celestial motions and times; the other, **Astrology**, which reveals the decrees of fatal events depending on the stars and the fortunes established for individuals. The difference between the two is this single point: that the former measures much, while the latter mentors—or rather, lies—much. <note>original: "illa multùm metiatur, hac mentiatur multùm" — a wordplay on 'metior' (to measure) and 'mentior' (to lie).</note> We shall speak first of Astrology; afterwards, we shall also discuss that particular part of Astronomy which they call the <term>Computational Art</term> <note>The mathematical calculation of planetary positions and calendars.</note>, as far as the powers of our intellect permit.

<margin>The Author’s protestation regarding the interpretation of Egyptian Astrology.</margin> Before I approach these matters, I protest before God and the holy court of heaven that I shall assert nothing contrary to the most wholesome laws established by the Sacrosanct Roman Church. Rather, I shall perform only the office of a bare "Oedipus" or Interpreter in the bringing forth of these most recondite matters; let no one persuade himself that I have any faith in so ruinous a faculty. For when I name Astrology, I do not mean that which measures the magnitudes and motions of the stars by mathematical reasoning—certainly a noble art, most honorable in its own merits, and highly approved at all times by the authority of the most learned men—but rather that which pronounces future events from the stars and brings force upon human will. This latter is forbidden by laws both civil and pontifical, mocked by Philosophers, cultivated by charlatans, and suspected by every good and prudent man.

<margin>Astrology is pernicious and vain.</margin> Concerning this [Astrology], relying both on reason and the judgments of the wisest men, I would not hesitate to affirm that among the deceptive arts, there is none that either deceives the credulous and unskilled more, or which harms more through the spreading of its deceits. It is all the more deadly than other superstitions because it seems to approach closer to the truth. It was first born in Egypt and <term>Chaldea</term> <note>Ancient Mesopotamia, famous for star-gazing.</note>, raised in <term>Greece</term>, and reached maturity in the <term>Roman Empire</term>, from whence it translated its roots into all parts of the world, with an outcome all the more ill-fated as it brought greater ruin to the scepters of Kings and Emperors. And since "from a bad crow a bad egg is born," <note>A Latin proverb meaning a bad parent produces a bad child.</note> I do not see what good or fruitful thing can be born from such a pernicious root of such great superstitions. At first glance and from a distance, it offers some appearance and habit of wisdom; yet if you consider it more closely, you find it cherishes nothing but a viper of madness in its breast. Once examined more exactly, you would abominate it like a certain <term>Lerna</term> <note>The Hydra of Lerna, a many-headed monster; here implying a multifaceted evil.</note> and a fallacy of darkness under the open light. It displays the heavens and the planets from afar, whence you might easily believe that in so sublime and lucid a spectacle, everything could be most truly foreseen; but soon, when you explore more attentively, you will see that the mirror is so high that the images of earthly things can by no means penetrate there. It is so bright that the weakness of our fleeting nature grows dim at its splendor. Then, if you approach nearer, you will see woven into its veil, instead of heavenly things, monsters of portentous images and strange spectacles of stars transformed into exotic animals; in a word, you will gaze with stupor upon a heaven full of fables—indeed, instead of the true heaven, a counterfeit heaven not made by God, but feigned by Astrologers. It is a wonder how, through these glooms and mists poured over the eyes of the unskilled, it represents to itself an image that is beautiful, venerable, and full of serious authority. The books of Astrologers [are filled] with old wives' fictions and the insane [follies] of idle
->men<-

He issues a formal disclaimer that his study of these ancient errors is purely academic and compliant with Catholic doctrine.</summary>

For you will find them for the most part so stuffed with delusions that it can hardly be discerned whether you carry away from them a greater occasion for laughter or for acquiring the truth. When you have dispelled these shadows and deceptions of right reason with a ray of light and the diligent ruler of careful treatment, you will see that nothing in those books is balanced, there is no authority in the authors, nothing rational in the reasoning, nothing harmonious in experiment, nothing constant, nothing true, nothing credible, nothing solid; but rather things mutually conflicting, false, vain, and ridiculous; so that you would hardly believe that those who wrote them held any faith in what they were writing. The Ancients possessed an Astrology wonderfully contaminated by innumerable superstitions and greatly exposed to diabolical illusions; the Arabs, having made it their own, pursued it with the highest devotion; from them, certain Latin writers pursue it with such insanity to this day, that I will not say they subject matters concerning the natural temperament of the human body to it, but with a certain detestable daring and rashness, they do not blush to attribute even those things which pertain to the supernatural to the same. Today, you will hardly find a condemned art, especially those containing the secrets of <term>polymantia</term> <note>The practice of multiple forms of divination or "many-prophesying."</note> or the divinatory faculty, of which <term>judicial astrology</term> <note>The branch of astrology used to predict specific events or human fate, often criticized by the Church as infringing on free will.</note> does not claim a part for itself, as will be seen in the context of this treatise. Therefore, so that the roots of these vanities may be more clearly shown, I will draw the first beginnings of my dissertation from the Astrology of the Egyptians, so that the Astrologers of our time may see from what an abominable workshop of total idolatry it proceeded, and learn to be wiser; for I would dare to solemnly affirm that all present judicial astrology, which they call <term>apotelesmatic</term> <note>From the Greek 'apotelesma,' referring to the effects or outcomes of the stars; essentially predictive astrology.</note> and consultative, retains to this day a hidden alliance with demons, a pact already then entwined with the ancient Astrology of the Egyptians: which will be clear throughout the following discourse. But since we have reserved individual points to be refuted in their proper places, lest we waste time in more extensive digressions, let us finally begin the business at hand.

# THE ASTROLOGY OF THE EGYPTIANS
## Part One

### C H A P T E R  I.
#### On the Origin and Progress of Astrology among the Egyptians.

# CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER I.

<note>The header indicates this is the seventh division of Kircher's massive work, "Oedipus Aegyptiacus," where he attempts to decode Egyptian wisdom through the lens of 17th-century scholarship.</note>

<unclear>Whether you consider</unclear> his immense capacity of mind, or his total knowledge of hidden things, or finally his desire to propagate his glory among posterity and to deserve well of the human race, he was the first. For here, as we have taught above, bringing back to the anvil <note>A metaphor for refining or reworking an idea</note> the laws of Astronomy—which he had received by tradition from Enoch through the propagation of Noah’s lineage—he spared no effort so that he might explore the truth of the Ancients' Astronomical Canons through the experiment of his own observation; and once explored, reduce them to that perfection which those unrefined times permitted.

<margin>The first division of the heavens into 12 parts.</margin>
These things being established, I say that Mercury first divided the sky into twelve signs, having invented particular characters for that purpose; he partitioned the year into 365 days; he first detected the motions of the planets; and finally, other matters which shall be discussed most abundantly in the following pages. It remains to be told by what method he accomplished this.

<margin>How Hermes is presented hieroglyphically.</margin>
For first, it is likely that he first observed the entire machine of the heavens revolving around two poles, according to the model of which Aratus <note>A Greek didactic poet who wrote about the stars</note> is the authority that he invented a similar sphere, being the discoverer of the courses of the heavens and the globe. Whence the Egyptians, intending to represent him hieroglyphically, painted a man with a canine face <note>Referring to Anubis-Hermes or Hermanubis</note>, in whose one hand was held a caduceus, and in the other a sphere; all of which you will find explained at length in the <term>Pamphilian Obelisk</term> <note>A reference to Kircher's own earlier work on the obelisk now in the Piazza Navona</note> on page 294. For when he discovered that in the celestial machine, once a revolution was completed in the space of a natural day, certain fixed stars proceeded as if perpetually unmoved, some very swiftly, and the rest with a motion midway between speed and slowness; he thought the same thing happened as in a material sphere, which when rotated, those parts which go around the poles are seen to be slow and as if unmoved, while conversely those which occupy the line of the middle globe proceed with the swiftest motion. And so, by the said observation, he detected the poles in the sky and the equinoctial line. <margin>The first observation of the poles and the equinoctial. Observation of the fixed stars.</margin> Truly, when he noted one and the same always immutable distance of all the stars among themselves, from this he easily fashioned the globe of the fixed stars. Furthermore, when he had noted that some stars held neither the same distance from each other, nor the same pattern of rising and setting, nor fixed places in the sky; <margin>Observation of the Planets.</margin> but discovered them wandering here and there in the ethereal expanse with a certain perpetual variety; he judged them to be not fixed, but led around by motions attributed peculiarly to each one: of which he found only seven subject to this instability: among which, since the Sun and Moon held the principal place, he first applied his mind to scrutinizing their motions. <margin>Observation of the motions of the Sun and Moon.</margin> Therefore, when he discovered that the Sun touched different points of the Horizon every day; and likewise in the middle of the sky marked different points of altitude or depression; he noticed that there was a certain and constant elongation of it toward the South and the North: which when it had completed, it soon withdrew in the opposite direction with a reversed motion. And from that emanated the invention of the Tropics, which he called the extreme "hostels" of the souls of the Gods ascending and descending, as will afterwards be proved from the "Cave of the Nymphs" described by Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher; the "Cave of the Nymphs" is an allegorical interpretation of Homer</note>. <margin>Observation of the Zodiac.</margin> Again, when he noted that the Sun passed through certain constellations in order every month; from there flowed the distinction of the <term>twelve-parts</term> <note>original: "dodecamoriorum"</note>, or the <term>Zodiac</term> <note>The belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs</note> divided into twelve signs, which he called the mansions of the Gods,

In no other way than through zealous and constant study of observation must he be judged to have finally arrived at the knowledge of the other phenomena and celestial laws. Therefore, I consider those to have spoken most falsely who have striven to ascribe the first invention of the obliquity of the Zodiac, the division of the signs, and the distinction of the mansions to Anaximander, Thales, or Eudoxus <note>famous Greek philosophers and astronomers</note>; since these things were already held in Egypt for many centuries as if they were the rudiments of a trivial school. It was from the Egyptians that the aforementioned Greeks first received these things, being many centuries later. Indeed, the partition of the Months (of which, according to the testimony of Holy Scripture, there was already knowledge at the time of the Flood) cannot be conveniently conceived without the motion of the Zodiac and the Sun through the twelve signs, and the Moon is necessarily joined to the Sun twelve times in the annual space established in its obliquity.

# CHAPTER I. OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>Hermes Trismegistus and the second Idris drew much from Ham.</margin>
...that he established a law utterly degenerate from tradition; which afterwards a certain <term>Trismegistus</term> <note>Thrice-Greatest</note>, descending from the Canaanite line of Ham, reduced into a better form—separating the lawful from the unlawful—and made it more conformable to divine Religion, as far as was permitted to a Pagan Philosopher supported only by the light of nature amidst such a depravation of things. We have proved in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* <note>Kircher’s 1650 work on the Roman obelisk in the Piazza Navona</note> that he was indeed that true and so greatly celebrated second Hermes Trismegistus. Furthermore, the Egyptians and Arabs maintain that Enoch, or that first Hermes, was the first after the sons of Seth to cultivate Astronomy and teach the reckoning of time and years; and that from his monuments left to the later world, our second Hermes deduced his own principles regarding the division of time and transmitted them to posterity. For the more secret Astrologers of the Egyptians hold it as certain that the civil year of the Egyptians was divided into as many days as the first Idris, or Hermes, had lived among men. For Holy Scripture expressly says that he lived three hundred and sixty-five years, exactly as many as the civil year of the Egyptians has days: for thus says verse 23 of Chapter 5 of Genesis:

<margin>Enoch lived as many years as there are days in a year.</margin>
->And all the days of Enoch were three hundred sixty-five years.<- <note>original Greek: Καὶ ἐγένοντο πᾶσαι αἱ ἡμέραι Ἐνὼχ τριακόσια ἑξήκοντα πέντε ἔτη.</note> Since indeed the second Idris taught this same method of partitioning the year to later Egyptians, as we have shown elsewhere, it is probable that he obtained these things from the monuments of the first Hermes, communicated to the later world through Ham. Since they recognized that this number of the years of Idris's life was by no means void of mystery, it is probable that from here arose that secret Egyptian <term>hieromantic</term> <note>sacred divination or priestly knowledge</note> doctrine concerning the revolution of the World: namely, that the celestial Gods change their stations in the great citadel every

<margin>The celestial Gods change their stations in the great circle according to the Egyptians.</margin>
hundred years, and after a completed circuit of 36,500 years, all things are restored to their original state. It is certain that Plato also had a scent of this, when he defined the circle of <term>rebirth</term> <note>original Greek: παλιγγενεσίας (palingenesias)</note>—which even to this day we call the Platonic Year—by the number of the said years. For since they observed the firmament to complete one minute in the great circle (that is, the Zodiac) nearly every hundred years, 100 multiplied by 360 will give 36,000; if to these you add the five <term>intercalary days</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπαγομένους (epagomenous); the 5 extra days added to the 360-day Egyptian calendar</note> multiplied by 100 years, you will have the number of 36,500 years: the completion of all things, the number of the Great Jubilee, and the return of the "monad" <note>the number one, representing unity or God</note> departing into multitude back into the monad—that is, into the original state of things. Just as Plato, having been so taught by the Egyptians, was of this opinion, they in turn speculated this from the mystical number of the years of Idris's life; and several more recent authors have followed him in this revolution of the firmament.

[The previous generation of] men handed down the knowledge they had received to their Hebrew descendants. In Egypt, Misraim first imbued his son and others with these same principles. Later, the second Hermes, known as Mercurius Trismegistus <note>The "Thrice-Great" Hermes, a legendary Hellenistic figure combining the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian Thoth, regarded as the author of a vast body of sacred texts.</note>, cultivated this study with the greatest zeal. According to Clement of Alexandria in the sixth book of his *Miscellanies* <margin>Clement of Alexandria</margin> <note>original: "Stromat." referring to the *Stromata*</note>, Hermes handed this knowledge down to later Egyptians in twelve books. From both the Chaldeans <note>Ancient inhabitants of Mesopotamia, famous for their star-gazing.</note> and the Egyptians, the Greeks "stole" this wisdom and claimed it as their own, even though all these ideas flowed from the same original school of thought.

Therefore, it should seem a wonder to no one that the Egyptians, Chaldeans (or Babylonians), and Greeks have competed for the title of the first inventors of astronomy. Each of these nations claimed the glory of this discovery for themselves, seeing how much it was held in the esteem and admiration of men. In this same way, when Sulpitius Gallus first detected an eclipse in Rome <margin>Sulpitius Gallus was the first to predict an eclipse in Rome; Thales did so in Greece.</margin>, he was considered its inventor, even though the discovery had already been attributed to Thales of Miletus in Greece many centuries earlier—and the knowledge of eclipses flourished in Egypt many centuries before that, as will be discussed in its proper place. Thus, although the inventions of things may emerge in one particular region, they have often been preceded by the same discoveries in other regions. Since I show this in many other places, I do not wish to dwell on it any longer. Let it suffice for now to have demonstrated—perhaps in a longer discourse than is proper—that Hermes was either the inventor or the restorer of astronomy in Egypt.

# CHAPTER II.

->Concerning the division of the signs, and the invention of the characters of the celestial signs.<-

Mercurius Trismegistus, looking out for the benefit of the human race and being intent on communicating the exact order of celestial matters to posterity, described each detail in his books, as Clement of Alexandria testifies. And because he observed that an influence is propagated from the star-bearing heaven in a continuous order down to the lower realms, he began his astrological arrangement there. Thus, having first noted through long experience and frequent observation of the Sun, Moon, and other stars the four principal cardinal points that produce all changes and variety <margin>The method of observation established by Mercury.</margin>, he fashioned a circle. In this circle, he arranged the said points by means of two diameters, *a-d* and *c-e*, intersecting each other at right angles—namely, *a d c e*. Those points which hold the middle line *e-c*, being equally distant from the poles of the world, he wished to be called the points of equality <note>The Equinoxes, where day and night are of equal length.</note>, because when the Sun reaches them, it makes the night equal to the day. He even established the Dog-headed Ape <note>The Cynocephalus, often associated with the god Thoth/Hermes.</note> as the symbol for this; for its nature is such, according to Horus <margin>The Dog-headed Ape is the symbol of the equinox.</margin> <note>Referring to Horapollo, an author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note>, that near the points of the equinox, it is accustomed to urinate twelve times [a day] by a certain hidden and inborn instinct; more on this in its proper place. However, those points *a* and *d*, which terminate the greatest elongation of the Sun as it travels back and forth, now into the South and now into the North, he called the "Limits of the Gods" <margin>The Tropics are the limits of the Gods.</margin> <note>The Solstices.</note>, because the divine powers circling the globe would never pass these fixed boundaries, but with their course reversed, would move now toward the South, now toward...

When he says four parts, he shows the four portions of the year, which the fourfold division of the Zodiac created. When he says it is divided into 36, he shows that each of the houses or habitations of the Gods was further divided into three other portions, which, according to Iamblichus, <margin>The Decans of the signs.</margin> he calls Decans. All of these things harmonize beautifully with what was brought forward just before. That all these things are the machinations of Mercury [Hermes], Iamblichus openly testifies—

# SECTION VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER II.
V

<margin>Iamblichus.</margin> Iamblichus writes with these words: *With these things thus distinguished, the doubts which you say you conceived in the Egyptian books you have read are easily resolved. For those opinions or inventions circulated under the title of Mercury <note>original: "Mercurii"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note> contain the matters of Mercury; and although they often speak in the style of the Greek Philosophers, they were nevertheless translated from the Egyptian language into Greek by men not unskilled in Philosophy.* See also <margin>Clement of Alexandria.</margin> Clement of Alexandria in books 5 and 6 of the *Miscellanies* <note>original: "Stromat." or Stromata</note> speaking amply concerning Mercury and his inventions, as well as Origen, Tertullian, and other Authors whom I have cited above, discussing these matters.

Having thus seen the first sphere of the Zodiac, and the rough sketch performed by Hermes, let us now see by what names, Divinities, animals, and characters they led this through the individual houses.

Therefore, since that star-bearing circle which we call the Zodiac is divided into 12 houses or mansions, and since they noticed that the lower things are opposed to the upper, and that every influence flows into the lower World from the powers of the superior, he [Hermes] equipped the individual houses with their own Powers or Divinities. And <margin>The First House or Altar of the Zodiac and its numbers.</margin> indeed, he attributed the first house to Anubis. Now Anubis was a Divinity of the Egyptians, a guardian of temples, and a preserver of heat and moisture; whose hieroglyphic symbol was the "goat-fish" <note>original: "hircopiscis"</note>, i.e. <note>Symbol for Capricorn: A goat-headed creature with a coiled fish tail</note> which he held bound to his hands by a leather strap. <margin>Anubis's hieroglyphic: Capricorn.</margin> The horns of the goat denoted the heat, or the fiery power of the Sun enclosed in the earth; but the tail of the fish denoted moisture, from which the first generation of all things proceeds; of which they said Anubis was the guardian, according to the testimony of Plutarch. He also says that Anubis was placed midway between the upper and lower hemisphere because, when the Sun is in Capricorn at its greatest elongation <note>the winter solstice</note>, and the earth is weakened by the solar rays, it remains closed as if in a womb, and through the arrangement of seminal principles, it contrives the preludes of a new generation, over which they said Anubis presided. Clement of Alexandria reports this expressly in these <margin>Clement of Alexandria.</margin> words in book 5 of the *Miscellanies*: *The Egyptians were also accustomed in certain solemnities to carry around four statues of Gods, which they called <term>Komasias</term> <note>A Greek term for festive processions</note>, two of which shone with the form of Dogs, the third a Hawk, and the fourth an Ibis. By the two dogs they understood the two hemispheres.* And a little later: *Others, however, wished to suggest by the two dogs the two tropics, which are like dogs observing and guarding, appointed by nature, prohibiting the further elongation of the Sun to the South or the North.* Thus, this house was like a certain gate for the ascent of the Gods, concerning which more will be said later.

<margin>II House: Canopus.</margin> The second house was attributed to the care of Canopus. Now Canopus, or in Egyptian <term>Kanob</term> <note>original: "κάνωβ"</note>, was the Divinity or Genius of activated subterranean water, and the exciter for exerting fertility; concerning which see the very full treatment in Volume I, in the Chapter on Canopus. In his place, the Greeks put Aquarius, in which they do not differ from the Egyptians; for the Water-jar, which the Greeks imagined was poured out by Aquarius, the Egyptians used to paint by combining Aquarius and the Hydra into one image according to their usual custom. See the figure in the Diagram of the ancient Zodiac, which follows a little later.

The third house or mansion was attributed to the Divinity Ichton, which Iamblichus explains in these words: <margin>The III House of the Zodiac was called Ichton and why.</margin> *To this, Mercury sets before one indivisible thing, which he calls the first exemplar, or expression, or image, which he calls Ichton, in which is the first intellect and the first intelligible, which is worshiped by silence alone.*

I say that this is the pattern, not only in the Intelligible World, but also in the starry realms, and the idea of the lower things to be produced. For by this, the seeds of conceived things are led into the light; with this as a guide, the gate of life assigned to all things is opened around this station of the year. Thus, they appropriately indicated this by the hieroglyphic symbol of the fishes; for at this time of year, fish produce a vast and abundant offspring, and swelling with seeds, they fill all the paths of watery nature. Consequently, the name of this Genius <note>A presiding spirit or guardian deity</note> has persisted to this day from the etymology of "fishes." See the figure of this overseer in the diagram shortly following.

<margin>IV House of Ammun.</margin> The fourth house or mansion was attributed to Ammun, a Prince of great authority among the twelve Powers. His figure was distinguished by ram's horns <note>original: "arietinis cornibus"</note>, which indeed indicated nothing else hieroglyphically but the fertility of that station or mansion, by which the seeds that <term>Ichthon</term> <note>Likely referring to the previous mansion's deity associated with the sign of Pisces</note> had arranged are produced by Ammun into a varied harvest of generable things. But since this Ammun has been treated most extensively in the first Volume, Treatise 2, in the chapter on Ammun, and in Book 3 of the *Pamphilian Obelisk* regarding the hieroglyphic significance of the Ram, we refer the reader there, where they will find everything pertaining to this matter gathered from innumerable authors.

<margin>V House of Apis.</margin> The fifth house or mansion in the Zodiac was destined for the <term>Apis Bull</term>. Now, Apis was the greatest deity among the Egyptians, the presiding lord of agriculture, by whose help they believed the abundance of all things necessary for human life was provided. For this reason, they believed him to be the prefect of this mansion, in which the harvest was gathered in Egypt and the fruits were brought to maturity. <margin>Why it was attributed to the sign of the Bull.</margin> These things indicated nothing other than the effects of agriculture, of which Apis was the symbol. For the seeds which <term>Ichthon</term> had arranged, and <term>Ammun</term> had produced into luxuriant offspring, Apis was believed to ripen into the fruits necessary for human life. He was represented hieroglyphically under the figure of a Bull, which astrologers have preserved for this mansion even to this day. Let the reader see what we have discussed most copiously concerning Apis in Volume I, Treatise 2, in the chapter on Apis, and in Book 4 of the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, page 256, regarding the hieroglyphic significance of the Bull.

<margin>VI House attributed to Hercules and Apollo.</margin> The sixth house or mansion of the Zodiac was consecrated to Hercules and Apollo—or as Plutarch prefers, Helitomenos and Harpocrates—or as the Greeks please, Castor and Pollux; from whence the sign of Gemini emerged. For the Egyptians say that Isis, after his death, lay with Osiris and from him conceived the twins Helitomenos and Harpocrates, and that they were afterwards translated into heaven and placed over this mansion. Hence the two stars in Gemini, which the Arabs <margin>Horus.</margin> call *Ras Algeuze* <note>original: رأس الجوزاء - The Head of the Giant/Gemini</note>, <term>Abenregel</term> <note>The Arab astrologer Albohazen Haly Abenragel</note> calls *Garuklas and Apollun* <note>original: قرقلس وافولون - Arabic corruptions of "Herakles and Apollon"</note>. Although these names are most corrupt after the manner of the Arabs, they nevertheless indicate nothing other than Hercules and Apollo, or Horus; these two are equivalent to Helitomenos and Harpocrates. By them, nothing else is indicated hieroglyphically except the doubling of the strength of the Solar heat, which acquires its greatest power in this mansion. And indeed, strength is aptly expressed through Hercules, and the force of heat through Apollo or Horus, by which the clouds gradually in Ethio—

->And thus far we have described the six houses of the ascending Gods;<-
now from this point of the seventh house, there follow the six houses of the descending Gods, as the Egyptians maintain—or as Porphyrius <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on Egyptian religion.</note> maintains, the mansions of souls (both views can be supported, since souls cannot descend without the guidance of the Gods, according to the testimony of Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD), another influential Neoplatonist.</note>); the symbol of this point, as well as of the opposite sign, was the <term>dog</term> <note>original: "canis"</note>, the guardian of the fixed limit; or because the Dog-star, which in Egyptian we call <term>Sothis</term> <note>The star Sirius, whose rising heralded the Nile's flood.</note>, arose at this time, acting as a kind of precursor to the coming Nilotic inundation.
<margin>The Dog Sothis in Egyptian rises at this time.</margin>

The seventh house or mansion was consecrated to the Divinity <term>Hermanubis</term> <note>A syncretic deity combining Hermes/Mercury and Anubis.</note>, that is, to Mercury, whom they exhibited under the appearance of an Ibis; they believed his duty was to heap up immense masses of vapors and, as if attracted and stolen from all the storehouses of moist nature, to dissolve them into rains; from which, subsequently, great benefit proceeded from the flooding of the Nile. But as to why they placed the figure of the <term>Crab</term> <note>The zodiac sign Cancer.</note> in the place of the Ibis, the reason was that the Crab among the Egyptians was not a symbol of any particular Genius <note>A protective spirit or minor deity.</note>, but a hieroglyphic of the sun's turning. For just as the Crab is so fashioned by nature that it observes a backward motion in its walking; so the Sun, after it has reached the final limit of its elongation, gradually fails from further motion and the days diminish, as if it seems to follow the likeness of the Crab's backward motion. However, the mansion was dedicated not to the Crab, but to Hermanubis, as has been said, in the form of an Ibis <note>original: "Ibimorpho"</note>. Hence the Ancient Egyptians did not paint a Crab, but an Ibis, the hieroglyphic of the Genius ruling in this lodging. See more on this symbol below, and those things pertaining to this matter curiously treated in Book 4 of the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, in the chapter on the Ibis.

<margin>Why the Greeks placed the figure of the Crab in place of the Ibis.</margin>

He was painted in various ways, sometimes under the form of a man <term>with the shape of a lion</term> <note>original Greek: "λεοντομόρφῳ" (leontomorpho)</note>, sometimes under the simple figure of a reclining Lion, as will be explained in its proper time and place. He was a singular Divinity among the Egyptians, and of the highest veneration, about whom frequent discourses were circulated; for they believed that all administration over moist nature was committed to him. But these things, as I have said, we shall pursue most extensively in their proper places.

# CHAPTER II.

...we have treated all these matters extensively in the first Volume, second Treatise, in the chapter concerning Isis.

<margin>10th House: Omphta.</margin>
The tenth house or station was dedicated to a Spirit <note>Genius</note> whom the Egyptians called <note>original: ⲰⲘⲪⲦⲀ</note> Omphta. This was a beneficent Deity because Omphta distributed in just measure those things which Momphta and Isis had set in motion through the moisture of the Nile's inundation. From this, the hieroglyphic of the Balance or Libra crept into this station; for Omphta was believed to be the just executor and weigher <note>trutinator</note> of arranged affairs, which they believed took place at this position in the Zodiac. He was depicted in human form, holding a measuring rod in his right hand and a grain-measure <note>modium</note> on his head, as appears below in the Zodiac.

<margin>11th House: Typhon.</margin>
The eleventh house or station was dedicated to Typhon, a Spirit of a malignant and wasting nature, by whose scorching power moisture was dried up, trees were stripped of their finery, and the earth was left parched, dry, and scaly, with its moisture driven deep into its bowels. And from this they tell the fable that in this Month of Athyr <margin>Osiris shut in the Ark by Typhon.</margin> Osiris was shut into an Ark by Typhon; and that snares were set for Horus, the beauty of the perceptible World; from which the Isiac lamentations and mournings took their origin. They aptly displayed this catastrophe of perishing fertility <margin>Hieroglyphic.</margin> through a bull whose testicles a Scorpion bites, to indicate that the generative moisture of the earth fails by a certain wasting and Typhonic power especially at this station, as has been explained elsewhere. Consequently, from this very hieroglyphic, it pleased posterity to honor this house with the symbol of the Scorpion.

<margin>12th House: Nephtys.</margin>
The twelfth house or station was called Nephtys, the Spirit presiding over subterranean heat, lest everything be destroyed by the Typhonic power. For, as Plutarch says, the Mistress of the lower earth does not permit the moisture to perish entirely by the adverse force of Typhonic desiccation, wishing a temperate state to remain perpetually, since the entire beauty and harmony of the World could in no way exist if the fiery power were to fail. This is the Spirit to whose care the arms of Osiris—that is, of the Sun—were committed, which were (according to Plutarch) the dart, the spear, and the bow. By these nothing else was denoted than the tempered force of Solar heat, by which she strives to preserve the moisture that the scorching power of Typhon seeks to destroy; so that even from that time to the present day, the sign of Sagittarius [the Archer] has remained for this Station.

And these are the twelve <term>dodecaemoria</term> <note>twelve-parts or signs of the zodiac</note>, the houses or stations of the twelve Spirits of the Zodiac, which the ancient Egyptians, by the tradition of Hermes, were accustomed to arrange according to the <margin>12 Deities arranged by the Egyptians according to the pattern of nature.</margin> pattern of nature. The Greeks made this arrangement entirely their own, changing it only slightly and veiling it in various other fables. Furthermore, to each of these Spirits of the twelve signs, three other assistant Spirits were joined, whom they called <term>Decans</term> <note>rulers of ten degrees each</note>, so that the entire <margin>Who are the Decans in the Zodiac?</margin> Zodiac is divided among 36 Spirits. To each of these, different duties in administering the World's economy were committed by the supreme Spirit of all Nature, whom they therefore called <term>pantomorphon</term> or <term>polymorphon</term> <note>original Greek: παντόμορφον / πολύμορφον, meaning "all-formed" or "manifold-formed"</note>. <margin>The Manifold Spirit.</margin> Moreover, Hermes, in the *Pimander* <note>A foundational Hermetic text</note>, calls the Zodiac a tabernacle, constituted by a circle divided into twelve houses, according to the Ideas of all nature. <margin>Authorities: Hermes in the Pimander and Asclepius.</margin> But let us hear his words: *“But I would have you tell me this besides: how the twelve avengers of darkness are driven away by the opposing powers.”* TRISMEGISTUS: *“That tabernacle...”*

# CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS 157 CHAPTER II.

That, O son, is established in the circle of the Zodiac, which consists of that number twelve; and the numbers are one and all-forming, according to the ideas of nature for the wandering and circuit of man. And in the *Asclepius* <note>A famous Hermetic dialogue between Hermes Trismegistus and his disciple Asclepius.</note> he further describes them in these words: There are many kinds of Gods (arranged in a circle), and of all of them, one part is called intelligible <note>original: "intelligibilis"; referring to things grasped by the mind rather than the senses.</note>, and the other part is called sensible. They are not called intelligible because they are thought not to be subject to our senses; for we perceive them even more than those we call visible. For a sublime reason, and that of the divine <margin>The Horoscopic Gods who are rulers of the heavens <note>original Greek: ὀυάρχαι (ouarchai)</note></margin> standing beyond the minds and intentions of men, if it does not receive the words of those speaking with a more attentive obedience of the ears, it will fly past and flow away, or rather flow back, and mix itself with its own powerful waters. There are, therefore, Gods who are the Princes of all species. These are followed by the Gods of whom the Prince is the Sun <note>astrological symbol for Sol: ☉</note>. To these, the sensible ones are similar in both their origins, who accomplish all things through sensible nature, one through another; each one illuminating his own work of the heaven, or whatever it is that is comprised by that name. Jupiter <note>astrological symbol for Jupiter: ♃</note> is Jupiter (whom the Egyptians call **Hemphta**); for through the heaven, **Hemphta**, or Jupiter, provides life to all. It is, however, of the Sun <note>astrological symbol for Sol: ☉</note>: for the good of light is poured into us through the orb of the Sun; there are thirty-six (who are called the **Horoscopii** <note>The 36 Decans of the Egyptian zodiac, each ruling ten degrees.</note>) of the stars always fixed in the same place; of these, the Sun <note>astrological symbol for Sol: ☉</note> is the Prince, whom they call **all-forming** <note>original Greek: παντόμορφα (pantomorpha)</note>, who makes different forms in different species. These words are so clear that they seem to have pointed directly to the doctrine of Hermes established by us a little while ago. Indeed, Iamblichus <margin>Iamblichus.</margin> describes them so beautifully that he might seem to have explained them. I, he says, will tell you the cause in the first place, for which the sacred and ancient writers of the Egyptians thought various things about these; and moreover, the Wise men of this age do not speak of them with the same reasoning. For since there are many essences in the universe, and they differ among themselves in many ways; their principles were also rightly handed down as many, having different orders, and some principles by some Priests, indeed total or universal ones, as Seleucus relates. Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus.</note> himself handed them down in twenty thousand volumes, or as Manetho recounts, he handed them down in thirty thousand volumes, and likewise six thousand five hundred and twenty-five, and in them he demonstrated all things perfectly. But other ancients introduced other principles of particular essences here and there. It is necessary, therefore, to declare the truth briefly about all these, and first what you first asked. The first God is before being, and alone, the father of the first God, whom he begets remaining in his solitary Unity, and that is super-intelligible, and it would be the exemplar of him, who is called his own father, his own son, the sole-father, and God truly good. For he is greater, and first, and the fountain of all, and the root of those things which are first understood, and which understand, namely of the ideas. From this One, surely, the self-sufficient God unfolded himself. And therefore he is called self-sufficient, his own father, and prince by himself. For he is the principle, the God of Gods, Unity from one, the principle of essence above essence: for from him comes essence, therefore he is named the father of essence. For he himself is Being above being, the principle of intelligibles. These are the <margin>The most ancient principles of all.</margin> most ancient principles of all, which Mercury places before the ethereal, empyrean, and celestial Gods: composing a hundred books about the empyrean ones, and as many about the ethereal ones, and a thousand about the celestial ones. But according to another order, he places the God **Emepht** <margin>Emepht.</margin> before the celestial Gods as a Leader, whom he says is an intellect understanding, and turning intelligences into himself. Before this one, he places the impartible One, which he calls the first...

# CHAPTER II.

<margin>Ichton.</margin> ...the first model, or expression, or image, which he calls <term>Ichton</term> <note>original: "Ichton"; likely a corruption of a Greek or Egyptian term for the "First Image" or "Idea"</note>; in which is the first thinking subject and the first object of thought, which is worshipped by silence alone. Beyond these, however, other Leaders preside over the craftsmanship of visible things. For the craftsman-intellect <note>original: "opifex intellectus"; the Demiurge or creative mind</note>, who is both the Lord of Truth and wisdom, insofar as he proceeds into the realm of generation and brings the hidden power of latent reasons into the light, <margin>Amun.</margin> is called <term>Amun</term> <note>The Egyptian deity Amun, interpreted here as the "Hidden One" who reveals himself</note> in the Egyptian language; but insofar as he accomplishes all things without falsehood and with artistic skill <margin>Phta.</margin> together with Truth, he is named <term>Phta</term> <note>Ptah, the Egyptian creator-god of craftsmen</note>: the Greeks, however, call him <term>Vulcan</term> <note>Hephaestus</note>, considering only his craftsmanship: but insofar as he is the bringer of good things, he is called <margin>Osiris.</margin> <term>Osiris</term>; and he has other names because of his different powers and actions. There is also another sovereignty among them over the whole of the Elements placed in the realm of generation, and over their virtues; of which four are masculine and four are feminine: a Sovereignty which they attribute to the Sun. Likewise, another Sovereignty over all nature involved in generation is attributed to the Moon. <term>Marsilio</term> <note>Marsilio Ficino, the Renaissance Neoplatonist</note>. You can arrange the order in these matters to agree with <term>Proclus</term> <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher</note> in this way. First is the "One" itself, existing above all that can be understood. Second is the "One Being," or the unity of Being, in which its unity is placed before its being: it can also be called the "intelligible intellect" and its own father. Third is the intellect that is both intelligible and intellectual at once, the unity of the intellect, and the first expression, <term>Ichton</term>. Fourth is the "intellectual intellect" already unfolded, the Leader of the celestial Gods, <term>Emepht</term>. Fifth is the craftsman-intellect, the nearest Leader of the worldly craftsmen, who are the celestial, empyrean, and ethereal Gods: this is perhaps the intellect of the **Soul of the World** <note>original: "Anima Mundi"</note>, which is named <term>Amun</term>, <term>Phta</term>, <term>Vulcan</term>, <term>Osiris</term>. <term>Iamblichus</term> <note>A Syrian Neoplatonist who wrote on Egyptian mysteries</note>. Dividing the heaven into two parts, or four, or twelve, or thirty-six, or doubles of these, or in whatever other way, they also set Sovereignties over these, either fewer or more. Again, they place one Leader over these, and thus the treatise of the Egyptians concerning principles, proceeding from above to the lowest things, descends from the one into the multitude—governed, clearly, by one God—everywhere an indefinite nature is imperiously contained under a certain defined limit, especially by the exalted unity which is the cause of all. Indeed, God produced Matter by "materiality," namely, derived from "essentiality," which the craftsman, taking up as vital, uses to make simple and impassible spheres. But he took the last part of it to make generable and corruptible bodies. With these things thus distinguished, the doubts which you say you conceived in the Egyptian books you have read are easily resolved. For those which are circulated under the title of <term>Mercury</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note> contain Mercurial opinions, even if they often speak in the style of Greek Philosophers; for they were translated from the Egyptian language into Greek by men not unskilled in Philosophy. I would wish, however, that whatever things touch upon the first causes of worldly things would also declare the ultimate principles. Likewise, whoever treats the planets, the Zodiac, the Decans, the Horoscopes, and the stars as powerful Leaders, should hand down the particular distributions of the principles. Accordingly, the dogmas which are in the <term>Salaminiaca</term> <note>Likely referring to the "Salmeschiniaka," ancient astrological/hermetic texts</note> contain the shortest part of the Mercurial arrangements. Likewise, those things which are treated concerning the appearances of stars, or their occultations, or the waxing or waning of the Moon, have their assignment of causes among the last things according to the Egyptians. Truly, the Egyptians do not think that all things are natural, but they distinguish Life—both Intellectual and animal—from nature, not only in the World, but also in men. And since they have placed intellect and reason, existing according to themselves, in charge, they believe that whatever happens, happens in this way; and they assert that the craftsman is the principal father of those things involved in generation.

# ## CHAPTER II

<margin>Explanation of the Barberini Tablet.</margin>
The globe, shaped like a circular child <note>original: "κυκλο-πειδόμορφος"</note>, shows the unity of the triform Deity, dwelling in the solitary contemplation of itself. The principal figure, however, indicates the descent of this same triform, all-shaped Deity into the vastness of all nature. Upon its head, it bears a Lion’s head inserted into a sextile Moon <note>Symbol: ☾</note>, by which power and dominion over the Sun <note>Symbol: ☉</note> and Moon <note>Symbol: ☾</note> are shown; this power is also declared by its seated posture. It bears a ram’s horn to demonstrate its fecundity and its Ammonian virtue <note>referring to the god Jupiter-Ammon</note>. In its left hand, it holds a Scorpion and a dog; by which Anubis and Typhon are aptly indicated, according to the testimony of Plutarch, and it represents the drying power of the Sun, which is exerted most greatly when the Sun <note>Symbol: ☉</note> enters Scorpio, while the trees are stripped of leaves and the earth of its grasses. In its right hand, it holds two Serpents and the figure of a Lion entwined with a staff; by these, the force and power over life and death, generation and corruption, good and evil, are indicated in the Kingdom of Momphta. Thus, through the Scorpion, a deadly animal, the death and destruction of things—or the preparation of evils—is indicated according to Horus; through the two Serpents, the double life of the World, celestial and elementary; and through the Lion of Momphta, the presiding spirit of moist nature is aptly indicated.

Furthermore, through the images placed around the many-formed Deity—serpents and others, such as staffs shaped like the hoopoe bird <note>term: cucuphomorphis; staffs topped with the head of a hoopoe, a symbol of gratitude or piety</note>, whips, and handled crosses <note>note: the Ankh</note>—represented under the figures of a Boy, a Lion, a Hawk, and an Ibis, they show the vital fecundity which they flow into the World, the Sun, the Moon, and the Elements for the variety of things; all of which will be explained more extensively in their proper places. It tramples the heads of two Crocodiles looking in different directions, by which it is beautifully indicated that it holds all pernicious Typhonic and Arimanian <note>note: likely referring to Ahriman, the Zoroastrian spirit of evil</note> force, which extends through the Rising and Setting, perfectly subjected to itself.

Beneath the Crocodiles, a curved surface is seen full of Genii <note>term: Genii; guardian spirits or minor deities</note>, followers of the all-shaped Deity and tutelary ministers of affairs, by whom the entire Kingdom of Momphta is administered through the fit arrangement of the seasons. Some of these are standing, others are sitting. The standing ones are the first three from the right and three from the left, with five intermediate ones in a sitting posture. Starting from the first on the right, the Genius is lion-headed <note>original: "λεοντικέφαλος"</note> <note>Symbol: ☉ ☾</note> <margin>Lion-shaped Genius <note>Symbol: ☉ ☾</note>.</margin> holding a grappling hook in its hand, clothed in a sacred veil, and holding a globe on its head; by this, the Genius is noted for conferring a corroborative force and solidity upon things against the dissipative force of matter. There follows a hawk-shaped Genius <note>original: "ἱερακόμορφος"</note> <note>Symbol: ☉</note>, that is, with a Hawk’s face, distinguished by a hoopoe-headed staff, by which <margin>Hawk-shaped Genius <note>Symbol: ☉</note>.</margin> the Solar force in heat and moisture—which is the cause of the variety of things—is indicated. There follows a third cat-shaped Genius <note>original: "αἰλουρόμορφος"</note> <note>Symbol: ☾</note>, either of the species of a Cat, or what is the same <margin>Cat-shaped <note>Symbol: ☾</note>.</margin> thing, a dog-headed <note>original: "Cynocephalus"</note> Lunar Genius.

To these, three other Genii respond from the opposite side, the first of which has a Hawk’s face with a feather in its hand, showing the swift force of Solar motion; the second in the form of an Ibis, with a feather in its hand, the swift force of Lunar motion; the third, by its dog-like form, indicates Anubis, the protector of the Horizon according to Plutarch. In the middle, the figure of a Serpent <margin>Symbols of the Zodiac.</margin> biting its own tail in a wavy coil is inserted, by which the year or the Zodiac is aptly indicated, according to Horus. It is wavy, or arranged in the figure of flowing water, to express the circuits which the Sun completes through the twelve signs and as many months—as if in the waves of the celestial sea—and while it performs this by its motion, it is the cause of the production of all things that are in the World. # CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER II.

...for the signs or Months are aptly indicated by circles. Because, however, five days are missing from the solar year to reach 360, they wished to signify these by five <margin>The 5 intercalary days.</margin> principal circles, over which as many Spirits <note>Latin: Genii; protective or guiding spirits associated with specific times or places.</note> preside. The mythology according to the mind of <margin>Plutarch, *On Osiris and Isis*.</margin> Plutarch is as follows: Rhea, they say, having secretly coupled with Saturn, was cursed by the Sun (who had detected the outrage) so that she should give birth neither in a Month nor in a year. But Mercury, captured by love for the Goddess, lay with her; afterwards, playing at dice with the Moon, he won as victor the seventieth part of each day and added them to the 360 days of the year. These five days are now called <term>Misi</term> <note>A Coptic-derived term for "birth."</note> by the Egyptians, and by the Greeks <margin>What is Misi? The birthdays of the Gods.</margin> <term>Epagomenoi</term> <note>Greek: ἐπαγόμενοι; "added" or "intercalary" days.</note>, that is, "additional" days, and are celebrated as the birthdays of the Gods. On the first of these days was born <term>Osiris</term>, Lord of all things; on the second day <term>Arueris</term> was born, whom some call Apollo and others the elder Horus; on the third <term>Typhon</term> leaped forth, not at his proper time or place, but breaking through with a blow to the side; on the fourth <term>Isis</term> in the marshes; on the fifth <term>Nephthys</term>, whom they also name the End, Venus, and Victory.

We, however, have restored these five minor deities from hieroglyphic doctrine so that <margin>Explanation of the 5 guardian Spirits.</margin> we may understand the first day to be dedicated to Hermanubis, the second to Anubis, the third to Isis, the fourth to Horus, and the fifth to Osiris as the true guardians of Egypt, whom the figure expressed here denotes. For Hermanubis, or the Ibis-headed Hermes, is expressed by an Ibis-shaped statue; Anubis by a <term>kynoprosopon</term> <note>Greek: κυνοπρόσωπον; "dog-faced."</note> or canine face; Isis by a female face with her veil; Horus by a child’s face; and finally Osiris <margin>What the symbols held in the hands of the statues indicate.</margin> by a leonine and maned countenance. They hold feathers in their hands to hint at the hidden motion of their activity. The circles on the heads of the first, second, and fourth indicate divine force and power over the World. The <term>eyed Phallus</term> <note>Latin: Phallus oculatus; a symbol of generative power combined with divine oversight.</note> placed upon the head of Isis in the middle indicates the multitude of seminal abundance, over which Isis stands as the passive principle of things. Finally, the fifth figure, Osiris, carries a serpent-bearing globe on his head to show that he is the active principle of worldly life.

And these are the moderators of the year, and the tutors and preservers of all things born in the lower World throughout the course of the entire year. Yet, because the happiness of lower things indicated by the said five guardian Spirits has opposing powers, by whose malice the things of nature could be variously <margin>Opposing Spirits.</margin> disturbed; hence they aptly placed at the side guardian Spirits who drive away evil (as indicated by the hooks, whips, and similar symbols of averting power, by which the malignant force is driven away from the Spirits, and the intended variety and abundance of things is preserved). Below these, however, are two images, <margin>What the spear, Hippopotamus, and pierced Crocodile signify.</margin> the first of which transfixes a Hippopotamus with a spear, and the other a Crocodile. By these is indicated the <term>Bebonian force</term> <note>A term for Typhon's destructive power, mentioned by Manetho.</note> (for so Manetho, in Plutarch, names the Typhonic force), by which they denote an obstacle or impediment. The Hippopotamus and the Typhonic Crocodile resist things proceeding rightly and tending toward their end; however, the spirit of Horus and Osiris finally destroys and scatters this. These things harmonize beautifully with what Plutarch recites in his book *On Osiris and Isis*, namely that at Hermopolis <margin>Plutarch.</margin> an image of Typhon is shown: <note>original Greek: Ἵππον ποτάμιον, ἐφ' ᾧ βέβηκεν ἵεραξ ὄφει μαχόμενος... "A river horse, upon which stands a hawk fighting a serpent, signifying Typhon by the horse, and the power and principle by the hawk."</note> a Hippopotamus upon which a Hawk stands fighting a Serpent, designating Typhon by the horse, and the power and principle by the hawk.

...pius, by whose power that [evil] is often not exhausted, but rather disturbed and disturbing because of its malice. You see in this figure a Divinity <note>original: "λeοντόμορφος" (leontomorphos) - lion-shaped</note> holding a serpent in the left hand, and with the right hand twisting a small spear against a hippopotamus; for Osiris, the life of all things, by the virtue of his rays—as if struck by certain spears—easily overcomes that Bebonian <note>A reference to Bebon or Babys, a name associated with Typhon/Set</note> force and kills the enemy of the end of natural things. Against this enemy, Mophta shows himself as a diligent antagonist, whom the lion-shaped statue <note>original: "λeοντόμορφος"</note>—equipped with a staff shaped like a hoopoe's head <note>original: "cucuphomorpho"</note>—indicates by following from behind and breaking its power. This same thing is shown on the opposite side by the figure of a hawk piercing a crocodile with a weapon. See Plutarch in the cited place. For they called all things that were evil and harmful, having a certain repugnance to nature, the effects and works of Typhon; when the Sun destroys these, he simultaneously reduces the world's disorder <note>original: "ἀκοσμίαν" (akosmian)</note> into a proper balance. Furthermore, by the dogs lying at the sides of the wavy serpent, the guardianship of the Sun's approach and retreat is indicated; or as Plutarch wishes, the rising of the Nile, which the celestial dogs <note>The stars Sirius and Procyon</note> move and promote by their rising. But that these things are so, Clement of Alexandria demonstrates in clear words in the 5th book of the *Stromata* with these words: *There are those, however, who wish the Tropics to be signified by the dogs, who guard and, like doorkeepers, observe the approach of the Sun to the South and the North.*

What the Divinities assigned to the Zodiac indicate.

These things having been thus explained, let us now set forth the duties of the individual Spirits <note>original: "Geniorum"</note> described in the Zodiac. By Anubis, therefore, or the dog-shaped Mercury, they understood nothing other than the guardian of the World's heat. By Ichton, the disposition of moisture for the perfecting of the generation of things. By Amun, the fertilizing power of heat. By Apis, the ripening of fruits and the harvest. By the Twins, Hercules and Apollo, the heating power of the Sun. By Ibis, the rising of Sothis <note>The star Sirius</note>, the precursor of the Nilotic inundation. By Momphta, the disposing power of the Nile's increase. By Isis, the abundance of grain to follow. By Omphta, the equal tempering of the earth for the scattering of seed. By Typhon, the final drying out of the earth and the enclosure of beneficial moisture into subterranean passages. Finally, by Nephtys, the rescue of moisture from all destruction. To these, just as many major gods and goddesses of the nations correspond, whom you may contemplate as shown on page 251 of the *Pamphilian Obelisk*. The Hebrews and Arabs also, imitating the Egyptians, likewise divide their Zodiac into the protections of twelve Angels; since we have shown their names in the Kabbalah of the Hebrews and Saracens, we have thought it superfluous to repeat them here to the nausea of the reader.

Why and how the Egyptians place Capricorn as the first sign.

Almost all astronomers begin the order of the signs from Aries; which the Egyptians also do: whence someone might perhaps wonder why we have attributed the first sign or twelfth-part <note>original: "dodecamorium"</note> to Capricorn or Anubis. I answer, that we can consider the order of the signs in this place in two ways.
