# CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER III.

...themselves, whether astronomically or mystically. Those considering the signs astronomically took their beginning from that point of the spring season when the day equals the night <note>The Vernal Equinox</note>; this is observed by astronomers even to this day. However, those considering them mystically—specifically regarding the administration of the Spirits <note>original: "Geniorum"</note> and Gods in the worldly economy—took the order of the signs and Gods from the point of the winter solstice, which they called the "ascent of the Gods." They did this so that if they began the arrangement of the houses of the Spirits from the spring equinox, the order of the ascending Gods would not be disturbed. And this is the reason why we, following the Initiates <note>original: "Mystas"</note> of the Egyptians, have preserved this order. Now that these things have been explained, let us see what the characters of the signs mean and from where they drew their origin.

-><margin>The origin of the signs and the characters of the 12 signs of the Zodiac.</margin><-

Mercury Trismegistus <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure identified with the Egyptian god Thoth, credited with inventing writing and science.</note>, after he had assigned his own Spirits to each of the twelve divisions <note>original: "dodecamorijs"</note> of the Zodiac, found it exceedingly laborious to always place full hieroglyphic images in astronomical work whenever he wished to denote a sign. Therefore, he established certain abbreviations drawn from those very images in place of the full figures. This custom has been preserved from that time until this very day through a certain continuous succession and tradition. But let us explain each one, making a beginning in the manner of the astronomers with Aries.

<margin>
I Sign $\Upsilon$
</margin>

The first sign in the astronomical manner is Aries <note>The Ram</note>, called *Amun* in Egyptian; it was depicted under the figure of a man conspicuous with the horns of a ram. However, in the shorthand business of astronomical computation, so that they would not be forced to always write the entire image, astronomers placed only the two horns of the Ram in this way:
<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: A square box containing a stylized depiction of two ram's horns, illustrating the origin of the Aries glyph.</note>
to which corresponds the symbol continued by later astronomers until these times, which follows: $\Upsilon$.

<margin>
II Sign $\succ$
</margin>

The second sign is Taurus <note>The Bull</note>, which the Egyptians call *Apis* <note>original: "απιν"</note>, a most great Deity; it was exhibited under the form of a Bull, as is still in use today. Therefore, lest they be forced to paint an entire bull every time this sign was mentioned, they placed only the head of the Bull with its horns, as follows:
<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: A square box containing a frontal view of a bull's head with prominent horns, illustrating the origin of the Taurus glyph.</note>
to which corresponds the modern character of Taurus: $\succ$.

<margin>

</margin>

The third sign holds the Gemini <note>The Twins</note>, whom the Egyptians call Hercules and Apollo, or *Hulitomenon* and *Harpocrates*. These were two hieroglyphic statues of each, joining their hands to one another. Lest they be forced to paint these when mention of this sign was made, they found this epitomatic <note>shorthand or summarized</note> character in place of the statues by which the said Twins were expressed, which astronomers use even to this day, as follows:
<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: A square box depicting two anthropomorphic figures (representing Gemini) seated or standing together, with arms joined/crossed, illustrating the origin of the Gemini glyph II.</note>
$\text{\textII}$.

->The sixth sign is dedicated to the Virgin ♍︎, whom the Egyptians name Isis, the discoverer of grain; for this reason, they depicted her hieroglyphically under the form of a Virgin conspicuous with a triple ear of corn. So that they would not always be forced to paint this image when she was mentioned, they formed three ears of grain bound by a tie, and the character of the Virgin emerged as follows: <note>Hieroglyphic symbol: Three ears of wheat or grain stalks tied together with a cord</note>. Later generations, not grasping the reason for this, placed this character ♍︎ in place of the three ears, which nevertheless does not deviate much from the ancient character. Moreover, they assigned three ears because in Egypt the harvest was performed three times a year, on account of the extreme abundance of the earth, which she herself represented.<-

IX Sign
<note>Zodiac symbol: Sagittarius (♐︎)</note>
</margin>
->The ninth sign is the Bow-bearer or Sagittarius, but he is called *Nephte* by the Egyptians, the <term>rival-in-art</term> <note>original Greek: ἀντίτεχνος (antitechnos), meaning a professional rival or opponent</note> of Typhon. ### C H A P T E R IV.

->On the origin, names, duties, and characters of the seven Planets.<-

Manilius rightly and wisely sings in Book 1 of the *Astronomicon*:

<margin>Manilius</margin>

> Teachable ingenuity conquered all by trying,
> Nor did it first impose an end and measure on things,
> Until reason ascended the heavens, and grasped the nature
> Of things from deep causes, and saw whatever exists etc.
> Which, after it traced each thing back to its own causes,
> It strove to know the nearby mass of the World from on high,
> And to encompass the whole heaven in the mind,
> And assigned to the signs their own forms and names,
> And noted what turns they played under a fixed law,
> And that all things are moved by the Divine Will of the World,
> With the stars changing fates in a varied order.

<margin>Hermes was the first observer of the motion of the planets.</margin> Our Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage of Egypt</note> was the first among mortals who, after he had completed the twelve-fold System of the Zodiac and seen that some stars were not fixed, but traveled back and forth in a wandering course through the spacious paths of the heavens, applied his burning mind to exploring the motions and the laws of those motions, in order to understand such an exotic matter. He discovered that seven stars especially, out of the entire army of stars, were endowed with this wandering nature—yet with this condition: that all of them, following the slanted arrangement of the Zodiac, completed their course only within a certain and defined period of years; some indeed more quickly, some more slowly; some treading the path of the Zodiac more directly and precisely, others more irregularly. And first, indeed, he noted the Sun, which with a constant and unswerving step—

<margin><unclear>Hermes, Book 15 on the nature of things, chapter 12; and Book 1 on Generations; and Book 4, chapter 11.</unclear></margin>

# CLASS VII. MATHEMATICAL HIEROGLYPHICS. CHAPTER VI.

<page-num>469</page-num>

...he observed with the greatest zeal and the experience of many years that [the Sun] held the middle line of the Zodiac; but that the Moon and the other five stars <note>The five planets known to the ancients: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> did not, but rather wandered back and forth within a breadth of six degrees. That this is so is expressly testified by the Scholiast on Hyginus <note>An anonymous commentator on the astronomical work of Gaius Julius Hyginus.</note>, whoever he may have been. "Mercury," he says, "was the first of mortals to show the obliquity of the Zodiac, and that the courses of the planets are completed beneath it." Nay, Trismegistus himself in the *Pimander* <note>The *Poimandres*, the first tractate of the *Corpus Hermeticum*, a collection of Greek texts attributed to the legendary sage Hermes Trismegistus.</note> testifies to this concerning himself in the following words:

**ASCLEPIUS:** In what way then, Trismegistus, are those things which are in the World changed along with those things which are moved? For you said that the wandering spheres are moved by the sub-sphere of the fixed stars <note>original: *aplane* (from Greek *aplanes*), referring to the sphere of the fixed stars which does not "wander" like the planets.</note>.

**TRISMEGISTUS:** That is not motion, O Asclepius, but resistance; for they do not travel in the same way, but in a contrary manner. Indeed, this opposition contains a stable reverberation of motion: for the repercussion is the agitation of a stationary state, and therefore the wandering Spheres, by running through each other in a contrary and clearly subordinate way, are agitated by a contrary meeting around an opposition of this kind by that which stands firm; which indeed cannot be otherwise; for the Bears themselves <note>The constellations Ursa Major and Ursa Minor.</note> which you know, which neither ever rise nor set but perpetually recur around the same point—do you think they move, or rather stand still?

**ASCLEPIUS:** They move, O Trismegistus.

**TRISMEGISTUS:** By what motion, Asclepius?

**ASCLEPIUS:** By a motion running eternally around the same point.

**TRISMEGISTUS:** But truly that circulation is the same motion contained by a stationary state, for it prohibits the "around the same" from that which is above it; and that which is above it, being hindered, presses upon the "around the same": and so the firm contrary agitation is perpetually established by the opposition itself. I will place an example before your eyes from the living things on earth, just as when a man swims: while the water is running against him, the repercussion of his hands and feet together makes the man stay still, so that he does not glide along with the water, or sink into it.

<margin>From Book 2 of the *Astronomy*, chapter 14.</margin>

By these words, what else does he indicate but the proper motion of the planets, by which they are carried from east to west in a direction contrary to the rapid movement of the world? Modern thinkers also demonstrate this motion by the diurnal motion, and by the motion of a man walking in a contrary direction within that same movement. But since these things are commonly known, it shall suffice to have indicated them. Therefore, let us proceed to the imposition of names and characters.

<margin>Mercury imposes names upon the planets.</margin>

Mercury, therefore, just as he was powerful in the highest and most admirable dexterity of wit, so he concealed his individual inventions with no less industry of mind. This is evident first in the imposition of the planetary Names. For when he saw that the whole order of nature rested upon these seven wanderers, and that all lower things were subjected to their fates, he judged that they should be called the greatest and principal Divinities <note>original: *Numina*</note> of the sensible World. The Sun indeed—whom he calls the most excellent God of the celestial Gods in the *Pimander*, and whom the remaining wanderers obey as a Prince and King—he therefore called **Osiris**, which in Egyptian signifies "many-eyed," and <term>Ach</term> <note>Kircher often attempts to link Egyptian names to Hebrew or Coptic roots; here *Ach* is presented as a term for "Holy Lord".</note> also signifies Holy Lord, because by the rays of his light he grants life to all gifts, as we shall explain more fully below.

<margin>The Sun, Prince and Divinity of heaven: Osiris or Potiris.</margin>

The Moon indeed he called **Isis**, the wife of Osiris: for from their conjunction and copulation he believed that visible variety, shining forth in the majesty of all nature, was born; by attributing a hot <unclear>seed</unclear> to the Sun and a most fertile one to the Moon, which are as it were the first elements of all generation. And he placed these two planets as intermediates between the elements and the remaining higher planets, as the arbiters of all nature, as shown above in the hieroglyphic constitution of the System of the World.

<margin>... ... ... Wife of Osiris, Queen of heaven.</margin>

The hieroglyphic of Saturn is composed of that of the Moon together with that of the Elements; that of Jupiter consists of the same, and is the same, except that it holds a different position; the character of Mars is composed of that of the Sun and that of Aries joined together by the straight line of the cross; the note of Venus is formed from that of the Sun and the Elements; and finally, the hieroglyphic of Aries is formed of two semicircles connected at a common point.*

### On the excellence of Egypt, and the study of Astrology.

**E**gypt was a climate of wonderful things, a mine of prodigies, the Garden of the High God on earth; no one who considers it now believes it once existed in its primary state. Although it is one city, it appears as if many were joined together along their shore. Gardens at the back of the cities, as if one, coalesced into each other; then fields were seen at the back of the gardens. Furthermore, it was a journey of one day from Alexandria even unto Aswan <note>original: "Afouan"</note>, and the gardens extended their excellence to one another. The Egyptians were formerly masters of a very great Kingdom, and being mixed from various nations—Copts, Greeks, and Amalekites—they likewise worshipped idols. After the flood, they were instructed in various sciences, especially incantations, prestigiatory magic, and Chemistry: and their images, made according to the influence of the stars, are found derived from here. Furthermore, <margin>Monf is the same as Memphis.</margin> the city of Monf, distant 12 miles from ancient Fustat <note>original: "Phestad"</note>, was the seat of the Kingdom. Their Priests excelled other Priests in learning and wisdom, just as the Greeks say of them. When they applied themselves to the stars for the sake of foretelling, they believed the stars infused sciences into them, announced future events, and taught them the art of natural things and divination. Know that in truth they taught the more abstract and hidden sciences, and they themselves had learned the most celebrated arts of divination and the most excellent laws; they made speaking statues, painted moving images, constructed buildings higher than all other buildings, and carved their sciences upon the hardest stones. Egypt consisted of 85 Provinces, of which 45 were in Sais in Lower Egypt, and 40 in Upper Egypt. And in each Province there was a leader of the Priests or Magi. However, that one among them who observed the 7 moving planets for 7 years, they called "ignorant"; but he who for 49 years observed each of the planets <margin>"Dripping" or "Infusing" is the same as Prophet.</margin> for 7 years, they called the <term>Infusing</term> or <term>Dripping</term> <note>Latin: "Stillans" or "Infundens". This refers to a high priest who "pours out" or "drops" celestial wisdom like dew.</note> one. Out of honor for him, the King rises, and he sits only near the King; nor does he govern anything except what belongs to the King. The Priests, having entered with the craftsmen, stand before the "Dripping" one, and each of the Priests, separated by the planet which he serves, does not abandon his equal: and he is called the servant of that planet, namely the Servant of the Moon, the servant of Mercury, the servant of Venus, the servant of the Sun, the servant of Mars, the servant of Jupiter, and the servant of Saturn. Then the "Dripping" one questions each of them, saying: "Where is your Planet found?" and he answers, "In such a sign, in such a degree, and in such a minute." Thus he also questions one or another, who instructs him: and when he has recognized the mansions of the seven planets, he says to the King, "It is fitting for the King that..."

# CHAPTER V.

->*Concerning the Spirits of the signs of the Zodiac, their powers, qualities, and how the Egyptians represented the complexity of all things through them.*<-

<margin>How the pyramidal influence from the celestial signs is to be considered.</margin> The Egyptians, under the instruction of Mercury <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage</note>, conceived that from the twelve <term>dodecamoria</term> <note>the twelve 30-degree segments or "houses" of the Zodiac</note> as many luminous and inverted pyramids were drawn down even to the center of the earth. The base of these occupied the very length and breadth of the dodecamoria, while the vertex rested upon the center of the earth, as I have said; they said that the entire order of nature was contained beneath these. They also displayed these hieroglyphically in the temple of Heliopolis <note>the "City of the Sun," a major religious center in ancient Egypt</note>, constructed in the form of a Zodiac, by means of twelve Obelisks, as was proven in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* on pages 171 and 177. Moreover, a principal Spirit presided over each pyramid’s influence upon the lower symbols; he governed everything subject to his pyramid, each according to the classes of natural things assigned to them. These effects differed with a notable diversity as often as the seven <term>Usiarchs</term> <note>original: *Usiarchos*; "rulers of substance," referring to the seven classical planets</note> or planets happened to fall into these regions of the dodecamoria. But because they saw that a whole dodecamorium did not always produce one and the same effect, but one at the beginning, another in the middle, and finally another at its end; they placed three other Spirits over each dodecamorium divided into three parts. These they called sometimes <term>Decans</term> <note>rulers of ten degrees of the zodiac</note>, sometimes <term>Horoscopes</term> <note>here meaning "markers of the hour" or specific degrees</note>, and later the Arabs called them <term>Faces</term>; and so 36 <term>Horoscopes</term> were contained in the entire circuit of the Zodiac, as the managers, dispensers, and administrators of all lower nature, whom we have shown above from Hermes and Iamblichus. And from here proceeded those twelve <term>mystical chains of all things</term>, by which lower things were connected with higher things in a certain wonderful manner. And these chains, most frequent among the hieroglyphic inscriptions, were like twelve bonds of nature, by which they linked the lower or <term>material</term> <note>original: *hyleos*; from the Greek 'hyle' for matter</note> things with the intermediate grades of celestial nature,

And they believed these were so aptly bound together with the supreme choir of the twelve signs <note>original: "dodecamorio," referring to the twelve 30-degree segments of the zodiac</note> of the immortal Gods, that whoever found a single chain <margin>12 Chains of things.</margin> corresponding to a certain specific sign, was considered to have likewise grasped the entire economy of the analogous classes of nature subject to a specific twelve-fold pyramid. They believed this knowledge was inserted into the soul devoted to wisdom by the supreme All-Forming <note>original: "Pantamorpho"</note> Divinity, or the providence of all things, coupled through love. For, as Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who heavily influenced Kircher’s view of Egyptian mysticism.</note> says concerning the *Soul and the Demon*, the said providence is equally beneficent and sincere, the adorner of all things, and consequently unencumbered by those who are refined, running through all things, especially because it is nowhere restrained. In no different a way, the Divinities subject to it are present to all, free from all, filling all things with themselves; they are mixed with many things in various places, and they love their offspring—that is, the series of subject things. For since Love provides for, preserves, and contains things divinely loved, the Gods love the super-celestial Gods; the celestial Gods love the celestial spheres committed to them; and the Divinities of the spheres love each of the orders of the material worlds destined for them. But let us hear the words of Proclus in the cited passage: <margin>Proclus, book on the Soul and the Demon.</margin> *“The sacred oracles therefore indicate that this Love of the Divine binds all things together and resides in all things. Truly, if it connects all things, it joins us to the prefectures of the Demons <note>In this context, "Demons" refers to "daimons" or intermediary spirits, not evil entities.</note>. Diotima <note>The female philosopher mentioned in Plato's Symposium as Socrates' teacher on the subject of Love.</note> called this a 'Great Demon,' since it fills the entire middle space between those things which are desired and those which desire. That which is to be loved claims the first rank for itself; the lover, however, takes the third rank from the beloved. Finally, Love occupies the middle between both, gathering and binding together in turn the desirer and the desired, and filling the inferior with the better. Now, among the intelligible and hidden Gods, it unites the intelligible intellect to the first and secret beauty through a certain life better than intelligence. Therefore, the Theologian of the Greeks <note>Likely referring to Orpheus or Plato.</note> himself calls that love 'blind.' In those things, however, which are outside the intelligible realm and not yet illuminated, it is an indissoluble bond for all things perfected by it. For a bond is a certain union, but one with much distinction. Wherefore the sacred oracles are accustomed to call the fire of this love a 'joiner'; for proceeding from the intelligible intellect, it binds all subsequent things to each other and to itself. It reconciles, therefore, all the Gods to intelligible beauty, the Demons to the Gods, and joins us to the Demons and the Gods. In the Gods it subsists primarily; in the Demons secondarily; and in souls through a certain third process pre-existing in the first. In the Gods, again, it is above essence—for every race of the Gods is of such a kind—but in Demons it is through essence; and finally in souls through the effect of illustration. And this threefold order seems similar to the threefold power of the intellect.”*

# CHAPTER V. EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: HIEROGLYPHIC EXERCISES.

...[the zodiacal] path: they superstitiously believed that whoever was born under a certain <term>dodecamorio</term> <note>A "twelfth-part" or specific sign of the zodiac</note> of the pyramid, influenced by such and such a presiding Planet, was loved by its <term>Genius</term> <note>A guardian spirit or tutelary deity</note> or Genii, as if committed to their faith and care. They believed that all talents, whether of nature or of grace, which belonged to that same <term>dodecamorio</term> or ruling planet, were granted to the individual. If these Genii were of a malignant nature and at odds with the Genii of the <term>dodecamoria</term>, the person born would also be of a bad character; but if they were beneficial and sympathetic, they asserted the newborn would be similar. Thus, the Egyptians ascribed the outcomes of events not so much to the stars themselves as to the Genii presiding over them. <margin>The vanity of Astrology.</margin> Hence there was such great ardor in appeasing them, and such great care and anxiety in winning their favor through sacrifices and <term>praxas</term> <note>original Greek: "praxeis" (πράξεις), meaning ritual acts or magical operations</note> ceremonies. This is quite different from the Astrologers of our own time, who rashly ascribe the fortune of men to a certain fatal necessity of the stars. But let us return to the subject at hand.

The <term>dodecamoria</term> were therefore arranged in such a way that celestial things corresponded with elemental things, and these in turn with celestial and Angelic things—and finally all things with the supreme moderator of all—by a certain exact analogy. Following the testimony of Psellus <note>Michael Psellus, a 11th-century Byzantine scholar known for his writings on demons and the occult</note>, they called these <term>seiras</term> <note>original Greek: "seiras" (σειρὰς), meaning chains</note>, that is, chains, by which the highest things were connected to the lowest, the lowest to the middle, and the middle to the highest in a wonderful proportion, according to the twelve Classes of the nature of beings. Among these <margin>The Fiery, Watery, Airy, and Earthy Trigon.</margin> were the four Elements: fire, air, water, and earth. They attributed Fire to Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius, which formed the fiery <term>trigon</term> <note>A "trigon" or triplicity is a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element</note> in the Zodiac. Earth they attributed to Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn, which formed the earthy trigon; Air to Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius, which formed the airy trigon; and Water to Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces, which formed the watery trigon. To these they joined all the remaining orders of beings which in any way agreed with one of these four mentioned Elements, including all their species: such as stones, metals, flowers, plants, trees, quadrupeds, birds, aquatic creatures, and the human complexion. Those which by their nature obtained a dry and warm temperament were attributed to Aries, as were other signs likewise warm and dry. <margin>Whence the triplicity of the signs of the Zodiac had its origin.</margin> From these same Classes, they assigned to the earthy sign those things which were cold and dry, expressing the nature and complexion of said sign: and likewise for the other airy and watery signs. And from this emerged that partition of the Zodiac into its trigons or triplicities. In like manner, they applied the nature and property of the seven Planets to the said twelve houses. However, since we have taught these and similar things at great length in the <term>Astrological Kabbalah of the Hebrews</term> <note>original: "Gabala Astrologica Hebræorum", referring to Kircher's own earlier work or section</note>, we refer the reader there: in this place, we have only judged it necessary to reveal those things which were said there according to the mind of the ancient Hebrews, so that they might be clearly seen to correspond in all things according to the mind of the Egyptians. Indeed, you may contemplate all these things in the following <term>pinace</term> <note>A table or illustrative plate</note>.

<note>original Hebrew: ועל דעת חכמת מצרים המזלות י״ב והם מושלות בכל דברי תחתיים מן עשבי הארץ עד החיות ושרץ היבשת ולכל אחד ממזלות מבנה מלאך המושל בכל מה תחתיו</note>

Indeed, according to the science of the Egyptians, there are twelve signs, and they dominate all those things placed under them, from herbs even to the animals and reptiles of the earth; and an Angel presides over each figure, ruling all things that are under him. Afterward, he describes the signs in a long discourse, assigning the individual things which pertain to its dominion according to innumerable classes of things, in exactly that order which we described in the preceding table. Lest I be forced to transcribe entire books, I shall hereafter endeavor to reduce these matters into tables, so that we might compensate for the massive volume of material with a certain brevity. Furthermore, they proceed in a not dissimilar fashion in describing the secrets of the seven planets, to each of which they first assign their own Spirits <term>Genii; protective or guiding spirits associated with celestial bodies</term>, and then they connect under each one the chains of things analogous to the planets, taking the beginning of their discussion from the Sun. But read the Arabian author himself discussing the seals of the seven planets in *Hieroglyphic Medicine*, where all things are explained more diffusely. Meanwhile, lest we stuff the book with exotic citations, it seemed best to place here a summary <term>anacephaleoticam; a Greek-derived term for a recapitulation or summary table</term> table, in which you will behold, placed before your eyes in a single synopsis, whatever the Author pursues with laborious speech and the most diffuse discourse.

They called these the Decans, or "Faces." The presiding spirits over each, according to the testimony of Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Egyptian god Thoth, credited with the invention of writing and magic</note>, they called sometimes "Overseers" <note>original: *Ephoros*</note> and sometimes "Horoscope Gods." They believed that one of the planets ruled over each of these; furthermore, they designated the effects that each Decan impressed upon a person at the moment of conception or birth through various hieroglyphics. However, so that the reader may more closely observe the harmony of the whole, we have arranged a table here in which everything that the Arab Abenragel <note>Albohazen Haly Abenragel, a 10th-11th century Arab astrologer</note> pursues through long discourses is condensed into a single synopsis.

->**Concerning the Twelve Houses.**<-

<margin>Sextus Empiricus <note>A Greek physician and philosopher (c. 160–210 AD) whose works are a primary source for ancient skepticism and descriptions of astrology.</note></margin>
The Egyptians, not yet content with such a laborious apparatus of astrological science, noted certain wondrous effects which the stars—both fixed and wandering <note>The "wandering stars" are the planets</note>—produced in certain regions of the sky. For they showed one effect according to the nature of the stars at rising, another at setting, another in the middle of the sky <note>The Midheaven</note>, another at the point of midnight, and finally others in the intermediate places, both above and below the Horizon. Hence, they divided the sky—following the division already previously established in the Zodiac—by another division into twelve intervals, six of which were above and just as many below the Horizon; these they named *aulai* <note>Greek: αὐλαὶ; "courts" or "halls"</note>, or "Ligatures," houses, and mansions of the Gods. And in these houses, they most diligently explored the position of both the signs of the Zodiac and the planets, as well as their configurations toward one another: oppositions, conjunctions, and aspects—trine, quartile, sextile, platic <note>An approximate aspect</note>, and partile <note>An exact aspect</note>. And thus, at last, they would judge concerning lot, fortune, nature, misfortune, and finally the <unclear>total</unclear> state of human life; they predicted storms, sterility, plague, the bounty of the harvest, and similar things used by astrologers even unto this day. And lest they should seem to attribute these things solely to the said regions of the sky and the virtues of the stars, they furthermore assigned to each house its own presiding, ruling, building, destroying, benign, and malevolent Spirits <note>original: "Genios"</note>; to whose power and will all things were committed by the supreme ruler of the universe. Hence, just as they greatly feared the unlucky aspects of contrary forces, so they desired with the greatest vows the beneficial influx of sympathetic Divinities. Having inspected and examined some *thoma* <note>likely referring to a sacred record or astrological chart</note>, they would strive with the greatest prayers to appease them through previous sacrifices and appropriate ceremonies (as will be said in its proper place and time)—the malevolent ones so that they might not bring harm, and the beneficial ones so that they might render them propitious and draw them into their own lot. But let us confirm all that has been said so far with the words of Sextus Empiricus, who describes these things quite graphically. First, therefore...

# CLASS VII. MATHEMATICAL HIEROGLYPHS. CHAPTER V.
Aa 2

It is established by them that earthly things have a certain agreement, which they call sympathy, with celestial things, and that by the influences of the latter, the former are always renewed.

->The mind and thought of earthly men is such<-
->As the Father of men and Gods wills the day to be.<-
<note>A Latin translation of a famous passage from Homer's Odyssey (18.136-137), often cited by ancient authors to describe how human nature is shaped by the heavens.</note>

The Chaldeans have looked quite curiously into that which surrounds us; they say indeed that seven stars <note>The seven classical planets: Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> hold the account of the acting causes in each of those things which happen in life, and that they assist the parts of the Zodiac. And the Zodiac circle itself, as we have received by tradition, they divide into twelve animals <note>original: *animalia*; referring to the signs of the Zodiac</note>; and each animal into thirty parts (for on this point let us agree with them for the present); and each part into sixty minutes (for so they call those things which are smallest and indivisible). Of the animals, which they call *zodia* <note>original: ζῴδια, meaning "little animals" or "carved figures"</note>, some they call masculine, others indeed feminine; and some indeed are bicorporeal <note>Double-bodied or dual signs</note>, others truly not; and some indeed are solid, others truly *tropika* <note>original: τροπικά</note>, that is, changeable or turning. And they call them masculine and feminine because they have a nature that assists in the generation of males and females; for Aries is a masculine sign, but Taurus feminine; Gemini masculine, and the rest in turn by a similar analogy, some masculine, others truly feminine. Moved by these things, as I believe, the Pythagoreans call unity <note>The number one</note> male, but the dyad <note>The number two</note> female, the triad again male, and by an entirely similar proportion and analogy the rest of the even and odd numbers. Some, however, also dividing each animal into twelve parts, use almost the same reasoning, so that in Aries they call the first twelfth part of it Aries, and masculine; the second Taurus, and feminine; the third Gemini, and masculine. They say the bicorporeal animals are Gemini, Sagittarius, Virgo, and Pisces; the rest are not bicorporeal. And the *tropica* or changeable signs are those in which, when the Sun is present, it transforms and causes the turnings of the surrounding air; of this kind are the signs Aries, and its opposite Libra, as well as Capricorn and Cancer: for in Aries the spring turning <note>The Vernal Equinox</note> occurs, in Capricorn the Winter, in Cancer the Summer, and in Libra the Autumnal. They consider Taurus, and its opposite Scorpio, Leo, and Aquarius to be solid <note>Fixed signs</note>. But truly, of all these, those signs which obtain dominance in each birth for the outcome of those things which are completed (which they call <margin>Concerning the 12 houses of the heavens.</margin> *apotelesmata* <note>original: ἀποτελέσματα; astrological effects or outcomes</note>, and from which they especially make predictions) they say are <margin>The center of the houses.</margin> four in number, which by a common name they call centers, but specifically one <margin>Midheaven.</margin> the Horoscope <note>The Ascendant or rising sign</note>, another *mesouranema* <note>original: μεσουράνημα</note>, that is, the midheaven, another <margin>What the Horoscope is.</margin> the Occident <note>The Descendant or setting sign</note>, and another the subterranean and *antimesouranema* <note>original: ἀντιμεσουράνημα</note>, that is, the position opposite the midheaven, which is itself also a midheaven <note>The Imum Coeli or bottom of the sky</note>. And the Horoscope is that which happened to be rising at that time when the Birth was being completed; the Midheaven is the fourth sign from it; the Subterranean is the position opposite the midheaven, which is diametrically opposed to the midheaven, so that (for it will become clear by example) if Cancer is the Horoscope, Aries is in the midheaven, Capricorn sets, and Libra is under the earth. But truly, of each of these centers, a certain animal <margin>What *apoklima* and *epanaphora* are.</margin> or sign preceding it they call *apoklima* <note>original: ἀπόκλιμα; a "falling away" or cadent house</note>, that is, a declination; but that which follows, *epanaphora* <note>original: ἐπαναφοράν</note>, that is, a succession; now indeed that animal which follows...

### CHAPTER V. 288 THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

That sign or constellation which is in the Ascendant <note>original: "Horoscopo"; the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</note>, if it be in the open, they call the "Evil Spirit" <note>original: "mali Daemonis"</note>; that which follows (following that which is in the Midheaven) they call the "Good Spirit"; but that which precedes the Midheaven, they call the <term>katomesēida</term> <note>original: "κατωμεσηίδα"; meaning the "lower middle" or "under-meridian"</note>, that is, the "Lower Gate," and the <term>antitheon</term> <note>original: "ἀντίθεον"; meaning "opposed to the god"</note>, which is to say, the unique lot and God. That which comes to the Setting <note>the West</note> is the "Idle Sign" and the "Principle of Death." That which is after the Setting, and is not open, is "Punishment" and "Bad Fortune"; this is situated diametrically opposite the "Evil Spirit." That which comes under the earth is "Good Fortune," which is situated diametrically opposite the "Good Spirit." That which recedes from the point opposite the Midheaven toward the East is the "Goddess," diametrically opposite the "God." That which follows the Ascendant is "Idle," which in turn is diametrically opposed to the other "Idle" point. 

Or to speak more briefly: the declining of the sign in the Ascendant is called the <term>Evil Spirit</term>; its <term>Epanaphora</term> <note>original: "ἐπαναφορά"; a planetary "rising" or "succession" following a pivot point</note> is called "Idle." In the same way, the declining of the Midheaven is called "God," while its <term>Epanaphora</term> is the <term>Good Spirit</term>. Similarly, for the point opposite the Midheaven, the declining is called "Goddess," and the <term>Epanaphora</term> is "Good Fortune." Likewise, the declining of the West is "Bad Fortune," and its <term>Epanaphora</term> is "Idle." They believe these things should be examined not lightly or as if doing something else, for they judge that the stars do not have the same power for doing good or ill if they are considered in the centers <note>the "angles" or pivots of the chart</note>, in the risings, or in the declinations, but are more effective in some places and less effective in others. 

There were also certain Chaldeans <note>a term often used for ancient Babylonian astrologers and astronomers</note> who attributed each part of the human body to a specific sign, as having a harmony with it and being affected by it. For they name Aries the head, Taurus the neck, Gemini the shoulders, Cancer the breast, Leo the sides, Virgo the hips, Libra the flanks, Scorpio the genitals and womb, Sagittarius the thighs, Capricorn the knees, Aquarius the shins, and Pisces the feet, as is clear in the figure.

# CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. 189 CH. 4.

I must say something regarding the division of the signs. For since there was no certain method of observation and inspection—because they did not contemplate the signs by their own boundaries, but rather by the observation of scattered stars—it occurred to them to divide the entire circle into twelve parts. Showing the way and the method, they say that when the Ancients had observed a certain bright star among those in the Zodiac circle, they filled a perforated jar <note>A clepsydra or water clock</note> with water and allowed it to flow into another vessel placed beneath it until that same star rose again, estimating that the revolution of the circle lasted from the rising of that sign until its return. <margin>By what method the Ancients measured the revolution of the Zodiac.</margin> Again, they took a twelfth part of the water that had flowed out and considered how much time it took for this portion to flow: for they said that in that time a twelfth part of the circle had returned. They held that the ratio of that part of the water to the total water was the same as the ratio of that part of the circle to the whole. From this relationship, I say, they marked the final boundary of a twelfth part starting from some notable star seen at that time, or from one of those stars rising simultaneously further North or further South. They did this same thing for the other twelve parts; such is the way and method by which they divide the Zodiac circle into so many parts. Moreover, that method by which the Chaldeans observed the Horoscope <note>The "Ascendant" or the point of the Zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth</note> from the beginning seems to agree with this analogy and proportion. <margin>How the Chaldeans observed the Horoscope.</margin> For at night, it is said, the Chaldean sat on some high promontory watching the stars; another sat by the woman in labor until she had given birth. As soon as she had given birth, he signaled this to the Master on the promontory; and he, upon hearing it, observed the sign that was then rising as the Horoscope. During the day, however, he attended to the Horoscopes and the movements of the Sun.

But these things concern the signs. Regarding the stars <note>The planets</note>, they say some are beneficent, others truly malefic, and others common: <margin>Some stars are beneficent, others malefic, others common.</margin> for instance, the stars of Jupiter and Venus are beneficent, while those of Mars and Saturn are malefic, and that of Mercury is common, since it is beneficent with the beneficent and malefic with the malefic. Others, however, believe these same stars are sometimes beneficent and sometimes malefic depending on their various configurations. For regardless of the sign, or the aspects and figures of other stars toward them, no malefic is entirely malefic, nor is a beneficent star entirely beneficent. Furthermore, they think the Sun and Moon preside over the seven stars, and that the remaining five have less power over the outcome of events. For this reason, the Egyptians liken the Sun to the King and the right eye; the Moon to the Queen and the left eye; and the five stars to the lictors <note>Attendants or guards of a magistrate</note> and bodyguards; the rest of the fixed stars they liken to the people. And of the five, they say Saturn, Jupiter, and Mercury agree with the Sun and bring him assistance; these they also call "diurnal" because the Sun, whom they aid, rules over those things born during the day. They say these same stars have greater power either because they are in their own houses, or in their exaltations, or terms, or because some are crowded by others as if by bodyguards, or because they look upon one another and take up certain figures between themselves, or because they are in the "centers" <note>The angular houses of a chart: 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th</note>. <margin>The houses of the planets according to the Ancients. What are the exaltations and depressions of the planets.</margin> As they themselves judge, the house of the Sun is Leo; of the Moon, Cancer; of Saturn, Capricorn and Aquarius; of Jupiter, Sagittarius and Pisces; of Mars, Aries and Scorpio; of Venus, Taurus and Libra; of Mercury, Gemini and Virgo. They call the "exaltations" of the stars their elevations to the heights, and finally "depressions" or "rejections" those places from which they are delighted or in which they have meager power. For they are delighted in their high elevations, but have meager power in

->depressions.<-

# CHAPTER V. THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

...regarding depressions or abasements: For example, the exaltation <note>original: "elatio"</note> of the Sun into the heights is **Aries**; it is exalted specifically and perfectly at its nineteenth part or degree. Its depression, however, is the sign diametrically opposed to it. Again, the exaltation of the Moon into the heights is **Taurus**; its depression is that which is situated diametrically opposite to it. For Saturn, it is **Libra**; for Jupiter, **Cancer**; for Mars, **Capricorn**; for Venus, **Pisces**; and their depressions, as I have said, are situated diametrically opposite to their exaltations in the heights. <margin>What the planetary terms are.</margin> They call the "terms" of the stars those parts in each sign in which each star has the most power, from a certain part to another certain part. Regarding these, there is no small disagreement among them, even in their tables. They also say that stars are "escorted" as if by bodyguards when they are in the middle of other stars in the sequence of the signs: for instance, if one star of the same sign holds the first parts, another the last, and another the middle, the one in the middle is said to be escorted by bodyguards by those holding <margin>The aspects or configurations of the planets.</margin> the parts at the extremes. Furthermore, stars are said to "aspect" one another and agree among themselves when they appear in a triangular or square figure. Stars are formed into a triangular figure and aspect each other when they have a space of three signs cast between them; and a square figure when they have two. It is observed that in a triangular configuration, a beneficent star <note>A planet considered to have a positive influence, like Jupiter or Venus.</note> combined with a malefic star <note>A planet considered to have a negative influence, like Saturn or Mars.</note> bestows a benefit and becomes more beneficent. A beneficent star with another beneficent star does only this; and a malefic with a malefic likewise. They are said to be "in the centers" when they are seen in any of the center points: either at the Horoscope <note>The Ascendant or eastern horizon.</note>, or at the Midheaven, or at the Setting <note>The Descendant or western horizon.</note>, or at that which is situated opposite the Midheaven <note>The Imum Coeli or bottom of the sky.</note>. But since these things have been set forth by us simply and roughly, it must first be understood that the **Chaldeans** <note>A term often used by ancient authors to refer to astrologers and astronomers of Mesopotamia.</note>, moved by two methods, offer their predictions of things to come, which they call <term>apotelesmata</term> <note>The effects or outcomes of the stars; astrological prognostications.</note>. There is a difference between them: for some are simpler, while others are more accurate. The simpler ones are those made from a sign, or from the simple and sole power of a star: such as, "this star, when it is in this sign, produces such an effect." The more accurate ones are those made through a conjunction, and as they themselves say, through the tempering together of many factors: such as, "if one star is in the Horoscope, another in the Midheaven, another in the point opposite the Midheaven, and others are held in this or that way, these things will happen."

->And this is the opinion of **Sextus Empiricus** <note>A skeptical philosopher (c. 160–210 AD) who recorded many astrological theories while attempting to refute them.</note> regarding the twelve domiciles of heaven; however, the **Egyptians** differ greatly from him; and so that this may be made clear, it seemed best to begin a little further back.<-

<margin>The Egyptians divide the heaven into 12 mansions.</margin> The division of the heaven into twelve mansions is an invention of the Egyptians, as was shown above from various authors; for just as they divided the Zodiac into twelve domiciles which they called "citadels," and which the Sun traveled through in its annual course, so also the celestial houses were divided equally, but in such a way that within the space of one natural day, the Sun with its attendants—the Moon, planets, and stars—would travel through each one. For since at any time one of the degrees of the Zodiac would be hanging over the horizon, it followed that the remaining degrees of the Zodiac signs would also be found in some of one of the twelve mansions, which must also be said of the planets and stars. Since, moreover, different houses were open to different influences of light and heat, they believed that anyone recently born was marked by various impressions according to the quality of each house; this is indeed the foundation of the entire <term>Genethliacal</term> <note>The art of casting birth charts or horoscopes based on the moment of birth.</note> art. # CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS 191 CHAPTER V.

In these houses, the Ancients considered a great force and power of celestial influences to be hidden. These <term>centers</term> <note>original: κέντρα (kentra)</note> were called by the Greeks and the Egyptians <term>dwelling places</term> <note>original Coptic: ⲙⲁⲛϣⲱⲡⲓ (manshopi)</note>, or the principal mansions of the Gods. More recent authors call them "cusps" or "angles." The remaining intermediate spaces they called <term>places</term> <note>original: topos</note>; since there were eight of these, they called them <term>opposing</term> <note>original: ἀντιφέροντα (antipheronta)</note>. Of these, four are "opposing"—that is, fallen or sluggish places—and the other four are <term>successions</term> <note>original: ἐπαναφοραὶ (epanaphorai)</note>, meaning those that follow. The <term>centers of the angles</term> or the cusps of the four cardinal points are shown in the following figure: first, the <term>rising</term> <note>original: ἀνατολή (anatole)</note> or the East. Second, the <term>mid-heaven</term> <note>original: μεσουράνημα (mesouranēma)</note> or the middle of the sky. Third, the <term>setting</term> <note>original: δύσις (dusis)</note>. Fourth, the <term>underworld</term> <note>original: ὑπόγειον (hypogeion)</note> or the bottom of the sky.

The reason why they began with quadrants is this: the Ancients imagined two great circles passing through the poles of the World. One is the meridian; the other is drawn through a point on the Ecliptic—specifically at the contact of the rising Horizon—and at the opposite point of the setting Horizon, intersecting the meridian at the poles of the World. By these two circles, the Zodiac is divided into four quadrants, and thus the other cardinal points immediately become apparent. The first of these, on the part of the rising Horizon, is the <term>horoscopic sign</term> <note>original: ὡροσκοποῦν σημεῖον (hōroskopoun sēmeion)</note>, which is the sign ascending at the time of birth. The second is the <term>mid-heaven</term>, the fourth sign from it. The third is the <term>setting</term>, the western point, which is the seventh sign from the Horoscope. And finally, the fourth is the point opposite the <term>mid-heaven</term>. For example: if <term>Aries</term> is the horoscope, <term>Capricorn</term> is in the mid-heaven, <term>Libra</term> is setting, and <term>Cancer</term> is at the bottom of the sky. In this way, they easily found the degree applied to the Horizon at a given hour using the arrangement of an armillary sphere.

The Ancients attributed these four quadrants to the four ages of man, as the <term>Greek author Demophilus</term> writes: <note>original Greek: Ὁ μὲν ὡροσκοπῶν δηλοῖ τὴν πρώτην ἡλικίαν, ὁ μεσουρανῶν τὴν μέσην, ἡ δὲ δύσις τὴν γεγηρακυῖαν, τὸ δὲ ὑπὸ γῆν κέντρον τὸν θάνατον, καὶ τὰ μετ' αὐτὸν γενομένην εὐδοξίαν, καὶ ἀδοξίαν.</note> "The <term>Horoscope</term> indeed manifests the first age, that is, childhood; the <term>mid-heaven</term> the middle, that is, the prime of life; the <term>setting</term> the completed age, that is, old age; and the <term>underworld</term> the decrepit age, which brings death and the works of glory or infamy that follow it."

However, other authors applied the four quadrants to the ages differently: for they ascribe the quadrant from the first to the tenth house to childhood, calling it <term>oriental</term>. The second, opposite to this, from the fourth to the seventh house, they called <term>opposing</term>, corresponding to old age. The third, from the west to the mid-heaven, they called <term>Libyan</term> <note>original: λυβικὸν (lybikon)</note> and applied it to youth or manhood. Finally, the fourth, called <term>anti-Libyan</term> <note>original: ἀντικυβικὸν (antikybi-kon)</note>, leading from the Horoscope to the bottom of the sky, they applied to the age near death. Furthermore, the operations signified by the twelve houses are called <term>Athla</term> <note>meaning "labors" or "contests"</note> by the Ancients; as <term>Manilius</term> says:

### CHAPTER V.

They are also used as amulets, which are customarily hung around the necks of children. They are called "Ligatures" <note>Latin: *Ligaturæ*; objects bound or tied to the body for protection</note> because no correct judgment can be established unless all the places of fortune are aptly combined among themselves and, as it were, bind and embrace one another. From this, the Greeks, hearing these words *Chatholoth* <note>A transliteration of a Hebrew or Near Eastern term for "destinies" or "connections"</note>, retained the term *Athla* <note>Greek: ἄθλα; meaning "labors," "contests," or "prizes"</note> assigned to them. There are twelve of these, according to the twelve-part face of the heavens, and they are distinguished from the places of birth: for the theme of birth <note>Greek: γενέσεως; *geneseos*</note> is one thing, and the theme of the Labors is another; the former denotes nature, while the latter denotes actions. In the primary birth-chart, the first house is the Ascendant <note>Greek: *Horoscopos*</note>, but in the actions or Labors, it is the Lot of Fortune <note>The "sors fortunae," a specific mathematical point in a horoscope</note>, and new actions arise and are established there, for they follow the Lot of Fortune as their Leader. For in the birth-chart, the "positioning" <note>Greek: θέσις; *thesis*</note> is considered intrinsically, but in the Labors, the "exposition" <note>Greek: ἔκθεσις; *ekthesis*</note> is considered extrinsically; and of the former, the Ascendant is the ruler, while of the latter, it is the Lot of Fortune. Thus says <margin>Hermes</margin> Hermes: *In specific times, he subjects bodily matters to the Ascendant, external matters to Fortune, and matters of the soul to the Midheaven, according to mathematical principles.* <note>Original Greek: Ἐν καιροῖς τὰ σωματικὰ τῷ ὡροσκόπῳ τὰ δ’ ἐκτὸς τῆς τύχης κ’ τὰ ψυχικὰ τῷ οὐρανῷ δ’ ταῦτα μαθηματικῶς</note>. Indeed, bodily things are like the day to the Ascendant, and possessions to the Lot of Fortune, spiritual things to the Moon, but practical actions to the Midheaven. Furthermore, what are called *Athla* by the Ancients are called by the Arabs *Al-Wajh* <note>Arabic: الوجة</note>, that is, the "Face."

Now that these things have been explained, contemplate everything said so far according to the mind of the Ancients in the following figure of the twelve celestial houses. In this figure of the twelve celestial dwellings, we have first placed for each house the Egyptian name of that house, which they call *Stathmous* <note>Greek: ΣΤΑΘΜΟΥΣ; "stations" or "mansions"</note>; then, in the inner houses, we have always placed in the first spot the tutelary Genii <note>Guardian spirits or guiding deities</note> of each. We have named the first house the House of Hermanubis <note>A syncretic deity combining Hermes/Mercury and Anubis</note>, that is, the House of Mercury, according to the mind of the Ancients; the second, the House of Typhon; and so on for the rest, which follow the Greek names. Then follow the *Athla*, that is, the meanings of the operations which are performed in each. In the outer boundary, we have added the "declinations" <note>Greek: ἀποκλίματα; *apoklimata*</note> and "ascensions" <note>Greek: ἐπαναφορὰς; *epanaphoras*</note> of each. In the inner square, we have added the four parts of the World corresponding to the cusps. Finally, in the center, we have displayed the hieroglyphic Diagram of the four Genii of the World, upon whom the Lot of Fortune chiefly depended; these are encircled by a serpent, the symbol of both the annual and diurnal revolution, over which the said Divinities were believed to preside. In the very center, the letter *eta* <note>η</note> signifies the Gate of the World, through which the Sun and Moon, marked by Cancer <note>Astrological symbol: ♋</note> and Leo <note>Astrological symbol: ♌</note>, proceed and animate all things by their fertile motion. But since we shall explain this hieroglyphic more fully in the following pages, we did not wish to dwell longer on its interpretation here. The skilled reader will better grasp my thought regarding the arrangement of the twelve mansions of heaven from the Diagram itself than I could provide even by the longest discourses.

### Conclusion.

**I**n this figure, you first see a double hemisphere, upper and lower, divided into twelve equal parts, which they called *topoi* <gloss>or mansions</gloss>. And indeed, at the four cardines <note>The "hinge" points of a horoscope: the Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli</note>—the East, the South, the West, and the Bottom of the Sky—they placed four figures as if they were presiding governors and arbiters of all fortune. In the remaining angles, which they called the <term>octotopos</term> <note>From the Greek for "eight places," referring to the eight houses of the zodiac that are not the four primary angles</note> due to their number of eight, they placed the followers of the principal guardian Spirits, some of whom were beneficial and others malevolent. Furthermore, they assigned certain lots of things pertaining to fortune to each individual house. In this manner, they believed that Mercury presided over the first house of life and bodily constitution, and whatever pertains to the forming of character; in a word, they reduced to this house every single thing that in any way belongs to the Mercurial classes in all of nature, and which by a certain analogy could be traced back to the goods of fortune, riches, honors, length of life, and the strength and beauty of the body. Likewise, they willed that <term>Rephan</term> <note>A Coptic or ancient name for the planet Saturn</note> or Saturn should preside over the fourth house of the deep night, along with everything savoring of a Saturnine nature. Over the tenth house, or the Midheaven, they placed Aphrodite or <term>Nephten</term> <note>Associated here with Venus/Nephthys</note> together with Jupiter; for this reason, they also called it the house of dignity, honor, and Royal happiness. Finally, they believed that <term>Typhon</term> <note>The Egyptian Set, associated here with destruction and the West</note> ruled over the seventh house, the angle of the West, the house of death. To the other individual houses of the eight-fold division, they attributed Spirits and natures suitable to them, as is evident from the figure.

### The application and use of the aforesaid in the business of Astrology, and their refutation.

**S**ince they kept the eyes of the mind continually intent upon the orders of the celestial motions, and noted that various influences were drawn down from the Governors of the highest habitation of the heavens, through the intermediate choirs of the planets, into the furthest seedbeds of the Elemental World; and since they saw changes emanating daily from the continuous motion of the heavens or the stars; they adapted the houses and mansions to the expanse of the zodiacal planets in this way, so that they might perceive from the System itself the encounter of qualities and influences, whether friendly or inimical. For if, at the hour of birth, they found happy and beneficial Governors in the house of happy fortune, they pronounced that person happy as well, from so many conspiring goods; but if they found beneficial governors ruling a certain house along with malevolent ones, they pronounced that the person born would attain such a lot of fortune; if, finally, they discovered malevolent governors joined with malevolent ones in any house, they were of the opinion that the person born would be subject to an unjust and unhappy fate. Therefore, with the greatest zeal, they noted the four cardines and explored what position the presiding Spirits held in relation to one another. But if they comprehended an inimical encounter anywhere, they immediately strove to appease the malevolent Spirits with the highest prayers, sacrifices, and ceremonies, lest they do harm; and the good spirits, so that they might persevere in the flow of good things. And in this way, they acted not only regarding the fortune of the person born, but in those matters which concerned sterility and fertility...

# CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER VI.
<sig>Bb 2</sig>

...they proceeded from matters concerning the fertility of the fields, the rising and falling of the Nile, medical elections <note>The practice of choosing the most astrologically favorable time for medical treatment</note>, and the omens for journeys and business affairs. Indeed, they dreamed that they knew above all else that all human happiness and unhappiness depended on the will of the Genii <note>Spirits or guardian deities</note>. See more of what we have brought forward regarding this kind of thing in the *Astrological Cabala* of both the Hebrews and the Saracens. But as for why the Egyptians adorned the houses <note>Astrological houses</note> in such an order, and with such significations and promises, Auenar <note>Abraham ben Ezra, a 12th-century Jewish scholar</note> explains this in his *Astrology* written in Hebrew, whom you may consult; since all such delusions of the Egyptians have long since been proscribed by the orthodox Church as the ruin and destruction of souls, I judged it not at all expedient to bring forward here a matter described in more copious words by Arabian and Hebrew authors.

## CHAPTER VI.

### *Concerning the 48 Asterisms, or the Mansions of the Gods* <term>causal-holders <note>original Greek: αἰτιόχων (aitiochon); those who hold or contain the causes of things</note></term>.

It is so ingrained in the condition of men that as soon as they behold certain abstruse and exotic things, they are carried away in admiration, and once carried away, they scrutinize the reasons of the hidden causes. This happened most especially to the Egyptians: living as they did under a face of perpetual celestial serenity, while they diligently contemplated those most orderly armies of the stars in the harmless vigils of the night with an intent sharpness of mind and eye, they were driven by a certain stupor. They persuaded themselves that it was impossible for that which was announced by such great portents to be idle, or for that which filled all things in the lower world with its irradiation through such miraculous effects to be unfruitful. Hence, after setting forth observations of many years, they divided the entire star-bearing sky into certain <margin>The division of stars into Asterisms made by the Ancients.</margin> classes, which the Egyptians first called the "Mansions of the Gods," and later the Greeks called "Asterisms" or "Iconisms" <note>Constellations or images</note>. For first, they uniquely worshipped the choirs of the twelve principal Gods included in the Zodiac as the moderators of the Universe, as seen above, since from their will and disposition all lots of good or bad fortune in the lower world depended. To these they joined, on both sides in the Northern as well as the Southern hemisphere, certain subsidiary cohorts of Gods distributed into various offices. In the Northern realm of Typhon <note>The Egyptian god of chaos and storms</note>, they placed certain austere and—to speak with Zoroaster—certain "implacable" powers; but in the Southern realm of Osiris, they placed those benevolent and highly favoring to the human race, as if set in opposition to the inclemency and austerity of the Northerners. From their <term>opposition of craft <note>original Latinized Greek: antitechnia; a conflict or counter-play of influences</note></term> and perpetual movement, the nurseries of the mixture of good and evil things arose. Hence, just as they contended with the greatest zeal to appease the Northern powers for the averting of evils, so they endeavored to draw the Southern powers into their protection through sacrifices and ceremonies established with singular industry. All of these things were explained at length above in the treatise on the *Hieroglyphic System of the World*, as well as in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, page 206.

# CHAPTER VI. THE EGYPTIAN GYMNASIUM OF HIEROGLYPHICS.

<margin>The 48 constellations invented by the Egyptians.</margin> This being established, I say first that the Egyptians were the first of all mortals to divide the sky into 48 images, as Hyginus <note>Gaius Julius Hyginus, a Roman mythographer and astronomer.</note> testifies. He says, "The signs and images by which the stars and planets are marked by astronomers are Chaldean and Egyptian." This division was appropriately made so that 24 images were placed under the South and just as many under the North; all of which they called the 
<margin>What are the stations or mansions of the Gods?</margin> stations or mansions of the Gods, as we have said. For they placed a certain "choragus" <note>A leader or conductor of a group.</note> over each image, to whom the remaining stars of one and the same constellation were joined like attendants. They assigned to each a certain protection over things contained in the lower world, and they declared him blessed who could know the chains of these constellations, by which the corresponding and matching classes in the lower world were connected. For once these were known, they thought it would not be difficult to attract good Spirits <note>Genii</note> appropriate to each matter into their own affairs—whether through sacrifices or various compositions taken from the aforementioned classes of natural things—through their accustomed rites, and to drive away the malignant ones. For as Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the famous Greco-Egyptian astronomer.</note> rightly says: *For the faces of this lower world are subject to the celestial faces*. In the midst of these Divinities, they placed Mithras, whom they also called <note>original: "Μιθρὶς"</note>—that is, the Mediator—which is the Sun. Like a Leader and supreme Monarch of the celestial world with the remaining company of planets, returning now to the South, now to the North, he visits the subsidiary forces of the said Divinities every year, inciting each one by his power to the conservation of the worldly economy. Since all these things have been established with their own authorities in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* on page 157, we refer the curious reader there. 
<margin>The Greeks converted the hieroglyphic images of the stars into Gods.</margin> Following these were the Greeks, who converted the hieroglyphic images of the Egyptians (which they did not understand) into the portraits of the Gods they themselves had invented, which posterity has used even to this day. But so that you may more clearly compare the primitive face of the sky described hieroglyphically by the Egyptians with the portraits of the Greeks, we shall first place here both hemispheres marked with the constellations of the Greeks, and then we shall also place the portraits of the Egyptians.

->**Greek Portraits of the North: 21 Northern Signs.**<-

I. **Ursa Minor** <note>The Little Bear</note>, Helice or Cynosura; Arabic الركبة *Alracaba* <note>The Knee</note>; Greek ἅμαξα, *The Wagon*; Hebrew עיש ובניה, *Gnash* <note>The constellation Ash/Arcturus</note> *the Hen with her children*. It contains 21 stars and occupies ♊︎ Gemini and ♌︎ Leo; it is of the nature of Mars and Venus.

II. **Ursa Major** <note>The Great Bear</note>, Greek ἅμαξα μεγάλη, *The Greater Chariot*; Arabic الدب الاكبر *Dubbe ellekbar*, *The Greater Bear*; Hebrew דוב גדול <note>The Great Bear</note>; to the Indians, *The Golden Sea*. It contains 57 stars and occupies ♌︎ Leo and ♍︎ Virgo; it is of a Martial nature.

III. **Draco** <note>The Dragon</note>, Greek Δράκων, *The Serpent, Python*; Arabic ثعبان *Taaban* <note>Serpent/Basilisk</note>; Hebrew התנין *Tanin*, *The Snake*. It contains 32 stars and occupies ♐︎ Sagittarius, ♑︎ Capricorn, ♒︎ Aquarius, ♓︎ Pisces, ♈︎ Aries, ♉︎ Taurus, ♊︎ Gemini, and ♌︎ Leo; it is of the nature of Jupiter and Saturn.

IV. **Cepheus**, to the Greeks Κηφεύς; to the Arabs قيفوس *Keiphus*; to the Hebrews להבה בעלה, *The Lady of Flame* or *The Inflamed One*. It contains 13 stars and occupies ♈︎ Aries, ♉︎ Taurus, and ♊︎ Gemini; it is of the nature of Jupiter and Saturn.

# EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM
<margin>CHAPTER VI</margin>

XIX. **Pegasus**, or the winged horse; Greek: *hippos* <note>original: ἵππος</note>; Arabic: *Alpharaso*, "the horse" <note>original: الفرس</note>; Hebrew: "the horned horse" <note>original: סוס בעל קרנים</note>. It contains 23 stars and occupies the signs of Aquarius, Pisces, and Aries; it is of a Mars-Mercury nature <note>In astrology, "nature" refers to the planetary influence or temperament a constellation exerts.</note>.

And these are the 48 Images with which the Greeks, led by mystical reasons, marked the entire heavens; which indeed, as will be seen later, they borrowed from the Egyptians and, having adorned them with various fables, made their own. Let us now reveal what those primeval images were with which the Egyptians honored the heavens.

# CHAPTER VII.
### How and why the Egyptians divided the Heavens into 48 Asterisms.

<margin>The Egyptians believed the Gods or Spirits inhabited the stars;</margin> It is a dogma of the Egyptians that the celestial Gods or Spirits inhabit the stars: for they thought the lower world subsists by their power and efficacy—not by some inherent flowing force of the stars themselves, but by the governing arrangement of the Divinities. These beings, sitting upon the stars as if on a royal throne, use the natural power of the stars as a kind of instrument for the management of lower things. They taught that in each individual <term>asterism</term> <note>a group of stars or a constellation</note> a primary Divinity resides, while in the remaining stars belonging to that same constellation, Spirits reside as followers and ministers of the principal Divinity. They believed their power descended in a kind of pyramidal flow, the base of which was defined by the size of the constellation itself, and the vertex at the center of the earth. They called these <term>aitheias</term> <note>original Greek: αἴθειας; likely referring to "ethereal" dwellings or "heights"</note> or the citadels of the Gods: for they judged that everything contained within pyramids of this kind was subject to the power and disposal of those same beings. We have already discussed the twelve Divinities of the Zodiac at length in Chapter Five; it remains for us to discuss the rest of the constellations, both northern and southern, with equal step. So that this may be done with greater method, it seemed best to first present the arrangement of the Icons according to the three "faces" of each sign, according to the mind of <term>Auenaris</term> <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a famous 12th-century Jewish scholar and astrologer</note> the Hebrew Astrologer, and the Indians.

->*The arrangement of Icons by which the Egyptians, according to the mind of Auenaris, subdivided the twelve-part signs of the Zodiac into three faces, and attributed appropriate Images to each face.*<-

The ancient Astrologers, as was said in the preceding pages, divided the Zodiac into 12 signs, which they called the citadels of the Gods, and each one...

# CLASS VII. MATHEMATICAL HIEROGLYPHS. CHAPTER VII.

from the 12 signs, they divided them again into three parts, which the Moderns have called faces or aspects, and <term>Decans</term> <note>From the Greek 'deka', meaning ten; these are 10-degree subdivisions of a zodiac sign</note>; in such a way, indeed, that they attributed ten degrees to each face. To these faces or aspects they attached certain <term>iconisms</term> <note>symbolic images or figures</note> or images, by which the nature of the influence prevailing in such and such a face would be expressed by a certain symbolic sketch. For from such and such a rising face, they predicted that the future condition of a person's birth would be whatever the symbolic constitution of the image had expressed. These images are to be conceived not only along the length of the Zodiac, but also according to its width, so that, for example, all those images found within a <term>Rhombus</term> <note>a diamond-shaped area of the sky</note> formed by two lines marking the boundaries of a face and meeting at each pole, are considered to belong to that face which the said two lines enclose. 

It should also be noted that there is no small difference between these iconisms and the <term>asterisms</term> <note>constellations</note>, of which the Ancients established 48 in the heavens. For the iconisms of the faces were considered according to the width of the Zodiac; but the asterisms were considered according to the width of the <term>equinoctial</term> <note>the celestial equator</note>. Hence, while authors here and there confuse the former with the latter, they have given occasion for the greatest perplexity. I believe this confusion arose because later Egyptians, introducing more and more schemes into the heavens and repeatedly adding new ones to the original iconisms, gradually filled the whole sky with innumerable characterizations of monsters, just as they filled the minds of later Astrologers with utter confusion. 

Therefore, so that we might avoid these sorts of quicksands, we shall first and separately exhibit <margin>Rabbi Auenar, Beneka the Indian, Abenragel.</margin> the images of the faces just as <term>Rabbi Auenar</term> <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a 12th-century Jewish scholar</note>, <term>Beneka the Indian</term> <note>An Indian source likely transmitted through Arabic texts</note>, and <term>Abenragel the Arab</term> <note>Al-Andarzaghar or Al-Buni, famous Arab astrologers</note> described them, following the Egyptian tradition; then we shall also exhibit, step by step, the 48 star-bearing iconisms which the ancient authority of the Sages consecrated to posterity as primordial specimens of wisdom. Thus, therefore, says Auenar:

->And in the third face there rises a youth sitting upon a throne, covered with a cloth, and in his hand are Teraphim.<-

*And in the third face there rises a youth sitting upon a spread seat, and in his hand are Teraphim.* What is understood by <term>Teraphim</term> <note>original: "Theraphim"; small household idols or oracular figurines mentioned in the Bible</note> was explained at length in the first volume, Synthesis 3, in the chapter on the Baalim; for it was an averting idol <note>an object used to ward off evil</note> which the Egyptians carried with them. But see the cited location regarding these. This is followed by another kneeling image, which Auenar describes from the Astrology of the Egyptians in these words:

->And a man lowered his head downward and he cries out to the Name [God].<-

*There rises also a man, bowing his head toward the lower parts, and he prayerfully invokes God.* This image is indeed nothing other than the image of a Tutelary Genius <note>a guardian spirit</note> supplicating a superior, and it is found everywhere among the hieroglyphics; it is often confused with the <term>Engonasi</term> <note>Greek: "the Kneeler," referring to the constellation Hercules</note> of the Greek star-patterns.

<margin>
Attendants of Apis, or Taurus.
</margin>

2 Within the kingdom of <term>Apis</term> <note>the sacred bull of Memphis, associated here with the sign of Taurus</note> there rise first, according to the Astrology of the Egyptians, the image of a man holding a sword in his left hand and a staff in his right; then truly a great Ship, upon which is a Lion. But let us hear the words of Auenar:

->And there shall rise in the first face of Taurus the Hero who has a sword in his left hand, and furthermore there shall rise a great ship in which is a lion.<-

In this passage, Auenar confuses the figures of the "faces" with the constellations themselves. What is indicated by the Giant, if not <term>Orion</term>? What by the Ship, if not that most celebrated <term>Baris</term> <note>a sacred Egyptian boat</note>, marked by a leonine figure, which we call <term>Mophta</term> <note>Kircher's term for a specific Egyptian genius or creative force</note>? It is here wrongly confused with the Ship of the Argonauts. The Indians, in place of the Lion positioned in the Ship, place a Ram; this fits beautifully with the figure of the Ram placed in the Ship on the <term>Bembine Tablet</term> <note>also known as the Mensa Isiaca, a famous bronze tablet depicting Isiac mysteries</note>. Furthermore, the Indian Astrologers say that beneath the Ship is the half of a dead woman, but they are mistaken; for the Egyptians placed <term>Horus</term> in this location, submerged in the Nile by <term>Typhon</term> <note>the Greek name for Set, the god of chaos</note>, in whose place the Greeks substituted <term>Icarus</term> submerged in the Eridanus. Again, in the Northern face, they say a man rises in Goat-like dress; by which nothing else is signified but <term>Erichthonius</term> <note>a legendary Greek king associated with the constellation Auriga</note> weighed down by the weight of a young goat. In the third face of Apis, there rises first <term>Anubis</term> distinguished by his dog-face, according to the testimony of Auenar, in whose hand is a serpent.

</margin>

*There rises there a Serpent dwelling in a tree, and a Wolf in whose hand is a sign, and a man in whose hand is a musical instrument with which he sings.* In place of the Wolf, the Greeks here place the "Beast" of the Centaur, and for the Musician, they place the Lyre.

...speaks in these words: *For the bears, that is, the Ursae themselves, which you know, never rise nor set, but perpetually recur around the same point.* <note>Kircher is discussing the circumpolar nature of the Great and Little Bear constellations.</note> Although others in place of the Greater Bear put an iron pig having a copper head; the Egyptians more correctly place a larger and smaller chariot, as was said above; others place a serpent-footed man entwined with snakes, of which kind we displayed Typhon <note>The Egyptian personification of chaos and evil.</note> in Volume One, Synthesis 3, in the Chapter on Typhon.
