# § II.
## On Egyptian Clocks.

<margin>The Egyptians used three types of clocks: Sciatheric, Natural, and Sympathetic.</margin>
I read that three types of clocks were used by the Egyptians: <term>Sciatheric</term> <note>Derived from the Greek words for "shadow-catching"; these are sundials.</note>, Natural, and Sympathetic. The first was that by which they learned the hourly times from the shadows of <term>Gnomons</term> <note>The rod or pin of a sundial that casts the shadow.</note>. This type was multifaceted. Some learned that it was such and such an hour from the shadows of Obelisks and pyramids, using fixed marks on the flat surface of the surrounding ground which the shadow of the tip would reach. In this way, we have shown elsewhere that the Obelisk erected at Heliopolis <margin>The shadows of Obelisks among the Egyptians showed the hours, midday, and the Solstices. Strabo. Solinus.</margin> indicated the hours. Strabo and Solinus teach that the Great Pyramid also exhibited the midday time of the entire year, as well as the Solstices and equinoxes, because its midday shadows never fell outside its base. Furthermore, the expression <term>eleven-foot shadow</term> <note>Original Greek: ἑνδεκάπουν σκία (hendekapoun skia)</note>—meaning the time for dinner—shows that they learned the hours by means of a staff planted in the surface of the earth, measuring the shadow of the staff by "feet" to reach a knowledge of the time for performing actions. Alternatively, it was called the <term>eleven-foot element</term> <margin>The Egyptians learned the hours by measuring the shadow of a staff in "feet."</margin> <note>Original Greek: ἑνδεκάπουν στοιχεῖον (hendekapoun stoicheion)</note>, because the hours were distinguished by the marks of individual letters, as Athenaeus left witnessed in the following Epigram.
<margin>Athenaeus.</margin>

Therefore, the Egyptians used this <term>Bowl-dial</term> <note>original: "Scaphio"</note> above all others, as the hieroglyphics produced in their time will show. Since they were already perfectly skilled in the use of the sphere, and the Bowl-dial was nothing other than a concave hemisphere in which the distinctions of the Sun’s parallels, along with the tropics and the equinoctial line, as well as the <term>unequal hours</term> <note>Hours that vary in length depending on the season, so that there are always 12 hours of daylight and 12 of night.</note> could be delineated with the greatest ease; in this way, they first divided the equinoctial line into twelve equal parts, and likewise the Tropic of Cancer <note>Astrological symbol for Cancer: ♋</note> and Capricorn <note>Astrological symbol for Capricorn: ♑</note>. # § IV.

->*On the Baboon Clock of the Egyptians.*<-

<margin>
The baboon measured the hourly times by urinating among the Egyptians.
</margin>
There was, among other things, another device no less ridiculous than it was mysterious. They observed in the <term>Cynocephalus</term> <note>Literally "dog-head"; the sacred baboon (Papio hamadryas) associated with Thoth, the god of wisdom and time.</note> (this is a certain species of ape) some hidden property or other, by which, when the Sun enters Aries and Libra <note>The times of the spring and autumn equinoxes.</note>, it would urinate twelve times during the day and twelve times at night by some hidden instinct of nature. From this arose the hydraulic clock peculiar to the Egyptians. They fashioned from bronze a <term>Cynocephalus</term> in a sitting position, from whose member water slipped down into an underlying oblong vial; the rising volume of water, gradually ascending within the sides of a cylindrical glass machine divided into twelve circles, showed the hours step by step. Thus says <term>Horus</term> <note>Referring to Horapollo, the purported author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note> in Book 1, Hieroglyphic 16, whom you may consult. See also the image of the Cynocephalus in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, page 300, where you will find everything described at length. You will find the clock itself below in the section on *Egyptian Mechanics*.

<margin>
Horapollo.
</margin>

### § V.

-> **On the Sympathetic Clock of the Egyptians.** <-

<margin>
The aquatic lotus constituted the sympathetic clock among the Egyptians.
</margin>

**T**he Sympathetic Clock of the Egyptians was known only to the Philosophers and initiates <note>original: "mystis," referring to those initiated into the sacred Egyptian mysteries</note>, who made use of it in their mystical consultations. It was, in fact, the aquatic lotus; this is a marsh plant endowed with such a hidden power of nature that as soon as the Sun rises, the plant also rises as if from the depths of the waters, gradually lifting itself until noon. At that point, standing entirely above the waters in its upright position, it seems to emulate the Sun. But as the Sun declines toward its setting, the plant also, through its own tilting from hour to hour, keeps the same laws for itself by its wondrous conversion, until it reaches the surface of the water. Finally, when the Sun goes below the Horizon, the plant itself goes under the waters, maintaining such a persistent submersion that it seems to long for the Sun <note>original: "deperire," to perish or pine for</note> as much while submerged beneath the waters as it had raised itself above them at noon. The Priests knew this hidden impulse of nature; for that reason, they implanted a wooden circle in the waters, as you see here—a rival to the solar circle—marked with its own hours. Thus it happened that they perfectly learned those hours from a certain hidden striving of nature, which could scarcely be discerned by a <term>shadow-clock</term> <note>original: "Sciatherico," an instrument like a sundial that tells time via shadows</note>. However, since we have already dealt with these matters in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* <note>Kircher's 1650 work *Obeliscus Pamphilius*</note>, and intend to treat the plants of Egypt again in a dedicated treatise, we refer the reader there. See also what we have said in *The Magnetic Art* <note>Kircher's *Magnes; sive de arte magnetica* (1641)</note>, Book 3, part 5, chapter 4.

# EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>
The Egyptians attributed individual planets to the individual days of the week.
</margin>

## CHAPTER IX.

### On Planetary Hours, and the Presiding Spirits of Each.

As in all things, so especially in the seven planets ruling the individual hours of the day, the Egyptians seemed to have placed a great mystery. For they were the first who attributed the individual days of the week to individual planets. They believed that for every hour from the rising of the Sun until the next sunrise, by day and by night, one of the presiding planets was in charge. From this source, even to this day, has flowed that <term>astrological vanity</term> <note>Kircher uses this term to distance himself from superstitious fortune-telling while still exploring the historical "science" of the Egyptians.</note>, because astrologers attempt almost nothing without first inspecting and understanding the hour of the ruling planet. But so that this hidden matter may be more clearly revealed, it seemed appropriate to begin the explanation from its deeper foundations.

### § I.

### What Planetary Hours are, and of what kind.

<margin>
What Planetary Hours are, and of what kind.
</margin>

The planetary hours described here are "unequal." They are called this not in an absolute sense according to the course of the Sun (like "equal" hours), but in reference to the presiding planets. Since they listed the seven planets in this order: <note>Saturn ♄, Jupiter ♃, Mars ♂, Sun ☉, Venus ♀, Mercury ☿, Moon ☾</note>, each planet was thought to dominate and preside over the individual hours of the day in a backward order. For if Saturn ruled the first hour of the day, Jupiter ruled the second, Mars the third, the Sun the fourth, Venus the fifth, Mercury the sixth, the Moon the seventh, and Saturn again the eighth, Jupiter the ninth, and so on. When these had revolved in order through the space of 24 hours, the first hour of the following day necessarily fell to the Sun, the second of that same day to Venus, the third to Mercury, and so through the rest, until after a full revolution of 24 hours, the first hour of the third day fell to Mars; as is exactly seen in the following table.

And from this Table it becomes clear why, in the days of the Week, the planets do not correspond to each other in their natural order, but are always separated by an interrupted sequence. <note>For example, following the sequence of the first hour of each day gives us Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn—the order of our modern week.</note>

## Gg

[...continuation of previous page] are distanced. The reason for this matter is none other than that the lordship of the planets is completed in a reverse order <note>The "reverse" or Chaldean order ranks planets by their perceived speed and distance from Earth: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon.</note> within the space of a 24-hour period, or a natural day. Thus, the twenty-fifth hour—which is the first hour of the following day—always falls to the planet that follows next in that reverse order. 

For example: in the Table for Sunday, the first hour of the day is assigned to the Sun, from which the day takes its name. The second hour belongs to Venus, which immediately follows the Sun in the reverse order; and so on for the rest, until the eighth hour. Once the lordship of the seven planets has revolved through those seven hours, the Sun begins its lordship again at the eighth hour. The remaining planets follow in order, as before, until the third hour of the night, at which point the Sun (the cycle of planets having revolved again) begins its rule once more. This repeat occurs again at the tenth hour of the night. After the Sun, the lordships of Venus for the eleventh hour and Mercury for the twelfth hour of the night follow. Once these are complete and the 24-hour revolution is finished, the first hour of the necessarily following day—namely, Monday—falls under the lordship of the Moon. The same logic applies to the rest, as is clear from the Table.

<margin>
The order of the days of the week, which are named after the planets, does not follow the [natural] order of the planets; and why.
</margin>

And from this, the reason is clear why the days of the week, though marked with the names of the planets, follow neither the natural order of the planets nor the simple reverse order as shown in the Table, but always follow one another in an interrupted sequence. I am not unaware that many who are ignorant of these matters devise various explanations for them. Dio Cassius <note>original: "Dion Nicæus." A Roman historian who provided one of the earliest accounts of the seven-day week's origin.</note> among others, in Book 36, thinks this discontinuity arises from the harmony or consonance called the <term>diatessaron</term> <note>The musical interval of a "fourth." In ancient Greek music theory, this was considered a fundamental building block of cosmic harmony.</note>. It was believed by the Ancients that the entire power of music was contained within this interval, and that it served as a stable foundation. 

Indeed, by applying the ratio of this musical consonance and comparing it with the adornment of the sky and the order of the celestial spheres and planets, they noticed a certain agreement and similarity. They decided that after one day was named after one planet, the following day should be named after the fourth planet following it in the reverse order.

# § II.
->**On the Rule or Dominion of the Planets.**<-

<margin>
The ancient Egyptian rule of the Planets.
</margin>

It was an invention of the Egyptians to arrange the secondary dominion of the Planets for each hour of the day, both during the daylight and the night; a system which the entire School of Astrologers embraces and kisses as if it were sacrosanct even to this day. It pleased the ancients so much that the very days of the week took their names from it, as we have seen. It is truly a swollen and fertile breeding ground of superstitions, from which, both in the past and today, countless monsters of portentous births have emerged and continue to emerge, as if from a Trojan horse. Indeed, hardly any Magical, Cabalistic, or Astrological operation is established that is not founded on this most vain observation of the planetary hour. We shall confute this more sharply once we have first shown the superstitious structure of this machination from its foundations.

<margin>
The Egyptians imagine seven Intelligences preside over the World.
</margin>

The Egyptians imagine, therefore, that in that great Hermetic year, seven Intelligences preside over the World according to certain sets of seven, each of which governs for 354 years and four months <note>This time period likely derives from the 354 days of the lunar year.</note>; they all perform various duties and offices. Consequently, they believe the World undergoes various and diverse alterations according to the influence and disposition of the seven wandering stars <note>The "wandering stars" are the five visible planets plus the Sun and Moon.</note>. The Hebrew astrologer Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>Kircher refers to him as Abraham Auenar.</note> recites these views from the mind of the Egyptians in his *Book of Reasons* in these words:

<margin>
Abraham Ibn Ezra.
</margin>

Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a German abbot and polymath known for his work on cryptography and angelology.</note>, in his small book *On the Seven Secondary Intelligences* <note>original: "de septem Secundeis"; these are the "second gods" or planetary spirits who act as God's administrators of history.</note> annexed to his *Polygraphia*, describes these Intelligences differently; in his work, he preserves neither the order of the Angels nor the same number of years of the World as Avenar. Thus, the first circle of the revolution of dominion, which the planetary Spirits performed in order, was 2480 years and 4 months; the second circle was completed in the year 4960 with 8 months, and so on until the consummation of the age. ### SECTION VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER IX.

...among the Hebrews it is found to belong to the domain of Anael <note>The angel associated with Venus in the previous table</note>, or another; so that the whole matter ought to be judged—by all those who are accustomed to weigh things with a finer scale of reason—as concocted, resting on no solid foundation of truth, and deserving of no merit.

<margin>The Egyptians attributed a specific ruling Planet to each hour of the day.</margin>I find indeed in the ancient monuments of the Egyptians that they taught something similar, as we shall later explain concerning the Sothiac or Canicular Year <note>original: "Anno Sothiaco sive Caniculari"; this refers to a cycle of 1,461 years based on the rising of the star Sirius, which the Egyptians called Sothis</note>. This was touched upon in the preceding pages and will be explained more fully in what follows, where we shall treat of the Platonic Year and the <term>palingenesia</term> <note>original: "παλιγγενεσίᾳ"; the Stoic and Platonic concept of the periodic rebirth or cyclical renewal of the universe</note> of all things. It is certain, however, that the Egyptians were the first to distribute Genii <note>Spirits or guardian deities</note> to each hour, who would have care of the things committed to their faith by night and by day throughout the course of the entire week. They did this in such a way that the first hour of the first day belonged to the dominion of the Sun (called Coepi), the second hour to the Genius of Venus, the third to the Genius of Mercury, the fourth to the Moon, the fifth to Saturn, the sixth to Jupiter, and the seventh to Mars. Once the dominion of Mars had revolved, the Sun repeated its dominion, and the others followed in the same order as has been stated; until, the revolution of 24 hours (namely, one natural day) being completed, the twenty-fifth hour—that is, the first hour of the following day—would belong to the Moon, from which that day also received its name <note>Monday, or "Moon-day"</note>. Thus, after another revolution of one day was completed, the dominion of the first hour of the third day would belong to Mars, the first hour of the fourth day to Mercury, the first hour of the fifth day to Jupiter, the first hour of the sixth day to Venus, and finally, the first hour of the seventh day would belong to Saturn. The names of the Genii, which we have extracted from the monuments of the Coptic Egyptians, are the following:

<margin>The seven Coptic Deities of the Genii or Angels.</margin>
*   ⲡⲓⲣⲓⲏⲗ ⲡⲟⲩⲣⲟ ⲛⲣⲏ: that is, <term>Piriel, Angel of the Sun</term>.
*   ⲥⲟⲩⲣⲟⲧⲓⲏⲗ ⲡⲟⲩⲣⲟ ⲛⲧⲉⲫⲁⲛⲟⲩ: that is, <term>Surotiel, Lord of Venus</term>.
*   ⲁⲛⲟⲩⲃⲓⲏⲗ ⲡⲟⲩⲣⲟ ⲛⲧⲉⲡⲓⲥⲁϫⲓ: that is, <term>Anubiel, Lord of speech and invention</term> <note>Likely a reference to Anubis or Thoth, the Egyptian god of writing and wisdom</note>.
*   ⲡⲓⲟⲥⲓⲏⲗ ⲡⲟⲩⲣⲟ ⲛⲧⲉⲓⲁⲙ: that is, <term>Piosiel, Lord of the sea and the depths</term>.
*   ⲣⲁⲫⲁⲛⲓⲏⲗ ⲡⲟⲩⲣⲟ ⲛⲧⲉⲭⲣⲟⲛⲟⲥ: that is, <term>Raphaniel, Lord of time and actions</term> <note>Raphan or Remphan was a name associated with the planet Saturn</note>.
*   ⲡⲓⲥⲧⲁⲧⲓⲏⲗ ⲡⲟⲩⲣⲟ ⲛⲧⲉⲡⲓⲱⲛⲧϩ: that is, <term>Pistatiel, Lord of lives</term>.
*   ⲧⲩⲫⲁⲛⲓⲏⲗ ⲡⲟⲩⲣⲟ ⲛⲧⲉⲡⲧⲁⲕⲟ: that is, <term>Typhaniel, Lord of destruction</term> <note>Associated with Typhon or Set, the god of chaos</note>.

And these Genii held dominion over all nature through the days and nights as if taking turns in succession according to the mind of the Egyptians. Thus, Piriel, the Angel of the Sun, would rule the first, eighth, fifteenth, and twenty-second hours of the first day; on the first, eighth, fifteenth, and twenty-second hours of the second day, Piosiel, the Angel of the Moon, would rule; and so on for the others, as has been said. <margin>The superstition of the ancients and moderns in observing the planetary hours.</margin> They observed these hours with such great superstition that they attempted almost no works without consulting them. This custom has been derived from them even down to our own times, and is approved by the common calculation of Astrologers...

| **12** | **Sellen**, | Genius of the favor of Princes. |

<margin>The vanity of the Egyptians in observing planetary hours is sharply criticized.</margin>

It should be noted at this point that this Table only contains the arrangement of the Genii’s dominion over the 12 nocturnal hours of the entire week; however, during the twelve hours of the daytime, the dominions of the Genii follow one another in the exact same order as they do in the nightly hours.

But let us explain this vanity a bit more fully. The Ancients arranged the dominions of the planets according to the order of unequal hours <note>Ancient "unequal" or "temporal" hours divided the day and night into 12 hours each, regardless of the season; thus, a summer daylight hour was much longer than a winter one.</note>; since these hours increase during the day when the Sun turns toward the North, and decrease at night—and the opposite happens when the Sun turns toward the South—it necessarily followed that the planetary reigns were unequal in duration. This was not the case regarding the day itself, but rather regarding the night when compared to the day and other parallels of the Sun. Thus, in the summer Tropic <note>The Summer Solstice.</note>, when in Rome, for example, the hours of the day are almost twice as long as the hours of that same night, the planetary reigns lasted nearly one equinoctial hour and 15 minutes, whereas at night they lasted no more than 45 minutes. Hence, I ask: how could these "astrologasters" <note>A derogatory term for superstitious or fraudulent astrologers.</note> have observed the hours so precisely as to invoke the Genius presiding over that hour—especially at night, when the Sun did not illuminate the <term>sundials <gloss>original: *Sciatherica*; instruments for measuring time by shadows.</gloss></term> erected for this purpose?

---

Certainly, they frequently fell into the gravest errors, believing an hour belonged to Mars when it still pertained to the rule of Jupiter. Truly, those monstrous names and offices of the planetary Genii—who are imagined by the Arabs, Hebrews, and Egyptians to preside over the protection of things at every hour—have no other origin than that drawn from the dark kitchen of the Devil. The horrendous superstitions which they practice to draw down some Genius at a settled hour, and to favor their prayers and solicitations, are such that I judge them more fit for stoking the fires of Vulcan <note>Meaning the fires of a forge or even hellfire.</note> than for the commendation of the public light; indeed, the chaste ears of Christians should shudder at them as most impious, and as inventions of an <term>evil demon <gloss>original: *Cacodæmone*; a malevolent spirit or devil.</gloss></term>. Nevertheless, it seemed right to review them here, both to show the context of this accumulated superstition and to more clearly demonstrate the <term>treatises <gloss>original: *Syntagmata*; organized collections or arrangements of information.</gloss></term> of Egyptian superstition. In this matter, I have followed Saint Irenaeus <note>A 2nd-century Church Father who wrote "Against Heresies."</note>, who, in order to show the unbridled lust and insanity of the Gnostics in dreaming up such things, wove together a long catalog of those same "little gods" whom they call <term>Aeons <gloss>original: *Æonas*; in Gnostic belief, these are emanations of the divine.</gloss></term>, along with their horrendous superstitions. I decided that I must do the same in this place for the caution of the pious: for this Table is a damned root...

CLASS. VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER X.

Hh

...the root of that so-called *Key of Solomon* <note>The *Clavicula Salomonis*, one of the most famous grimoires of planetary magic from the Renaissance.</note>; from which an entrance lies open to the eternal precipices of the infernal abyss, leading to the final destruction of those who use them; from this, magicians complete all their execrable crimes with the help of demons. From here Cornelius Agrippa, Paracelsus, Pietro d’Abano, and other masters of a damned and diabolical art drew their teachings, which I advise all men of fearful conscience to flee as they would Scylla and Charybdis <note>Two legendary sea monsters of Greek mythology; Kircher uses them to represent the "danger on all sides" found in these magical texts.</note>. But who revealed those fanatical names of Angels to them? None other than the Evil Spirit <note>original: *Cacodemon*</note>, the master and craftsman of this whole deceptive art. This indeed is clearly evident from the effects they are said to produce, which are most pernicious, indeed entirely diabolical; no one is so reckless, not to say stupid, that they do not see such things could not apply to good Angels. Therefore, they are merely the works and inventions of magicians and men devoted to diabolical arts.

# CHAPTER X.
## On the Twenty-Eight Mansions of the Moon.

<margin>The Mansions of the Moon are a superstitious seedbed and are rightly called the stables of demons.</margin>
<margin>The 28 Mansions of the Moon are an Egyptian fiction.</margin>
To the planetary hours and their Genii are added the 28 Mansions of the Moon, with their own assigned Genii. In Coptic they call them ⲛⲓⲙⲁⲛϣⲱⲡⲓ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉ ⲡⲓⲓⲟϩ <note>original: *ni-man-shōpi n-te pi-ioh*</note>, that is, the habitations or lodgings of the Moon; in Arabic they are called منازل القمر <note>original: *Manāzil al-Qamar*</note>, the hospices of the Moon. Some also call them the stations of the Lunar Gods. I would more rightly call them the "stables of demons," since they are filled with so many boasting superstitions that there is scarcely an astrological invention into which the Mansions of the Moon do not enter. This is, moreover, a fiction of the Egyptians, who, defining the Moon’s course by the number of 28 days, assigned to it one station for each natural day, together with a Genius for that station as a kind of administrator and guardian. With the greatest zeal, they would first inquire after the planetary hour; then they would consider which station the Moon was in at that same hour; and thus, from the hostile or friendly gathering of Genii, they judged whether their work should be begun or not begun.

<margin>The gate of the mansions of the Moon according to the Egyptians is the Milky Way.</margin>
But before we arrive at the explanation of the Mansions, it seemed appropriate to first explain their "gate" in this place. The Egyptians call the "Gate of the Lunar Mansions" that circle which astronomers commonly call the Milky Way; in Coptic it is called ⲡⲓⲙⲱⲓⲧ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉ ⲡⲓⲧⲟϩ <note>original: *pi-mōit n-te pi-toh*</note>, which word, as I said in the *Supplement to the Coptic Prodromus* (Chapter 5), is Egyptian or Coptic, and we interpret it as the "way of straw" or "chaff." For by this name the Egyptians call that white circle which the Greeks call the <term>γαλαξίαν</term> (Galaxy) or <term>τοῦ γάλακτος κύκλον</term> (the circle of milk), and the Latins call the *via lactea* (Milky Way). Ovid, indeed, describes it as the path by which the gods approached Jupiter, in these words:

<margin>How the Milky Way is named by various peoples.</margin>
> ->*There is a high path, visible in the clear sky:*<-
> ->*It is named "Milky," notable for its very brightness.*<-

---
->By this<-

# CHAPTER X. THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

->By this way the Gods travel to the kingdoms of the great Thunderer,<-
->And to his royal house, etc.<-
<note>original: "Hâc iter est Superis ad magni regna Tonantis..." Kircher quotes Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*, referring to the Milky Way as the path to the palace of Jupiter (the Thunderer).</note>

The "Milky Circle" is so named by the Poets because of the milk spilled by Juno; for more on this matter, consult Hyginus, Phornutus, and other mythologists. This path, I say, is called in Coptic the "Way of Straw" or "Chaff"; a naming convention followed by almost all other Eastern peoples. It consists of two words, the first being ⲙⲱⲓⲧ ⲛ̀, meaning "way," and the other ⲧⲟϩ, meaning "straw" or "chaff"; the ⲛ̀ is the mark of the genitive case <term>nota regiminis: a grammatical indicator showing possession or relationship</term>, as we have taught in our Coptic Grammar. The Arabs, Syrians, Ethiopians, Hebrews, and other Easterners show that this interpretation of ours is the true one. The Arabs usually call the <term>Galaxian</term> <note>original: γαλαξίαν (Greek), the Milky Way</note> <note>Arabic: المجرة</note> *Al-Majarra*, as if you were to say "a flow or trail of scattered straw." The author of the *Scala*, as well as Abenragel, describes it thus: <note>Arabic: المجرة وهي طريق التبن</note> <margin>The author of the Scala, Abenragel, Mor Isaac.</margin> *Al-Majarra, and it is the way of straw or chaff.* Mor Isaac, in his Syriac Philosophy, calls this milky circle the "path of straw" in the same manner with these words:

-><note>original Syriac: ܘܐܦ ܒܚܝܠܗ ܕܡܠܟܘܬܐ ܡܫܡܗ ܒܫܒܝܠܐ ܕܬܒܢܐ — "And also by the power of the kingdom it is named the path of straw."</note><-

Indeed, the zone seen in the circle of the twelve signs is called the "way of straw or chaff." The Ethiopians too, as I have heard from the Abyssinian priests here in Rome, call it *Chafara tsamangadu*, the "way of straw"; just as the Hebrews call it *Netiv ha-teven*, all of them subscribing to the fables of the Egyptians. <margin>Egyptian fable concerning the Milky Way.</margin> For the Egyptians imagine that Typhon <note>A monstrous serpent-like deity in Greek and Egyptian myth, often associated with chaos and storms.</note>, fleeing toward the Indians, scattered a bundle of grain-ears that had been placed in his way across the sky; hence the name "Way of Straw" has remained for that region to this day.

The Egyptians, therefore, as I was saying, establish twenty-eight "Stations of the Moon"—that is, the same number of constellations—which the Moon reaches in each of her periods (that is, in the space of twenty-eight days). <margin>How the Egyptians name the 28 Stations of the Moon.</margin> They call these places by the Coptic name ⲙⲁⲛⲙⲱⲟϩ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉ ⲙⲉⲧⲉⲟⲥ, which means "the dwellings or inns of the Moon" (in Arabic <note>Arabic: المنازل القمرية</note> *the lunar lodgings or lunar stations*). ⲙⲁⲛⲙⲱⲟϩ is the plural for "mansions," ⲛ̀ⲧⲉ is the mark of the genitive, and ⲙⲉⲧⲉⲟⲥ means "Moon." We see that astrologers, from the earliest times to the present day, have observed these lunar stations as being significant and worthy of knowledge, both for exploring changes in the weather and for choosing the most fruitful times to begin works; this is because the influence of the stars in the aforementioned places of the zodiac introduces various effects into worldly matters. <margin>Each of the 28 Lunar Stations consists of 12 degrees and 24 minutes.</margin> Each station consists of exactly 12 degrees and 24 minutes, as will be clear to anyone dividing a circle [of 360 degrees] into 28 parts. Although these stations used to begin at the "head of Aries" in the eighth sphere, modern astrologers now start them from the 22nd degree of Aries due to the movement of the apogees <note>The "movement of the auges" or apogees refers to the precession of the equinoxes, which shifts the position of stars relative to the calendar over centuries.</note>. The order of the Lunar Stations and their explanation follows.

<margin>Order and explanation of the 28 Lunar Stations.</margin> I. ⲕⲁⲧⲱⲛ (*Katon*) in Coptic means "Fish," signifying in this context the "Station of the Fish." In Arabic it is called <note>Arabic: بطن الحوت</note> *Batn al-Hut*, the "Belly of the Whale" (or Fish). This is the first station of the Moon, so named because of its "pernicious humidity." It used to begin at 0 degrees of Aries and ended at 12 degrees and 24 minutes of the same sign. The Genius <note>A guiding spirit or intelligence associated with a celestial body or location.</note> of this station, according to the Arabs, is <note>Arabic: فياييل</note> *Kiaiel*; it is a station for the infestation of one's enemy.

### CLASS VII. MATHEMATICAL HIEROGLYPHS. CHAPTER X.

II. <term>Pikstorion</term> <note>original: πικστωριον</note>, that is, the *Fish of Horus*, which in Arabic is <note>Arabic: الشرطين (al-Sharaṭayn)</note> the *Station of the Moon*, which the author of the *Scala* describes in these words: <note>Arabic: الشرطين وهو راس للحمل (al-Sharaṭayn wa-huwa ra's al-ḥamal)</note> *Sartin, and it is the head of Aries.* Abenragel <note>A 11th-century Arab astrologer</note> says it thus:
<note>Arabic original: الشرطين وهو منزل القمر في برج الحمل فهو راس للحمل</note>
That is, *Sartin is the lunar station in the sign of Aries, and it is commonly taken for the head of Aries itself.* Its beginning is at 12 degrees and 24 minutes of Aries, and its end is at the twenty-fifth degree of the same sign. Its presiding Genius is <note>Arabic: حياييل (Ḥayāyīl)</note> *Hiaiel*; it is the station for the reconciliation of a Prince.

III. <term>Kolion</term> <note>original: κολιων</note>, the *connecting station*, in Arabic <note>Arabic: بطين (al-Buṭayn)</note> *Bathin*. Ibn al-Khamis <note>referencing the author "Chamus"</note> describes it so:
<note>Arabic original: بطين هو منزل القمر فهو مثلث عند بطن الحوت</note>
*Bathin is a lunar station, and it is the triangle near the Belly of the Whale.* We say this station is none other than what the Triangle—or the <term>Delta</term> <note>original: Δέλτα</note>—the head of Aries, and the Northern Fish of nearly the same latitude establish. The beginning of this station starts from the twenty-fifth degree of Aries <note>Astrological symbol for Aries</note>, and its end is in the ninth degree of Taurus <note>Astrological symbol for Taurus</note>. Its Genius is <note>Arabic: جنحاييل (Jankhāyīl)</note> *Ginchiael*, and it is a station of prosperity and good fortune.

IV. <term>Orias</term> <note>original: ωριας</note>, that is, the *Station of Horus*, in Arabic <note>Arabic: الثريا (al-Thurayyā)</note> *Altarieh*; it is the lunar station which the Pleiades <note>The "Seven Sisters" star cluster</note> provide for the Moon. However, they called it the Station of Horus from *Horias*, because Horus—by whom they signify the fertility of the world through <term>hieroglyphs</term> <note>original: ἱερογλύφως</note>, according to Plutarch—exercised himself most greatly in Taurus, the house of Venus, in the company of the Pleiades. For this reason, the Hebrews also call these same Pleiades <term>Succoth Benoth</term> <note>original: סוכות בנות</note>, that is, the *assembly*, or *daughters of the tabernacle, covered daughters, and brooding ones*: for just as a Hen cherishes and sustains her chicks, so does the Station of Horus in Taurus sustain the lower world. From this, they say its idol was a Hen with her chicks. Thus says Rashi <margin>Rashi.</margin> <note>The OCR reads "Raffi," a common early modern misreading of the Hebrew script for the famous commentator Rashi.</note> on chapter 5 of Amos, and in Job:
-> <term>Succoth Benoth was an image of a Hen with her chicks.</term> <note>original Hebrew: סוכות בנות דמות תרנגלת עם אפרוחיח</note> : <-
These *Succoth Benoth* are the same as the *Horias* of the Egyptians, and the <note>Arabic: الثريا</note> *Altarieh* of the Arabs, which is the same as the Taurine station <note>Arabic: الثريا</note>: for *Altarieh* finds its name from no other source than the Arabic word <note>Arabic: ثور</note> *Tzuor*, which signifies a Bull <note>Taurus</note>. Rabbi Jonah <note>Ibn Janah, a famous medieval Hebrew grammarian</note> expressly teaches this in these words on Amos 5. <margin>R. Jonah.</margin>
-> <term>Succoth Benoth are the seven stars in the Zodiac which in the Ishmaelite tongue, that is, Arabic, are called Altarieh.</term> <note>original Hebrew: סוכות בנות הוא ז' כוכבי במזלח אשר בלשון אשמאליס אלتוריא</note> : <-
Truly, regarding these matters, consult the *Egyptian Temple*, that is, the first volume of the *Oedipus*, where many curious things are passed down. The words of Abenragel, who in his *Astrology* describes the mansions of the moon, correspond to these things, saying:
<note>Arabic original: الثريا هو منزل القمر في برج الثور وتسمي دجاجة السماء مع بناتها</note> <margin>Abenragel.</margin>
*Altaria is the lunar station in the sign of Taurus, and it is called the Hen of Heaven with her daughters.* There are some who confuse <note>Arabic: الثريا (al-Thurayya/Pleiades)</note> with <note>Arabic: نعش و بنات نعش (Na'sh and Banat Na'sh)</note>, that is, with the daughters of the bier and the bier of Lazarus, which others call Arcturus, and others the Lesser Bear. But what we think of it, and what should truly be determined...

# THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

<margin>CHAPTER X.
Athenaeus.</margin>

We teach regarding this in the first volume of this *Oedipus*, where we noted the Egyptian Temple. Certainly, I find in the writings of Athenaeus <note>A 2nd-century Greek rhetorician and grammarian</note> that the Pleiades are called <term>Pleiades</term> <note>original Greek: Πλειάδες</note>—that is, "doves"—by Aeschylus, Pindar, and Simonides. Nor does Homer look elsewhere when, in his description of Nestor’s Cup, he sings of <term>peleiades</term> <note>original Greek: πελειάδας</note>, or doves, serving ambrosia to Jupiter, meaning by this the <term>Pleiades</term>. But to return to our purpose: this station is called <term>Opias</term> <note>original Coptic: ⲱⲡⲓⲁⲥ</note> and by another Coptic name <term>Exastron</term> <note>original Coptic: ⲉⲝⲁⲥⲧⲣⲱⲛ</note>, as if you were to say "six stars." By these words, it is most clearly indicated that nothing else is meant but <term>Al-Thurayya</term> <note>Arabic: الثريا</note>, that is, the *Pleiades*; and Ovid agrees with this:

->*The Pleiades begin to support their father’s shoulders,*<-
->*Of whom seven are said to be, though they are usually six.*<-
<note>Reference to Atlas holding the heavens and the "Lost Pleiad" myth.</note>

The beginning of this station is the ninth degree of Taurus, and its end is the twenty-second of the same. But perhaps this is more detailed than was necessary. Its presiding Genius is <term>Delbaiel</term> <note>Arabic: دلباييل</note>; and it is a station of enmity and vengeance.

V. <term>Tompion</term> <note>original Coptic: ⲧⲱⲙⲡⲓⲟⲛ</note> and the *Station of the Elder Horus*, in Arabic <term>Aldebaran</term> <note>Arabic: الدبران</note>; it is called the "Station of Horus" because, just as it occupies nearly the same region of the sky as the preceding one, so also it finds its name from the most effective operations of Horus in this station. Concerning this, Abenragel <note>An 11th-century Arab astrologer</note> writes thus:

-><term>Aldebaran is a mansion in the sign of Taurus, and it is the Eye of the Bull.</term> <note>original Arabic: الدبران هو منزل في برج الثور فهو عين الثور</note> <note>Symbolic sun-like mark</note><-

That is, *Aldebaran is the station of the Moon in the sign of Taurus, and it is called the Eye of the Bull.* All modern astrologers follow the Arabs, who thereafter take Aldebaran for the eye of Taurus. By the Greeks it is called <term>Lampadias</term> <note>original Greek: λαμπαδίας</note>, so named for its remarkable brightness. Its beginning is the 21st degree of Taurus, its end the fourth degree of Gemini <note>Astrological symbol ♊</note>. The Genius is <term>Huajel</term> <note>Arabic: هوابيل</note>; it is a station for the favor of Great Men.

VI. <term>Klauos</term> <note>original Coptic: ⲕⲗⲁⲩⲟⲥ</note> and the *Lock* or *Enclosure*; the station of the Moon thus called in Arabic is <term>Al-Han'ah</term> <note>Arabic: الهنعة</note>, and it is nothing other than two stars in Gemini. The first of these, which precedes their feet, is called <term>Propous</term> <note>original Greek: προπούς, "before the foot"</note> by the Greeks, as Geminus witnesses; the other, <term>the one upon the wrist</term> <note>original Greek: ὁ ἐπὶ τοῦ καρποῦ</note>, is of the second magnitude and is called <term>Ras elgeuze</term> <note>Arabic: راس الجوزا</note> by the Arabs—that is, the *Head* of Gemini <note>Astrological symbol ♊</note>. I find these stars described by the Arabs with two other names, namely <term>Garakles</term> and <term>Apullun</term> <note>Arabic: قركلس وافلون</note>; as this matter left me perplexed, I eventually discovered that they wished to indicate, by these corrupted Greek names, Hercules and Apollo (by which names I read that the <term>Didymoi</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ Διδύμων</note> or Twins were called among the mythologists). This station begins at the fourth degree of Gemini and ends at the eighteenth of the same. Its Genius is <term>Phigiaiel</term> <note>Arabic: فيجاييل</note>; it is a station of benevolence and love.

VII. <term>Klaria</term> <note>original Coptic: ⲕⲗⲁⲣⲓⲁ</note> and to the Arabs <term>Al-Hen'ah</term> or <term>Albenaah</term> <note>Arabic: الهنعة</note>, is a station of the Moon which Abenragel describes thus:

-><term>Al-Hen'ah is the mansion of the moon in the sign of the Twins, which they call the shoulder of the Twins.</term> <note>original Arabic: الهنعة هي منزل القمر في برج التومان يسمونها كتف التومان</note> <note>Symbolic sun-like mark</note><-

*Albenaah is the Moon's station, which they call the shoulders of the Twins.* It begins at the eighteenth degree and ends at the thirtieth of Gemini. Its Genius is <term>Zifaiel</term> <note>Arabic: زساييل</note>; it is a station for the acquisition of goods.

### CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER X.

...the *Nile Cubit* <note>original Latin: *cubitus Nili*</note>, called in Arabic **ذراع الاسد** <note>original: *Dhira al-Asad*</note>, meaning the *Lion’s Cubit*. I believe this station is wrongly named by the Arabs as the "Lion's Cubit," since it is still a whole sign away from that constellation. It is therefore called **ⲡⲓⲙⲉϩⲓ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉⲕⲱⲙ** <note>Coptic: *Pimehi n-te-kōm*</note>, that is, the *Cubit of the Nile*, because around this lunar station, the rising of the Nile began to appear on the Nilometer <note>A structure used to measure the Nile's water level</note>, which was divided into cubits; we have written extensively about this elsewhere. This station begins at the start of Cancer and ends at its 13th degree. Its Genius is **طياييل** <note>original: *Hathaiel*</note>; it is a station for victory in war.

**IX. ⲡⲓⲉⲣⲉⲙⲓⲇⲓⲥ** *the station of descent or influence*, in Arabic **النثرة** <note>original: *Al-Nathrah*</note>; it is the station of the Moon in the sign of Cancer. Thus says Abenragel <note>A 11th-century Arab astrologer</note>:
->**النتره منزل القمر في برج السرطان**<-
<margin>Coptic</margin>

### CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER X.

**XXIV** **ϣⲛⲉⲃⲣⲏⲧⲟⲥ** <note>Coptic: *Shnebritos*</note> **Blessedness, or the swallowed arm**, in Arabic **سعد البلع** <note>original: *Saad elbelaa*, meaning the Luck of the Swallower</note>; this is the station of the Moon which begins at the 29th degree of Capricorn and ends at the 9th degree of Aquarius. This is also called **ذنب الجدي** <note>original: *Dhanab al-Jady*</note> **the tail of the Goat** <note>the constellation Capricorn</note>, from the first-magnitude star fixed at the root of the tail. Its Genius is **خخاييل** <note>original: *Chachaiel*</note>; it is the station of the fertility of the flocks.

**XXV** **ϣⲛⲉϣⲛⲉⲩⲧⲏⲥ** <note>Coptic: *Shneshneutis*</note> **Blessedness of blessednesses, or the arm of arms**, in Arabic **سعد السعود** <note>original: *Saad elsaaud*, meaning the Luck of Lucks</note>; this station of the Moon is in the zodiac division of Aquarius, beginning at the ninth degree of Aquarius and ending at the 21st of the same. Certain Arabs also call this region **فم الحوت** <note>original: *Fam al-Hut*</note> **the mouth of the fish**; for it is, to speak with the Greeks, **the body of the fish, called the southern solitary one** <note>original Greek: σῶμα τοῦ ἰχθύος. λεγομένη νοτίου μονάζοντος</note>; and it seems, according to the mind of the ancients, that this star-cluster should be referred to the "Southern Fish" <note>the constellation Piscis Austrinus</note> rather than to Aquarius. We, therefore, say that this station occupies that region which the Greeks called **the pouring of water** <note>original Greek: χύσιν ὕδατος</note>, and because of its winding paths, they called it **the broken way** <note>original Greek: ἁγμονὸν, *hagmonon*</note>. In Vitruvius <note>a Roman architect and author</note>, this is read corruptly as *agmonon* instead of *hagmonon*; which I would wish the learned to note; for Hesychius <note>an ancient Greek grammarian</note> expressly interprets *hagmonon* as **the pouring out of dim stars** <note>original Greek: τὴν ἄμαθον ἀστέρων χύσιν, literally "the sandy pouring of stars"</note>. The Genius is **ددلييل** <note>original: *Dedaliel*</note>; the station of the abundance of the earth's goods.

**XXVI** **ϣⲛⲉϣⲃⲉⲣⲓⲁⲛ** <note>Coptic: *Shneshberian*</note> **The hidden arm**, in Arabic **سعد الاخبية** <note>original: *Saad elachbieh*, meaning the Luck of the Tents</note>; this is the station of the Moon which begins from the twenty-first degree of Aquarius and ends at the fourth degree of Pisces. The Genius is **صخاييل** <note>original: *Szakzaiel*</note>; the station of pleasures.

**XXVII** **ⲁⲣⲧⲉⲗⲟⲥ** <note>Coptic: *Artelos*</note> **Station of the first sprouting**, in Arabic **الفرع المقدم** <note>original: *Alphara elmakoddem*, meaning the foremost spout</note>; this is the station of the Moon whose beginning is from the fourth degree of Pisces and its end in the 17th degree of Pisces. Its Genius is **تطاييل** <note>original: *Tataiel*</note>; the station of droughts.

**XXVIII** **ⲁⲣⲧⲉⲗⲟⲥⲓⲁ** <note>Coptic: *Artelosia*</note> **The latter sprouting**, in Arabic **الفرع المؤخر** <note>original: *Elphara elmuchhar*, meaning the rear spout</note>; this is the station of the Moon extended from the 17th degree of Pisces up to the 30th degree of the same. The Genius is **هرخزييل** <note>original: *Harchaziel*</note>; the station of floods.

-># PART II.<-

->### On the Egyptian Calculation, and the Reason and Method for Correctly Establishing the Year.<-

-># CHAPTER I.<-

->#### *On the Origin of the division of time into years, days, and hours.*<-

<margin>The Egyptians divided the year into as many days as the years Enoch lived.</margin>It has been shown more than enough from Plutarch, Diodorus, Herodotus, and others that the Egyptians were the first among mortals after the flood to focus on Astronomy, to have divided time into years and days according to the course of the Sun and Moon, and to have discovered the system for intercalating <note>intercalation: the insertion of extra days into a calendar to keep it synchronized with the seasons</note> days. To make this more clearly evident now:

It must be known that there was a secret tradition of the Hierophants <note>Hierophants: high-ranking priests who interpreted sacred mysteries</note> (as we hinted at earlier in the section on Astrology, and in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* page 28) that the civil year of the Egyptians consisted of as many days as there were years in the life of Enoch—that first Hermes from before the flood, whom the Arabs call Adris, and the Egyptians call the first Osiris, or also Hermes. For Enoch, as the sacred text of Genesis testifies, reached 365 years of his life before he was translated <note>translated: taken up to heaven without dying</note>. *And all the days of Enoch were three hundred sixty-five years.* Since we have previously reported that the second Hermes, whom we called Trismegistus, established the year with this many days, it is likely that he obtained this method from the monuments of the first Hermes, which were communicated to the world after the flood through Ham. Indeed, not only the ancient astronomers but also later mathematicians, and most notably their prince, Ptolemy, used this full and simple civil year of the Egyptians. Others in this place say the author of the <term>ἐπαγομένων</term> <note>original Greek: epagomenon; these are the "added" or "intercalary" days</note> or intercalary days was Afeth, the thirty-first of the Kings of Egypt; so says Eusebius in his *Chronicle*: *Afeth, the 31st of the Egyptian Kings, reigned for 20 years.* He added the intercalary days to the year, and in those times, as they say, the Egyptian year of 365 days was produced, which previously was completed in 360. But since we have already attributed the invention of this thing to Mercury Trismegistus, who was much more ancient, I do not see how these accounts can be consistent. From Misraim <note>Misraim: the biblical grandson of Noah and legendary founder of Egypt</note>, the founder of the Egyptian Monarchy, until Afeth (whom we say is the same as Mispharmutosi the second), 924 years are counted, according to the testimony of Eusebius himself: <term>From the first King of those under Misraim in Egypt until Concharus, 606 years, or rather 700 full years, under 25 Kings.</term> <note>original Greek: Ἀπὸ τοῦ πρώτου Βασιλέως τῆς κατὰ Μεσρέιμ τῆς Αἰγύπτῳ ἕως τῆς Κονχάρεως ἔτη ϛχ’ ὅ γ’ καὶ πλήρη ἔτη ψ’, Βασιλέων κέ :</note> <margin>Eusebius makes King Afeth the author of the <term>intercalary days</term>, but incorrectly.</margin> From Concharus to Afeth, 224 years are numbered according to the same author; these joined to the 700 make 924 years, and thus the invention of the intercalary days would fall around the years of the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt; this ought not, nor can it, be said for any reason. For if we are to stand by the *Chronicle* of Eusebius computed from the fragments of Manetho <note>Manetho: an ancient Egyptian priest and historian</note>, it must be said that either Afeth has been confused with another King of this name...

<summary>Kircher argues that the 365-day Egyptian year was originally modeled on the 365-year lifespan of the biblical patriarch Enoch, whom he identifies with the Egyptian Hermes. He disputes Eusebius’s later dating of the calendar's reform, claiming it is far older than the 16th century BCE.</summary>

<keywords>Enoch, Hermes Trismegistus, Egyptian calendar, intercalary days, Eusebius, chronology, Misraim, 365 days, astronomy</keywords>

--- Page 250 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Egyptian chronology from page 248. It specifically addresses King Aseth's role in refining the calendar and explains the mechanics of the Sothic cycle—the 1,460-year loop where the Egyptian calendar realigns with the solar seasons—distinguishing between the "wandering" civil year and the fixed Julian year.</meta>

Regarding the King, whom we called Maspharmutosin II above, this most intricate knot must be more accurately untangled. To that end:

I say that King Aseth was nearly contemporary with Mercury <note>original: "Mercurio," referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note>; for Eusebius places him third before Tutemosin. Aseth, being inquisitive, brought the inventions of Mercury back to the anvil <note>a metaphor for refining or reworking an idea</note> and reorganized the epagomenal days <note>epagomenal: the five extra days added to the 360-day year to reach 365</note>. Rejecting the various crude opinions of that rough age regarding the form of the year, he retained only this one as more exact. To adorn it with a mysterious quality, he distinguished each of these five intercalary days with the names of Gods. Thus, among posterity, he was known as the inventor of this mechanism—not because he was truly its first inventor, since Mercury first publicized the 365-day year after the flood through a tradition passed down from Enoch via Ham, as we have said. In this way, I believe this passage should be understood, pending better judgment; for with this established, both the order of chronology and the logic of time will be more skillfully consistent.

### CHAPTER II.
-> *On the Sothic, or Canicular, Period.* <-

**T**he Egyptians, becoming gradually better instructed through long experience in celestial observation, saw that the year they then commonly used (consisting of 360 days) did not quite correspond to the Sun's period in the Zodiac. <margin>The 365-day Civil Year of the Egyptians was twofold: fixed and wandering.</margin> Noting that the Sun's period exceeded that year by five days, they defined the Solar year as twelve months consisting of 300 days <note>original Greek: *Ἑκατονθήμερος*, literally 'hundred-day-period', which Kircher glosses as *trecenarijs* or 'consisting of three hundreds,' referring to the base 300 days of the ten 30-day months prior to the final 60 days and the 5 extra days</note> with an appendix of five epagomenal days at the end of the year, without any quarter-day. This was thereafter regarded by everyone as the true civil year. This year, in turn, was either fixed or wandering; the former served civil business, while the latter served the sacred actions of the Hierophants <note>Hierophants: high-ranking priests who interpreted sacred mysteries</note>.

Thus, the Egyptian year was simple and uniform, without any extra hours or leap days <note>original: "biſſextis," referring to the bissextile or leap day</note> that are usually intercalated in the Julian calendar every four years. Therefore, if compared with the Julian year, <margin>The Egyptian year is always uniform.</margin> after four years, the start of the months move back by one day; after eight years, by two days; and so on gradually, until after 1,460 Julian years have passed, the first day of the first month returns to the same Julian month and day from which it started. <margin>The minor Canicular or Sothic period of the Egyptians.</margin> Some call this circle of years the Canicular Period or Sothic Period <note>original Greek: *ἔτος κυνικὸν, ἄτος Σωθιακὸν*; *Canicular* refers to the Dog Star, Sirius</note>. The Minor Canicular Period is a system of 4 Egyptian years, consisting of 1,460 days; whereas the Minor Julian Period is 4 Julian years, consisting of 1,461 days. The Julian period exceeds the Egyptian by one day due to the intercalation of the four quarter-days. For a single Julian year exceeds the Egyptian by almost six hours, which, growing over four years into 24 hours, necessitates the intercalation of an entire day. Furthermore, the Greater Egyptian Canicular Period <margin>The greater Canicular or Sothic period of the Egyptians.</margin> is a system of 1,461 Egyptian years, in which interval the civil month of Thoth <note>Thoth: the first month of the ancient Egyptian calendar</note> returns to the Julian Thoth from which it started. The Julian Canicular Period, however, is a system of 365 minor Julian periods.

<summary>This page discusses the Egyptian calendar's development, crediting King Aseth with formalizing the 365-day year by adding five days named after gods. It explains the Sothic cycle (or Canicular Period), where the Egyptian 'wandering' year realigns with the solar year every 1,460 years.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of the Egyptian calendar, moving from the introduction of the 365-day year by King Aseth to the mathematical and religious implications of the "Sothic Cycle." It addresses a scholarly dispute regarding whether the Egyptians used leap years (intercalation) and introduces the concept of the "Year of God," citing classical authors like Theon, Ptolemy, Censorinus, and Geminus to distinguish between the fixed civil calendar and the wandering priestly calendar.</meta>

### CHAPTER II. THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

...of 365 days; specifically 1,460 Julian years, but 1,461 Egyptian years, <margin>The Year of God among the Egyptians.</margin> in which interval the month of Thoth <note>The first month of the Egyptian calendar.</note> returns to the same Julian day. And this span they call the <term>Great Canicular Year</term> <note>original: "ἔτος κυνικὸν μέγα"; Canicular refers to the Dog Star, Sirius</note>, or the <term>Year of God</term> <note>original: "ἐνιαυτὸς Θεοῦ"</note>. This division and naming of years has stirred up no small amount of dispute not long ago between two men of great reputation; however, I have decided this must be settled solely by the authority of ancient writers. For in this matter, as it is both obscure and uncertain, one ought to believe only as much as can be proven from reliable authors, <margin>The state of the controversy against the Egyptian years and cycles.</margin> lest any room be granted to fictions and shameful inventions. The hinge of the controversy, therefore, turns on this: First, whether the Egyptians, besides the common solar year which was "loose and wandering" <note>A year without leap days that shifts through the seasons</note>, also employed four-year cycles <note>original: "lustra"</note> or Sothic cycles? Second, whether they called it the **Year of God**? Third, whether they employed intercalation <note>The insertion of a leap day</note> to fix the years in place? I shall treat each of these briefly in order.

<margin>Theon of Alexandria.</margin> Theon describes the Egyptians using a wandering and loose year in these words: <note>original Greek: "Ἐξ ἧς λαμβάνομεν..."</note> *From which we understand that the day according to the Egyptians... for the year according to the Greeks, or rather as given in Alexandria, consists of 365 days and one quarter, whereas according to the Egyptians, as we said, it is 365 only. It is clear that every four years, one day is added to the Alexandrian count.* Subsequently, "Month" and "day" are used according to the Egyptians in this manner. For since the <term>prophetic</term> <note>original: "προφήτης"; here meaning 'standard' or 'foretelling'</note> year of the Greeks or Alexandrians consists of 365 days and one quarter, but that of the Egyptians only 365: it is evident that every fourth year, one day is added to the Alexandrian system. In these words, he indicates that the Alexandrians had adopted a fixed year—namely the Augustan year—but that the ancient Egyptians <margin>Ptolemy.</margin> conducted a simple and uniform year without an intercalary day. All of this is confirmed by Ptolemy in the *Almagest*. Regarding the Sothic cycles, which they called the <term>Year of God</term>, <margin>Censorinus.</margin> Censorinus reports they were used in these words: *"The Moon does not pertain to the Egyptian 'Great Year,' which the Greeks call <term>Canicular</term> and we Latins call the <term>Dog-Star Year</term>; this is because its beginning is taken when the star Sirius <note>original: "Caniculae sidus"</note> rises on the first day of that month which the Egyptians call Thoth. For their civil year has only 365 days without any intercalation; thus, every four years among them is roughly one day shorter than the natural four-year period, and so it happens that in the 1,461st year it revolves back to the same starting point."* This year is also called the <term>Solar Year</term> by some, and by others the <term>Year of God</term>. <margin>The Egyptians had a twofold method of calculation.</margin> To understand these things, it must be observed that the Egyptians had a twofold method for their calculations: one was established for fixing the years and bringing them into order, and was used commonly throughout Egypt along with the Alexandrians; even to this day, the Coptic Christians observe it. The other was peculiar to the Priests and Hierophants <note>High-ranking priests who interpreted sacred mysteries</note>; hence it was called the mystical <margin>The Hierophantic method of calculation among the Egyptians.</margin> or "hierophantic" and secret method, known only (as I said) to the Sages of the priestly order. It used no intercalation, just like the civil year, but it "gave the reins" to its years, allowing them to wander, and accounted for the increasing days and years by a certain secret and mystical skill related to the movements of the Sun. But lest we seem to have said anything without proof, it remains for the testimonies of reliable authors to be declared. <margin>Geminus.</margin> First, Geminus, an ancient astronomer, discusses these "Hierophantic years" in his book *On the Sphere*: <note>original Greek: "Οἱ μὲν γὰρ τῶν ἑορτῶν..."</note> *For those who lead the festivals and sacrifices have followed the Greeks. For they do not lead the years according to the sun, nor the months or days according to the moon, but they use a certain unique arrangement; for they wish the sacrifices to the Gods...*

That the festivals of the gods should not occur at the same time and year, but should pass through all the seasons of the year, so that summer, winter, autumn, and spring festivals might be celebrated in turn; for the year consists of 365 days, and they lead twelve months of thirty days, and they set apart five [extra] days; but they do not add the one-fourth [the leap day], for the reason mentioned, so that their festivals may rotate.

<margin>Why the Hierophants used a wandering year.</margin> For the Egyptians, he says, followed a purpose and opinion contrary to the Greeks; for they do not direct their years to the Sun, nor their months and days to the Moon, but they rely on a specific foundation. For they strive to represent the sacred rites of the Gods not at the same times of the year, but they wish those rites to wander through all the seasons of the year, so that the same festival might be summer, winter, autumn, and finally spring. Indeed, they observe a year of 365 days, and twelve thirty-day months; to these they add five days besides. They do not insert the quarter-day <note>The extra six hours that create a leap year</note> for the stated reason, namely, so that their solemnities might recede <note>Move backward through the calendar</note>. And this is the specific institution of the **Hierophants** <note>High-ranking Egyptian priests who guarded sacred secrets</note>, who intentionally loosened the reins of their year so that solemn and festive days would not be confined to any fixed season, but would gradually be led through all of them. Thus, the Alexandrians and those following the Egyptian [calendar] begin the year together, and throughout that year the Alexandrians observe the days and months clearly according to the Egyptian system, having anticipated the years according to the Egyptians; and at the beginning [of the cycle] they follow again. Because indeed, according to the Greeks or Alexandrians, as has been handed down by us, the year consists of 365 days with a quarter, while according to the Egyptians it is only 365, as we have said; it is evident that the Alexandrian year gains a full day every four years; and in 1,460 years, it gains 365 days, which is to say, one Egyptian year <note>This refers to the Sothic Cycle: 1,460 Julian years equal 1,461 Egyptian wandering years</note>. ## CHAPTER II. 252 HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>Strabo.</margin> ...brings forward among other things. Their practice is this: to manage the days not according to the Moon, but according to the Sun, so that to twelve thirty-day months they add five extra days every year; furthermore, since a certain small portion of a day exceeds the completion of the whole year <note>referring to the six hours that make a leap year</note>, they compose a fixed period from whole days and whole years, in which the remaining portions of individual years complete a full day.

<margin>Lucian.</margin> At this point, some surprisingly contend that the Egyptian years were lunar, persuaded by that passage of Lucian, who in his book *On Astrology* discusses it thus: <note>original Greek: "Καὶ οἱ μὲν ἔτι σφίσι μείζον ἡ σελήνη καὶ ἡ ταύτης αἶσα σοφὴ ἐγίνετο. ἔπειτα κύκλῳ, καὶ τὰ ἡλίου ἐμάθοντο."</note> *"And for these people [the Egyptians] indeed, the Moon and its allotted portion were even more significant; then, in a cycle, they also learned of the Sun."* And these Egyptians indeed measure the months by the Moon and its revolution; but they define the year by the Sun and its circuit. 

<margin>The lunar, two-month, and three-month years of some Egyptians.</margin> To explain this, it must be known that just as there were various religions for various people in Egypt, so too the system of months was diverse. For some of the ancient Egyptians, when they noted the Moon completing its circuit every month, they used this circuit as a "year," so that the lunar month—in which the Moon passes through the Zodiac—was called a "Lunar Year" by them. However, when they saw that this system of calculation was contrary to their customs, they abandoned it and established sometimes a two-month year, sometimes a three-month, or a four-month one. Yet, seeing that they were still not satisfied in the distribution of time, they made the Lunar year precisely 360 days, so that individual 30-day months corresponded precisely to the 12 signs of the Zodiac. But let us hear Censorinus: 

<margin>Censorinus.</margin> "And in Egypt indeed, the most ancient practice was for the year to be two months long; afterwards, it was made four months by King Piso; most recently, they extended the year to 12 months and five days." With this agrees the statement of the Hebrew author in the book *On New Moons* <note>original Hebrew: "Moledim," referring to the calculation of the new moon</note>:

> Our Rabbis of blessed memory say <note>original Hebrew: "אמרו ח'ז'ל"</note> that of old they calculated the years according to the way of the Egyptians; that is, they calculated the years according to the lunar cycles; and it is written in the books of calculations that our father Abraham <note>original Hebrew: "אבינו אברהם"</note> of blessed memory delivered this system to the Egyptians.

From these things it is clearly evident that the Egyptians also established their years according to lunar cycles—not all of them, but some **Nomes** <note>administrative districts of ancient Egypt</note> more devoted to the worship of the Moon; however, the greater part of Egypt <margin>Some Egyptians used Lunar years, others Solar.</margin> used Solar years, as is testified by those things we brought forward a little earlier, and as will be more clearly evident in what follows. But let us return to where we digressed.

It is now our task to prove from authors that both [types] were called the "Year of God." And this has already been proven from Censorinus a little before. Now, however, we bring forward a witness beyond all exception, Horapollo, who, dealing with the hieroglyphic representation of the year, discusses it thus in Book 1, Chapter 5: 

<margin>Horapollo.</margin> <quote>“When they signify a year, they draw a quarter of an aroura. An aroura is a measure of land of one hundred cubits. And wishing to say a year, they say 'a quarter,' since they say that from one rising of the star of the God [Sothis] until another rising, a quarter of a day is added over the three hundred and sixty-five days. Wherefore every four years, the Egyptians count a 'Divine Day,' for four quarters complete a day.”</quote> <note>Hieroglyphic description: Although Kircher does not provide a visual figure here, he transcribes Horapollo's description of the hieroglyph for "year" (Annus) as a "fourth of an aroura" (τέταρτον ἀρούρας), a land measure of 100 cubits, representing the extra quarter-day in the solar cycle.</note> 

Immediately, he says, when signifying a year, they paint a fourth part of an year. Moreover, an <term>aroura</term> <note>original: "ἄρουρα," a Greek unit of land area, roughly 2/3 of an acre, used here to explain the fraction of a year</note> (from which the word *arvum* [field] comes to the Latins) is a measure of land comprising a hundred cubits. Therefore, wishing to say "a year," they say "a fourth," because from one rising of the star, the name of which is <term>Sothis</term> <note>The Egyptian name for the star Sirius, whose rising heralded the Nile flood</note>, to the next, as they report, a fourth part of a day is interspersed; so that the "Year of God" consists of 365 days. ### CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER II.

Every fourth year the Egyptians also count and intercalate an extra day, since four quarters of a day complete a full day. <margin>The "Year of God" is the same as the "Year of the Sun" among the Egyptians.</margin> Since the Egyptians call the Sun "God," it is no wonder that the Solar Year <note>Symbol: circle with a dot (Sun) preceded by characters i τ and followed by ⲑ</note>—called in Coptic **ti-rompi** <note>original: ϯⲣⲟⲙⲡⲓ; Symbol: ⲑ with a cross below</note> or **ti-rompi** through a mixture of terms—is named thus. For it is better known than it needs to be stated that Osiris, or the Sun, was called the "Great God" by the Egyptians (according to the testimony of Plutarch), and Isis was the Moon. <margin>Plutarch.</margin> From this also, the historian Apion mentions that a statue of Osiris, or <margin>Apion the Historicus.</margin> Serapis, was cast from a nine-cubit emerald—a stupendous miracle among them. All these things show that honor was held for this Solar Deity, Osiris, above all others.

-><-

Now indeed (which is a matter of greater difficulty), it must be briefly explained why they expressed the "common year" <margin>Why the common year is signified by a fourth part of an aroura.</margin> by a "fourth part of an *aroura*" <term>aroura: an ancient Egyptian unit of land area, typically 100 square cubits</term>, which was comprised of only one hundred cubits, and why they named that same year "the fourth" <note>Greek: τέταρτον (tetarton)</note>, as if you were to say "a quadrant." For since Horus describes a double year in this cited passage—one smaller year of 365 days, and another <margin>The double year among the Egyptians.</margin> "Cynic" or Canicular year <term>Canicular: related to the Dog Star, Sirius</term>, which comprised four solar years with one intercalary day added—they defined this year by the rising of Sothis <note>the star Sirius</note> repeated four times. Thus, when three hundred and sixty-five days were finished, six hours were added each year to the course defined by the Sun's motion; these hours would produce a full day after a rotation of four years. 

The Egyptians, I say, finally intercalated one day in the fourth year of Sothis, and only then considered a full year to be complete (which was in reality a four-year period, one day longer than a civil four-year period). This year the Greeks call *kynikon* ["Cynic" or "Dog-like"], the Latins—as Censorinus <note>original: Gensorinus</note> well notes—call the "Canicular" year, and the Copts call **ti-rompi** <note>original: ϯⲣⲟⲙⲡⲓ</note>. This is because its beginning is taken from the first day of that month which the Egyptians call Thoth <note>original Coptic: Ⲑⲱⲑ (Thoth) followed by a symbolic representation of the Sun/Month</note>, when Sothis rises. For their own specific solar year, being "unbound" and "wandering," has only 365 days without any quarter-day. Therefore, a four-year period is approximately one day less than a natural four-year period, and thus it happens that in 1460 years, it returns entirely to almost the same beginning. 

In the works of Horus, therefore, the "turning year" is taken for the civil year, and they denote it by a fourth part of an *aroura*; and wishing to say "year," they say "the fourth" [*tetarton*], or "quadrant." To what purpose is this, if not because six hours are a fourth part of a day? And furthermore, just as the civil year is a fourth part of a Canicular Lustrum <term>Lustrum: here used to mean a four-year Sothic cycle</term> or Sothic cycle; so too 365 years are a fourth part of the "Great Year." These 365 years, multiplied by four, produce 1460—that Great Canicular Year, which we defined above as the Egyptian System of 1460 years. Again, just as six hours accrue to each simple year, which after four years become a whole "artificial" day, so to each 365-year period accrue 91 days and one quarter, which after 1460 years grows into a whole Great Canicular Year, which we defined as the System of 1461 years. 

Horapollo beautifully wove this reasoning in when he said: <margin>Horapollo.</margin> "From one rising of the star Sothis until the next rising, a fourth of a day is added" <note>original Greek: Μετὰ τὴν ἀνατολὴν τοῦ ἄστρου τοῦ Σωθέως μέχρι τῆς ἄλλης ἀνατολῆς τέταρτον ἡμέρας προστίθεται.</note>; from which, he says, they count a superfluous day every fourth year. This the Alexandrians call the "Cynic" year, the Copts the "Sothic," and others the "Hermetic," from Hermes its first [inventor].

...supreme instructor, whom they also depicted in the form of a Dog, and whom they believed, once translated into Heaven, shone in the form of Sothis <note>The Dog Star, Sirius</note>. You see, therefore, how the Priests fixed their years, and by what reasoning they "loosened the reins" of the same; they fixed them, clearly, by the command of the Princes for the direction of civil actions, but they loosened them for mystical reasons brought forward above from Geminus. And this "solid" civil year of theirs was defined by a span of four years, in which Eudoxus <note>A Greek astronomer who studied in Egypt</note> thought the periods and the circuit of the seasons were completed; of which Pliny also makes mention in these words: *Eudoxus thinks that if one wishes to observe the smallest circuits, the same cycles return after exactly four years—not only of the winds, but also for the most part of the other seasons; and the beginning of this Cycle is always in the intercalary year at the rising of the Dog Star.* Nothing clearer than this can be said. Harmonious with these things are also what Horapollo brings forward in Book 2 of the *Hieroglyphics*, chapter 85, where he expressly says that the Egyptian year consists of four years in these words: <note>original Greek: Ἄνθρωπον ζήσαντα τέλειον βίον θέλοντες σημῆναι, κορώνην ζωγραφοῦσιν, αὕτη γὰρ ζῇ ἑκατὸν ἔτη κατ᾿ Αἰγυπτίους. τὸ δὲ ἔτος τεσσάρων ἐνιαυτῶν.</note> "Wishing to signify a man who has lived a full life, they paint a Crow; for this bird lives a hundred years according to the Egyptians. However, the 'year' [intended here] consists of four usual years." The author of the *Scala Magna* <term>Scala Magna: a famous medieval Coptic-Arabic encyclopedic dictionary</term> expressly says:

->The Coptic months are twelve. Their year is 365 days, with the five days of the *Nisi* <note>The epagomenal or "added" days; original Arabic: النسي</note>, and every four years a leap day at the beginning of the year, *Neuruz* <note>Nowruz</note>, which is a Persian word. <note>Symbol: Star/Sun</note><-

*The months of the Copts are 12, and their year is 365 days with 5 days of Nisi, and every four years a leap day at the beginning of the year Neuruz, which is a Persian word.* The Coptic reading in the same place corresponds to this:

->The twelve months of the Copts, and the five epagomenal days, the day of intercalation every four years at the beginning of the year, namely Neuruz.<-

*That is: The twelve Coptic months, and the five epagomenal days, the day of intercalation every four years at the beginning of the year, namely Neuruz.* This is confirmed by another Arabic manuscript treatise on the Computation of the Copts, which that distinguished man <term>Abraham Ecchelensis: a Maronite scholar and linguist who assisted Kircher with Oriental languages</term>, my singular friend, granted as a loan, who discusses the year of the Copts thus:

->Many of the Wise believe the Solar Year to be 365 days and a quarter day simply; and therefore the months in this world are so ordered that the beginning, for example, of the Coptic months is the month of Thoth and Paophi, or the beginning of the Greek months, or the beginning of the Syrians is Elul and Tishri; and it is said that this ordering was made by the sons of Adam from the beginning of days. <note>Symbol: Star/Sun</note><-

<note>original Arabic: يوما سوا ولذلك يجتمع الربع في كل اربع سنين فيصير يوما ولذلك يكبسوا السنة الرابعة تكون ثلثمائة وستة وستون يوما</note>

And establishing it, they fixed the year so that the Solar year would be 365 days with a quarter of a day equally; and therefore, collecting this quarter every four years, they completed one day, and by intercalating the same, they established a year of 366 days. But if anyone is not yet satisfied by the cited passages, we bring forward Diodorus <margin>Diodorus Siculus.</margin> Siculus, also cited above, who, speaking of the inhabitants of Thebes, discourses thus:
> They do not arrange the days according to the Moon, but according to the Sun, setting months of thirty days; they add five days and a quarter to the twelve months, and in this way they complete the cycle of the year.
<note>original Greek: Τὰς δὲ ἡμέρας οὐκ ἄγουσι κτ' σελήνην, ἀλλὰ κτ' τὸν ἥλιον τριακονθημέρους μὲν τιθέμενοι τοὺς μῆνας, πέντε δὲ ἡμέρας καὶ τέταρτον τοῖς δώδεκα μησὶν ἐπάγουσι, καὶ τούτῳ τῷ τρόπῳ τὸν ἐνιαύσιον κύκλον ἀναπληροῦσι.</note>

The days, he says, are not taken according to the Moon, but the Sun, so that they attribute 30 days to each month, and introduce five days with a quadrant <note>a quarter-day</note> to the twelve months, and by this reckoning they fulfill the entire cycle of the year. Therefore, among the Egyptians, besides the "vague" or loose year, a fixed and <term>embolismic</term> <note>from Greek "embolismos," meaning intercalary or "inserted," referring to the leap day</note> year was also very much in use, since without it, the greatest confusion would necessarily arise in the administration of public affairs. Indeed, so far were the Egyptians from first receiving this intercalation from the Greeks and Latins, <margin>The Greeks received the method of intercalation from the Egyptians.</margin> that rather the Greeks first learned the true reckoning of the year and the method of intercalation from those same Egyptians. But lest anyone think I am dealing only in words, I hold for my side that most grave author of the highest reliability, the <term>eyewitness</term> <note>original: αυτόπτω (autoptō)</note> Strabo, who in the middle of his 17th book teaches that Eudoxus first brought this reckoning of the intercalated day and year into Greece, having received it from the Egyptians, in these words: <margin>Strabo.</margin>
> For Eudoxus traveled here with Plato, and they spent thirteen years with the priests there. For as these priests were outstanding in their knowledge of heavenly things, yet were secretive and reluctant to share concerning time and its observances, they were eventually discovered; and although they [the priests] possessed certain theorems, the Barbarians <note>a common Greek term for non-Greeks, here meaning Egyptians</note> concealed most of them. These men [the priests] handed down the portions of the day and night that exceed 365 days for the completion of the annual time. But the year was unknown among the Greeks until that time, as were many other things, until the younger astronomers received from those who translated the memoirs of the priests into the Greek language, and even now they receive things from them and from the Chaldeans.
<note>original Greek: Συνανέβη γὰρ δὴ τῷ Πλάτωνι ὁ Εὔδοξος δεῦρο... καὶ τὰ τῶν Χαλδαίων.</note>

<margin>Eudoxus received intercalation from the Egyptians.</margin> That is: For Eudoxus set out there with Plato; and both were involved with the Priests for 13 years, as some have recorded. Those Priests, while they excelled in the science of celestial matters, otherwise kept it secret and did not wish to communicate it with anyone; yet, overcome by both time and submissive service, they explained some precepts, while the Barbarians meanwhile concealed very many others. They handed down the particles of day and night running beyond 365 days toward the completion of the year. The year was ignored at that time among the Greeks, just as were many other things; until the younger Astronomers received those things from those who translated the records of the Priests into the Greek language, and even still they receive them both from those and from the Chaldeans. From which it clearly appears that long before the invasion of Egypt by Alexander the Great, the Egyptians knew and practiced the <term>intercalation</term> <note>original: ἐμβολισμόν (embolismon)</note> of the year arising from the four quadrants of the day; indeed, that Eudoxus first handed down to the Greeks the secret received from the Hierophants <note>high priests of the mysteries</note> who had been won over by gifts and submission.

Besides this fixed year intended for civil actions, they had, as I said, another year, which was known only to the Priests, which we have partly proved (and shall prove further a little later) they called the <margin>The fourfold Year of God of the Hieromants.</margin> "Year of God"; and it was fourfold. The first was a year of four year-quadrants, or...
