### CHAPTER II. 256 OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM ###

<margin>The first year of God or the Canicular Lustrum.</margin> ...or composed of four three-month periods, which they also called the year of <term>Horus</term> <note>Horus was the Egyptian god of the sky and sun; here, his "year" refers to a single season</note>. Thus Censorinus, in the passage frequently cited, says these words: *There are those who hand down that Horus instituted this three-month year, and that through it Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter pass, and it is called a year; and the Greeks call their annals <term>horai</term> <note>original Greek: ὥρας — meaning seasons or hours</note>, and their writers <term>horographers</term> <note>original Greek: ὡρογράφους — writers of seasons or annals</note>.* Furthermore, it has been proven from Horapollo and Censorinus that the fixed year and the Canicular or Sothiac Lustrum <note>A four-year period ending with the rising of the dog-star, Sirius</note> was called the <term>year of God</term> <note>original Greek: ἐνιαυτὸς Θεοῦ</note>. This opinion is confirmed by <term>Haly</term> <note>Likely Ali ibn Ridwan, a medieval Arabic astronomer</note>, the Arabic Chronographer, in these words:

<margin>Haly.</margin>->And the great year of the Egyptians is composed of four simple years, and they call it the year<-
->of the God, because each one of them is marked with the name of a God.<- <note>Decorative floral ornament</note>

Furthermore, the "great year" of the Egyptians is composed of four simple years, which they also called the "Year of God," because each one of them was distinguished by the name of some God. No testimony could be more illustrative than this. From this, the Persians also seem to have taken the opportunity to name that great year of 1,440 years <term>Salchudai</term> <note>Persian: سالخدای — literally "Year of God"</note>, and the month (or twelfth part of this great year) the "Great Month," <margin>The Persians received their method of arranging the year from the Egyptians</margin> called in <term>Persian</term> <term>Bozurah mahe</term> <note>original: بزورج ماه — Great Month</note>, and in <term>Chaldean</term> <term>Sabara</term> <note>original Hebrew/Chaldean: סחרא — cycle</note>, or corruptly <term>Sarus</term>, from which comes the "Sari" of the Chaldeans. For if 120 civil years constitute one month, then twelve such months—which equal 1,440 years—will be one "greatest year." It was called in Persian <term>Salchudai</term>, or <term>equal to God</term> <note>original Greek: ἰσόθεος</note>, from the days of the months being <term>synonymous</term> <note>original Greek: συνωνύμοις</note> with the Persian Gods, as we shall declare elsewhere. You see, therefore, that even the Persians, as neighbors to Egypt, coordinated their years in imitation of the Egyptians; as those who were similar in mysteries and mystical disciplines, they did not differ in their methods of arranging years. Therefore, what for us is the space of time comprised between two leap years—namely a Lustrum, <margin>What the Sothiac or Canicular Lustrum is.</margin> or the Julian four-year period—this was for the Egyptians the Sothiac or Canicular Lustrum, both consisting of 1,460 days. After the completion of these, an <term>intercalation</term> <note>original Greek: ἐμβολιμὸς — the insertion of a leap day</note> of one accumulated day occurred, as has been proven from the Greek, Arabic, Latin, and Hebrew authors cited above.

<margin>The method of Egyptian intercalation is explained.</margin> At this point, someone might perhaps wonder how the Egyptians intercalated days and years after every lustrum (both small and large), when it is well known that the Egyptians, above all others, most greatly hated <term>intercalation</term> <note>the adding of leap days</note>, viewing it as a disturber of the mystical arrangement of solemn feasts. This is shown in the Scholia of Germanicus in these words: *The Apis bull is led by the Priest of Isis to the place called <term>ANO</term> <note>Greek: ΑΝΩ — meaning 'Above' or 'Upwards'</note>, and they are bound by a sacred oath that they will admit neither a month nor a day to be intercalated—which would change the feast day—but will keep 365 days exactly as instituted by the ancients.* From this passage, authors of great reputation took the opportunity to deny all Egyptian intercalation. But I respond: in this place, one should not understand the *civil* arrangement of the year of the Egyptians (which was considered the same as the civil year of the Alexandrians and Greeks, as is clear from the authors cited above), but rather that *Hierophantic* or mystical arrangement of the Priests. This consisted in the secret arrangement of the sacred rites established in honor of the Gods; and just as they were bound by oath to keep all mysteries in silence, so they were bound regarding this mystical arrangement of the years.

<summary>Kircher explains that the Egyptians used a four-year cycle called the "Year of God," which influenced Persian and Chaldean chronologies. He clarifies a historical confusion by arguing that while Egyptian priests swore oaths against leap years to keep their sacred calendar "pure," a civil calendar with leap years still existed for practical use.</summary>

...since it could not be made to agree with an intercalary day <note>a leap day</note>, they loathed it as something repugnant to their mystic rites. For since the <term>epagomenai</term> <note>original Greek: αἱ ἐπαγομέναι — the five "added" days at the end of the Egyptian year</note>, or the "Days of Nisi" <note>An Arabic/Coptic term for the epagomenal days</note>, were named after certain Gods, and the birthdays of those same Gods were celebrated on the days that bore their names; if a sixth added day were introduced, to which God would it be dedicated? Whose "epoch" or birthday would they celebrate? These days were, as we showed in the *Prodromus*:

-> The watch of the star * of the son * of his guard * of Apophis <-
<note>Translated from the Coptic: ⲟⲩⲉⲣϣⲓ ⲛ̀ ⲥⲓⲟⲩ * ⲛ̀ ⲡⲉϣⲫⲉⲛ * ⲛ̀ ⲧⲉϥⲩⲗⲁⲕⲏ * ⲛ̀ ⲁⲡⲟⲩⲫⲁⲥ. This refers to the traditional names or protective watches associated with the extra-calendrical days.</note>

<margin>Plutarch.</margin> according to the testimony of Plutarch. Therefore, if a sixth added day were introduced, two "added" or ill-omened days would occur in succession, which was contrary to the established law of the <term>Hierophants</term> <note>High priests or interpreters of sacred mysteries</note>. Consequently, they deliberately "loosened the reins" of the calendar, so that once a circuit of 1460 years was completed, the ancestral Gods could be said to have traveled through the entire world; Plutarch teaches this quite clearly in his book *On Osiris and Isis*. When this period was finished—

<margin>When the new moon of the Canicular Lustrum began.</margin> the new moon of the <term>Canicular Lustrum</term> <note>A four-year period associated with the Dog Star, Sirius</note> began on that night which followed the afternoon of the five Days of Nisi, with the Dog Star rising <term>acronychally</term> <note>Rising at sunset</note> on the night preceding the month of <term>Thoth</term> <note>The first month of the Egyptian year</note>; and that entire year was called <term>Sothis</term> <note>The Egyptian name for Sirius</note>. In the following year, on the same night preceding Thoth, they observed the rising of the Dog Star, which did not rise in the evening as in the first year, but at midnight; then the second year of the Lustrum began. In the third year, the rising of the Dog Star appeared before the Sun, and from this the third year of the Lustrum began. In the fourth year, the Dog Star could not be seen, because in the meridian of Egypt it rose in the opposite part of the other hemisphere; thus the fourth year of the Lustrum began from the noon of Thoth. In this way, a quarter of a day was inserted between each year of the Lustrum, and this was done without any <term>intercalation</term> <note>original Greek: ἐμβολισμῷ — the insertion of a whole leap day</note>. But gradually, one day would "creep in." Therefore, the entire controversy among authors seems to have arisen because they thought the Egyptians' civil method of reckoning was the same as the Alexandrian one, whereas we say they are different. For just as the "fixed" year of the Egyptians is the same as the Alexandrian, so the "vague," "loose," and "un-intercalated" year remained solely in the hands of the Egyptian Priests and Astronomers, as was proved at length in the preceding pages. Geminus, in chapter 6, clearly asserts that the Festival of Isis, which in the time of <term>Eudoxus</term> <note>A Greek astronomer (c. 390–337 BC)</note> coincided with the winter solstice, later in his own time was a whole month away from it; this would not have happened if the Egyptians had used only a fixed year and not a vague and loose one. For as Geminus himself testifies in the cited passage—

<margin>How the Egyptian festivals wander through all the days of the year.</margin> in four years, the Egyptians fall one day behind the Sun; in forty years, they fall ten days behind; and so their festivals would occur earlier by that many days, so that they would not be held in the same quarters of the year. Thus, in the space of 120 years, they celebrate their festivals 30 days earlier—that is, an entire month earlier—with respect to both the solar year and the seasonal quarters. Hence, says Geminus, that error which is circulated among the Greeks: because of the long duration of time, it was considered worthy of approval and was believed to be true even up to our own times. For many of the Greeks think that the Festival of Isis, according to the Egyptians and according to Eudoxus, falls on the winter solstice; this is entirely false, for the Festival of Isis is separated from the winter solstice by an entire month. That error flowed from the aforementioned cause; for 120 years earlier, it happened that the Festival of Isis was celebrated at the winter solstice itself; but in every four years, a variation of one day occurred; and thus—

namely, that the Copts and Ethiopians observe the said four-year period to this very day. For just as the ancients called each year of that period by the name of some God, so too the aforementioned peoples designate each year of that same four-year cycle, not indeed by the name of a profane God, but by the names of the four Evangelists. Thus, the first year from the leap year is called Matthew, the second Mark, the third Luke, and the fourth John. The <term>Coptic Computation</term> describes it in these words:

->“The leap day happens every four years, and they call each of them by the names of the four Evangelists.” ❈<-
<note>original Arabic: يوم الكبيس في كل اربع سنين ولكل وحده منهم يسمونها باسم اربع انجيلين</note>

->“To know the year of the Evangelists, take the Year of Mercy,”<-
->“and divide it by 4; if the remainder is 1, it belongs to Matthew;”<-
->“if 2, it belongs to Mark; if 3, it belongs to Luke;”<-
->“and if it is divided equally by 4, it belongs to John.”<-
<note>translated from the original Ge'ez/Ethiopic provided in the text</note>

That is, *To know the year of the Evangelists, divide the Year of Grace by the number 4; if 1 remains, it will be the days of Matthew; if 2, the days of Mark; if 3, the days of Luke; but if the division by 4 is even, then it is the days of John.* In the same way, the ancients called the first year Sothis, the second Isis, the third Serapis (or Osiris), and the fourth Horus, as Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a foundational figure in modern chronology</note> also rightly notes. Therefore, by dividing the years from the Era of Nabonassar <note>A Babylonian era used by ancient astronomers, starting in 747 BC</note> by four, they found the year corresponding to the God, by the exact same logic that the Egyptian Copts and Abyssinians <note>Ethiopians</note> find the day of the Evangelists.

...occurring in these months, which we have provided as collected from various authors. By applying this to the first day of the month of Thoth, you will learn the day and year of the first <term>vague year</term> <note>The "vague year" was the Egyptian civil year of 365 days, which lacked a leap year and thus "wandered" through the seasons</note> and the placement of festivals for that entire year. Once that year has passed, applying the first day of Thoth to the second day of the month of Thoth shows the position and arrangement of all festivals occurring in that year. Thus, for any given year, if you wish to know the placement and arrangement of Egyptian festivals appropriate to that year, you will apply the first day of Thoth on the inner wheel to the given day or year on the outer rim, and you will achieve your goal. 

Note, however, in this place, that just as the <term>Sothic Lustrum</term> <note>original: Lustrum caniculare; a four-year period</note> composed of a four-year span marks 1,460 days, so the Great Sothic Lustrum marks the years of that cycle. Since, according to what was cited above, the civil year consists of 365 days, which when multiplied by 4 makes 1,460 days—exactly how many days the four-year Sothic period contains—so 4 multiplied by 365 years produces that Great Sothic Lustrum, encompassed in a span of 1,460 years. 

Therefore, the outer circle, divided into 365 degrees, can be applied both to the days of the four-year Sothic period and to the years of the Great Lustrum; thus, the Egyptians showed marvelous genius in such a beautiful arrangement. Indeed, the festivals that were appropriate for the Great Lustrum were adapted to the smaller Sothic period of 1,460 days; so much so, that the Gods are not only thought to circle that Great Orb in the space of 1,460 years, but could also be said to have circled the smaller Orb of days encompassed in the four-year period. Consequently, since the <term>Hierophants</term> <note>High-ranking priests who interpreted sacred mysteries</note> could not perform the worship due to the Gods over that Great Lustrum because of the shortness of human life, they performed it for the Gods within the Lustrum of 1,460 days. Now, let us explain the sacred rites and the use of the wheel.

### CHAPTER II. ###

...the growth and conception around the winter solstice. <note>original: τὴν περὶ τομὰς χειμερινὰς ἀύξην καὶ κύεσιν</note> Therefore, it is said that when Isis felt herself to be pregnant, she hung an amulet upon herself on the sixth day of the month of **Paophi**, and gave birth to **Harpocrates** <note>The Greek name for the child-god Horus, often depicted with a finger to his lips as a sign of silence</note> around the winter solstice, imperfect and premature. This is because at that time the first flowers and early buds are born; for this reason, they offer the first fruits of sprouting beans. In this entire month, they also celebrate sacred rites to **Omphta**, whom Plutarch calls **Omphis**, a benevolent deity: "Another name for the God is Omphis, which Hermaeus says means 'benefactor.'" <note>original: Ἔτερον δ’ ὄνομα τοῦ Θεοῦ τὸν Ὄμφιν εὐεργέτην ὁ Ἑρμαῖος λέγει</note>. Regarding this name, see the more extensive treatment in the preceding description of the hieroglyphic Zodiac.

<margin>Month 3, Athyr.</margin> On the 17th day of the month of **Athyr**, the death of **Osiris** is celebrated. For they say that **Typhon** <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian god Set, the brother and murderer of Osiris</note> enclosed Osiris in a chest and cast him into the sea through the Tanitic mouth <note>One of the primary branches of the Nile delta</note>; for this reason, that place is still called "the Admirable" by the Egyptians. "They say these things were done on the seventeenth day of the month of Athyr, when the sun passes through Scorpio, in the twenty-eighth year of Osiris's reign." <note>original: Ταῦτα δὲ πραχθῆναί λέγουσιν ἑβδόμῃ ἐπὶ δέκα μηνὸς Ἀθὺρ, ἐν ᾧ τὸν σκορπίον ὁ ἥλιος διέξεισιν, ὀγδόον ἔτος καὶ εἰκοστὸν ἐκείνου βασιλεύοντος τοῦ Ὁσίριδος</note>. And elsewhere: the fact that he is said to be enclosed in a chest is nothing other than the hiding and diminishing of the water: "Therefore they say that Osiris vanished in the month of Athyr, when, as the Etesian winds <note>Strong, cool Mediterranean winds that blow in summer and cease in autumn</note> completely fail, the Nile recedes and the land is laid bare." <note>original: Διὸ μηνὸς Ἀθὺρ ἀφανισθῆναι τὸν Ὄσιριν λέγουσι, ὅτε τῶν ἐτησίων ἀπολειπόντων παντάπασιν ὁ μὲν Νεῖλος ὑπονοστεῖ, γυμνοῦται δὲ ἡ χώρα</note>.

<margin>Month 4, Choiac.</margin> On the 19th day of the month of **Choiac**, the sacred rites of **Cistophoria** <note>The "carrying of the chest," a mystery rite common to many Greco-Egyptian cults</note> are celebrated; Plutarch recounts the rituals of the solemnity in these words: "On the nineteenth day, at night, they go down to the sea, and the <term>stolistæ</term> <note>A class of priests responsible for dressing the divine statues and maintaining the sacred wardrobe</note> together with the priests carry out the sacred chest, which contains a small golden casket inside, into which they pour drinkable water, and a shout is raised by those present, crying out that Osiris has been found; then, mixing fertile soil with water and adding expensive spices and incense to the mixture, they fashion a small moon-shaped image, and they clothe and adorn this, signifying that they consider these Gods to be the nature of earth and water." <note>original: Τῇ δὲ ἐννάτῃ ἐπὶ δέκα νυκτὸς ἐπὶ θάλασσαν κάτεισι... [to end of Greek block]</note>.

<margin>Month 5, Tybi.</margin> On the 7th day of the month of **Tybi**, the return of Isis from Phoenicia is celebrated: so says Plutarch in the cited passage: "Therefore, sacrificing on the seventh day of the month of Tybi, which they call the 'Arrival of Isis from Phoenicia,' they mold a bound river-horse <note>A hippopotamus, which Kircher identifies as a symbol of Typhon's chaotic power</note> out of sacrificial cakes." <note>original: Διὸ καὶ θύοντες ἑβδόμῃ τοῦ Τυβὶ μηνὸς, ἣν καλοῦσιν ἄφιξιν Ἴσιδος ἐκ Φοινίκης, ἐπιπλάττουσι τοῖς ποπάνοις ἵππον ποτάμιον δεδεμένον</note>. By this, they signify that the Typhonic power was routed by Isis. In this same month, the solemnity of **Nephtes** <note>Nephthys, the sister of Isis and consort of Set/Typhon</note> is celebrated.

<margin>Month 6, Mechir.</margin> In the month of **Mechir**, the priests used to purify their inner shrines and offer sacrifices to **Canopus** <note>An Egyptian deity represented by a jar with a human or animal head, symbolizing the cooling waters of the Nile</note>; for those rituals and ceremonies, see the first volume of this *Oedipus*, in the chapter on Canopus.

<margin>Month 7, Phamenoth.</margin> In the month of **Phamenoth**, they celebrate the festival which they call the "Entry of Osiris into the Moon": so Plutarch says: "On the New Moon of the month of Phamenoth, they hold a festival, calling it the 'Entry of Osiris into the Moon,' which is the beginning of spring." <note>original: Ὅτι τῇ νουμηνίᾳ τοῦ Φαμενὼθ μηνὸς ἑορτὴν ἄγουσιν, ἔμβασιν Ὁσίριδος εἰς τὴν Σελήνην ὀνομάζοντες, ἔαρος ἀρχὴν οὖσαν</note>.

It explains how physical elements like the receding Nile and the growth of seeds were ritualized through symbolic sacrifices and processions.</summary>

...they believe that to be the beginning of Spring. In this way, they obscurely suggest the power of Osiris—that is, the Solar power—within the Moon; for the Moon is Isis, the wife of Osiris. Therefore, they call the Moon the "Mother of the World" <note>original: Mundi matrem</note> and assign to her a nature mixed of both sexes <note>Reflecting an ancient belief that the Moon possessed both male and female generative qualities</note>, because, having been filled and made pregnant by the Sun, she in turn emits and scatters generative principles into the air.

<margin>Month 8: Pharmuthi.</margin>In the month of Pharmuthi, they celebrate the feast of Ammon, as we showed above in the hierarchy of the Zodiac; for Amun is the Ram-headed Deity, the overseer of fertility, whose signs show themselves most strongly when the Sun is ascending in Aries <note>The Ram</note> near the beginning of Spring. At the same time they celebrated a feast, according to <margin>Pausanias. Plutarch.</margin>Pausanias, which they called the "driving out of Typhon" <note>Typhon is the Greek name for Set, the god of chaos and winter's cold</note>: and according to Plutarch, they used to kill a Crocodile, of which Typhon was the symbol; secretly suggesting by these rites that when the Sun moves into Aries—the house of Ammon—the darkness and the intensity of the cold (the effects of Typhon’s power) are driven out and dispelled by the power of Ammon. See what we have handed down concerning these things in the cited place, and in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, regarding the meaning of the Ram on folio 269.

<margin>Month 9: Pachon.</margin>In the month of Pachon (or <term>Pachon</term> <note>original: παχὼν</note>), which corresponds to May, they performed sacred rites to Serapis <note>A Graeco-Egyptian deity who combined traits of Osiris and Apis</note>—that is, the subterranean Osiris—whose benefit shines forth most greatly in this month, with the earth luxuriously blooming with every kind of sprout and herb. Hence Plutarch interprets this word <term>Sarei</term> <note>original: Σάρεϊ</note> as "joy," since the Egyptians call the feast of joy "Særei." But for a more extensive treatment of these things, see Volume 1, in the chapter on Serapis. Furthermore, in this month the <term>sphragistae</term> <note>From the Greek for "sealers," these were priests responsible for examining and sealing sacrificial animals to ensure they were "pure"</note> (or sealers) sacrificed red bulls, as Plutarch testifies: "to the sealers (acting as sacred heralds), a tongue was poured out <note>likely meaning extended or carved</note> while sinking to the knee, having the hand folded behind..." <note>original: τοῖς σφραγισταῖς (ὡς ἱεροκήρυκας) γλῶττα μὲν ἐγχέας ἀνθεῖτο εἰς γόνυ καθειμένῃ, τὴν χεῖρα δὲ ὀπίσω πεπλεγμένην ἔχοντα</note>. Moreover, the carving of the seal was expressed as <note>Hieroglyphic description: A man kneeling on his knees, with his hands tied behind his back, and a sword hanging over his throat.</note> (as Castor asserts) *a man sinking onto his knees, with his hands drawn back behind his back, and a sword threatening his throat.*

<margin>Month 10: Payni.</margin>In the month of Payni, they inflicted punishments upon Asses for the sake of the detestable Typhon, whom they say resembled an Ass both in laziness and stupidity, as well as in color; hence: "And making cakes in sacrifices, in the months of Payni and Phaophi they imprint the shape of a bound ass upon the meal-cakes." <note>original: Καὶ πόπανα ποιοῦντες ἐν θυσίαις, τῇ δὲ Παϋνὶ καὶ τῷ Φαωφὶ μλῶις ἐπιπλάττουσι σχῆμα ὄνον δεδεμένον</note> *In the months of Payni and Phaophi, making cakes in sacrifices, they imprint the figure of a bound Ass upon them.*

<margin>Month 11: Epiphius.</margin>In the month of Epiphi, which corresponds to July, the "preludes of Memphis" were performed as the Sun entered Leo; all the rites and ceremonies looked toward the fortunate rising of the Nile; concerning which there is more in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* in the hieroglyphic description of the Lion. On the last day of this month, they hold the birthday festival for the eyes of Horus, and they bring forth Songs invoking him who is hidden in the arms of the Sun. Thus Plutarch: "In the sacred hymns of Osiris they call upon him who lies hidden in the arms of the sun, and on the thirtieth day of the month of Epiphi they celebrate the birthday of the eyes of Horus, as they consider not only the moon, but also the sun to be the eye and light of Horus." <note>original: Ἐν δὲ τοῖς ἱεροῖς ὕμνοις τοῦ Ὀσίριδος ἀνακαλοῦνται τὸν ἐν ταῖς ἀγκάλαις κρυπτόμενον τοῦ ἡλίου... καὶ φῶς ἡγούμενοι</note> *In the sacred hymns of Osiris they invoke him who hides in the arms of the Sun; and on the last day of the month of Epiphi they celebrate the birthday of the eyes of Horus, for they think not only the Moon, but also the Sun to be the eyes of Horus.*

<margin>Month 12: Mesori.</margin>In the month of Mesori, they celebrate the solemnities of the Nile, namely at that very time when the rising of the Nile begins. "And they call not only the Nile, but simply every liquid the outflow of Osiris, and in the sacred processions the water-vessel always leads the way in honor of the God, and they write with a royal [symbol]... and the divine watering is like the mythic motion of all things, by which the nature seems to resemble a generative part; and they sing of the phallic nature at the feast of Pamylia." <note>original: Οὐ μόνον δὲ τὸν Νεῖλον, ἀλλὰ πᾶν ὑγρὸν ἁπλῶς Ὀσίριδος ἀποῤῥοὴν καλοῦσι... τὴν δὲ τῇ παμυλίων ἑορτῇ ἄδοντες φαλλικῶ</note>

# OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

->ROTA<-
<note>This word, "ROTA" (Wheel), likely refers to the cyclical nature of the Sothic period discussed below or serves as a printer's mark.</note>

<margin>CH. II.</margin>

"Behold the dryness (it is said of the gods) and the salvation, and the generative organ is the birthday of the gods." <note>original Greek: ἰδὲ, ἀυχμία (φησὶ θεῶν) καὶ σωτήριον, ὃ δ' αἰδοῖον γενέθλιον θεῶν. This quote, likely from Plutarch, links dryness/heat with the divine and the phallus with the creation of the gods.</note> Furthermore, they do not only call the Nile, but simply all moisture, the <term>efflux of Osiris</term> <note>original: Osiridis effluxum; the divine substance flowing out of the god to fertilize the earth</note>; and in the procession before the sacred rites, a water vessel always precedes in honor of the God. They also depict the King and the southern climate of the world by a fig leaf, and they interpret the fig leaf as the irrigation and movement of all things; its nature is seen to be similar to the genital member. Furthermore, when they celebrate the **Pamylia** festivals <note>An ancient Egyptian festival celebrating the birth of Osiris</note>, which are performed by employing a **phallus**—that is, an image of the male member—they present and carry around an image which has a triple penis. They are secretly suggesting that God is the principle of all things, and every principle multiplies that which is produced from it; and thus moisture is the principle of all things, without which the sensible World, which they call **Horus**, cannot be preserved.

And these are the solemnities which the Egyptians were accustomed to celebrate throughout the course of the year in honor of the Gods they worshipped. These festivities, if you look at the common and civil year, were fixed and immobile; but they were wandering and loose if you consider the method used by the <term>Hierophants</term> <note>High priests who interpreted sacred mysteries</note>. For they wanted the Gods to wander through all the regions of the world in a space of 1,460 years, and to pass through every degree of the Zodiac and day of the months in the succession of time; this was so that no part of the world, nor any portion of the annual time, should be left without the necessary presence of the Gods, as we showed above from **Geminos** <note>A Greek astronomer and mathematician</note>. However, all the sacred rites were referred back to four Numina <note>divine powers</note> in particular: namely, first to **Sothis**, who is Mercury; second to **Isis**; third to **Osiris**; and fourth to **Horus**, whom they also call **Kemin**. Just as these four Numina are restored to their own principles every four years (that is, 1,460 days), so in 1,460 years—in the course of that great <term>Sothic</term> period—they return to the point from which they had progressed. We have expressed these four Numina in the inner circle, each with its own hieroglyphics. And let these remarks suffice concerning the Great Sothic Year.

<note>Within the serpent quadrants, the year is divided by the four major deities, each assigned a "Hierophantic" or priestly year of 365 and 1/4 days:</note>
*   **I.** Year of **Sothis**: 365 days. Hierophantic Year: 365 1/4 days.
*   **II.** Year of **Isis**: 365 days. Hierophantic Year: 365 1/4 days.
*   **III.** Year of **Osiris**: 365 days. Hierophantic Year: 365 1/4 days.
*   **IV.** Year of **Horus**: 365 days. Hierophantic Year: 365 1/4 days.

->**The Sothic Lustrum or CANICULAR**<-
->**or the Great Greater Canicular Period of 1461 years.**<-
<note>The Canicular cycle is named after the "Dog Star" (Canicula or Sirius). Because the Egyptian civil year was exactly 365 days (missing the 1/4 day of the solar year), the seasons and festivals slowly drifted. It took 1,461 Egyptian years to return to the starting point where the rising of Sirius coincided with the New Year.</note>

Note, Reader, that the fixed festivals of the Months show the specific day of the Month by their points; however, the names of the twelve Gods shown in Coptic letters indicate that these Gods have no fixed seats, but move forward. Thus, in the space of 1461 years, they complete the entire circle of the 12 Months. This cycle is called the Year, or the Great Hierophantic <term>Lustrum</term>.

<margin>CHAPTER II.</margin>

### ->Explanation of the Chronological Wheel, in which everything said thus far regarding the Months and Festivals is encompassed in a single synopsis.<-

**T**he outer circle contains the 365 days of the entire expanded Egyptian year; below this are the names of the Egyptian Months, each of which contains 30 days, along with the five extra days which the Egyptians call <term>Nisi</term> <note>Also known as epagomenal days, these were five days added at the end of the year to bring the total to 365.</note>. Beneath this, a circle is placed where the <term>portioned year</term> <note>original Greek: ἐνιαυτοῦ μερίζηται (eniautou merizētai)</note>—that is, the year of 360 days—is divided into twelve months, together with the five extra days. And this is the "fixed year" of the Egyptians: four of these years constitute a <term>Sothic lustrum</term> <note>A "lustrum" usually means five years, but here Kircher uses it for a 4-year cycle.</note>, also called the "minor canicular cycle" or the cycle <term>of the August Gods</term> <note>original Greek: Θεῶν σεβαστῶν (Theōn sebastōn)</note>. In this cycle, the first year is held sacred to **Sothis** (that is, Mercury); the second to **Isis**; the third to **Osiris**; and finally, the fourth to **Horus**. This aforementioned cycle corresponds to four Julian years containing a <term>leap day</term> <note>original: bissextum</note>. It can be considered in a twofold manner: either as a civil four-year period, or as a mystic and <term>hierophantic</term> <note>Related to the interpretation of sacred mysteries.</note> one. The former (civil) usually intercalates one day after four years, while the latter (mystic), scorning all intercalation, "loosens the reins" and allows time to drift forward. For this reason, we have arranged another wheel, rotatable at its center, upon which we have placed the festivals of the Egyptian Gods and other solemnities. It is called by Authors <term>the Great Year of God</term> <note>original Greek: ἐνιαυτὸς μέγας τοῦ Θεοῦ (eniautos megas tou Theou)</note>, the "great wandering Sothic year," or the "canicular cycle," and it consists of 1460 years, after which period the cycle returns roughly to the first day of the month of **Thoth**. The Gods and their festivals wander through all the months of the fixed year over a span of 365 leap-day cycles; thus, there is no day in the months that the Gods cannot be said to have traversed. And this is the great "hierophantic" or "hieroglyphic" year, by which they mystically indicated that there is no part of the World which the Gods do not penetrate with their beneficial presence, animate, and preserve through their necessary influence.

<margin>The serpent biting its tail signifies the year.</margin>

They represent this aptly through a serpent forming a circle and biting its tail with its head, according to the testimony of Horus. <note>Hieroglyphic description: Kircher refers to the Ouroboros as a symbol for the cyclical nature of the Sothic year.</note> In its revolution, it effectively created four circles, by which the "minor Sothic lustrum" of four years was indicated. Over each of these years, they placed a presiding Deity adorned with their specific hieroglyphics.

<margin>Horus. The four Deities presiding over the Sothic Lustrum.</margin>

Here you see **Sothis** presiding in the first circle—that is, Mercury—seated and distinguished by a canine head, as the Author of the arrangement of the year and seasons; in the second circle occurs **Isis**, seated and conspicuous with a female face, who was said to preside over the second year; in the third circle sits **Osiris** upon a throne, distinguished by a Hawk’s head, presiding over the third year; in the fourth circle is seen **Horus** in that figure which you see, the governor of the fourth year. For just as these Deities traverse the entire four-year Sothic cycle in a space of 1460 days, so these same Deities are said to complete the "great cycle" in 1460 years, together with the rest of their followers and the festivities offered to them. Furthermore, just as one day is added every four years in the minor cycle, so when the major cycle is completed, a year is added so that they may be restored to their original positions.

Note also that just as the year of the minor cycle consists of 365 days, so one "year" of the major cycle is considered to be 365 years, which, when multiplied by 4—

CLASS VII. MATHEMATICAL HIEROGLYPHICS. 267 CHAPTER III.

...multiplied, they produce a circuit of 1460 years. This period—from its first institution, which we suppose was established by Hermes <note>Kircher identifies the Egyptian god Thoth with the Greek Hermes and the "Hermes Trismegistus" figure.</note> in the year 1837 BC, as we showed in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*—has been completed twice up to our present year of 1653. Thus, today, the first day of the month of Thoth, according to the calculation of the Hierophants <note>Priestly interpreters of sacred mysteries.</note> regarding the great wandering year, falls on the 25th day of the month of Phamenoth. For if you add the year 1837 BC (when, by hypothesis, Hermes established this calculation) to 1653 AD (the present year), you will have a total of 3490 years. When divided by the years of the great canicular lustrum <note>original: "lustri maioris canicularis"—the Sothic cycle of 1460 years based on the rising of the Dog Star, Sirius.</note> of 1460 years, it gives a quotient of 2, with 570 days remaining. These 570 days make up one year, six months, and 25 days, which corresponds to the 25th day of the month of Phamenoth.

These things being established, if you wish to know which months the festivals and solemnities of the Gods correspond to today, proceed as follows: Turn the wheel of the great Sothic year (or canicular lustrum) so its marker, which resembles a lily, is over the 25th day of Phamenoth. For on this present day, the beginning of this Sothic Cycle corresponds to that date by our hypothesis; and the days of the months, to which the festivals and solemnities arranged in the circuit of the wheel correspond, will provide the answer you seek. You will operate no differently in this Sothic Cycle when it is adjusted to the indicators of any other times. 

If, however, you desire to know which Deity from the four <term>August Gods</term> <note>original Greek: Σεβαστῶν (Sebastōn), referring to the four gods presiding over the 4-year cycle: Sothis, Isis, Osiris, and Horus.</note> presides over this present year, operate thus: Divide the 570 days remaining from the previous division by 365, and you will have a quotient of 1, and 205 remaining days, which are the days of the second year of the canicular cycle. You shall therefore pronounce that **ISIS** <note>original Greek: ΙΣΙΝ (Isin)</note> presides over this present year. Moreover, the beginning of the great wandering canicular Cycle falls on the twenty-fifth of Phamenoth, as was said, which corresponds to March 21st, the day of the equinox. 

We have handed down these things according to the mind of the Hierophants. However, those who wish to adapt this greater cycle to the Egyptian or Alexandrian years <note>The fixed calendar established under Augustus, which included a leap year.</note> should divide the 3490 years since the institution of the Cycle by 1461; the result will be 2 and 578/1461. These remaining fractions, when resolved into days, will give one year, seven months, and eight days, which will be the 8th day of the month Pharmuthi, corresponding to the third of April. Having prefaced these matters, it now remains for us to say something about the modern Calculation of the Copts.

Furthermore, the said *Supplement* has perhaps reached the notice of only a few, and moreover, it teems with many errors due to the negligence of the printer and the proofreader.

# THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM OF OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS #

<margin>CH. III.</margin> they call the *Era of the years of our Father Adam* <note>original Arabic: "تاريخ السنين ابونا ادم"—Tarikh al-sinin abuna Adam</note>, as mentioned by Maximus the Monk <note>A 7th-century theologian and scholar of chronology</note> regarding Adam, which they used in organizing both the Solar and Lunar cycles and the sequences that follow those cycles. Another era dates from the beginning of the Kingdom of the Greeks; regarding these years, see my work the <term>Prodromus</term> <note>Kircher's *Prodromus Coptus*, published in 1636</note>. A third is the technical Era of Diocletian, which is used for dating books, letters, and monuments; Albateni <note>The 9th-century Arab astronomer Al-Battani</note> calls this the *Coptic Era* <note>original Arabic: "تاريخ القبطي"—Tarikh el-Kupti</note>. The Copts themselves call it the *Era of the Holy Martyrs* <note>original Coptic: "ⲛⲓⲁⲛ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉ ⲛⲓⲙⲁⲣⲧⲩⲣⲟⲥ"—Ni-an ente ni-martyros; or Arabic: "تاريخ الشهداء الطهار"—Tarikh al-shuhada al-tuhar</note>. In Coptic, this is *the year of the Martyrs* <note>original Coptic: "ϯⲣⲟⲙⲡⲓ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉ ⲛⲓⲙⲁⲣⲧⲩⲣⲟⲥ"—Ti-rompi ente ni-martyros</note>. Some add to these eras or epochs a fourth: that of Nabonassar, King of the Chaldeans. However, since only astronomers use this and it has no place in civil reckoning, we have deliberately chosen to omit it. Indeed, the Era of Nabonassar was not a civil era, nor was it commonly known to the Egyptians, but only to astronomers who borrowed it from the Chaldeans. As our most learned Petavius <note>Denis Petau (1583–1652), a famous Jesuit chronologist</note> <margin>Petavius.</margin> proves in a learned letter sent to me, this was accomplished through the work and diligence of Callisthenes. Callisthenes, who was a student of Aristotle, followed his master’s urging while in the company of Alexander the Great; he sent the most ancient Chaldean observations recovered from Babylon back to Greece. From there, they were brought to Egypt and employed by astronomers, most notably by Ptolemy, who seems to have borrowed them from Hipparchus. Simplicius testifies to all of this in his commentary <margin>Simplicius.</margin> on the second book of Aristotle’s *On the Heavens*. Thus, whatever we said regarding this era in the *Prodromus*, we do not wish it to be understood otherwise than we have stated here. Nor do we believe the era dating from the death of Alexander (also called the Era of Philip) should be confused with the era of *the Two-Horned One* <note>original Arabic: "ذو القرنين"—Dhu al-Qarnayn, a title often associated with Alexander the Great</note>, since one differs from the other by nearly 12 years—a matter which can be read at greater length in the works of Petavius, whom I praised above.

Regarding the Era of the Years of the World <note>Anno Mundi</note>, it should be noted that the Greeks and Latins, departing without cause from the true calculations of the Holy Bible, reckon 5,199 years from the creation of the world to the birth of Christ. This number exceeds the true reckoning of Moses by one thousand two hundred and fifty years. Furthermore, the Greek founders of chronological systems imitated the Egyptians by interpreting the eras of the world in various ways to fit their mathematical methods. From this liberty were born three technical eras, which later generations accepted as the true years of the world, though they were actually devised or transformed by masters for the purpose of calculation: these are the Dionysian, Alexandrian, and Antiochian eras, concerning which see Petavius in his *On the Doctrine of Times* and Scaliger. Since these eras are not "natural" but rather inventions for the sake of calculation, they differ greatly. The Hebrew era reckons 3,760 years from the creation of the world to Christ. Thus says the Hebrew book of calculation, the title of which is:

->*The Gleaning of the Harvest concerning the Secret of Intercalation:*<-
<note>original Hebrew: "לֶקֶט קָצִיר לְסוֹד הָעִבּוּר"—Leket Katzir l'Sod ha-Ibbur</note>

That is, *The collector of stalks concerning the mystery of calculation, or intercalation*. For what we call "Calculation," they call—naming the whole by a part—*Intercalation* <note>original Greek: "ἐμβολισμόν"—embolismon</note>, or in Hebrew <term>Ghibbur</term> <note>original Hebrew: "עִבּוּר"—Ibbur</note>. This literally means *pregnancy*, a most elegant metaphor, as if the year carries an added month within itself, just as a pregnant woman carries a fetus in her womb. In this book, therefore, from the creation of the world to the era of Christ, they count:
3,760 [years]

The Copts, however, arrange their Ecclesiastical year beginning from August 29th, which falls on the first day of the month of Thoth <note>The first month of the ancient Egyptian and Coptic calendars.</note>, the day of the beheading of St. John the Baptist—even though it is celebrated on the 2nd day of Thoth in the Martyrology, due to the specific solemnities of the first day of the year. Concerning this, the *History of the Copts* <note>original: "Tarich el Kupti"</note> says:

The beginning of the year is Thoth, and it is the day of the martyrdom of the Saint and Prophet John the Baptist, son of Zechariah the Priest. <note>original Arabic: بدو السنه توت ويوم استشهاد القديس والنبي يوحنا المعمدان ابن زكريا الكاهن</note>
<note>Decorative ornament (small star/flower) centered below Arabic text.</note>

*That is: The beginning of the year is the Month of Thoth, and the day is consecrated to the martyrdom of the Holy Prophet John the Baptist, son of Zechariah the Priest.* These words harmonize exactly with the Syriac or Antiochian Calendar, as is evident:

The dawn of the morning of Thoth, and the day of the killing of John the Baptist, and the departure of Adam our father, and the beginning of the year of the Egyptians. <note>original Syriac: ܢܘܓܗ ܨܦܪܐ ܕܬܘܬ ܘܝܘܡ ܩܛܠܗ ܕܝܘܚܢܢ ܡܥܡܕܢܐ ܘܡܦܩܢܐ ܕܐܕܡ ܐܒܘܢ</note>
<note>Decorative ornament (small star/flower) centered below Syriac text.</note>

*That is: The Beheading of St. John the Baptist, and the death of our Father Adam, and the beginning of the year of the Egyptians.* This is also confirmed by the Greek <term>Hierokeryx</term> <note>A "Sacred Herald" or preacher; here likely referring to a liturgical text or office.</note> in these words: "The Beheading of John the Baptist, and the death of our ancestor Adam, and the beginning of the years of the Egyptians." <note>original Greek: Ἀποκεφαλισμὸς Ἰωάννου τοῦ Βαπτίστου, καὶ θανάτη τοῦ προγόνου ἡμῶν Ἀδάμ, καὶ ἀρχὴ τῶν τῶν Αἰγυπτίων ἐνιαυτῶν.</note> This feast is celebrated twice by the Copts: first on the 1st of Thoth, when he was beheaded, and second on the 30th of Mechir, when his head was found, as is shown in the Coptic Calendar.

The method by which the day of the week on which the 1st of Thoth (or the feast of the beheading of St. John the Baptist) falls can be found is beautifully taught by the Ethiopian or Abyssinian calculation in the following words:

### CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. 271 CHAPTER III. ###

The [calendar] of the Egyptians is demonstrated thus: for since 25 solar years, excluding leap years, contain 9125 days, and there are in them 309 lunations <note>A lunation is the time between two successive new moons.</note>—which according to astronomical calculation consist of 9124 days, 22 hours, 51 minutes, and 18 seconds—all lunations will return after 25 years to the same day on which they were previously made, anticipating [the time] by only one hour, 8 minutes, and 12 seconds. This can by no means be said of the nineteen-year cycle <note>The Metonic cycle, commonly used in Western Easter calculations.</note> when applied to the said years of the Egyptians. And from this also emerges the reason why the Ancients never intercalated <note>Inserted an extra day, like a leap year.</note> sacred years, but intercalated civil or Alexandrian years every fourth year. But regarding this cycle [we spoke] a little more extensively before; now let us proceed to the Coptic computation, or that used by the Church of Alexandria. It uses a double cycle: Solar and Lunar. The former they call in Coptic <term>pi-kyklos nte-phre</term> <note>Coptic: πικυκλος ν̄τεπηρη</note> or in Arabic <term>dawr al-shamsi</term> <note>Arabic: دور الشمسي</note> (*The Solar Cycle*); the latter they call <term>pi-kyklos nte-pioh</term> <note>Coptic: πικυκλος ν̄τεπιοϩ</note> or in Arabic <term>dawr al-qamari</term> <note>Arabic: دور القمري</note> (*The Lunar Cycle*). The cycle of the Sun consists of 28 years, and that of the Moon of 19 years. By these they investigate all things pertaining to the arrangement of Easter and other feasts, as is clear from the following Table <note>original: "Pinacio"</note>, which I have thought fit to present to you here, excerpted from the books of the Copts.

### P R O P O S I T I O N I.
#### How to find the Solar Cycle.

<note>Original Arabic: "If you want to know the Solar Cycle, subtract twenty-eight twenty-eight from the year of the Coptic era, and the remainder is the solar cycle of that year you are in."</note>

> *If you wish to know the Solar Cycle, cast away from the years of the Era of Diocletian <note>Also known as the Era of the Martyrs, beginning in 284 AD.</note> as many times as possible the number 28, and the remainder will give you the Cycle of the year currently in progress.*

---

### P R O P O S I T I O N II.
#### How to find the Lunar Cycle.

<note>Original Arabic: "If you want to know the Lunar Cycle, subtract one from the year of the Coptic era, and also subtract nineteen nineteen, and the remainder is the Lunar Cycle."</note>

> *If you wish to know the Paschal or Lunar Cycle, subtract 1 from the years of the Era of Diocletian, and again [subtract] 19 as many times as possible; for the remainder will give the requested Lunar or Paschal Cycle.*

---

### P R O P O S I T I O N III.
#### How to find the Day of the Month.

# CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. 273 CH. III. #
Mm

If you wish to know the day of the week <term>feria</term><note>From the Latin *feria*, referring to the days of the week where Sunday is the 1st day, Monday the 2nd, etc.</note> of the month, take the character of the year, or the sign (in the column) opposite the cycle of the Sun; to this add the character of the month (in its own column) and the sum will give the day of the week sought, after casting out 7 as many times as you can.

### PROPOSITION IV.

#### To find the Easter Cycle by another method.

->If you want to know the calculation of the cycle <term>kyklos</term><note>The Arabic text uses *keyquls*, a transliteration of the Greek *kyklos* (cycle).</note> of that year you are in, how much it is: subtract the years of<-
->our father Adam <note>The "Years of Adam" refers to the Anno Mundi or the Era of the World, a common starting point for Eastern Christian chronologies.</note> nineteen by nineteen, and whatever remains that does not reach nineteen, that is the cycle of that year,<-
->because the cycle completes from one to nineteen, and when it reaches nineteen, it returns to one. ☼<- <note>Translated from the original Arabic text.</note>

*When you wish to know the number of the Lunar cycle of this year in which you are, what it may be, cast out 19 from the years of our father Adam as many times as you can, and that which remains, and is not 19, that will be the cycle of this year, because the cycle is a revolution of years from one to 19, and from there back to one.*

---

### PROPOSITION V.

#### To find the Foundation of the Year.

->And if you want to know the <term>Foundation</term><note>Arabic: *al-As*, meaning base or foundation; used here for the Solar Cycle.</note> and its calculation, which is the cycle of the Sun—this calculation grows from one<-
->to seven and from seven it returns to one—and if you want the cycle of the year you are in, then take<-
->the years of our father Adam and add to them their quarter; and whatever fraction there was, like a quarter or a half, leave it;<-
->and when the quarter is gathered with the root [the original sum], join its total and cast it out seven by seven, and whatever remains that does not reach seven,<-
->it is the cycle of the Sun for that year you are in, and it is the Foundation. ☼<- <note>Translated from the original Arabic text.</note>

*This is: If you wish to know the foundation of the year (which is a certain fixed cycle of the Sun, proceeding from 1 to 7, and from there returning to one), take the years of our father Adam, and add to them their quarters; and if there should be fractions of numbers, you will leave them; and if the quarter was complete with the root, you will join its sum, and cast out from it seven as many times as you can; and if what remains is not seven, it will be the cycle of the Sun of this year which is currently running, and this is the foundation sought.*

---

### PROPOSITION VI.

#### To find the day upon which the beginning of any month falls.

->If you want to know which day will be the first of the month, look at the sign of the month you want<-
->and add to it the Foundation of that year; and whatever is gathered with you, cast out seven from it; and whatever remains<-
->from the seven—if one remains, the first of the month is Sunday, and if two remains, it is Monday. ☼<- <note>Translated from the original Arabic text.</note>

*If you wish to know which is the first day of the month, look at the character of the month you wish, and add it to the foundation of the current year, and from the total subtract seven, and the remainder out of seven: if it is 1, the first day of the month will be the 1st day of the week [Sunday]; if 2, it will be the second day of the week [Monday], and so on for the rest.*

And

And the rules for Ethiopian Reckoning correspond perfectly <note>original: *ad unguem*, literally "to the fingernail," a Latin idiom for precision</note> to these Rules; we would have gladly included them here if the constraints of time permitted. For the same reason, I am omitting the expanded Arabic-Coptic-Latin Martyrology <note>A liturgical calendar listing saints and martyrs according to their feast days.</note>. However, so that the curious Reader may know which day of the Julian months <note>The Julian calendar was the standard calendar of the Roman Empire and much of the Christian world until the Gregorian reform.</note> corresponds to which Egyptian day, I have thought it necessary to subjoin here a Table <term>Pinax</term><note>From the Greek *pinax*, meaning a tablet or register; Kircher uses it for a reference table.</note> of days.

To this we have added another, namely a Table of months, in which we have placed the months of the Hebrews, Syrians, and Arabs in a parallel arrangement, corresponding as much as possible to the months of the Copts, so that if anyone wished to compare one with another, they might have the means to do so. It must be noted, however, that since most of the Eastern months are lunar and arrange their days according to the New Moons <term>Neomeniae</term><note>The first appearance of the crescent moon marking the start of a month in lunar calendars.</note>, they do not correspond in every respect to the days of the Coptic months—which are solar and fixed—but rather change their positions; nor do the solar days of the Easterners always correspond to the Egyptian days, but have different positions within the same month. A third Table contains the Nomenclature of the days of the week used by various peoples of the East; which we have therefore added to the Month-Table <term>Menopinacio</term><note>A technical term Kircher uses to describe a monthly almanac or calendar table.</note>, lest we seem to have omitted anything the Reader might desire.

## OR ARCHITECTURE.

Farewell, most worthy Prelate, and favor my studies.

# CLASS VIII
## Egyptian Mechanics.

### P R E F A C E .

<margin>The method by which Egyptian Mechanics is treated here.</margin>
**F**ollowing the direct thread of order from the Astrology of the Egyptians—that is, from the Heavens—we now descend into their earthly habitations, so that the prodigious fruits produced at all times by the ingenious industry of the Egyptians might shine forth from the wonders of this treatise. While we do this, let no one think we shall provide in this place a Mechanics supported by mathematical demonstrations, for that would be entirely outside our scope; rather, relying on historical accounts, we offer that which places before the eyes of the curious Reader the stupendous genius and prodigious inventions of the Egyptians. Furthermore, we shall explain the hieroglyphic principles <note>By "hieroglyphic principles," Kircher refers to the symbolic or sacred meanings the Egyptians supposedly embedded even in their machines and buildings.</note> shining forth within them, reserving the remaining matters concerning mathematical principles for that great Work which we call *Universal Mechanics*.

<margin>Division of the treatise on Egyptian Mechanics.</margin>
We have titled this Class *Egyptian Mechanics*, and it is divided into three primary species used by them: the first was Architectural; the second Organic, which considers the various types of instruments usually employed in the erection of buildings, columns, and statues; the third was <term>Thaumaturgic</term> <note>original: Θαυματουργική; "wonder-working." In the 17th century, this referred to mechanical marvels like automatons or optical illusions that seemed magical.</note>, and consisted in the construction of certain hidden machines drawn from the innermost springs of nature. These indeed they adorned with such genius and subtlety that posterity believed them to be not the works of men, but of Demons, so entirely <term>marvelous</term> <note>original: καὶ παράδοξα; Greek for "and paradoxical" or "beyond belief."</note> did everything seem. And although I do not deny that the work of Demons was occasionally involved in them, nevertheless, works of this kind by no means exceeded the limits of human power, but had their principles founded in the innermost recesses of nature. It will be my role in this place—that is, the role of Oedipus <note>Kircher frequently refers to himself as "Oedipus," the mythological solver of the Sphinx's riddles, as he attempts to "solve" the mysteries of ancient Egypt.</note>—to demonstrate this through various ways and reasons. Therefore, let us begin the business with the good God's favor.

### P R E L U D E  I .

->**Concerning Egyptian Measures.**<-

**S**ince, therefore, mention of Egyptian measures and weights will be made throughout this treatise, lest the curious Reader be entangled in a confusion of measures used by other Nations with those of the Egyptians, it seemed best to provide a prelude here concerning each one. In this way, he might more securely form a judgment regarding the authorities for the things to be introduced, which ancient writers describe throughout.

Certainly, among other subjects in which the tireless industry of <term>Philologists</term> <note>Scholars of language and historical texts.</note> has toiled to determine up to now, the matter concerning weights and measures occupies no small place; indeed, as it is abstruse, so is it difficult, and by no one...

# CLASS VIII. EGYPTIAN MECHANICS. PREFACE I.

...hitherto explored by me. <margin>A difficult treatise on weights and measures, and why.</margin> I find no other reason for this difficulty than the diverse uses and customs of different nations—nations that I would not only say differ from one another, but even towns that seem to disagree among themselves. Added to this is the varying condition of the times and the will of Princes; as the necessity of public affairs demands, new laws are established while old ones are voided, or the value of things to be acquired through civil contracts is increased or diminished. Consequently, from this perpetual cycle of changes, a great uncertainty in these matters must necessarily arise. This is true in all things dependent on the will of Princes, but it holds especially in this subject of weights and measures, which are, as it were, the instruments of justice by which that which belongs to each person is determined. Let no one wonder, therefore, if they see such inconsistency among the authors <margin>Ambiguity among authors regarding the measures of the Ancients.</margin> debating this subject; for if you except the names themselves, the determined quantity of weights and measures—especially those of the Ancients—is not only uncertain but so corrupted by the ambiguity of authors that hardly any certain knowledge of them can be obtained. When, therefore, I beheld this disaster in literature, not without grief, I decided that the sources themselves must be approached so that something certain could finally be established, as will appear from the following names. These have been extracted from the Coptic Nomenclator, which the Copts call the *Scala Magna* <note>original: "Scalam magnam"; literally "The Great Ladder" or "Great Scale," this refers to a famous medieval Coptic-Arabic dictionary.</note>, printed by us in Rome in the year 1643, <margin>The Coptic Nomenclator or *Scala Magna*.</margin> and are explained more fully in this place.

Four types of measures are proposed in the *Scala*: <margin>Four types of Egyptian measures.</margin> of the first type are measures of distance, which we use in trade and the measurement of fields, such as: the foot, palm, ell, arm, pace, cubit, reed, stadium, mile, <term>parasang</term> <note>An ancient Persian unit of distance, roughly 3.5 miles.</note>, and league. Of the second type are measures of dry goods, such as were used among the Hebrews: the Cor, Gomer, Ephah, and Kab; and among the Greeks: the Medimnus, Choenix, and Kotyle; and among the Romans: the Modius. Of the third type are measures of liquids, such as the Hebrew Bath, Hin, and Log; the Greek Amphora, Urna, Metreta, and Congius; and the Roman Sextarius and Cyathus. Of the fourth type are the names of various weights, such as the Hebrew <term>Kikkar</term> <note>original: "Kicarim"; the Hebrew talent.</note>, Mina, Shekel, and Gerah; and the Greek and Roman Talent, Pound, Ounce, Denarius, and Drachma. Although each of these is treated in the *Scala*, because they might lead the reader into various doubts, I have decided to describe them more clearly here.

The measures of the ancient Egyptians suitable for measuring distances were: <margin>Egyptian measures for measuring distances.</margin>

-> The span :: a measure :: and :: the measuring reed :: the stadium :: the mile :: <-

<margin>The Pilikos (or Piluces).</margin> The *Pilikos* <note>original: ⲡⲓⲗⲓⲕⲟⲥ</note> is an Egyptian measure, the same as the Greek *lichas* and the Arabic *Pheter*; it is the distance between the thumb and the index finger when they are stretched out as far as possible. Thus says Pollux <note>Julius Pollux, a 2nd-century Greek grammarian and lexicographer.</note>: *If indeed you stretch the thumb against the part opposite the index finger, the middle space is called a lichas*; <note>original: Εἰ δὴ τὸν μέγαν δάκτυλον τῷ λιχανῷ ἀντιτείνας, τὸ μέσον λίχας</note> and it is ten "digits" <note>A "digit" or finger-breadth was a standard small unit of measure.</note> long. Thus the cited author:

<- The Pilikos <-

PREFACE I. EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS, THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

The distance from the thumb to the tip of the [index] finger makes ten fingers. <note>original Greek: Ποσὸν δὲ ἀπὸ τοῦ μεγάλου δακτύλου πρὸς τὸ τοῦ δακτύλου ἄκρον, δακτύλους δέκα.</note> <margin>What is an *orthodoron*?</margin> But longer than the *lichas* <note>The span between the thumb and index finger</note> is the *orthodoron* (which I interpret as the "straight palm"), namely the distance between the first part of the palm, which they call the *karpos* <note>The wrist</note>, and the tip of the middle finger. So say Pollux and Hesychius.

The Egyptians call the palm <term>ⲧⲉⲣⲧⲱ</term> <note>Coptic: *Tertō*</note> and the Arabs call it *shabar* <note>Arabic: شبر</note>. It consists of four fingers and is called a *dochme* by the Greeks. <margin>What is a *tertō*?</margin> So says Pollux: <margin>What is a *dochme*?</margin> "A *dochme* is the four fingers filled out" <note>original Greek: Δοχμὴ δὲ ἐστὶ, πλησθέντες οἱ τέσσαρες δάκτυλοι</note>. The <term>dochme</term> is indeed four closed fingers, for we measure with the hand held crosswise. Aristophanes uses this measure in *The Knights*. The Sausage-seller, speaking of leather, mocks Cleon: "And before the day was spent, it was larger than two palms." <note>original Greek: καὶ πρὶν ἡμέραν φαγῆναι, μεῖζον ἢ δυεῖν δοχμᾶιν.</note> In truth, *dochme*, *daktylodochme*, *palaiste*, and *doron* all signify the same thing, and each is described by Hesychius as "four-fingered."

The measure <term>ⲟϩⲟⲧ</term> <note>Coptic: *Ohot*</note>, which the Arabs call <margin>What is an *ohot*?</margin> *al-ba' al-qama* <note>Arabic text: الباع القاماً, meaning the fathom of a man's stature</note>, is the same as the "ell." It is the extension of both arms in length, which is equal to the height of a man; from the Coptic, we interpret this as the **greater cubit**. To understand this, it must be noted that the cubit varied among the Egyptians. <margin>The cubit was varied among the Egyptians.</margin> For one was 24 fingers, another 32. One was equal to a reed, or a pole, or a rod; another equaled the stature of a man. So says the Arab Abulfeda in the *Prolegomena* of his *Cosmography*; these are his words:

<margin>Abulfeda</margin>
> "Know therefore that there is much controversy between the Ancients and the moderns concerning the cubit, the mile, and the parasang. Regarding the finger, they have agreed on this: that every finger is the measure of the space filled by six equal grains of barley placed side-by-side according to their width. But in the cubit they differ somewhat. For the Ancients, one cubit was 32 fingers, while for the moderns it is 24; thus the cubit of the ancients exceeds the cubit of the moderns by 8 fingers. This is the secret of the priests." <note>Translated from the Arabic text provided in the manuscript.</note>

That is to say, the **greatest cubit** is equal to a reed or pole as well as to the stature of a man, as will be proven below. <margin>The greatest cubit.</margin> Furthermore, the Rabbis also affirm that a finger consists of 6 grains of barley in these words:

<margin>The Rabbis.</margin>
> "Every cubit has six palms, and one palm has four fingers by the thumb, and a finger has six grains of barley; and this is the cubit of Moses, the cubit of the Law and the Prophets." <note>Translated from the Hebrew: ויש לאמה ו' טפחים...</note>

Every cubit has six palms, and a palm four fingers at the thumb, and a finger six grains of barley; and this is the true legal cubit, and the cubit of building—that is, the one used by the Law in the description of buildings and structures. <margin>The legal cubit.</margin> Which <margin>Rashi</margin> <term>Rabbi</term> <note>Likely referring to the commentator Rashi</note> affirms in this place: <margin>The minor cubit is equal to the legal cubit of 24 fingers.</margin> "A finger has six grains of barley," which harmonizes with the Syriac: "A finger is the measure of six grains of barley." From these points it is clear that the minor cubit, namely of 24 fingers, is equal to the Mosai-

<sig>co</sig> <note>The text breaks here, continuing "-aic" on the next page to complete the word "Mosaico" or Mosaic.</note>

### SECTION VIII. EGYPTIAN MECHANICS. PREFACE I.

Nn 2

...[common] or legal. Now, a cubit is a length equal to the distance from the <margin>What is a cubit?</margin> bend of the arm, or its outer prominence, to the tip of the middle finger; or, what is the same thing, the distance from the middle of the chest to the elbow or the bend of the arm; for this space is entirely equal to the former, according to the testimony of Pollux: <note>Julius Pollux (2nd century CE), author of the *Onomasticon*, a Greek thesaurus and encyclopedia.</note> *The distance from the point of the elbow to the tip of the middle finger is a cubit. It contains a foot and a half, and the distance from the middle of the chest to the elbow is equal to the former.* <note>original Greek: Ἀπὸ δὲ τῆς ὠλεκράνου πρὸς τὸ μέσου δακτύλου ἄκρον τὸ διάστημα πῆχυς. ἔχει τὸν πόδα, καὶ μίσου, κὶ διάστημα ἀπὸ τοῦ μέσου τοῦ στήθους πρὸς τὸ ὠλέκρανον τῷ προτέρῳ ἴσον.</note> That is, *From the bend of the elbow to the tip of the middle finger, the interval of the cubit contains a foot and a half, to which interval the distance from the middle of the chest to the bend of the elbow is equal.* As I have said, a cubit of this kind contains six palms, and a palm contains four finger-widths of the thumb; consequently, one cubit consists of twenty-four fingers, which is the unit we have already explained as the common cubit of the Egyptians and the legal cubit of the Hebrews. From this, it is clear that such a cubit, taken four times, perfectly fulfills the length of a man (which is measured by the extension of the arms) and his height or stature. With these premises established, let us now proceed to the rest.

->ΠΙΚΑϣ ϸΠΕΝΙϯϣϣΗΙ and even ΠΙΚΑϣ ϸΠΕΝΙϯϣϣΗΙϥ<- <margin><term>ΠΙΚΑϣ ϸΠΕΝΙϯϣϣΗΙ</term>: A measuring rod.</margin> In the *Scala* <note>Referring to Kircher's *Scala Magna*, a Coptic-Arabic dictionary.</note> I interpreted this as a "measuring rod"; and applying a more diligent scrutiny to this word, I finally discovered that it signifies the "rod of the Ibis" or "Egyptian Stork." Thus, this word is understood to be composed of <term>ΠΙΚΑϣ</term> (*Pikash*) and <term>ϸΠΕΝΙϯϣϣΗΙϥ</term> (*Shpenitishshêif*), of which the former signifies a leg, shin, rod, or reed, and the latter signifies the Ibis or Stork; as if you were to say, the <term>step</term> or <term>ell</term> of the Ibis. This is because it was first discovered and observed from the gait of the Ibis. For as Clement of Alexandria <margin>Clement of Alexandria</margin> rightly says: *Indeed, it seems that among the living creatures, the Ibis provided the Egyptians with the primary concept of number and measure.* <note>original Greek: Ἀριθμὸς δὲ ἐπινοίας καὶ μέτρο μάλιστα τῷ ζώω ἡ Ἶβις ἀρχὴν παρεσχῆσθαι τοῖς Αἰγυπτίοις.</note> <margin>The step of the Ibis: a measure of the Egyptians.</margin> For the ancient Egyptians were accustomed, for the most part, to employ measures established from the gaits of animals; since these animals always acted the same way by natural necessity, the measures adopted were established upon a more certain and solid foundation. What sort of measure this "step of the Ibis" was, however, now remains to be investigated. I find that it certainly equaled the height of a man, and was simultaneously the measure of the "Ibiac triangle." Thus says Abenephi <note>Ahmad ibn Wahshiyya, a 9th/10th-century Arabic author often cited by Kircher for Egyptian lore.</note> concerning the sacred worship of the Egyptians; his words are as follows:

<margin>Abenephi.</margin>
->وباع المصريين هو طول الانسان فاسمة باع كبير الكركي ومساحة المثلث<-
->الكركي وهو سر الكهنة ۞<-

*The <term>Baa</term> <note>Arabic: *Bāʿ*, usually meaning a fathom or the span of outstretched arms.</note> is an Egyptian measure equal to the height of a perfect man; and they <margin>What is the great step of the Ibis?</margin> called this the "great step of the Crane" <note>Kircher equates the Arabic *al-kurki* (crane) with the Ibis.</note> and the measure of the Ibiac triangle; and this was the secret of the Priests.* What the "Ibiac triangle" is, we have discussed elsewhere; but as for what or how great the "Ibiac step" was, it can hardly be said how much effort I have spent in finding it; nevertheless, by God's grace, I have extracted the secret, as I shall show. For since the height of a man consists of four common Egyptian cubits, and one cubit consists of six palms, and a palm of four fingers; then one common cubit must necessarily consist of 24 fingers, and consequently the <term>ⲟⲩⲉⲣⲕⲟϯ</term> (*uerkoti*) or *Baa* (which we interpreted above, as well as in our *Scala*, as the measure of the space of both arms perfectly extended in length) will consist of 96 fingers. But the mystic or sacred cubit of the Egyptians, which they call the "step of the Ibis," I have found to be of just as many fingers...

He cites Greek authorities like Pollux and Clement of Alexandria alongside Arabic sources to prove that these units formed a "sacred secret" among Egyptian priests.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical mathematical and metrological investigation from page 283. While the previous page established the common cubit based on human anatomy (24 digits), this page introduces the "Greater Egyptian Cubit" (32 digits) and its relationship to the stride of the sacred Ibis and the measurement of the stadium. It bridges Greek, Coptic, and Arabic traditions to harmonize these ancient units.</meta>

<header>OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC ACADEMY</header>

<margin>
PREFACE I
</margin>

I find this by the following reasoning. Since the leg or shin of the Ibis, <margin>Abenephi. Abulfeda.</margin> according to the testimony of Abenephi <note>Abenephi is Abu Bakr ibn Wahshiyya, a 9th-century polymath; Kircher frequently cites his work on Egyptian secrets.</note> and Abulfeda, <note>Ismael Abulfeda (1273–1331), a renowned Syrian geographer and historian.</note> is equal to the **greater cubit** of the Egyptians, namely 32 digits; and since the Ibis also completes an **equilateral triangle** <margin>The triangle of the Ibis.</margin> <note>original Greek: τρίγωνον ἰσόπλευρον</note> when walking, as Plutarch testifies; the "Ibis-triangle" will therefore be 96 digits, which is **equal in perimeter** <note>original Greek: ἰσοπερίμετρον</note> to three cubits of **ninety-six fingers** <note>original Greek: ἑξακαιενενηκονταδάκτυλον</note>—that is, 32 digits each—and corresponds to the height of a human being, whose stature consists of four [common] cubits. And this is that mystery of the Priests of which Abenephi speaks, which the Coptic name **cubit** <term>ⲟⲩⲁϩⲟⲧ</term> <note>Kircher transliterates this as *Ouahot*.</note> also confirms. They were accustomed to write this in two ways: first, as **cubit** <term>ⲟⲩⲁϩⲟⲧ</term>, meaning 32 digits; second, by this reasoning: **cubit** <term>ⲟⲩⲁϩⲟⲧ</term> by which they denote the "greatest cubit," which they also call **the reed of the stride** <term>ⲡⲓⲕⲁϣ ⲛⲧⲉⲡⲓⲥⲧⲉⲛⲧϩⲱⲃ</term>, that is, the three-cubit pace of the Ibis, or the "stalk," or the "cane," or the tripled leg of the Ibis. In Arabic, the *Scala* <note>The *Scala Magna*, a famous Coptic-Arabic dictionary.</note> calls this **the Kari reed** **القصبة الكري**; this pace exactly corresponds to human height. We may not undeservedly call this a **six-foot** pace <note>original Greek: ἑξάποδον</note>, for geometers assign a stature of just as many feet to a well-proportioned man. However, concerning the mysteries hidden beneath this pace, and how they represented Mercury <note>The god Thoth, often associated with the Ibis.</note> under this measure, I have already spoken elsewhere.

<margin>
The stadium
</margin>
**The stadium** <term>ⲡⲓⲥⲧⲁⲇⲓⲟⲛ</term> means the same thing as the Latin *stadium*, called in Arabic **the ghalwa** **الغلوة**; and among the <margin>The stadium varied among the Egyptians.</margin> Egyptians, it was varied. Some made it 65 canes or perches, others 85; nor are there lacking those who define it by a space of 400 cubits. Thus says the author of the *Scala*:

-> **The stadium is sixty-five reeds; and it was also found in an ancient copy that the stadium is eighty-five reeds; it is also said that the stadium is four hundred cubits.** <note>Floral ornament</note> <-

> That is: A Stadium is 65 reeds, and it was also found in an ancient manuscript that a Stadium is 85 reeds or perches; it is also said that a Stadium is 400 cubits or arm-lengths, and it is called an "arrow's throw."

And this last measurement corresponds exactly to the stadium of the Greeks, since <margin>Suidas.</margin> Suidas says **a stadium has 800 feet** <note>original Greek: στάδιον ἔχειν πόδας ωʹ</note>, and <margin>Herodotus.</margin> Herodotus agrees with this; since a foot is 16 digits, or four palms, according to the words of the cited Herodotus in *Euterpe*: <note>Herodotus, *Histories*, Book II (Euterpe).</note> **The fathom is measured as six feet, or four cubits; the feet being four palms, and the cubit being six palms.** <note>original Greek: Ἑξάποδης μὲν ἡ ὀργυιὴς μετρεομένης, καὶ τετράπηχυς· τῶν δὲ ποδῶν μὲν τετραπαλάστων ἐόντων, τοῦ δὲ πήχεος ἑξαπαλάστου.</note> Thus we measure a pace by six feet, and by four cubits: for feet are four palms, <margin>Suidas.</margin> but a cubit is six palms. Suidas confirms this: **the cubit has 24 fingers** <note>original Greek: ὁ πῆχυς ἔχει δακτύλους κδʹ</note>. A foot, however, has 16 fingers. Solon uses this same measurement in his laws, as found in <margin>Plutarch.</margin> Plutarch.

Since, therefore, the Egyptian stadium is said to have 400 cubits, and the greater Egyptian cubit is (as proved above) 32 digits—that is, two feet, one of which equals 16 digits—therefore 400 cubits will equal 800 feet, which is precisely a stadium, as will be clear to anyone calculating it. Therefore, the Egyptian stadium is equal to the Greek stadium, which was necessary to demonstrate. However, if we take the "reed" to be the pace of the Ibis, which we determined to be 96 digits, then the stadium of 85 reeds would be a space of 340 smaller cubits, or what is the same thing, 510 feet. From this, we gather that there were three types of stadium among the Egyptians: the Large, the Middling, and the Smallest. The Large is 400 cubits; the Middling 340; the Small 260 cubits. The first one, however, is the true Egyptian one.

<note>Catchword: nus</note>

# CLASS VIII. EGYPTIAN MECHANICS. 285 PREFACE II.

<term>pi-emlion</term> <note>original Coptic: πιεεμλιον</note> a mile, in Arabic <term>al-mil</term>. <note>original Arabic: الميل</note> Furthermore, one mile consists of seven stadia, while one parasang <note>A Persian unit of distance, roughly 3 to 3.5 miles.</note> consists of three miles. So says the Author of the *Scala*. <note>The *Scala Magna* is a medieval Coptic-Arabic dictionary used by Kircher.</note>

<margin>
<term>pi-emlion</term>
A Mile.
</margin>

> The mile, which is seven stadia; <note>original Arabic: غلوات (ghalawat), often used for the Greek stadium.</note> every three miles make a parasang, and a parasang is one thousand four hundred cubits, <note>The text here says 1400, though the calculations below suggest this may be a scribal error for a larger number.</note> and in steps it is three thousand paces. ۞

A mile contains seven stadia, and three individual miles constitute one parasang, and the parasang is 1,400 cubits or arms, which are a space of 3,000 paces. With this Abulfeda <note>Ismael Abulfeda (1273–1331), a Syrian geographer.</note> agrees in all respects, defining the Egyptian mile as follows:

> As for the mile, among the Ancients it is three thousand cubits, and among the Moderns four thousand cubits. The difference between them is merely in name, for the actual extent of the mile is the same for everyone, even if the number of cubits varies. According to the commentators, one mile is 96,000 digits. If you divide this by 32, the result is 3,000 cubits; and if you divide that same number by 24, it yields 4,000 cubits (one mile). As for the parasang, among both the Ancients and Moderns it is three miles; the only difference is in the varying name of the cubit. If you take the cubit of the Ancients, one parasang will be 9,000 cubits; according to the cubit of the more recent people, it is 12,000 cubits, which according to the commentators is 300,000 digits minus 12,000 digits. <note>This equals 288,000 digits (3 miles x 96,000 digits).</note> Know that the parasang among the Ancients is 9,000 cubits and the mile 3,000 cubits; among the Moderns, the parasang is 12,000 cubits. Know that the mile in both interpretations is a third of a parasang, and every parasang is three miles.

->*That is: The mile indeed among the Ancients consists of 3,000 arms or cubits, and among the Moderns 4,000. The difference consists only in this: that although the name "mile" is the same for everyone, the number of cubits varies. According to the Interpreters, one mile is 96,000 digits; if you divide these by 32, there will be 3,000 cubits; and if you divide the same number by 24, there will result 4,000 cubits (one mile). The parasang, however, among both the Ancients and the Moderns, is three miles; the only difference is in the varying designation of the cubit. For if you take the cubit for the cubit of the ancients, one parasang will be 9,000 cubits; and according to the cubit of the more recent, 12,000 cubits, which are, according to the interpreters, 300,000 digits minus 12,000 digits. You should know, therefore, that the parasang among the Ancients is 9,000 cubits, and the mile 3,000 cubits; but among the Moderns, the parasang is 12,000 cubits. And know that the mile among the Moderns is one-third of a parasang, and a parasang is 3 miles. Truly, whoever compares these things more exactly with what has been said above will find a remarkable harmony between the facts. But leaving these things aside, let us turn our attention to the measures of dry and liquid goods.*<-

That is: a **Saa** is a **Corus**, <note>The *Corus* or *Kor* is a large ancient unit of capacity for grain or liquids.</note> or a vessel of flour holding four **modii**. <note>A *modius* was a Roman "bushel," roughly 8.7 liters.</note> The Hebrews describe it thus:
