The **Corus**, a measure for dry goods, contains ten **Ephi**, and these are thirty **Sata**. <note>The *Satum* or *Seah* is approximately 7.3 liters.</note> But before we proceed further, we must first explain what an **Ephi** and a **Satum** are: for since the **Corus** is the largest of all measures, not only for dry goods but also for liquids, all others are to be understood as parts of the whole.

As for what the Egyptians call the **oiphi** <note>original Coptic: ⲟⲓⲫⲓ</note> (or without the article, **iphi**) and the Arabs call **Al-waibah**, <note>original Arabic: الويبه</note> <margin>Hesychius.</margin> **Hesychius** calls this the *oiphi* in a corrupted form; he describes it with these words: *A certain Egyptian measure of capacity,* <note>original Greek: Μέτρον τι τοχωρητικόν Αἰγύπτιον</note> that is, the **Oephin** or <margin>**Choenix.**</margin> **oiphi** is an Egyptian measure containing four **choenices**. <note>A *choenix* was a Greek daily ration of grain, about 1 liter.</note> Now, a **choenix** is equivalent to two Roman **sextarii**, <note>A *sextarius* is roughly a pint.</note> with a weight in wine or <margin>**Ephi. Satum. Cabus. Log.**</margin> water of 40 Roman ounces; thus the **Ephi** or **oiphi** measure would contain eight **sextarii**. The Hebrew **Ephi**, however, is a tenth part of a **Corus**, and is equal to a **Bathus**; <note>The *Bath* is the liquid equivalent of the dry *Ephah*.</note> they differ only in this: the **Ephi** is a measure for dry goods, while the **Bathus** is for liquids. Furthermore, an **Ephi** contains three **Sata**. So says the *Yalkut*: <note>The *Yalkut Shimoni*, a medieval compilation of Jewish midrash.</note>

<margin>Author of the *Yalkut*.</margin>
->An Ephi contains three Sata; a Satum contains six Cabi; a Cabus contains six Log; and a Log contains six eggs. <note>original Hebrew: איפה ג' סאים וסאה ו' קבים וקב ו' לוגין ולוג ו' בצים</note><-

From this it appears that the measures of the Egyptian **Corus** and the Hebrew **Corus** are different: <margin>The Egyptian Corus differs from the Hebrew.</margin> for the **Corus** of the Egyptians is a vessel containing four **modii** of flour; but the **Corus** of the Hebrews contains 47 **modii**—unless perhaps they take a **modius** to mean seven **Sata**, which we shall discuss below. Since, therefore, the **Corus** differs from the **Corus**, who does not see that the **Ephi** consequently differs from the Egyptian **oiphi**? But even the Egyptian **Bathus** differs from the Egyptian **Ephi**, which measures we said were <margin>**pi-bathos n-hēes** <note>original Coptic: ⲡⲓⲃⲁⲑⲟⲥ ⲛⲏⲉⲥ</note></margin> the same among the Hebrews. The Egyptians call the **Bathus** the **pi-bathos n-hēes**, <margin>The Egyptian Bathus.</margin> that is, a **Bathos** of oil, for **hēes** means "oil" in the Coptic language; which the Author of the *Scala* <note>The *Scala Magna*, a Coptic-Arabic dictionary.</note> explains in these words: *The kaphiz <note>A measure of weight or volume used in the Islamic world.</note> of oil is sixty Kost.* <note>original Arabic: القفيז الزيت ستين قسط</note> Now, as to what a <margin>What a **Kost** is. Serapion the Arab.</margin> **Kost** is, **Serapion the Arab** explains in these words:

->The Kost among the Romans is a pound with two-thirds [more], that is, 20 ounces. <note>original Arabic: قسط عند الروميون هو رطل مع اثنين الثלثين</note><-

That is, the **Kast** among the Romans is a pound with two thirds, which is 20 ounces. <margin>Aben Sina.</margin> **Aben Sina** <note>The famous Persian polymath Avicenna (c. 980–1037).</note> supports this with almost the same words. Those among the Latins who distinguish between **Kist** and **Akfat** are merely distinguishing the singular from the plural; for **Kist** and **Akfat** are the same measure, differing only in number. I note this so that a reader unfamiliar with the language does not stumble when encountering such things. # CLASS VIII. EGYPTIAN MECHANICS. PREFACE II.

We said in the Supplement that the **Corus** and the **Ghomor** <note>The *Corus* and *Ghomor* (or *Omer*) are ancient units of dry measure, often mentioned in the Bible.</note> were the same measure; but I have found that among the Egyptians, this too differs from the **Corus**; for the <term>Egyptian Ghomor</term> <note>original Coptic: πικοροϭ ncoϫ</note> signifies a **Saam**, or a vessel of flour containing 4 **modii**. <margin>The <term>Egyptian Ghomor</term> <note>original Coptic: πικοροϭ ncoϫ</note>.</margin> This <term>Egyptian Ghomor</term> is of two types: the greater and the lesser. The greater, which is also called the **Greater Modius**, <note>original Coptic: πικοροϭ nκομορ</note> contains thirty other **modii**. Thus says the Author of the *Scale*: <note>original Arabic: المد الكبير ثلاثون مدا — "The great modius is thirty modii."</note> *A Greater Modius of 30 modii*; and the lesser modius or **Komor** <note>original Coptic: πικομορ</note> contains fifteen modii, as stated in the *Scale*: <note>original Arabic: المد الصغير خمسة عشر مدا — "The small modius is fifteen modii."</note> *A Lesser Modius capable of holding 15 other modii.* From these I conclude that the <term>Egyptian Ghomor</term> is taken in this place for the **Corus** of the Hebrews, and the **modii** of which it consists are taken for **Sata**. <note>A *Satum* or *Seah* is roughly 7.3 liters; 30 Sata make one Corus.</note> By this reasoning, we shall reduce the **Ghomor** of the Egyptians to the Hebrew **Corus**, which we have proven consists of 10 **Ephis** and 30 **Sata**. Therefore, this **modius** is taken here for one Hebrew and Italian **modius** and a half, which makes one **Satum**; thus the Hebrew **Corus** and the Greater Egyptian **Komor** are accepted as the same measure. The Lesser **Komor**, however, consists of 15 **modii**, being exactly half of the greater. From these premises, we shall easily determine the remaining measures of the Egyptians.

The <term>Modius of the Saa</term> <note>original Coptic: πϭαπιϫι</note> is a measure containing 22 **Koft**. <note>The *Koft* or *Qist* is a measure of volume, often equated with the Greek *xestes* or Roman *sextarius*.</note> Thus says the Author of the *Scale*: <note>original Arabic: الصاع تسع اثنين وعشرين قسط وهذا الاسم في الاهـق المسيحى وذكر للجوهري ان المن مكيال وهو رطل عند اهل الحجاز ورطلان عند اهل العراق الصاع اربعة امداد — "The Sa'a holds twenty-two qist, and this name is found in the Christian 'Ahaq' [Apocalypse/Ecclesiastical lexicon]. Al-Jawhari mentions that the 'mann' is a measure which is one pound for the people of Hijaz and two pounds for the people of Iraq. The Sa'a contains four modii."</note> <margin>The <term>Modius of the Saa</term> <note>original Coptic: πϭαπι ϫι</note>.</margin> *This is to say: The Modius contains 22 Koft, and this name is found in the Apocalypse; Al-Jawhari mentions it as well, saying: This modius is a measure that is worth a pound among the Hijazi Arabs, and two pounds among the Iraqis; but the Saa contains four modii.*

Let us now explain the Author's words. He says first, then, that the **modius** or measure of the **Saa** contains 22 **Koft**. Since we have shown above from **Antho Serapion** that one **Koft** consists of 20 ounces of a pound divided into 12 ounces; it follows that the **Modius of the Saa** consists of 36 pounds and 8 twelfths. <note>36 and 2/3 pounds.</note> This **modius**, however, as **Al-Jawhari** rightly says, varies among different nations, which produces no small confusion in the ambiguity of such measures for those not paying attention to the specific circumstances of the words. He adds at the end that one **Saa** consists of four such **modii**, specifically those of which one consists of 36 pounds and 8 twelfths, so that one **Saa** consists of 145 pounds and 8 twelfths. From this it is clear that the <term>Egyptian Ghomor</term> is equivalent to the **Saa**: for the **Saa** is a **corus** of flour of four such **modii**, one of which we said holds 36 pounds and 8 twelfths. <margin>Saa.</margin> It is also clear that the Egyptian measure <term>Modius of the Saa</term> is the fourth part of the <term>Egyptian Ghomor</term>. Finally, you may gather that the **Lecythus**, <note>A *Lecythus* is a Greek oil jar.</note> the **Cantarus**, or the small flask of **Elijah**, which the Copts call the <term>Flask of Elijah</term> <note>original Coptic: πικαπσκικ nτεηλιας</note> is worth four **Koft**. Thus the Interpreter: <note>original Arabic: قله ايلياص اربعة قسط — "The jar of Elijah is four qist."</note> which are 6 pounds and 8 twelfths; <margin>Lecythus.</margin> the **hydria**, <note>A *hydria* is a large water jar.</note> however, which the Copts call the <term>Water-Pot</term> <note>original Coptic: ϯϵϵ spic</note> contains 19 **Koft**. Thus our Author: <note>original Arabic: وجره تسع عشر اقساط — "And a jar contains nineteen qist."</note> and the **hydria** contains ten **modii**; that is, <margin>Hydria.</margin>

<margin>**The Log.** <note>original Coptic: ⲡⲓⲗⲟⲕ</note></margin> **The Log** <note>original Coptic: ⲡⲓⲗⲟⲕ</note> in Coptic seems to sound the same as the Hebrew **Log** <note>original Hebrew: לוג</note>, even if the measure differs; for we have shown above that the Log holds six eggs. ### -> On the Artaba. <-

<margin>Artaba.</margin> The **Artaba** <note>original Coptic: ⲧⲁⲣⲧⲁⲃ</note> is a most famous Egyptian measure, which is commonly called *Arvaba* by corruption, *Alertob* <note>original Arabic: الاردب</note> by the Arabs, and *Ardubuo* <note>original Syriac: أردبو</note> by the Syrians. What kind of measure this was, and how large, is a matter of controversy among authors. <margin>Suidas.</margin> Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedist</note> says: *The Artaba is a Median measure, yet it is an Attic medimnus.* <note>original Greek: Ἀρτάβη μέτρον Μηδικόν, οὔτε Ἀττικὸς μέδιμνος</note> The Artaba is a measure of the Medes (that is, of the Medes), an Attic <term>medimnus</term> <note>A Greek dry measure</note> of grain; the Attic medimnus is a measure of six <term>modii</term>, according to the testimony of <margin>Cornelius Nepos.</margin> Cornelius Nepos in his *Life of Atticus*. Some say it is a measure common to the Persians and Egyptians. Thus the interpreter of Aristophanes says regarding the Artaba in *The Acharnians*: *It is a Persian and Egyptian name.* <note>original Greek: Περσικὸν δὲ καὶ Αἰγύπτιον ὄνομα</note> We say that the Egyptian **Artaba** <note>original Coptic: ⲧⲁⲣⲧⲁⲃ</note> is a liquid measure containing five modii; thus a certain anonymous Greek [writer] on weights and measures says in [the works of] Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola, a 16th-century scholar famous for his work on ancient weights and measures</note>: *The Egyptian artaba holds five modii; however, the Egyptian modius, like the Italian one, contains eight choenices.* <note>original Greek: Αἰγυπτία ἀρτάβη ἔχει μοδίους ε'· ὁ δὲ μόδιος ὁ Αἰγύπτιος, καὶ ὁ Ἰταλικὸς ἔχει χοίνικας η'</note> I find that St. Jerome was of the same opinion, <margin>St. Jerome.</margin> whose words in Book 11 of his *Commentary on Isaiah* are these: *And for the 30 modii, which we have set for the Corus (which in Hebrew is called the **Chomer** <note>original Hebrew: חומר</note>), the Seventy [translators of the Septuagint] rendered it as 17 artabae, which is an Egyptian measure and makes thirty modii: for if six artabae hold thirty modii, each one will hold five modii.*

### CLASS VIII. EGYPTIAN MECHANICS. SECTION II.

Others, however, hold the opposite view, such as Fannius, who makes it [the Artaba] smaller than what we have stated.

<margin>Fannius.</margin>
> *There is also in the lands which the foreign Nile floods,*
> *The Artaba, which exceeds three <term>modii</term> <note>A Roman unit of dry measure, roughly 8.7 liters</note> by a third part,*
> *For a double Artaba will be filled by ten modii.*
<note>original Latin: "Est etiam in terris, quas aduena Nilus inundat, Artaba, cui superat modij pars tertia post tres, Namq; decem modijs explebitur Artaba duplex."</note>

That is to say, the Egyptian Ardaba contains three *modii* and a third part of a *modius*. Epiphanius disagrees with this, claiming that the Egyptian Artaba consists of 72 <term>sextarii</term> <note>Approximately 546 ml</note>, <margin>Epiphanius.</margin> or one Attic <term>Medimnus</term> <note>A large Greek unit of capacity, about 52 liters</note>; and thus it would be equal to the Median Artaba. "The Artaba," he says, "this measure is also Egyptian and consists of seventy-two sextarii." <note>original Greek: Ἀρτάβη, τοῦτο τὸ μέτρον καὶ Αἰγυπτίῳ ἐστὶν ὅτι δὲ ἑβδομήκοντα δύο ξιστῶν.</note> By this reasoning, according to Epiphanius, the Artaba would be the same as the <term>Ephi</term> <note>The Hebrew Ephah, a dry measure of about 36 liters</note> measure. 

However, so that such various opinions regarding the Artaba may be resolved, I say that the Egyptian Artaba was <margin>The Triple Egyptian Artaba</margin> threefold. The first, and larger one, contained six <term>choenices</term> <note>A Greek dry measure, roughly 1 liter</note> more than the Attic Medimnus; Herodotus is the authority that the Persian Artaba was also this large, which is frequently confused with that of the Egyptians: <margin>Herodotus.</margin> "The Artaba is a Persian measure containing one Attic medimnus plus six Attic choenices." <note>original Greek: Ἡ δὲ ἀρτάβη μέτρον ἐστὶ Περσικὸν χωρέον μεδίμνου Ἀττικοῦ πλεῖον χοίνιξι Ϛ' Ἀττικῇσι.</note> 

Here a notable error of the translators comes to light, for they read Γ (meaning 3) instead of Ϛ' (meaning 6), having been deceived by the Greek number six (Ϛ'), which is very similar to the notation for three (γ'); I would wish for the learned to take note of this. We have said that the second Artaba, capable of holding an Attic Medimnus, was also used by the Medes. It was shown above that the third is equal to five *modii*. But now let us demonstrate this very thing from the original sources. The Egyptians call these three Artabas **ni-ertob** <note>original Coptic: ⲛⲓⲉⲣⲧⲱⲃ</note>, as is clear from the *Scala* <note>A Coptic-Arabic dictionary</note>. The first is called **ni-nishi ni-ertob** <note>original Coptic: ⲛⲓⲛⲓϣⲓ ⲛⲓⲉⲣⲧⲱⲃ</note>, that is, the *Great Ertob*; the second is **ni-meso ni-ertob** <note>original Coptic: ⲛⲓⲙⲉⲥⲟ ⲛⲓⲉⲣⲧⲱⲃ</note>, that is, the *Middle Ertob*; the third is **ni-s-ertob** <note>original Coptic: ⲛⲓⲥⲉⲣⲧⲱⲃ</note>, or the *Common Artaba* found everywhere; all of which the interpreter explains beautifully:

<note>original Arabic: والاردب كبير من وحده وستة امداد والاردب وسطه وهي مد وحده والاردب صغير فهي خمسة امداد ۞</note>

*The Large Artaba contains one great modius (which we said above is equal to a Medimnus) and six small modii besides (which we have equated with choenices); the Middle Ertob contains one modius, that is, an Attic Medimnus; and the Lesser Ertob contains five modii.* All of these points agree perfectly with what has been said; and the Hebrew description in the *Baal Aruch* <note>A famous 11th-century Talmudic dictionary by Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome</note> also agrees:

<margin>Baal Aruch.</margin>
**Ardab: a small measure of water; the middle is explained as the daily ration for laborers or craftsmen; the third signifies the large measure common in the land of Egypt even to this day.**
<note>original Hebrew: ארדב מדה קטנה ומציא פי׳ חשוכי את האומנים ומדה גדולה נהוגה בארץ מצרים עד היום</note>

From all that has been said thus far, it is clear that six Artabas of the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint translators of the Old Testament</note> were equal to the Hebrew <term>Corus</term> <note>A large biblical unit of capacity, about 220 liters</note>; this is a fact that Eupolemus the Greek—a writer of both great antiquity and authority—left recorded in the works of <margin>The 70 Interpreters. Eusebius.</margin> Eusebius; consult him in the place cited. And let these remarks suffice regarding the Artaba.

Regarding the **Pi-drachme** <note>Coptic: ⲡⲓⲇⲣⲁⲭⲙⲏ</note>, which **Al-Samanudi** interprets as the drachma, it is the eighth part of an ounce. The following words follow:
<note>original Arabic: الدرهم ثمن اوقية وفي نسخة ثلثي اوقية</note> -> ۞ The <term>dirham</term> <note>Arabic term for drachma</note> is an eighth of an ounce; and it is read in an ancient copy that they are two-thirds of one Ounce. <-
The **Drachma** was, as the name itself indicates, the Greeks' own weight and a stamped coin; when the Greeks held power, it was transferred to the Romans and frequently used by them. Conversely, the Romans' weight and name for the ounce was transferred to the Greeks and Arabs. It was, as among the Romans and Greeks, so too among the Egyptians: the eighth part of an ounce. So says **Fannius** <note>A Roman poet who wrote on weights and measures</note>: "An ounce is made of twice four drachmas." <note>original Latin: Vncia fit drachmis bis quatuor.</note> **Suidas** says: "Each [one hundred] drachmas are a part of every mina." <note>original Greek: Ἕκαστον δὲ δραχμαὶ πασῶν μνῶν μέρος.</note> One hundred drachmas make one mina. From this it is clear that a pound or <term>as</term> <note>A Roman unit of weight</note> consists of 96 drachmas; if you add four to these, you will have the Attic Mina of 100 drachmas. **Dioscorides, Galen, Columella**, and others agree with this; you may see them in the works of **Villalpando, Mariana, Agricola**, and others.

And by this reasoning, the **Hebrew Shekel** and the **Stater** weigh the same—

St. Matthew.</margin> *Those who received the <term>didrachma</term> <note>A Greek silver coin worth two drachmas, used for the Temple tax</note> came to Peter and said to him: Does your teacher not pay the didrachma? The **Kite** <note>Coptic: ⲕⲓⲧⲉ</note> is the Census, or the Roman half-ounce; according to the Egyptians these are the same thing, distinguished <margin>Stater, Shekel, and Census are the same.</margin> only by names.

# CHAPTER I.
## On the Architecture of the Egyptians.

<margin>The Egyptians were outstanding in Architecture.</margin>
**T**he architecture of the ancient Egyptians shone most brightly in that prodigious magnificence of Obelisks, Colossi, Pyramids, Temples, Tombs, and Labyrinths. And if the things written about them by eye-witnesses such as **Herodotus** <note>A 5th-century BCE Greek historian known as the "Father of History"</note>, **Pausanias** <note>A 2nd-century CE Greek traveler and geographer</note>, **Diodorus** <note>Diodorus Siculus, a 1st-century BCE historian who wrote a massive universal history</note>, **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the 'Natural History'</note>, and the histories of the Arabs are true—things which almost exceed the limits of human belief—I do not fear to assert that these works were so great that, whether you look at their excellence and perfection, or the difficulty of the efforts required to execute them, they seem to have taken away all hope from future architects of ever reaching the same perfection. For if the work proves the craftsman, what kind of architects must we claim them to have been, and with how divine a genius were they endowed? Certainly, the highest and most singular symmetry and proportion of parts, and the joining of floors, required a supreme geometer and arithmetician, just as the erection of such unusual structures rightly demanded a supreme mechanic and master of statics. But so that we may proceed in order, it seemed best to begin first with the Pyramids, and then we shall follow with the remaining structures in order.

# §. I.
## The Pyramids.

<margin>
The Pyramids of Memphis according to Herodotus.

**H**ow great was the magnificence, splendor, and beauty of the Pyramids erected in Egypt through the supreme and most lavish generosity of Kings can be gathered from this, among other things: that by the unanimous consensus of writers, even at the time when Roman pride trampled upon every corner of the world, they were numbered among the Wonders of the World. And although unusual masses of such towers were seen founded in various places in Egypt, those of Memphis, above all others, were the greatest cause for admiration, and stood as a marvel of the world. Herodotus—who, according to Pliny, lived around the year 300 from the founding of the City <note>original Latin: "ab Vrbe condita," referring to the founding of Rome in 753 BCE. Kircher's dating here follows older chronologies.</note>—testifies particularly to these things in his book *Euterpe* regarding one of those he inspected himself:

<margin>

> Twenty years were spent in the making of the pyramid; each face of its four sides measures eight plethra <note>original Greek: "ὀκτὼ πλέθρα." A plethron was a Greek unit of measure roughly equal to 100 feet</note>, it being square, and its height is the same. It is made of polished stone, most perfectly fitted together, with no stone being smaller than thirty feet. This pyramid was not built with a smooth surface but with steps, which some call "scales" <note>original Latin: "scalas"</note> and others call "small altars" <note>original Greek: "βωμίδας," meaning little altars or pedestals</note>.

Indeed, twenty years were consumed on this Pyramid, of which each side (for it was four-sided) is eight <term>plethra</term> or <term>iugera</term> <note>iugera: A Roman acre. Kircher is equating the Greek plethron with the Roman iugeron for his readers</note> in length, with an equal height, made of stones hewn and most elegantly joined, none of which are less than 30 feet. These face toward Libya <note>meaning the Western/Libyan desert</note>, 120 <term>stadia</term> <note>A Greek unit of distance, roughly 1/8th of a mile</note> from Memphis and 45 from the Nile. These

The entire structure consists of hard stone, difficult to work but destined to remain for eternity. For almost a thousand years, as some say—or as others hand down, more than three thousand four hundred years—this mass has remained intact until our time. They say those stones were brought from Arabia over a very long journey. It was built using mounds <note>original Latin: "Aggeribus," referring to earthen ramps</note>, as machines had not yet been invented at that time. Certainly a marvelous work, especially in a land sandy on all sides, where no traces of either a mound or a cut stone remain; so that the great mass seems to have been built not by men, but by Gods. The Egyptians attempt to tell certain wonders about these, claiming the mounds were made of salt and nitre <note>Natron/saltpeter</note>, and were later liquefied by the rising of the Nile, vanishing completely without human labor. But this is far from the truth. For the mound was constructed by a multitude of men and demolished by a multitude. For 360,000 men, they say, were assigned to that work, which they finished in roughly 20 years. ### CHAPTER I. THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

on each side, it contains 250 steps from the base to the summit, each of which is the height of five shoe-soles <note>original: "solearum calcei"</note>, and nine inches in length. This mass is of such vast width that a most skilled and strong archer, standing upon its peak and shooting an arrow into the air, could not launch it with enough force to fall outside the base of the mass, but it would land upon the steps themselves. Its summit ends in a flat space measuring 2 paces in diameter, upon which 50 men can stand. There are also two other pyramids of immense size, though far smaller than the first; the smallest of these three is a third larger than the one located at the <term>Testacean Hill</term> <note>The Pyramid of Cestius in Rome, built around 12 BCE as a tomb for the magistrate Gaius Cestius. It is located near Monte Testaccio.</note> in Rome. Besides these three, many other smaller ones are scattered here and there through that sandy soil—more than a hundred—not a single one of which is seen to be as damaged as the Roman one. Thus says Belon. These details largely agree with the report made by **Marcus Grimani**, the Prelate of Aquileia and later Cardinal. <margin>Marcus Grimani.</margin> Being a great student of antiquities, he measured it himself while he was in Egypt handling the affairs of the Venetians; he climbed it and penetrated into the interior. He measured this pyramid in standard <term>paces</term> <note>A "passus" or pace was roughly five feet, though measurements varied locally.</note>, the size of which is thought to have slightly exceeded the measure of three ancient palms. Each of the four sides comprises about 270 paces; the entire pyramid consists of "revived" <note>Kircher likely refers to "redivivo lapide," meaning stone reused or perhaps "living stone" (quarried bedrock).</note> and very hard stone, and its tiers <note>original: "præcinctiones," referring to the horizontal levels or platforms of the pyramid.</note> extend to a quite suitable length. They are so fitted and arranged throughout the whole work that they provide an ascent to the very highest peak, though it is extremely difficult and inconvenient; for each tier is about three and a half palms high, and they do not provide enough of a protruding flat surface for the feet of those climbing to rest upon them comfortably or safely. From the base to the summit there are about 210 tiers, and each maintains exactly the same height, so that the total height of the structure appears entirely equal to the width of the base below.

I find, however, that above all others, **Prince Radziwiłł** <note>Mikołaj Krzysztof "the Orphan" Radziwiłł (1549–1616), a Polish-Lithuanian noble whose account of his 1582–1584 pilgrimage became a bestseller.</note> observed them most precisely in his history of his travels on page 161. <margin>Radziwiłł.</margin> I have decided to include his words, though they are somewhat long, so that every detail may be brought to light. *In the early morning,* he says, *one hour before daybreak, we departed from our lodging and came to the old city <note>Fustat, or Old Cairo.</note>, which is a quarter of a mile from the new city, traveling always among gardens. Two hours after sunrise, having crossed the Nile and completed five miles of the journey, we arrived directly at the pyramids. Since much has been produced about them by other authors, I shall briefly note what I saw myself in person. It is established by the testimony of all that the city of <margin>Site of Memphis.</margin> **Memphis**, celebrated in both sacred and secular literature, was formerly here; now, except for certain meager ruins toward the south, no traces of it appear. Sterile sands cover everything. Nevertheless, seventeen pyramids are still seen intact, <margin>17 pyramids remain at Memphis.</margin> of which two are larger; the third, built by the courtesan <term>Rhodope</term>, is especially elegant, yet it has a height of scarcely 60 or 70 cubits. These three pyramids are clearly intact and are numbered among the wonders of the world. The two larger ones are of a stupendous and incredible magnitude; however, one excels the other, which is said to be 300 cubits in height, as well as in width and length. On the inside, it has skillfully crafted and very large steps, by which one ascends to the very summit just as on the outside. It also has chambers, the two largest of which are built one above the other, and these contained the sepulchers of the Kings of Egypt. In the lower one, there still remains a tomb [large] enough...* <note>The Latin "fatis" at the end is an OCR error or abbreviation for "satis" (enough/sufficiently), likely leading into a description of the sarcophagus's dimensions.</note>

Furthermore, by which Kings, at what cost, or by what method or skill, and whether these masses of pyramids were raised by the <term>Jews</term> <note>original: "Iudæis"</note> established in <term>Egyptian</term> servitude (as pleases almost all authors); or whether the same <term>Hebrews</term> completed the mounds and ditches by which the <term>Nile</term> is diverted (for all things appear to have been made by art, not by nature), I leave to the historians to judge. It is appropriate to marvel greatly at this: although the said pyramids were erected upon a high mountain which consists entirely of living rock, yet as much as can be gathered from the type of stone, it appears they were not fashioned from the stones of that same cliff; nor can it easily be investigated from where, or by what means, such a heap of stones could have been carried there; especially since even the overflowing <term>Nile</term> runs three miles distant from the structure. But neither can this be understood: since any stone is three <term>cubits</term> <note>An ancient unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger (about 18–21 inches).</note> long and wide, and more than one and a half cubits high, by what labor and skill they could have been dragged up such a high mountain and placed at the summit. <margin>The size, shape, etc., of the greatest pyramid, according to Radziwiłł.</margin> The greatest pyramid of all is constructed with a certain singular skill from stones of this kind, cut and squared, in the form of a certain natural mountain; and although it rises from the base gradually into a peak in a quadrangular shape, yet those square stones are seen to be composed with such wonderful art in an unequal order that the whole mass represents the appearance of a mountain formed by nature. The ascent is heavy and laborious on account of the thickness of the stones, yet it is secure; and although I used a suitable pace, I barely ascended the summit of the pyramid within an hour and a half, where there is a square level space, encompassing a span of ten cubits on each side.

The second pyramid, a little smaller than the previous one, stands at a distance of two arrow-shots from it; the interior entrance into it is not open, though they claim it is hidden. On the outside, one can climb up to the middle, since it has stones arranged in the same manner as the former one, except that they are a little flatter and smaller. From the middle upward, however, the stones rise up so smoothed over that to proceed further is impossible; which appears to have been done with that specific purpose: but then the third part of the same pyramid, all the way to the summit, has stones placed as if neglected and in disorder, just as in the lower part, so that unless that smooth series of rocks, which rises for several dozen cubits, stood in the way, its summit could easily be climbed just like the first.

The third pyramid, at the side of the second toward the city, belongs to that <term>Rhodopis</term> <note>A legendary Greek courtesan. Ancient traditions (likely confused) sometimes attributed the third pyramid to her rather than the Pharaoh Menkaure.</note> whom we have already mentioned, built entirely of hewn stone so that it cannot be climbed; from which, at three bow-shots also toward the city, is a head with neck and shoulders projecting, belonging to the same woman <note>Kircher is referring to the Great Sphinx, which was often buried up to its neck in sand during this period and mistaken for a female monument.</note>, seven cubits in height, of a wonderful appearance, carved out of a single piece of living rock. Some maintain that from that larger pyramid which we entered, through a subterranean cavern cut into the rock—which we saw covered over with stones—a narrow and hidden passage lay open into this head, and from there oracles were issued, while the common people of the Gentiles believed they were uttered through the mouth of the head itself. Thus far <term>Radziwiłł</term> <note>Prince Mikołaj Krzysztof Radziwiłł (1549–1616), a Polish-Lithuanian noble whose travelogue "Hierosolymitana Peregrinatio" was a major source for Kircher.</note>: who indeed described everything so exactly that nothing seems possible to be added to or taken away from it.

Among others, the most illustrious man **Pietro della Valle** <note>original: "Petrus à Valle"</note> surveyed the same pyramids with wonderful industry and curiosity in the year 1616, and by examining each and every thing and comparing them with authors, he observed them exactly and minutely; from whom also by word of mouth (for he was, while he was among the living, among the few, a truly [dear] friend...

<margin>Pietro della Valle <note>A famous Italian traveler (1586–1652) who spent years exploring the Ottoman Empire, Persia, and India.</note></margin>

> *Twelve miles from the river, one finds the first pyramids, which are those three large ones described by Bellonius* <note>original: "il Belonio"; referring to Pierre Belon, a 16th-century French explorer and naturalist.</note> *my guide; and those same ones that we sighted while coming to Cairo, along with an innumerable quantity of other smaller ones. Regarding the beauty of the great ones, it will suffice to say to Your Lordship that Bellonius spoke little of it, and that I consider them deservedly to be wonders of the World; and when I say this, coming from Italy and from Rome, Your Lordship can believe it to be true.*
<margin>The architecture of the pyramids.</margin>
> *There is no great elegance of architecture, nor fancy sculpted details, whimsies, or other ornaments with which we are accustomed to decorating our buildings; nor is there the difficulty of supporting great vaults in the air, like our domes and other structures that we consider ingenious. This is because the intention of those people was not to make something charming to the eye, but to create a structure that would be eternal—as it has been, and will be, in my opinion. For this purpose, there was no better shape than that solid form of the pyramids, which is nothing other than a square body made of massive pieces of marble* <note>While the traveler calls it marble, the pyramids are primarily constructed of limestone and granite.</note> *which, as it rises, always diminishes by steps; according to which proportion, compared to its height, it does not rise very steeply. From these three conditions—being composed of solid material, such as fine and very hard marble; having a base that is little burdened; and a full pyramidal body that always tapers upward—it follows that it is rendered extremely stable against every movement of the sky, the earth, and time, taking on no less firmness than the form of a natural mountain. At first glance, this seems like a small thing: for gathering so much marble in a sandy plain where there is none is no great feat. Egypt has very large mountains not far away; transporting them via the Nile is very easy; and from the Nile to that spot, which is a short distance, it is all level plain; and in the pyramid, simply composing them in a square figure one above the other is not great craftsmanship. The size of the pyramids does not seem less excessive; for in fact, you would believe that in height it does not much exceed the dome of <term>St. Peter’s</term> <note>The Papal Basilica in Rome; its dome was the architectural marvel of the era.</note> in Rome. I truly did not have the time or patience to measure; but to the eye, and as far as I understood from various curious people who have taken the trouble, I believe that the measurements of Bellonius are accurate: that is, that the pyramids are about three hundred or three hundred and fifty paces wide at the base on each of the four sides; and about two hundred and ten to two hundred and fifty <term>steps</term> <note>original: "gradi"</note> high, which it is impossible to count exactly because they are ruined in some places; and each step is a little more than two <term>palms</term> <note>A traditional unit of length based on the width of a hand; in Rome, a "palmo" was about 8.8 inches.</note> wide and a little less than four high. Thus, for the reasons already stated, they do not appear so marvelous at first sight; and they had this same effect on me. However, when a man approaches closely and considers better the vastness of the stones—much larger than the architraves of the portico of the <term>Rotunda</term> <note>The Pantheon in Rome, famous for its massive monolithic columns and portico.</note> or the stones of the <term>Colosseum</term>, and any others I have seen—and I think how with such ease they were handled all the way up to the top, where they must have been carried either with ropes or bridges; and furthermore, that they were composed with such accuracy of measurement, each placed in its spot so precisely and with such judgment; I begin to recognize the artifice, and to understand that those men were not lacking in knowledge.*

> But when one climbs toward the middle, and finds the doorway, carved with a marvelous precision within a mass of stones of extraordinary size; these, although so immense, are arranged above in an arch, and they adorn it with very beautiful architecture; it must be confessed that there is something of quality here. Because, if we admire the door of the Pantheon <note>original: "Rotonda"; the common name for the Pantheon in Rome due to its shape.</note> in Rome, which is erected on level ground, for its size—where the jambs and the architrave are a single piece (as many believe)—we should admire much more those seven or eight stones in the pyramid (each of which, in length and breadth, is perhaps no smaller than the entire width of the Pantheon’s door) which, having been pulled so high, and with a very beautiful design fitted together at the angles, form an arch and a vault for a small little door.

> The wonder increases upon entering inside and walking along that path which Belon describes, which goes all the way to the center where they placed the body in the tomb: which path, as he says, is square like the shaft of a well, not vertical, but sloping and quite steep, so that it is difficult to walk there; and they did this because they truly did not want anyone to go there to move and disturb those corpses. Indeed, the door, when the body was replaced, was closed and covered with the same large stones in such a way that from the outside it did not appear where it was; and since all the rest of the pyramid was a solid mass, even if it had been searched for, it was almost impossible to find it without dismantling the pyramid. 

> This path, where one enters with lights because there is no vent at all, I do not believe to be less than two hundred paces long, because it goes, as I have said, all the way to the center; and it goes not vertically, but sloping, which makes the line longer. It is very straight and is carved entirely between four very equal rows of stones, one of which forms the ceiling, one the floor, and two the sides. The width and height are such that a single man can walk there bent over, but not upright; and I believe they did this to make access more difficult. The stones around are so large that one often finds them—and thus nearly all of them—to be twenty, twenty-five, and thirty palms <note>A "palmo" or palm was a historical unit of measurement; the Roman palm was approximately 22.3 cm.</note> in length, and even more.

> ...placing the foot, one must take a very long stride. In such a way that climbing this path, although it is not extremely long or high, is nevertheless very tiring; and one can argue from this either that they made it this way on purpose to make it difficult to climb, or else that in those times the men of Egypt were taller in stature than they are today, if indeed it was easy for them in this manner. But I went there and examined it minutely with great pleasure; and in fact, considering well the handling of those massive pieces of stone, and their arrangement and fitting with such fine order, it seemed to me that I found there an architecture and a craftsmanship such that I, for my part, could not desire anything greater. 

> Having climbed this like a staircase, one enters the burial chamber, which is somewhat square; and having measured it myself, I found it to be twenty-one of my feet wide, and about forty long. Seven single stones cover the whole ceiling, each of which rests on either side of the width; and the rest is suspended in the air, forming a very flat vault, like one of our lofts <note>original: "solaio"; referring to a flat ceiling or attic floor common in Italian architecture.</note>. The tomb <note>The sarcophagus in the King's Chamber.</note> stands at the head of the room crosswise in an isolated position; it is a very large and quite thick basin made of a single piece of that hardest stone of Egypt, which Belon <note>Pierre Belon, a 16th-century French traveler and naturalist mentioned on the previous page.</note> in several places calls Thebaic stone <note>original: "Thebaica"; granite quarried from the region of Thebes (Aswan).</note>. I tested its hardness, because with a steel hammer I had, it was not possible to break off even a scale; and what pleased me greatly was that, striking it with the same hammer, it rang exactly like a bell, giving off a sweet sound, and so loud that if it had not been in a closed place, it would have been heard from a great distance. 

> There is no lid on the tomb, either because it was broken or because it was never placed there; if it is even true, as the ignorant locals say, that the King who had that pyramid built was not buried there; and that for this reason it is open, unlike the other nearby pyramids, which are all closed, and no door can be found for them. Be that as it may, the tomb was placed in there during construction; because to bring it in afterward, given the narrowness of the entrance and other difficulties, would have been impossible. 

> I had no less pleasure in seeing the pyramid from the outside; for I climbed with some little effort to the very top, where one enjoys a most beautiful view, discovering the sea and Egypt with much of the surrounding country. Up there at the highest point, in 그that part which looks toward Italy, I took pleasure in leaving my name carved there, along with that of some other person toward whom I bear no ill will. I also took pleasure in having several arrows shot from that summit by my *Capigi* <term>Kapıcı; an Ottoman palace guard or door-keeper</term> and by other Turks who were with us, with the greatest force possible; nevertheless, despite whatever effort they made, the arrows always fell back onto the steps of the pyramid; nor was there anyone who could <gloss>Note: the tilde over the 'e' in 'potēsse' indicates a nasal contraction common in early printing.</gloss> push even one of them beyond the steps, nor make it reach the bottom by a long shot. 

> Having سپس descended, I took another look from the outside at the smaller pyramids, which cannot be climbed; and also nearby at the Sphinx, which truly is a beautiful piece of rock, carved just as it is depicted. I do not remember having read whether it is natural rock in that place, or if it was brought from elsewhere; as seems more likely, since the countryside is flat and sandy. In that place one cannot tell, because the sand has grown very high, and the Sphinx stands perhaps half buried within it; only the head and the neck are visible outside, with a little of the shoulders and the back. If it was brought there, I value it much more than the obelisks <note>original: "guglie"; literally 'spires,' a common term for Egyptian obelisks at the time.</note>; because in fact it is very large, although by its shape and manner of resting on the ground, there is no doubt that it is easier to handle than the obelisks—at least less dangerous to break.

...[The next] day, which was the ninth of December, having risen early in the morning and struck our tent, we set out to see certain other pyramids further away, which Belon <note>Pierre Belon (1517–1564), a French naturalist who also wrote about his travels in Egypt.</note> likewise mentions; that is, he mentions many of them, but not yet another which is quite large, and to go see it, one walks a great distance forward into the sandy countryside, toward the South. These pyramids are called those of the Mummies, because they are near—or rather within—the region of sand where the mummies are found. Throughout the journey, one sees nothing but plains of very fine yellow sand, like that which we use for letters <note>original: "che adopriamo per le lettere"; referring to "pounce," a fine sand used to dry ink on paper before the invention of blotting paper.</note>, and extremely dry; and all around, step by step, are scattered pyramids of various sizes, but all of the same form. 

This larger one, which I went to see, stands many miles inland, and is quite large and beautiful: but by time it is so worn on the outside that the steps are ruined, and it is difficult to climb to the top, nor did I care to go up there. I very much wanted to see it inside, for it has its mouth open; and I found it, to my taste, much more beautiful than the other one seen before: because [while] that one went down, made in the manner of a well, [this one] begins a bit higher up; and, whether for this reason or another, it is without doubt twice as long as the other. It is also flatter and easier to walk: but it goes down so far that I certainly believe it reaches the very bottom among the foundations. 

Despite it being so flat, the journey nevertheless proved very troublesome for us: because, as the pyramid is more worn on the outside, a great multitude of large stones has fallen inside from the mouth, which in many places have so entangled the path that several times we had to go "swimming" over the stones, as the Doctor in Naples does upon the water <note>A local Neapolitan reference, likely comparing their crawling/sliding motion over the rubble to a specific swimming style or a well-known performer.</note>. And at times we passed through narrows so tight that they gave me pause; for if by chance one of those stones had moved a little, or through the malice of someone above (since after all one is in the land of infidels) another had been thrown down, closing the entrance a bit more, we would have been finished, and forced to remain dead inside there, buried alive. 

In faith, this thought occurred to me, and if I had to return another time, I would want to leave a good guard at the door for every respect; with orders also that if we were delayed too long, they should come down with good pickaxes, because those outside, being superior in position, could help: but those inside, even if they had pickaxes and every other tool, it would not be possible; because one man alone, who fits in the passage at a time, cannot send weight upwards; and of being heard shouting, there would not be a hope in the world. 

Enough; we others, without such diligence, passed through well: and at the foot of the descent we did not find a climb as in the other pyramid; but immediately and instantly the burial chamber, quite large and very high: and the vault is not flat as in that other, but made at an angle at the top, narrowing continually <note>A description of a corbelled vault, typical of the burial chambers in the pyramids at Sakkara and Dahshur.</note>. From this chamber, through a very low little door, one enters another similar chamber of the same size and construction; for perhaps the pyramid was made for more than one person: but neither in one nor the other chamber did I find any tomb <note>original: "auello"; a sarcophagus or stone coffin.</note>; and it must be that either they were not there, or they have been broken and destroyed. It is indeed true that in the second chamber, one sees very high up a door left among the marbles, into which, throwing a stone, I heard that it went quite far in; but the height is such that it would require a great ladder to climb it; and some of the locals say that above in that third chamber lies the sepulcher: I do not know, as I could not see it; but it could be; placed there perhaps so that the body, due to the difficulty*

Joseph Ben Altiphasi <note>Yusuf al-Tifashi (1184–1253), an Arab author known for writings on gems and Egyptian history.</note> describes them thus in his book on the history of Egypt, with which the reports of Ben Salamas, in the book titled *The Garden of the World’s Wonders*, agree.<-
<margin>Joseph Ben Altiphasi. Ben Salamas.</margin>

<note>This section translates the Arabic text block, which is framed by decorative floral ornaments in the original manuscript.</note>

On the mention of ancient relics and grand buildings in the land of Egypt: 

The pyramids in Egypt are grand and large, the largest of which are the two pyramids at Giza <note>original: "Jiza"</note> near the Nile. It is said that their builder was Shur, son of Shahluq, son of Sharyak, before the Flood. It is also said that Hermes, the Thrice-Wise <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note>, whom the Hebrews call Enoch and who is Idris—peace be upon him—built them when he knew of the coming Flood. He deposited within them gold, silver, and all precious items, including talismans <note>original: "al-daqur"</note> and tools. Each pyramid has a square base and a conical <note>pyramidal</note> shape; the height of its pillar is three hundred and seventeen cubits <term>cubit: an ancient unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18-22 inches</term>. It is surrounded by four equal-sided faces, each side being four hundred and sixty cubits. 

Despite its great size, it is built with such mastery of craft, perfection of design, and excellence of proportion that nothing in it has changed, even though winds howl and earthquakes shake; the masonry does not allow even a hair to pass between the stones. Each stone is five cubits long and two cubits thick. It is said they have doors leading to vaulted passages <note>original: "azaj"</note> under the earth; each passage is twenty cubits long. There is a door made of a single stone that turns on a pivot <note>original: "lawlab," literally a screw or spiral mechanism</note>; when closed, it cannot be recognized as a door. The eastern passage is on the southern side, and the western passage is on the western side. Each leads to seven chambers, each chamber named after one of the seven planets. These chambers are all locked with a single lock. In each chamber is a hollow golden idol; one of its hands is over its mouth, and on its forehead is an inscription. If read, the mouth opens, and inside is found the key to the locks. 

The Eastern Pyramid is the burial place of Shur, the son of the King; in the Western Pyramid is his brother... and in the Colored Pyramid <note>likely the "Red Pyramid" or "Mykerinos"</note> is buried Afros, son of Hujrat. The Sabians <note>A religious group mentioned in the Quran, often associated by medieval writers with the origins of alchemy and Hermeticism</note> claim that one of them is the tomb of Agathodaimon <note>original: "Agathaymun"</note>, who is Seth, and the other is the tomb of Hermes, and the colored one is the tomb of Sab, son of Hermes.

### Concerning the Antiquities of Egypt.

The pyramids in Egypt are very large, specifically the two located in the trench <note>original: "fossa"; likely referring to the plateau excavation</note> of ancient Misr <note>original: "Mesrae"; a common name for Cairo or Egypt in general</note> on the western side of the Nile. It is said that Shur son of Shahluq son of Shariak built them before the Flood; and it is said that Hermes Trismegistus, on account of his wisdom—who is called Enoch in Hebrew, and is Idris—peace be upon him—knowing of the future Flood, built them and stored within them all his goods, books, and whatever he held precious. 

Every pyramid is square and of a polished figure; if you look at the perpendicular elevation, it is 317 cubits. It is surrounded by four equal surfaces of sides, each side being 460 cubits. It was constructed by ingenious architects with such artistry that nothing in it is subject to change: for whether violent winds rush upon it or earthquakes shake it, nothing is ever taken away from it. The individual stones of which it consists are 5 cubits long and two cubits high. It is said to have doors above hidden subterranean channels; each channel is 20 cubits long, and they have doors made of stone through which access to the dwelling is opened by a screw mechanism <note>original: "per cochleam"</note>. It is not known where that door is, and the eastern channel faces South,

### ->CALCULATION <note>original Greek: "ΨΗΦΙΣΜΟΣ" (Psephismos)</note> or Reckoning of the entire Architecture of the Great Pyramid.<-

Among so many authors, we find Herodotus and Pliny to agree most especially; of whom the former, as he stands out in antiquity (for he lived about 300 years from the founding of the City [Rome], according to the testimony of Suidas and Pliny), so the latter, by the excellence of his writing and his curious investigation of matters, rightly holds a chief place among those worthy of trust. We begin, therefore, from his words. Pliny says, then, that the base of the pyramid was 8 *jugera* <note>A Roman unit of area; one jugerum is roughly 5/8 of an acre</note>, and each of the sides 883 feet; if these are multiplied by each other, a square number of 779,689 feet will be born. We have, therefore, the area of the base. If you wish to know its volume <note>original: "cubum"</note>, one side must be cubed—that is, 883 must be multiplied into the square (assuming, however, that the height is equal to the base of the pyramid)—and 688,465,387 will be produced, which is the prism <note>The volume of a rectangular block with that base</note> of the said base. Since indeed a pyramid is the third part of its prism, as Euclid demonstrates in Book 12, divide the given volume of 688,465,387 by 3, and the quotient 229,488,462 will give the solidity of the Great Pyramid in cubic feet. If you desire to have its weight, multiply the weight of one cubic foot—for example, 200 pounds—by 229,488,462, and the product will give the total number of pounds that the entire mass would weigh if it were entirely solid.

<note>Geometric diagram (fig 1): A perspective view of a pyramid used to calculate its dimensions. Points 'a, b, c, d' mark the square base, and 'e' is the apex. 'f' is the center of the base, and 'g' is the midpoint of one side. The lines demonstrate the internal right triangle 'efg' used to calculate the vertical height 'ef' relative to the slant height 'eg'.</note>

Furthermore, those who say that the four surfaces of the said pyramid are equal and equilateral must necessarily assert, by the force of geometric reasoning, that the height of the pyramid is less than the length of the side of the same; I demonstrate the matter thus. Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ be the base of the pyramid, and the surfaces be $e a c$, $e d b$, $e c d$, $e a b$, whose sides are equal to sides $a b$, $b d$, $c d$, $c a$, and consequently equilateral. These things being granted, imagine within the solidity of the pyramid a right-angled triangle $e f g$, whose side $e g$ is in the middle of the equilateral triangular surface, $e f$ is perpendicular <note>original: "normalis"</note> to the base $c b$, and side $f g$ indicates the semi-base, or half the width of the said pyramid, which is $b g$, up to the axis $f e$, which shows the perpendicular of the pyramid or its height. Since, therefore, in this right-angled triangle those sides are shorter which form the right angle (such as $f e$ and $g f$), it necessarily follows that line $e f$ is shorter than line $e g$, which subtends the right angle <note>i.e., the hypotenuse</note>; and thus it is clearly evident that the height of the pyramid is less [than the slant height].

You shall investigate the quantity of the sides of the said triangle $e, f, g$ in this way. Since the sides of the pyramid $a, b, b, d, d, c, c, a$ are each 883 feet according to Pliny, the line $f, g$ will necessarily be half of the said sides, which is $441 \frac{1}{2}$ feet. With this established, let it be that as the sine of the complement of the inclination <note>In modern terms, this is the cosine of the angle of inclination</note> of the pyramid's side is to the right sine of that same inclination—that is, as the sine of 30 degrees is to the sine of 60 degrees—so $441 \frac{1}{2}$ is to another value; and once the operation is performed, the line $f, e$, the sought-after vertical height of the pyramid, will result. You will find the side $e, g$ thus: Let it be that as the sine of the complement of the pyramid's inclination is to the total sine <note>original: "sinum totum"; in early trigonometry, this refers to the radius of the calculation circle, representing the value of 1 (or 100,000 in older tables)</note>, so $441 \frac{1}{2}$ is to another value; and the line $e, g$, the sought-after height of the sloping side of the pyramid, will result. Or, by means of tangents or secants, let it be that as the total sine is to the tangent sine, or to the secant of 60 degrees, so $441 \frac{1}{2}$ is to another value; once the operation is performed, the same result as before will emerge, namely the height of both sides $e, f$ and $e, g$. And this is the calculation according to the report of Herodotus, which nevertheless can hardly be consistent if it is compared with those things which other authors observe regarding its height.

Others suggest that the height of this pyramid was equal to the length of its base. If that were so, let the axis of height $f, e$ be 883 feet, as in figure II; and the quality of the line $e, g$ will be obtained in the following manner. Let the number of the line $f, e$ (883) be squared, and likewise the side $f, g$, which we said was $441 \frac{1}{2}$ feet; let the squares be joined into one. If you extract the square root from this sum, it will show you the quantity of the line $e, g$, the sought-after slant height. However, since this height, once assumed, exceeds what is reasonable, we have decided that a middle opinion must be held, which in this matter considers the perpendicular height less, but rather focuses on that which the line $e, g$ expresses in the figure. Let us therefore assume the angle of the slope of the surface to be 55 degrees; let it be that as the sine of the complement of $f, g$ is to the total sine $e, g$, so $441 \frac{1}{2}$ is to another value; once the operation is performed, the quantity of the line $e, g$, the sought-after height, will result. If you now desire to have the perpendicular height, that is, of the line $e, f$; let it be that as the sine of the complement of 55 degrees is to the right sine $e, f$, so $441 \frac{1}{2}$ is to another value; and once the operation is performed, the sought-after perpendicular height—that is, the quantity of the line $e, f$—will result.

## ->Architectural Conclusion.<-

And from these matters demonstrated—perhaps more at length than was necessary—the wonderful genius of the Architect is clearly evident, both in adorning such a miraculous structure and in moving such vast stones, each into its proper place. For this work could by no means have been accomplished without machines, constructed with the highest industry and in a truly <term>Archimedean</term> <note>Refers to the mechanical principles of Archimedes, the ancient Greek mathematician famous for his work with levers, pulleys, and the displacement of weight.</note> fashion. But what hoisting machines shall we suppose were used to bring stones from the mountains of Arabia, separated by such a distance, through such pathless and obstructed routes, to the designated location? Who in this modern day could find an Architect whose spirit would be sufficient to attempt such a thing? For it is built of stones, each 30 feet in length according to Herodotus, so joined together that without any pulling apart of the stones it remains whole to this day; with a circuit of 2,533 feet, of which the individual sides occupy nearly as much space as the length of the <term>Agonal Forum</term> <note>The Circus Agonalis in Rome, now known as the Piazza Navona.</note> in Rome. Thus, this fabric surpasses all the sumptuous buildings of the Romans—such as the Baths, Amphitheaters, etc.—by many leagues, whether you look at the magnitude, the exorbitant expense, or finally, the magnificence and genius.

While I am writing this, Titus Livius Burattini <note>Tito Livio Burattini (1617–1681), an Italian polymath, inventor, and architect who traveled extensively in Egypt and served the Polish crown.</note>, a distinguished Architect who traveled to Egypt with the express purpose of investigating all the monuments of antiquity with the greatest diligence, drawing what he investigated to entrust a treasure to posterity, transmitted to me, among many other things, a drawing of this pyramid. This was sent together with an <term>Ichnographia</term> <note>A ground plan or floor map, usually used in architecture to show the horizontal section of a building.</note> of the desert in which it is found and the subterranean crypt which opens the way to the Mummies; which I have thought should be placed here together with the letters given to me.

**A**mong the other memorable things of the Egyptians established by King Amasis, <note>Amasis II, a pharaoh of the 26th Dynasty (reigned 570–526 BCE) known for his building projects and connections with the Greek world.</note> there is also this: that he brought a certain shrine made from a single, solid stone over a period of three years, with the help of two thousand men, from the city of Elephantine <note>An island in the Nile, near Aswan, famous for its granite quarries.</note> to Sais, a journey of 20 days; concerning which Herodotus writes exactly in the <term>Euterpe</term> <note>The traditional name for the second book of Herodotus’s *Histories*, named after the Muse of music.</note> near the end.

This mass was brought from a distance of 20 days' journey over a period of three years, as has been said. How much the mass was moved by machines in individual years, months, and days, I leave to the Arithmeticians to calculate.

**W**hat those most elegant authors—Herodotus, Diodorus, Strabo, and after them Pliny—write concerning the Egyptian Labyrinth seems to surpass all human belief. # CLASS VIII. EGYPTIAN MECHANICS. 307 CHAPTER I. 

<sig>Qq 2</sig>

Its size, arrangement, and magnificence are described in various ways by various authors; nor should this seem strange to anyone, since those who entered the Labyrinth, amidst such a great multitude of things to see, each thought it best to report that which most drew them into wonder. Thus, as new and more wonderful things continually presented themselves to be examined, the minds of the observers were easily confused by the countless details; and just as they could not observe each thing distinctly, they passed them down to posterity in a confused and indistinct manner. Certainly, Pliny asserts that Daedalus <note>The legendary Greek architect of the Cretan Labyrinth.</note>, captured by admiration for this structure, took the opportunity from it to build another Labyrinth in Lemnos, although he imitated only a hundredth part of it, since he could not disentangle himself from the inextricable structure of the building even with the supreme genius with which he was endowed.

<margin>Location of the Egyptian Labyrinth.</margin> The Labyrinth is located at Lake Moeris toward Crocodilopolis <note>The "City of Crocodiles," known to the Egyptians as Shedet.</note>, according to the testimony of Herodotus and Pliny, who also claim it to be the Tomb of Moeris. It is first divided into twelve, according to Herodotus, and into sixteen according to Pliny, <margin>Dwellings of the Labyrinth.</margin> dwellings; namely, as many halls, or rather ample chambers and vast buildings, as all of Egypt was formerly divided into prefectures, which they call <term>Nomes</term> <note>From the Greek 'nomos', referring to the administrative districts of ancient Egypt.</note>. Furthermore, it contained temples of all the Egyptian <margin>Temples of the Labyrinth.</margin> Deities, within which were included several pyramids forty cubits high. According to Strabo, the individual halls of the Nomes were surrounded by columns and continuous with one another; the paths leading to them are opposite a wall that encircles the halls arranged in order. Before the entrance <margin>Crypts of the Labyrinth.</margin> gate, however, there are many long crypts which contain paths intertwined with such great and wonderful tortuosity that no one can enter any hall, nor leave, without a guide, deceived by that inexplicable wandering of the ways. Here there are also very high dining rooms and porticos, each built <margin>Dining rooms and porticos of the Labyrinth.</margin> with ninety steps, supported by columns of porphyry stone <note>original: "porphyrite lapide"; a hard, purple-red volcanic rock highly prized for imperial monuments.</note>, among which are images of the Gods, statues of Kings, and a supreme collection of monstrous images. The placement and arrangement of some of these houses, by the ingenious invention of the Architect, is such that as soon as their doors are opened, a formidable thunder seems to be heard. But worthy of admiration above all things is that <margin>Roofs of the Labyrinth.</margin> the ceilings or roofs of the individual houses, as well as the widths of the crypts, are built from entire stones—according to Strabo—of truly unusual size, with no intervention of wood or any other material. In a word, the entire extension of the structure included three thousand houses, which could equal even a huge city. But let us hear Herodotus exactly describing the details in his *Euterpe* <gloss>in Euterpe, book 2</gloss>. His words are:

<margin>Description of the Labyrinth from Herodotus.</margin>
> *While twelve Kings were reigning in Egypt, they decided to leave some monument common to them all, and from that decision they made a Labyrinth a little above Lake Moeris, especially toward the City called "of the Crocodiles," which I looked upon as greater than its fame. For if someone calculates the walls and the appearance of the work from the narration of the Greeks, he will conceive less than the labor and expense of this labyrinth; for although the temple at Ephesus is worthy of mention, and that in Samos; yet the pyramids were greater in report, each of which is comparable to many and great works of Greece. But the Labyrinth surpasses even those. For there are twelve halls covered with a roof, with gates opposite one another on both sides: six toward the North—*

<margin>3,500 dwellings of the Labyrinth.</margin>...halls contiguous to each other, with just as many facing the South, all enclosed by the same wall. There are two sets of dwellings within it: one subterranean, the other superior, built upon the first. In each set there are three thousand five hundred <note>Kircher's text states 3,500 (tria millia quingenta), though standard editions of Herodotus usually cite 3,000 dwellings in total (1,500 above and 1,500 below).</note> dwellings. We ourselves have seen the upper ones, and what we have witnessed, we now describe; the subterranean ones, however, we know only by report. For the Egyptian overseers of the Labyrinth were unwilling to show them by any means, saying that they contained the tombs of the Kings who were the authors of the Labyrinth's construction, as well as the tombs of the sacred crocodiles. Thus, we have learned of the lower parts by instruction, but the upper parts we viewed ourselves, finding them to be greater than any human works. Indeed, the winding paths and the exits through the roofs, and the passages through the halls, where they were so varied, filled me with infinite admiration. One passes from a hall into chambers, from chambers into bedrooms, from bedrooms into other terraces, and from chambers into other halls. The ceiling of all these, as well as the walls, is made of stone, adorned everywhere with engraved figures. Each hall is mostly arranged with white stone and encircled by a perimeter of columns. At the corner where the Labyrinth ends, there stands a pyramid forty paces high, in which large animals are carved, and to which a path leads underground. This is the description observed by Herodotus, a curious inspector and admirer of all things; following his description, I would have gladly presented a rough and superficial <term>Ichnography</term> <note>A ground plan or floor map.</note> of the entire structure here, if time had permitted, so that the reader might "recognize the lion by its claw" <note>original Latin: "ex ungue Leonem"; a proverb meaning one can judge the scale of a great work from a small fragment</note> and judge the excellence of the genius of the architect of such works. But perhaps we shall provide that elsewhere.

<margin>The Tomb of Ismendes is distinct from the Labyrinth.</margin> Furthermore, what Hecataeus <note>Hecataeus of Abdera, a Greek historian and philosopher.</note> reports in Diodorus Siculus concerning the Tomb of Ismendes <note>Ismendes is a Hellenized name for a pharaoh, often identified as Ramesses II, the "Ozymandias" of legend.</note> does not seem to agree with the accounts of Herodotus and Pliny. He makes no mention of the halls which they call "Nomes" <note>Administrative districts of ancient Egypt.</note>; nor does he arrange the dwellings in the same order as Herodotus; nor does the location, which the cited authors place next to Lake Moeris, match. For he says that it was built in the territory of Thebes; since this is many days' journey distant from Lake Moeris, we are necessarily forced to assert that it was a different structure—regardless of what some authors say who confuse the construction of the Tomb of Ismendes with the Labyrinth. However, because this construction of Ismendes is by no means inferior to the Labyrinth in terms of magnificence or vastness according to Hecataeus’s account, we shall also include here its description from the very words of Hecataeus, who was an eyewitness, as found in Diodorus.

<margin>Description of the Tomb of Ismendes.</margin> He says that the tombs of the ancient Kings were of such miraculous workmanship that they could hardly be equaled by posterity. The Priests report that forty-seven Royal Tombs are contained in their written records, of which only seventeen remained by the time of Ptolemy Lagos <note>The founder of the Ptolemaic Kingdom in Egypt.</note>; many of those had also been destroyed by the time we reached those places in the 180th Olympiad <note>Approximately 60–57 BCE.</note>. These things are handed down not only by the Egyptian Priests, but many Greeks agree with us, including Hecataeus, who traveled to Thebes in the time of Ptolemy Lagos and wrote Egyptian histories. Reviewing them individually, he records that the monument of the King, who is Simandius <note>Another variant of the name Ismendes/Ozymandias.</note>, was ten stadia in circumference. In its approach was a gate constructed of various stones; he says the length of this was two plethra <note>original Latin: "iugera"; here referring to the Greek "plethron," a measure of roughly 100 feet.</note> and the height was 45 cubits. After passing through this, those entering found a square stone peristyle, each side of which spanned four plethra. In it, instead of columns, were figures of animals made from a single stone, 16 cubits high, fashioned in the ancient style...

Two others, smaller, reached only to its knee—one on the right and one on the left—representing the King's daughter and mother. This work was remarkable not only for its magnitude but also for its wonderful artistry and the excellent nature of the stone, as in such a massive block there was neither a single crack nor a blemish. Upon it was written:

->**I AM OSYMANDYAS, KING OF KINGS; IF ANYONE WISHES TO KNOW HOW GREAT I WAS AND WHERE I LIE, LET HIM SURPASS ONE OF MY WORKS.**<-

The first part of the wall contained a sculpture of the siege of the city (namely, of the Bactrians) from the side where the river washes against the walls. The second wall was sculpted with captives without genitals and without hands, being led by the King; this was a sign that they were base in spirit and weak in body. The third side contained various sculptures and beautiful paintings of the King’s sacrifices and triumphs over his defeated enemies. In the middle of the peristyle was an open-air altar of the most beautiful stone, excellent in its workmanship and wonderful in size. 

On the last wall lay two massive statues carved from a single stone, twenty-seven cubits long, toward which three entrances from the peristyle opened. Near these was a house supported by columns, the side of which spanned two *iugera* <term>iugerum: a Roman unit of area; here used to describe a length of 480 feet</term>. Inside it were wooden statues in no small number, representing those who passed judgment in court. These were sculpted on one side of the wall, thirty in number, and in the center of the judgment was the Chief, from whose neck hung Truth <note>original: *veritas*; likely referring to the goddess Ma'at or the "Symbol of Truth" worn by Egyptian judges</note>, with his eyes partially closed, surrounded by a heap of books. These images signified that judges ought to be incorruptible and look only upon the truth. 

Then there was a walkway filled with chambers, and in them various kinds of banquets prepared with sweet tastes. CHAPTER II. 312 THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS' GYMNASIUM OF HIEROGLYPHICS.

...findings. Pliny asserts that brick ramps <note>original: *pontes latericios*</note> were constructed, through which immense stones were rolled to their designated place by the strength of laborers; but this cannot be maintained when the weights were greater than what the immediate application of hands could move. For Statics <note>the branch of mechanics dealing with weights and equilibrium</note> teaches that a weight which cannot be moved by the labor of two hundred men applied directly can be moved with no trouble by the labor of eight or ten men using machines. Therefore, they necessarily used machines to both move and erect such massive blocks; it remains to be explained what sort of machines these were.

<margin>Knowledge of tempering iron among the Egyptians.</margin>
I assume, therefore, first: that the Egyptians possessed a perfect knowledge of tempering metals—both gold and silver, and most importantly iron—handed down from the first Fathers <note>referring to the biblical Patriarchs or the earliest post-flood generations</note>. For how could it be possible for them to cut, hew, and polish such immense masses of statues, even those made from a single block of porphyry (which, as we have seen, is the hardest kind of stone), without the quality and tempering of the finest iron? We know how much our own craftsmen sweat even in the fashioning of small porphyry vessels; it is likely, therefore, that they possessed a wondrous tempering technique, entirely unknown to us, for penetrating the porphyry mountains themselves and for cutting, hewing, and polishing the stones.

<margin>Mechanical principles implanted by nature.</margin>
I assume, second: that Mathematicians and Engineers <note>original: *Mechanicos*</note>, a great number of whom were maintained at public expense for this purpose, devoted themselves solely to this: that by inventing new machines, they might advance the proud building projects of the Kings.

I assume, third: that mechanical principles are implanted by nature, as experience teaches from bodily movements, the lifting of heavy weights, or the striking of things; from this, the logic of levers and hammers found its origin. For when we attempt to drive a nail into a wall, we do not use our hand or any other hard object held in the hands, but a hammer, which acts like a lever; so also, we attempt to push and raise a stone more easily not by the direct application of hands, but by placing a piece of wood beneath it. These things are too well known to need further discussion. With these points established, let us begin.

<unclear>they took care of</unclear>. Furthermore, for pulling and transporting huge stones over long distances, they prepared two rollers <margin>The method of dragging stones.</margin> or cylinders proportioned to the weight to be carried. A platform made of the sturdiest trees was laid over these, arranged in such a way that they did not touch the cylinders directly; and upon these, they placed the stones, which were firmly bound. Then, by attaching ropes to the axles of the cylinders, a great multitude of men pulled them to the designated place across mounds of earth piled up like mountains. To ensure that no obstacle occurred on the way, all pits and inequalities in the paths through which the stones were to be conveyed were first filled with stones, sand, and earth. <term>Vitruvius</term> <margin>Vitruvius.</margin> <note>A famous Roman architect and engineer (1st century BCE) whose work *De Architectura* is the primary source for ancient construction methods.</note> records that Ctesiphon and his son Metagenes used this same artifice for transporting the columns destined for the Temple of Ephesus.

There were three usual methods and ways for moving larger machines: either they had to be transported from the quarry to the designated place, whether by land or by river; or immense Colossi <margin>Threefold method for moving larger machines.</margin> had to be erected; or finally, stones of the loftiest mass had to be positioned in their set place. The first was called <term>ἑλκτικὴ</term> <note>original: *helktikē* — the art of dragging or pulling.</note>, that is, traction to be carried out by force; the second was <term>ἐγερτικὴ</term> <note>original: *egertikē* — the art of lifting or elevating.</note>, that is, the elevating or nautical method; the third was called <term>μαγγαναρία</term> <note>original: *manganaria* — the art of complex mechanics or engines.</note>. I shall speak of each.

Upon these they placed the immense stones, and thus, with a huge multitude of men or <unclear>beasts of burden</unclear> applied to the ropes, they <unclear>conveyed</unclear> them to the designated place; this method was especially effective after the recession of the Nile, while the earth was still muddy and slippery.
