# HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>How Ctesiphon transported columns to their place.</margin>
...he used a not dissimilar artifice; for when he was about to transport massive columns into their place, once the columns were finished, he cast bronze axles <note>original: "axes æneos"</note> into the ends of the columns, corresponding to their circumference, with lead. Then, he inserted these axles into giant wheels, and in this way, the load was rolled along by the power of the wheels at the Architect's will. These bronze axles were later used for more firmly stabilizing the columns upon their bases and under their capitals. Inspect the adjacent figure.

<note>A massive cylindrical stone column is shown horizontally, its ends fitted into the centers of two enormous wooden wheels or drums. This contraption is mounted on a heavy wooden chassis which is being pulled by a team of four horses. A driver sits atop the frame. This represents the machine designed by Ctesiphon for transporting the columns of the Temple of Artemis.</note>

<margin>The use of rollers.</margin>
Others say that the Ancients used <term>rollers</term> <note>original: "scytalis" — cylindrical wooden rollers used to move heavy weights.</note>, upon which polished and smooth wooden boards were laid; they then moved the load placed upon them to the desired station by using levers. I would not want this to be understood as a method for a journey of great distance, for that constant movement of the rollers, and the changing of the boards placed upon them almost every fifteen paces, would have been exceedingly inconvenient; however, in a small space, it could have provided no small use for rolling a heavy weight.

...it might be less. This having been completed, they drove ships, firmly joined together, by means of oars under the Obelisk itself, which was hanging by its ends on the banks on both sides. <margin>By what ingenuity the Obelisk of Nectabis was brought to Alexandria.</margin> Once the ships had been driven under the Obelisk by this device, they gradually lightened the ships by unloading stones, until they received the hanging Obelisk; having been received in this manner, they led it through a canal into the Nile, and then to Alexandria, just as is clear from Figure II of Schema I, placed in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* <note>original: "Obelisco Pamphilio" — one of Kircher's other famous works on Egyptian archaeology</note>, folio 90, from which the reasoning of the whole mechanism can easily be perceived. But for the confirmation of what has been said, let us bring forward the words of <margin>Pliny.</margin> Pliny, Book 36, Chapter 9: "At Alexandria," he says, "Ptolemy Philadelphus set up one obelisk of 80 cubits <note>original: "cubitorum" — a cubit is roughly 18 inches</note>, which King Nectabis had cut out without a flaw; it was a much greater work in transporting and erecting it than in cutting it out. Some record that it was transported by the architect Satyrus: Callixenus says it was by a raft; but others say a canal was led from the Nile right up to where the Obelisk lay; and that two broad ships, loaded with foot-square stones of the same rock <note>original: "pedalibus ex eodem lapide" — ballast stones</note> to double the measure of the weight, were so placed that they went under the Obelisk as it hung by its ends on both banks; afterwards, the ships, lightened by the removal of the stone blocks <note>original: "laterculis"</note>, received the assigned burden. Six such were cut out in the same mountain, and the craftsman was gifted fifty talents." Thus Pliny. 

Without doubt, those who followed used a similar industry, received by tradition from their ancestors, in transferring great masses. Some maintain that the Obelisks were moved to their appointed places at that time when the inundation of the Nile in Egypt was at its height; for when the waters rose high above the lands, nothing was easier than to transport the burden outside the channel of the Nile to any level place in Egypt. Yet if necessity so required, they rolled the Obelisk, placed upon low sledges <term>chamulcis</term> <note>original: "chamulcis" — heavy, low-slung carriages or sleds designed for massive weights</note> or cylinders, to the place of erection; where, once the foundation was laid—which was mostly native rock or cliff—they finally erected the Obelisk with the help of capstans <note>original: "ergatorum"</note> and pulleys <note>original: "trochlearumque"</note>, protected against all violence [damage] by wooden beams and boards, stuffed with wool, hay, and straw.

<margin>The ships by which the Obelisks were carried.</margin> Indeed, Pliny and Ammianus Marcellinus report which ships the Roman Emperors used for bringing the Obelisks from Alexandria to Rome. <margin>The ship which had brought the Obelisk of Augustus perished by fire at Puteoli.</margin> The ship of Augustus Caesar, by which his larger Obelisk had been brought, although it was preserved at Puteoli <note>a major Roman port city near modern Naples</note> like a miracle for a perpetual memory of the event, finally perished in a fire by some accident. But the ship by which Caius Caligula had brought that Obelisk of Nuncoreus <note>Kircher is referring to the Vatican Obelisk, which Pliny attributed to a king named Nuncoreus</note>—more wonderful than all that have ever been seen on the sea—stopped at Ostia, where it was submerged by Claudius, Caligula’s successor, to serve as the foundation for a harbor tower built upon it, which lasts to this day. <margin>The ship which had brought the Obelisk of Nuncoreus served in the foundations of the Tiberine Ostia. Suetonius. Pliny.</margin> Thus Suetonius in the *Life of Claudius*, and Pliny in the cited place.

The ship by which the Ramesseus Obelisk was brought by the Emperor Constantine was a framework compacted from beams and huge trees, equipped, according to the witness of Marcellinus, with three hundred oars. The principal mast <note>original: "arbor principalis"</note>, besides others from which the sails were spread, was of such thickness that two men could not embrace it. Indeed, as far as can be gathered from the acts of the Emperor Constantius, from Ammianus Marcellinus, and other historians, its form was that which we have presented in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, folio 90, which you may consult in the cited place.

# CHAPTER II. EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM.

<margin>Three ships by which the Obelisks were brought from Egypt to the City <note>The "City" always refers to Rome in this context.</note>.</margin> Authors mention three ships by which Obelisks were carried from Egypt to the City: Pliny mentions two, and Ammianus mentions one; they testify that all of them were of a certain maximum and prodigious magnitude. Regarding the ship in which Augustus brought his obelisk into the City, which was permanently dedicated at the shipyards of Puteoli <note>Modern-day Pozzuoli</note> as a marvel but later consumed by fire, we have spoken shortly before. Concerning the ship by which Caius Caligula transported his Obelisk to Rome, <margin>Pliny.</margin> Pliny (Book 16, Chapter 40) relates these things among others: *A fir tree of remarkable beauty was seen in the ship which, by the order of Gaius the Prince <note>Caligula</note>, brought the Obelisk now standing in the Vatican Circus, along with four blocks of the same stone to support it. Nothing more wonderful than this ship was ever seen on the sea. It carried one hundred and twenty thousand modii <note>A Roman unit of dry measure, roughly 2 peck or 9 liters</note> of lentils as ballast. Its length occupied a great part of the left side of the harbor of Ostia; for there it was sunk by Prince Claudius, with three moles <note>massive piers or breakwaters</note> as high as towers built upon it using Puteolan dust <note>original: "Puteolano puluere" — volcanic ash used to make hydraulic cement that hardens underwater</note> and brought there for that purpose.* In Book 35, Chapter 9, he says: *The Divine Claudius, after it had been preserved for some years—that ship which Caius Caesar <note>Caligula</note> had imported, more wonderful than anything ever seen on the sea—sunk it at Ostia for the sake of the harbor, after towers made of Puteolan dust had been built upon it.* These accounts agree with the report of <margin>Suetonius.</margin> Suetonius in the *Life of Claudius*: *He constructed the harbor at Ostia,* he says, *by drawing an arm around it to the right and left, and at the entrance, where the sea was already deep, he threw up a mole. To make the foundation of this mole more stable, he first sank the ship in which the great Obelisk had been brought from Egypt; and having piled up stones on top, he placed a very high tower upon it in the likeness of the Pharos of Alexandria, so that ships might direct their course by the lights at night.* It is likely that Constantius Caesar constructed his ship according to this model—the ship which we have shown as described by Ammianus Marcellinus in the place cited in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*. The said authors indicate in express words that these were of the type of ships they call <term>Rates</term> <note>rafts or flat-bottomed barges</note> or <term>Crates</term> <note>frames or heavy structures</note>.

<margin>Domenico Fontana.</margin> Finally, whoever desires to know the method observed in the Obelisks erected by Pope Sixtus V should consult the machines employed by the architect Domenico Fontana, which are most elegantly engraved in copper and described at length by Mercati, Bargaeus, and others.

### CLASS VIII. EGYPTIAN MECHANICS 387 CHAPTER III. ###

...to examine the names used by the Egyptians. It has been passed down by Hero <note>Hero of Alexandria, a 1st-century engineer</note> or Philo <note>Philo of Byzantium, a 3rd-century BC engineer</note> why the aforementioned mechanical powers are reduced to a single nature, even though they differ greatly in their visible shapes. These names are: the wheel and axle <note>original: "axis in peritrochio"</note>, the lever <note>original: "vectis"</note>, the compound pulley <note>original: "polyspastos"</note>, the wedge <note>original: "cuneus"</note>, and finally that which is called the endless screw <note>original: "cochlea infinita"</note>. And to begin with the simplest lever:

---

<note>Woodcut illustration: A man (labeled B) uses a long wooden lever (AB) placed over a stone fulcrum (labeled C) to pry up a large square stone block (labeled D).</note>

---

<margin>What a lever is.</margin> A lever is an instrument, made of either wood or iron and long in shape, which, when placed under a weight at one end and pressed down by hand at the other, lifts the weight without any difficulty. This is seen in the figure, where **D** is the stone, **AB** is the lever, and **C** is the <term>hypomochlium</term> <note>original Greek term for a fulcrum or support point</note>. For as <margin>Hero the Mechanic.</margin> Hero correctly discusses in the works of Pappus <note>Pappus of Alexandria, a 4th-century mathematician who preserved Hero's lost works</note>, when the Ancients wanted to move great weights, it was first necessary to lift them from the earth. However, they had no handles to grip, because every part of the base of the weight rested on the ground. By digging a little and placing the end of a long piece of wood under the load, they placed a stone near the load under the wood, which is called a <term>hypomochlium</term> [fulcrum], and in this way they moved the load. Since this movement seemed very easy to them, they convinced themselves that in this way any great weights could be lifted. They discovered that the weight was moved more easily the closer the <term>hypomochlium</term> was to the stone; for by this means the lever acquired a greater length <note>Referring to the "effort arm" of the lever</note>. The longer the lever was, as the Mechanics demonstrate, the more easily the weight was moved. And these are the first foundations of Mechanics, which we all use not so much by learned art as by a certain instinct of nature. Indeed, no human action involving the application of force can be identified that is not performed, even without our noticing, by the aid of the <term>lever</term>.

Furthermore, since the nature of weights was sometimes so great that levers could not perform their task when used for lifting massive structures, they engineered another type of machine. In this machine, a multiple arrangement of levers in a circle might achieve the same result in lifting masses to a great height as levers do for masses resting on the surface of the earth. And this they called the <term>axis in peritrochio</term> <note>Literally "axle in a wheel"; known today as the wheel and axle or windlass</note>. <margin>The wheel and axle.</margin> It was an instrument made of a cylinder and a wheel, on whose circumference spokes were arranged to take the place of levers, as appears in the following figure. For they wrapped ropes around the cylinder **AB**, to which the wheel **S** was attached, and from the end of these ropes hung the stone **L**. It happened that as the wheel was turned by its spokes, the cylinder would wind up the ropes and finally lift the stone. They set up this machine mostly in the sea, where stones had to be lifted, and so strongly fixed it there—

This instrument had a twofold use: upright and inverted. ### The Egyptian Wedge

<margin>The Egyptian Wedge.</margin>
The **W**edge was most often employed in stone quarries; it is a wooden or iron instrument of pyramidal shape by which immense stones are split. For when this is placed inside a crack in some stone and struck by a heavy blow of a mallet, it violently forces itself into the crack and powerfully presses on both sides, finally splitting the rock. They possessed many instruments of this kind which, being placed in order within the fissure and struck, caused the stone to split. In those mountainous regions where immense masses for columns, obelisks, and statues had to be extracted from a single stone, <margin>Philo of Byzantium. Use of the wedge in splitting stones.</margin> Philo of Byzantium <note>A Greek engineer of the 3rd century BC</note> reports in his booklet *On the Five Static Faculties* <note>original: "de quinque facultatibus Staticis"</note> that the Ancients used the following industrious method. Above the rock, they would establish a wooden machine, or rather a <term>pegma</term> <note>a framework or scaffolding</note>, furnished with a rotating transverse cylinder; to this cylinder, they would hang by a very thick rope a steel column of immense weight; and below, within the crack of the rock, they would place a wedge proportioned to the size of the steel cylinder. Thus, with the rope pulled, the cylinder was raised; once it was elevated to a certain height, the workers would loosen the rope and let it fall onto the wedge. Pressed by the immense weight of this falling mass, the wedge split the rock with great force, and by following the fissure of the crack with a new arrangement of the instruments—

->## The Egyptian Multi-Pulley System.<-

<margin>The Egyptian Multi-Pulley.</margin>
**A**nother capability was provided by the multi-pulley <note>original: "polyspastum"</note>, which utilized a pulley-wheel inserted into a frame <note>original: "trochleâ mangano infertâ." A *manganon* refers to the block or housing of the pulley.</note>, around which a rope was wound; by this means, a pulled weight could be moved with no effort. The arrangement of such pulley-wheels varied according to the size of the weights. When a single pulley-wheel was used, as occurred with smaller weights, it was then called a *monaxos* <note>original: "μονάξος" – single-axle</note>; if two pulley-wheels were used, a *dispastos* <note>original: "δίσπαστος" – double-pulley</note>; if three, a *trispastos* <note>original: "τρίσπαστος" – triple-pulley</note>; and they were named so on into infinity. There was a twofold use for these multi-pulleys: for they served either for raising weights on high, or for dragging them across the ground. However, I thought it best to present the machine for both uses here to the eyes of the Reader, so that the visual representation of the machine might compensate for a lengthy description of it.
<margin>Variety of uses for the multi-pulley.</margin>

<margin>Disadvantages of the multi-pulley.</margin>

If the weights—such as the massive bulk of Obelisks or giant Colossi—were too large to be raised by the power of a single <term>capstan</term> <note>original: "ergata" — a vertical-axle windlass used for winding rope</note> and <term>multi-pulley</term> <note>original: "polyspastus" — a system of many pulleys working together to multiply force</note>, they would then increase the number of multi-pulleys to match the number of capstans. Thus, by employing a vast multitude of men or pack animals, with each group moving their own capstans in perfect unison, they finally lifted the masses. These masses were first enclosed in wooden scaffolding or a "wooden garment" to prevent damage to any part of the statues or Obelisks, and they were raised with as much ease as there was harmony in the labor. <margin>A forked wooden machine used in the construction of pyramids.</margin> In the construction of the pyramids, however, they did not use a central timber fixed into a platform. Instead, they employed a certain forked wooden machine, to which a pulley was attached at the upper part to thread the ropes. Outside the base of the pyramid, another machine was applied—which I interpret as a <term>capstan</term> <note>original: "ergaton"</note>—around which the other end of the rope was wound. This machine, rotated by the strength of men or animals, gradually placed the stone in its designated spot. They moved the aforementioned forked machine up each level of the pyramid, completing the work step by step; thus, there were either as many machines as there were levels of the pyramid, or the same machine was moved from level to level. But let us hear the words of Herodotus himself from his second book, where he discusses the Pyramid of Cheops:

> This pyramid was built in the form of steps, which some call stairs and others call "little altars." After they had first constructed it in this way, they raised the remaining stones using short machines made of wood, lifting them from the ground onto the first tier of steps. When the stone reached this tier, it was placed onto a second machine that stood on that first level; from there, it was dragged to the second tier onto another machine (for there were as many machines as there were tiers of steps). Alternatively, they transferred the same machine—if it was a single one and easy to carry—to each successive tier whenever they moved a stone.

From this, it is clearly evident that machines were first successfully devised by the Egyptians, who, more than any other nation in the world, always had their minds intent on erecting the greatest and most prodigious structures. Later, these inventions were passed to the <margin>Herodotus, Philo.</margin> Greeks through Daedalus <note>The mythical master craftsman of Greece</note>, according to the testimony of Herodotus and Philo, and from there they were transferred to the Romans. It is so true that Archimedes, Vitruvius, and Pappus took all their principles from here that even Archimedes himself admits it; <margin>David Rivaldus.</margin> this is testified by Rivaldus in his *Life of Archimedes*, where Archimedes sincerely confesses that he learned many things regarding mechanics in Egypt through his friendship with Hero <note>Hero of Alexandria, a famous mathematician and engineer</note>.

# CHAPTER III.
## *Concerning the Wonder-Working Machines of the Ancient Egyptians.*

<margin>Wonder-working machines of the Egyptians.</margin> This chapter is titled "Concerning the Wonder-working Machines of the Ancient Egyptians"—that is, concerning structures built with such miraculous and great industry that all authors who mentioned them believed they were constructed not by human art, but by the magical aid of demons. For it is the nature of such machines that while the hidden and concealed <term>clever devices</term> <note>original Latin: "technasmata" — referring to the internal gears or hidden mechanisms</note> are not visible, they nevertheless breathe motion and life, holding spectators as if thunderstruck by the novelty of the thing in intense admiration. <margin>They were of many kinds.</margin> They are of many varieties. Some displayed the miracles of art through sound alone, such as the **Statue of Memnon**; others feigned life through motion alone; some were adorned by the craft of water-works. There were also those which, through sound, motion, and other circumstances, were established with such industry that they were not undeservedly called <term>Wonder-workers</term> <note>original Greek: "Θαυματουργοὶ" (Thaumatourgoi) — literally "miracle-workers," used here for creators of complex automata</note> by posterity. <margin>Who was the author of the Wonder-working machines?</margin> Furthermore, who the architect of all these things was is as uncertain as the inaccessible antiquity of this invention itself, since the Arabs assert they were in use even before the Great Flood, as will be said later. <margin>Hesiod.</margin> **Hesiod**, the most ancient of poets, makes **Vulcan** <note>The Roman name for Hephaestus, the divine blacksmith and inventor.</note> the inventor of these, when he recounts that golden statues moving themselves in every direction were fabricated by him. <margin>The tripods of Vulcan.</margin> He also skillfully describes how Vulcan fashioned **tripods** that were mobile in every direction, competing among themselves, and returning to the place from which they had come. <margin>The statues of Daedalus.</margin> Some wish to believe that **Daedalus**, having been instructed by Vulcan, drew all of Greece into admiration of him through the prodigious works of these machines. <margin>Homer.</margin> According to the testimony of **Homer**, he had constructed—with the help of Ariadne—youths who performed dances with outstretched hands; # CHAPTER III. OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS, HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin> It is better known than it needs to be said that Apollonius and other philosophers celebrated for their fame in miraculous things took [their knowledge] from [the Egyptians]; even Aristotle himself seems to have acknowledged this in the Preface to his *Mechanics* with these words: *When craftsmen construct various instruments using the nature found in a circle, they hide the principle so that only the marvelous part of the machine appears, while the cause remains hidden.* <note>original Latin: "non manifestâ causâ"</note> He confirms this in the second book of *On Generation* and in his book *On the Motion of Animals*, where he shows the motion of animals through a certain comparison drawn from automated machines. Thus, the use of these <term>automata</term> <note>Self-moving machines or mechanical devices that mimic life.</note> existed long before Aristotle, from time immemorial. For what things were made by their help by Philo of Byzantium and Archimedes, and by Ctesibius—the son of an Alexandrian barber and the master of Hero—are well known from their works on hydraulics, organs, hydrology, and other automated machines animated by the help of toothed wheels and <term>screws</term> <note>original Latin: "vitium" – referring here to the spiral or "worm" gear.</note>, as <margin>Pappus.</margin> Pappus relates in Book 8. Indeed, in the course of time, these were raised to such excellence and perfection that nothing seems to be denied to modern craftsmen in that faculty, as we shall describe more abundantly, God willing, in our own *Universal Mechanics* in due time. Therefore, let us return to the automated machines of the Egyptians; in describing them, we will first cite the authors, and then we will reveal the hidden reasons for constructing machines of this kind, as far as it is possible to conjecture, through just as many problems.

When it is struck by a ray of the sun—which happens in the morning—then it certainly produces the greatest admiration, for they claim it speaks as soon as the first ray reaches its mouth. For the eyes are shining and joyful when exposed to the sun, like those who are well able to endure the sight of the sun, whom the Greeks call <term>Antalioi</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνταλίους</note> or <term>Euhelios</term> <note>original Greek: Εὐήλιος</note>, meaning 'sun-facing.' Of this the Satirist also makes mention when he sings:

->The golden image of a sacred long-tailed monkey shines,<- <margin>Horace. <note>Kircher has mistakenly attributed this to Horace; it is actually from the Roman poet Juvenal, Satire XV.</note></margin>
->Where the magic strings resound from the broken Memnon.<-

<margin>The statue of Memnon produced sound by magical art, or by the help of a Demon.</margin> We have seen the appearance and position of the statue of Memnon; it remains for us to explain what produced that prodigious sound. Most authors think it was a work of magic; I also think this, being persuaded both by the antiquity of the work and the condition of the statue; for if it had been something purely mechanical—an industrious invention of human wit—certainly it could not have continued its effect for nearly eleven hundred years, from its origin until the time of Apollonius of Tyana. It is more likely, therefore, that it was a <term>talisman</term>—if what the authors cited just before recorded about it is true—compacted within the said statue through the usual conjurations of Demons, who would produce the said effect. Nevertheless, let us see how this same effect might also be accomplished through natural industry.

# PRACTICAL DEMONSTRATION I.

->*To construct a Memnonian statue that gives forth the sound of a string at the rising of the Sun.*<-

<margin>How the Memnonian statue can naturally give forth a sound.</margin>
Since histories say that the statue of Memnon gave forth a sound similar to a <term>cithara</term> <note>A stringed instrument of the lute family, often associated with Apollo.</note> at the rising of the Sun, I have decided that the manner in which this could have happened should be shown in this place by <term>Physical-Mathematical reasoning</term>. No one is ignorant of the fact that <term>rarefaction</term> <note>The process by which a substance, like air, becomes less dense and expands, typically due to heating.</note> possesses great power in the nature of things. Let a base or <term>Abacus</term> <note>The flat slab forming the uppermost member of the capital of a column, or here, the pedestal of the statue.</note> be made, proportioned to the Memnonian statue, and let it be marked A B C D, divided by a <term>diaphragm</term> <note>An internal partition or dividing wall.</note> E F. Next, let the side of the Abacus marked D F be made from a thin metallic plate which easily catches the heat of the Sun, and let it face the rising Sun. Furthermore, let a hole R be made in the bottom of the diaphragm, through which a pipe or channel is led. Within the chamber of the diaphragm A B E F, let a subtle, thin, and very easily movable wheel be arranged, with its axle inserted into each side of the chamber. This wheel, rotatable on its axle, should have small wooden boards within the outer circumference, like certain paddles, inserted into it in a circle and equipped with a quill tip. Around the circumference of this wheel thus prepared, let as many metallic strings as you wish be stretched across in a circuit—of greater or lesser thickness for a greater variety of harmony—which are to be tied to the sides. You will then have a machine adapted for producing the sound of a <term>cythara</term>. For as soon as the side of the Abacus D F B, turned toward the rising Sun, has grown hot from the sun's presence, it will rarefy the air hidden within (which was cooled during the night) by the coming heat. This air, unable to be compressed, will prepare its escape through the pipe R with considerable force; and the pipe, being placed near the paddles of the wheel revolving in a circle, will turn the wheel. As the wheel turns, it will strike the strings stretched over it with the quill tips quite forcefully; finally, it will present to those standing by that sound similar to a <term>lyre</term> or lute, with no one [suspecting] the hidden mechan—

If, however, one wishes to animate a statue placed upon a pedestal with both motion and sound, another channel must be arranged, led secretly from the bottom of the <term>diaphragm</term> <note>An internal partition within the machine's base.</note> through the middle of the statue. For through this channel, the air escaping with great force will animate the pipe and stir the eyes into motion, whereby the statue will aptly mimic life in both sound and movement. And experience has taught that these things meet with success in a similar machine which I myself saw to be constructed; when exposed to the Sun, it gave forth a most clear harmony and all the movements I have described. For I have determined not to pass down anything in this place that was not first made known to me by experiment. Nevertheless, it is clear that the machine of Memnon was not constructed by this art, but by magic, or rather the mechanism of an enclosed Demon, because strings could not have lasted for so long a time. Hence, so that they might last, it would perhaps be more advisable to adorn the circumference of the wheel with delicate feathers inserted into it, as is done in <term>clauicymbalis</term> <note>Harpsichords or similar early keyboard instruments where strings are plucked by quills.</note>; for these, when the wheel is turned, will strike those strings and produce a sound not unlike a <term>cithara</term> <note>An ancient stringed instrument related to the lyre.</note> that will last a long time. However, so that the enclosed sound may be perceived by bystanders, it would not be useless for holes to be made in the upper or side part of the receptacle; for in this way the escaping sound will present itself more clearly to the ears.

# PRAGMATIA IV.
->An Echo that produces thunder for those opening a certain chamber.<-

<margin>How thunder is artificially produced.</margin>
We heard above, as Pliny recounted, that some chambers of the Theban Labyrinth were so constructed that as soon as the chamber door was opened, a very powerful sound like thunder was immediately perceived; we have decided to explain how this was done and by what artifice. The whole matter depended on the arrangement of the vault, which, being winding <note>original: *tortuosa*</note> and having various hollows <note>original: *sinus*</note> suitable for multiplying the voice, caused the creaking of the door to be multiplied within the sinuous coils of the walls, producing, as I said, the sound of thunder. <margin>The Ear of Dionysius at Syracuse.</margin> Anyone who understands the artifice of the "Ear of Dionysius" <note>A famous limestone cave in Syracuse, Sicily, known for its acoustic properties where even a whisper can be heard clearly at a distance.</note> constructed in the city of Syracuse will easily grasp the principle of this thunder. It has a winding entrance shaped like a snail shell, constructed with such skill that someone clearing their throat or shaking a cloak in the entrance clearly perceives the sound of thunder or the blast of a cannon. But whoever wishes to understand the reason for this hidden mechanism described more clearly should consult Book IX of our *Musurgia*, where we demonstrate the architectural principles of the Ear of Dionysius and other echo-producing places found throughout Europe with mathematical reasoning; there, they will easily see how the structure of the Theban Echo was built to produce thunder.

# PRAGMATIA V.

I thought it necessary to explain how this could have been done. <margin>The shrine of Serapis.</margin> The <term>Serapeum</term> <note>The temple or sacred precinct dedicated to Serapis.</note> was built in a round shape, as are all shrines of the Sun, and was notable for its hemispherical dome; in its center was placed the statue of Serapis, of such size that it touched the sides of the shrine on both ends. Thus, so that the rays of the rising Sun throughout the course of the whole year might touch the mouth and face...

<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of how Egyptian priests used architecture and astronomy to create "miraculous" solar effects. It follows a discussion on acoustic illusions, shifting focus now to the manipulation of light to animate the statue of the god Serapis.</meta>

<header>CHAPTER III. 350 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM</header>

...they touched; in the circular base of the dome <note>original: *tholi*</note>, they purposefully constructed circular openings, like windows, according to the rising and setting amplitudes <term>amplitude: the angular distance of the sun's position on the horizon from the east or west point</term> of the Sun, using astronomical reasoning. That is, they were arranged according to the amplitudes or declinations of the Sun from the equinoctial point, both toward the South and toward the North, so that the rising Sun would always fall directly into one of the aforementioned slits, according to its rising or setting amplitude. Consequently, the rays would necessarily and infallibly strike the mouth of the statue positioned in the center of the round structure. From this, the common people, ignorant of the secret <note>original: *mysterij*</note>, came to believe that Serapis was being greeted with a kiss by the Sun, whose soul they believed the god to be. Indeed, as the Sun was setting, lest it seem to have departed below the horizon without greeting the Deity, it would strike the statue with a kiss, as if paying a perpetual tribute to its lord.

But let us demonstrate the matter through mathematical reasoning. Let there be a circle, or the spherical base of the dome, labeled

Specific astronomical positions on the eastern (right) arc are labeled F (winter solstice), C (equinox), and G (summer solstice).</note>

B E C D, within the center of which, at point A, imagine the head of Serapis to be placed. Let round holes be arranged along the circumference of the base, within the maximum rising and setting amplitudes, so that they perfectly correspond to the Horizon. Let the rising amplitude be comprised between F, C, and G; of which F represents the winter <note>the winter solstice</note>, C the equinoctial, and finally G the summer—the maximum amplitude of the Sun on the horizon. Let all things be considered to be arranged in a similar manner for the setting amplitude. Between the stated width of the amplitude F–G, let those window-like slits be placed, so that between every [zodiacal] sign two slits intervene. It will follow that while the Sun rises in the first point of Capricorn <note>the winter solstice, usually December 21st</note>, the ray entering through the opening F will necessarily illuminate the face of Serapis. It will do the same when positioned at point C of Aries and Libra <note>the spring and autumn equinoxes</note> while rising; the same at point G of the summer sign of Cancer; and it will perform the same at any other intermediate point, as well as at the points of the setting amplitude. For since the base of the dome perfectly corresponds to the plane of the Horizon, and the solar rays are directed straight into the openings—which exactly correspond to the solar positions on the Horizon—they will necessarily always strike the central portion of the statue, as is evident from the figure. Thus, at every sunrise, the Sun will appear to kiss the face of the statue. The proposition is therefore clear.

The reasoning is clear from the construction; for since the lines—both the hourly lines and those of the signs—depicted on the hemi-cycle of the dome correspond exactly to the face of the heavens through which the Sun wanders all year, and the hourly spaces in the sky match the hourly spaces in the dome, it follows that the effect of illuminating Serapis must necessarily occur at the given hour. Thus, the logic of the Egyptian mechanism is clear.

# PRACTICAL APPLICATION VI.

->*A Statue placed atop a Shrine that turns toward the Sun.*<-

<margin>How the statue of Memnon can be greeted by the Sun at every hour of the day.</margin>The Arabs report that this machine was constructed by King Nacraus, as the curious reader may see in the Arabic words in the first volume, Work I. The translation of those words is: *“And he built a city in Egypt named Salgia, and in it he made a garden which he surrounded with a wall made of stones of various colors and overlaid with gold; and he planted in it various kinds of fruits, and a river flowed beneath it. He also planted a tree there that was fertile with every kind of fruit, and he built a pavilion <note>original: *tabernaculum*</note> of red stone, on the top of which was an idol that turned with the Sun, etc.”* However, it remains to be explained how this image was rotated along with the Sun.

<margin>A statue can be turned with the Sun in two ways: sympathetically and mechanically. Theophrastus on the Egyptian Lotus.</margin>Two methods can be assigned to this mechanism in this context: either sympathetic or artificial <note>original: *artificialis*, meaning man-made/mechanical</note>. The sympathetic method could be achieved using some material that has a natural sympathy with the Sun, just as Theophrastus writes concerning the **Egyptian Lotus**. For if these materials were inserted into the more prominent parts of the statue (acting as its limbs), and the statue itself were balanced very lightly and precisely upon a sharpened iron pin, the material being "attracted" by the Sun would cause the statue to turn. See more on these and similar matters in what we have discussed in the third book of *The Magnetic Art* <note>Kircher's own book, *Ars Magnetica*</note> regarding Heliotropic Clocks. The other method, being as practical as it is solid, likely performed its rotation through wheels, in much the same way that clocks are driven today. Since we have shown in the preceding pages that the Egyptians possessed knowledge of geared machines <note>original: *dentatarum machinarum*, literally "toothed machines"</note>, nothing was easier than to take an image—previously balanced with precision—and animate it into a motion corresponding to the Sun's movement by means of wheels measuring that motion and attached weights. As these matters present no great difficulty, we have chosen not to dwell on them.

## § II.

->**On machines relating to sacrifice.**<-

<margin>Various Egyptian machines relating to sacrifices.</margin>The Egyptian character was so constituted that they did not merely adorn altars, temples, and statues transformed by a certain mystical and exotic metamorphosis, but they also believed it contributed greatly toward inspiring both reverence and admiration for the sacred rites to bestow movement upon statues in imitation of all-transforming <term>pantamorphic nature<note>original: *pantamorphæ*. Referring to the ability of nature to take on all forms or shapes.</note></term>. This was done so that men ignorant of the mysteries might recognize the will of the Gods—or more truly, of Demons—at least through the movement, gestures, and actions of the statues. This was indeed a marvelous invention of the Priests for the purpose of leading astray the blind hearts of mortals. There were various types of these machines. Some were presented at the entrance of the temple, and others upon the altars. These were indeed fashioned with such ingenuity that not only did the common people believe something divine resided within them, but even those authors who made mention of them judged them to have been constructed by an art superior to human genius. Many such devices are those which <margin>Hero of Alexandria</margin>Hero transmits in his *Pneumatics*, which he testifies to have received from the Ancients and organized into order with these words: *“Since the study of pneumatics <note>original: *spiritalium*. In this context, it refers to the study of air, vacuum, and water pressure.</note> was deemed worthy of the greatest study by the Ancients, both by Philosophers and Mechanics—the former treating its force and capacity through reason, the latter even through the practical application of sensible things—we have considered it necessary to put into order what was handed down by the Ancients, and to explain what we ourselves have discovered.”* Hero, therefore, wished to consign to posterity those things worthy of admiration handed down by the Ancients and put into practice; wherefore we have seen fit to explain these machines one by one in this place.

### PRACTICAL APPLICATION I.

#### Upon the Altar of the Great Mother of the Gods of many breasts, as soon as the candles were lit, the breasts poured forth abundant milk.

<margin>The Great Mother of the Gods scattered milk through the fraud of the Priests.</margin>Many authors believe this work to have been constructed by the art of conjurers and the Demon; but we shall clearly show in this place that it was the deceitful machination of the Priests. They proceeded in this manner. A structure A B C K L was made, furnished with its columns B K and L C, upon which a hemispherical, hollow dome <note>original: *tholus*</note> A B C was placed; inside this was a grate G H, upon which the idol F, fashioned with protruding breasts, was established. The columns B K and C L had movable arms S and T, which could be moved up and down, and were equipped with candle-holders. The dome A B C was closed by a pulley <note>original: *trochleam*</note> placed at position A. Once this was done, a small altar-vessel <note>original: *arula*</note> M N was filled with milk; inside this, a siphon <note>original: *syphon*</note> X B K I was led from the dome through the bottom of the vessel K L all the way to the highest point I of the vessel N M. From the bottom of the vessel, another siphon N M was extended into the statue, and at point F it was divided into small channels <note>original: *canaliculos*</note> according to the number of breasts; and thus the machine was prepared. For at the time of sacrifice, as soon as the fire was lit on the small altar C D, the air within the altar was rarefied <note>To "rarefy" air means to heat it so that it expands, creating pressure inside a sealed container.</note>. Seeking more space, the air sought an escape for itself through the siphon D E; from here, it was first carried through the Dragon’s siphon F Y, where, through a fitting pipe in which it ended, it caused the Dragon to hiss. Then, the air was carried through the two lateral siphons G M and N X into the small vessels OH and SV. By pressing upon the liquid there—milk in one and wine in the other—the pressure forced the liquids through siphons into the bowl of the altar. Thus, Dionysus and Diana <note>Kircher uses the Roman names Diana and Dionysus to represent the Egyptian deities Isis and Osiris, following the Renaissance tradition of syncretism.</note> seemed to pour milk and wine themselves, with the Dragon as if applauding their actions with its hisses. 

Since these events were not understood by the standing commoners, nor was the reasoning of the hidden mechanism known, it is no wonder that they believed these things happened through the favor of the Gods. For Osiris (or Dionysus) was considered the inventor of the vine and milk, Isis was the Spirit <note>original: Genius</note> of the waters of the Nile, and the Asp was the Solar <term>Agathodaemon<note>original: Ἀγαθοδαίμων; a "Good Spirit" or protective deity in the Greco-Egyptian tradition, often depicted as a serpent or dragon representing divine providence.</note></term>, the cause of all these mentioned things, as we have explained elsewhere. Since sacrifices were performed to obtain benefits common to all and to appease the Gods, the Gods seemed to demonstrate that these prayers were granted by the very act of pouring milk, wine, or water, and by the hissing of the Dragon, once the sacrificial fire was lit. Thus, the purpose of the device is clear.

From the base C, a pipe is led into the vessel H L, joined below at D to a brass sleeve <note>original: "æneæ matrici"</note>; through this sleeve, however, another pipe E M F is passed in the manner of an axis, which is inserted at F and M like poles so that it may be rotatable. This pipe has an opening at G, which exactly corresponds to the orifice of the pipe C D within the sleeve. The pipe at E also has a mystic wheel N S inserted, in the center of which the orifice of the pipe ends in a lion’s head. When this is finished, if the wheel or the pipe H S is turned by the handles, the axis E M F inserted into it and turned within the sleeve D, as soon as the opening aligns with the opening of the small pipe C D, the water of the vessel A B, working its way through the small pipe C D into the pipe E M F, will break out with great force through E and the mouth of the lion. If, however, the opening of the axis does not align with the opening of the sleeve, the water will not be poured out, since the opening of the sleeve is exactly blocked by the exterior thickness of the axis. The whole ingenuity, therefore, was placed in this: that the axis E M F be inserted as exactly as possible into the hollow of the sleeve, yet still turn easily within it. It was nothing other than a type of stopcock <term>epistomium<gloss>a valve or tap used to control the flow of liquid, commonly used in ancient plumbing</gloss></term>, which we use today most familiarly in almost all barrels and the pipes of fountains, both for closing and opening them. By this method, therefore, when the wheel was turned, the water of the Nile would be dispersed, as is clear from this device. Furthermore, they signified by the wheel the heavenly Intelligences, which they called Iynges <note>original: "Iyngas"; in Neoplatonic and Hermetic thought, these are intermediary spirits or "messengers" that transmit divine influence</note>, the ministers of the Supreme Deity, by whose influence Mophta <note>Kircher's name for the "Genius" or presiding spirit of the Nile and moist nature</note>, the governor of the moist nature, supplied the sacred water, which was necessary both for producing all things and especially for ritual purifications <note>original: "lustrationibus"</note>.

This produced an undulating motion, making the figures appear to the distant onlookers like a choir of dancers <note>original: "tripudiantium choreas"</note> celebrating the sacrifices offered. It is said that King Menes <note>the legendary first king of Egypt</note> was greatly delighted by these things (designed by the architect Chomnisæus). These systems were constructed with such skill that, in the dark inner sanctuaries <term>adytis<gloss>the innermost, most sacred part of a temple, usually off-limits to the public</gloss></term> by the light of lamps, they expressed the movements of the Divinities almost as if they were alive. This was a clever invention indeed, whether of the Priests or of an evil spirit <term>Cacodaemonis<gloss>literally "bad spirit"; Kircher often attributed pagan "miracles" to demonic influence or deception</gloss></term>, intended to keep the dull and ignorant commoners in the madness of idolatrous servitude, under which they suffered in a marvelous way. Thus, nothing more powerful or effective could be devised for the cult of these false gods.

### §. III.

->*Concerning Clepsydras, or the Clocks of the Egyptians.*<-

<margin>
The hydro-pneumatic clocks of the Egyptians.
</margin>

The Egyptians believed that the exact observation of time and hours was of great importance for the proper conduct of their ritual elections. Consequently, they possessed a remarkable knowledge of the science of timekeeping beyond other nations, and they applied themselves to it uniquely. The many and various clocks they used sufficiently declare this; indeed, Hero <note>Hero of Alexandria, a Greek mathematician and engineer of the 1st century AD</note> reports in his work on pneumatics that he described these in an entire book, but this has been lost to the ravages of time. However, as much as can be gathered from the words of Pappus <note>Pappus of Alexandria, a 4th-century mathematician who commented on Hero's work</note> and Hero himself, most were constructed using hydro-pneumatic art, as will be more clearly seen from the mechanical devices soon to be introduced. It should be noted, therefore, that there were three types of [clocks] among the Egyptians...

### PRACTICAL APPLICATION I.

->*The Egyptian Baboon, pouring water from its member, shows the hours in a vessel placed beneath it.*<-

<margin>Horapollo.</margin>
**H**orapollo indicates the mechanism of this clock with these words: *Again, to signify the equinoxes, they paint the same animal, a seated Baboon <term>Cynocephalus<gloss>Literally "dog-head"; refers to the Hamadryas baboon, which was sacred to Thoth, the god of wisdom and time</gloss></term>; for during the two equinoxes of the year, it passes urine twelve times a day, specifically once every hour; and it does the same at night. Wherefore, not without reason, the Egyptians carve a seated Baboon on their water-clocks <term>hydrologijs<gloss>devices for measuring time by the flow of water</gloss></term>, from whose member (that is, the penis) water flows out; and this is because it signifies the twelve hours into which, at the time of the Equinox, day and night are equally divided.* Furthermore, lest that opening, sharply and skillfully constructed, through which water flows and is excreted into the clock, should either become too wide or too narrow (for both are of great consequence, since if it is wider, it pours out water with great speed and does not correctly achieve the measure and dimension of the hour; but if narrower, it releases the water-flow more gradually and slowly than is proper), they devised this remedy: scraping away whatever hair there is up to the tail, they fashion an iron tube of that thickness for the aforementioned use <note>original: "ferream quandam fistulam"; Horapollo's original Greek text is somewhat obscure here, but Kircher interprets it as a method for ensuring a precise, constant diameter for the water's exit</note>. Moreover, it seemed to them that they did this not without some reason, just as in other matters; and also because it is the only one of all animals that barks twelve times a day, once every hour, during the equinox. 

<margin>The water-clock Baboon.</margin>
We have heard the manner of the hieroglyphic water-clock related by Horus <note>Horapollo</note>; it will be our further task to show in this place with what diligence it was constructed. First, therefore, they made a seated Baboon out of bronze, hollow inside, such as is shown today in the Royal Museum of Monte Pincio, [belonging to] Francisco Gualdo, an Ariminensian Knight. They placed this above a four-columned pedestal <term>Abacum tetrastylon<gloss>a flat-topped stand supported by four pillars</gloss></term> marked A B, within which was placed a glass cylinder C D, closed at its base and open at the top. Inside this glass cylinder, a siphon <term>diabetes<gloss>in ancient mechanics, a 'diabetes' refers to a siphon or a leveling tube used to regulate water height</gloss></term> E F was arranged, whose internal channel I K, perfectly joined to the base of the cylinder, ended in a vessel G H placed below. On the circumference of the glass cylinder, or even on the siphon itself, the twelve hours would be described within as many circles, as the following figure shows. Once this was done, the Baboon was filled through orifice M with Nilotic water, of which it was the symbol, which was then drained through the member of the Baboon into the glass cylinder. And since the channel of the member was constructed with such diligence that through it the water would be exactly drained over a space of twelve hours (which they verified by comparing it to an accurate Sun-dial), therefore the siphon E F also, together with the glass cylinder, in that...

The opposite occurs in the water ascending within the siphon. Note also that the channel IK should not be of any random width, but so proportioned that the space IK between the hourly lines exactly matches the flow of twelve hours. <meta>This page continues the discussion of hydraulic timekeeping. ### CHAPTER III. THE EGYPTIAN GYMNASIUM OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>
This clock, and the one before it, only showed equal hours.
</margin>
This water clock <note>original: *hydrologium*</note> was indeed ingenious and very well-suited for showing astronomical hours <note>Standardized hours of equal length, used by astronomers rather than for daily civic life</note>. However, just like the previous one, it only demonstrated the hours perfectly on the equinoctial days, when the artificial day is equal to the night. Since the ancient Egyptians followed an older system in which every day and every night were each divided into twelve hours, these hours were necessarily longer or shorter depending on how close the sun was to the tropics. Because of this, it was impossible to have a stable and constant rate of water flow to measure them. Therefore, we shall now attempt to explain how a clock can be constructed so that the hours of the days and nights are shown according to a constant law throughout the entire course of the year.

# PRACTICE III.

### ->An ancient Egyptian water clock that demonstrates unequal hours.<-

<margin>
A clock for unequal hours.
</margin>
Let the machine be set up in a suitable place where there is a perpetual supply of water. Let there be a lion's head, or <term>Momphta<gloss>Kircher's name for a specific Egyptian symbol, often associated with a lion, representing the Nile's flow or solar power</gloss></term> marked **A**, which pours water into the reservoir **B C**. To prevent this vessel from overflowing, let the excess be discharged through the channel **T V**. Inside the vessel **B C**, there should be a bent siphon **D**, through which the water discharges into a glass vessel placed within a <term>tetrastylon<gloss>A structure with four columns</gloss></term> **G G H I**, upon whose columns the reservoir **B C** rests. This four-columned structure stands upon another reservoir **H I K L**, into which the water—having flowed from the siphon **D** of vessel **B C** into the glass cylinder—discharges itself through a <term>diabetes<gloss>From the Greek word for 'passing through'; here a regulated drainage pipe or siphon</gloss></term> **E F**. This is the construction of the machine; what follows is the method for marking the unequal hours upon the glass cylinder.

To ensure that the water within the glass cylinder exactly demonstrates the unequal hours throughout the entire year, proceed as follows. First, take a piece of paper equal to the height of the glass cylinder **E F**. On this, you will separately draw the hour lines in this manner: find the maximum and minimum length of the day for the location where the clock is to be set up. At Memphis, this was fourteen hours and ten hours <note>Referring to the hours of daylight at the summer and winter solstices respectively</note>. Then, describe a parallelogram **A B C D**, whose sides **A C** and **B D** are each to be divided into 24 equal parts. Divide the top side **A B** into six equal parts using seven lines that descend parallel to the base **C D**. On each of these, the symbols of the Zodiac signs should be inscribed, as seen in the following figure. This done, starting from the bottom, count ten spaces on side **A C** and fourteen on side **B D**, and draw a straight line **E F** between these points. With this established, the space **E C**, as well as **F D**, should be divided into twelve equal parts, and straight lines should be drawn through the corresponding hours.

<note>This grid represents the surface of a glass cylinder "unrolled" into a flat map. The horizontal axis shows the signs of the Zodiac (starting with Capricorn ♑ at the winter solstice and moving to Cancer ♋ at the summer solstice). The vertical axis tracks the rising water level. The diagonal lines are calibrated so that even though the water rises at a constant speed, it hits the 'hour' marks at different heights depending on the season, thus showing 'unequal' or seasonal hours.</note>

Once the straight lines have been drawn, you will have the lines of the water clock <note>original: *hydrologij*</note> ready to show the hours. This entire parallelogram should be painted onto the surface of a glass cylinder, and you will have the whole task finished. For as the water discharges itself through the bent <term>siphon<gloss>original: *syphonem*; a tube used to carry liquid from a higher level to a lower one</gloss></term> **D** into the glass cylinder, in such a way that the water precisely fills the cylinder up to **A B** within the space of 24 hours, it will necessarily happen that as the water on side **A C** passes from **C** to **E**, it will measure the length of the shortest day—ten hours—through the twelve hour-spaces into which the part **C E** is divided. At the point **V** <note>The equinox</note>, it will show the twelve hours of the equinox exactly. Finally, at **F**, it will accurately demonstrate the length of the longest day—fourteen hours—through the twelve spaces into which the part **D F** is divided. You will observe that the same happens consequently in the remaining lines of the zodiac signs. After the point **E F**, however, the water, gradually increasing, will begin to show the nocturnal hours. 

When the water has reached the final line, it will begin to enter the <term>discharge pipe<gloss>original: *diabetem*; here referring to an internal siphon used to empty the vessel</gloss></term> **E F**. Through this pipe, by the same proportion of motion with which it had risen inside the glass cylinder, it will empty itself into the vessel placed below, marked **H I K L**. This is done with this caution: that the water which had shown the hours while the Sun was in Capricorn by rising in the space **C E**, should show the same hours while falling in the space **B F**. In the same way, the water which had shown the hours while the Sun was in Cancer by rising in the space **F D**, should show the same while falling in the space **A E**, as the numbers written next to them clearly show. The same logic applies to the lines of the other signs; thus, as the water is falling, the line opposite to the one through which it had risen must always be used, as the characters of the signs at the base indicate. 

<margin>This clock is perpetual.</margin> 
Therefore, this water clock is perpetual, owing to the constant flow of water through the lion's mouth <note>original: *os leoninum*; a common decorative fountain outlet</note>. The entire ingenuity of the device consists in the construction of the bent siphon and the discharge pipe. Both of these must be reduced to such thinness and precision that the water from the reservoir **B C**, passing through siphon **D**, fills the cylinder **G I** precisely in the space of 24 hours, and at exactly the same time, the same water empties itself through the discharge pipe **E F** into the vessel **H I K L**. This cannot be achieved except through diligent observation over a period of time; furthermore, the greatest care must be taken regarding the proportion of the vessels—

[...continued from the previous page] must be maintained. But since the water would flow perpetually and the cylinder would therefore always be full, the lion's mouth should have a <term>stopper<gloss>original: *epistomium*; a valve, faucet, or spigot</gloss></term>. This is so that when the glass cylinder has become full of water, it may be closed until the entire volume of water has depleted itself over the span of twenty-four hours. Then, for a new demonstration of the hours the following day, it is opened again; thus, every other natural day, the stopper is closed and reopened. 

We have provided for a perpetually flowing supply of water for this specific reason: as long as the upper reservoir (marked B C in our diagrams) remains full, the water falling through the <term>siphon<gloss>original: *syphonem*</gloss></term> with a perfectly steady pressure will cause the water level inside the glass cylinder to rise at an equal rate. This constant rise would not happen if the water level in vessel B C were allowed to drop gradually, as we shall demonstrate at length in our work on *Hydrostatic Mechanics*.

->*The Use of the Clock*<-

If you wish to know the hour, first look for the line corresponding to the sign of the Zodiac in which the Sun currently resides. Observe where the water level in the vessel intersects that line; the specific hour line it touches at that point is the <term>unequal hour<gloss>original: *hora inæqualis*; also known as seasonal or temporal hours, where the periods of daylight and darkness are each divided into 12 hours regardless of the season, meaning an "hour" is longer in summer than in winter</gloss></term> you are seeking. 

When the water is rising within the glass vessel, use the signs noted on the front (A B); however, when the water is decreasing, you must use the signs described on the base (C D), just as we explained in the preceding sections. Thus, we have constructed a water clock <note>original: *Hydrologium*</note> that demonstrates the unequal hours throughout the entire course of the year. 

These are the matters regarding Egyptian Mechanics that I have thought necessary to point out. He who desires to know more of the wonders of Egypt should read the histories of the Arabs, especially the famous author Schiangia; Salamas Kandati, in the work he calls the *Garden of the Wonders of the World*; Joseph Ben Altiphafi, and the countless others I have cited throughout the preceding pages. I would gladly include their narrations of Egyptian portents here, had I not already provided them in the first volume of my *Oedipus*. 

Furthermore, since many of these wonderful <term>contrivances<gloss>original Greek: *τεχνάσματα* (technasmata); clever devices, often implying artificial or mechanical skill</gloss></term> are reported to have been constructed by the aid of demons and the magic arts, I have judged it best to omit them by design.

<note>Decorative Initial Q: A large woodcut initial containing a figure seated at a desk, appearing to be a scholar or physician engaged in writing or study.</note>**HOW GREAT**, Most Eminent Prince-Elector of the Holy Roman Empire, is the splendor and magnificence of your virtues, there is no need for me to recount in my writings; the world knows it, and historians will bear witness. And although you are perpetually pressed by the burden of such duties incumbent upon you—a weight surely heavier than <term>Mount Etna<gloss>Kircher uses this classical allusion to emphasize the crushing weight of political responsibility</gloss></term>—yet no matters can befall you so great that they might tear you away from the companionship of learned men, whom you love and cherish, or from your desire to grasp the more recondite arts. In this, unless a common <term>self-love<gloss>original: *philautia*; a Greek term for vanity or excessive self-regard</gloss></term> deceives me, you will perhaps find pastures not ungrateful, but suited to your genius. If I learn that these things have indeed not displeased Your Electoral Highness, you will give me courage, so that—stimulated by this kindness and clemency of yours—I may soon bring to light other and still other offspring of my wit, reserved for your glorious Name. Farewell, Prince-Elector of the Holy Roman Empire, and as you have cherished me thus far with your humanity and benevolence, do not cease to cherish me hereafter.

CAP. I. 346 OEDIPUS AEGYPT. HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM.

# SECTION IX
## Iatrics, or Hieroglyphic Medicine.

<note>Iatrics (from the Greek *iatrikos*) refers to the art of healing or the study of medicine. Kircher uses this section to decode what he believes are medical secrets hidden in Egyptian symbols.</note>

### P R E F A C E.

<margin>The triple mode of healing among the Egyptians: Physical, Prayerful, and Amuletic.</margin> SINCE a large portion of hieroglyphic inscriptions is filled with the secrets of Egyptian Medicine, I thought it timely to discuss its origin, discovery, and application in this place, so that its primary components may become known. The Egyptians employed a triple system of medicine. The first was <term>Physical</term> or **Practical** <note>original: *oeconomicum* - here referring to the general management of health and the body</note>, by which the infirmities of the human body were driven away through plant-based natural remedies common to all. The second was called <term>Euchetic</term> <note>original: *εὐχητικὸν* - pertaining to prayer</note> or prayerful, by which they believed they could dispel any diseases through prayers and hymns to the Gods. The third was <term>Amuletary</term> <note>original: *ἀποφυλακτικὸν* - protective or prophylactic</note>, also called symbolic, sidereal, or astral; through this, they were convinced that by using figures of the Gods assigned to specific diseases—adorned with various hieroglyphic symbols and accompanied by incantations—a person could be restored to their former health from whatever infirmity they suffered, by drawing down the power of the stars <note>original: *Deastris attractis* - literally 'attracting the little gods' or astral influences</note>. We have decided to treat each of these in order, intending this one goal: that the doctrines of the wicked arts—which, through the Devil's sowing, have spread their roots to this very day—may be uprooted. Thus, as is our sole purpose, the secrets of hieroglyphic doctrine may be revealed through a truthful interpretation.

# C H A P T E R I.
->On the Origin, Invention, and Condition of the Medicine of the Ancient Egyptians.<-

<margin>Adam, instructed by God in the art of healing, passed it on to his descendants.</margin> Just as the **Protoplast** <note>A theological term for Adam, the 'first-formed' human.</note> Adam is read to have been divinely instructed with an infused knowledge of all things, so it is most certain that he also possessed a remarkable knowledge of the medicinal properties implanted in stones, plants, and animals. For when the mass of the human race became corrupted after his Fall, and was subjected to the tyranny of countless evils and infirmities, this science seemed absolutely necessary for the preservation of human health; otherwise, man—destitute of all divine and human aid—might accuse God’s mercy, which has no end, of being excessively harsh. Therefore, by the wise counsel of God, it happened that Adam passed on the knowledge of natural things communicated to him to his descendants, so that man, weighed down by so many evils and driven to distraction as if by despair, would not cast away all hope of recovery. Hence, <term>Abenezra</term> <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a famous Jewish scholar and philosopher whom Kircher frequently cites for ancient traditions.</note> has shown quite beautifully that after the naming of the animals was completed, God led Adam through all the paths of Paradise, [showing him the properties] of each plant...

<summary>Kircher introduces the three branches of Egyptian medicine—physical remedies, prayers, and astral amulets—and argues that all medical knowledge originated with Adam, who received it from God to help humanity survive the diseases that followed the Fall.</summary>

...[He] gave them the ability to inspect the natures of plants, trees, fruits, and stones, and taught them which virtue was equipped for the expulsion of any disease. From this, it happened that Adam considered it no less necessary to provide for his own health than for the safety of his children, while he passed down the knowledge communicated to him by God, his Teacher, to his sons in a continuous succession. This is the part of the <term>Natural Kabbalah</term> <note>Kircher views "Natural Kabbalah" not just as mystical wordplay, but as a divinely revealed understanding of the hidden powers within the natural world.</note> which Noah, having received it from his predecessors, handed down to his sons, and they in turn poured it into the rest of posterity. But let us hear the words of Rabbi Abenezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar, poet, and philosopher.</note> on this subject:

<margin>Rabbi Abenezra.</margin>
And Adam was led through all the paths of the Orchard to see all the woods, trees, herbs, and stones; and the Lord taught him all their natures to heal every pain and illness. <note>original Hebrew: והובא אדם בכל נתיבות הפרדס לראות כל עצים ואילנות ועשבים ואבנים ולמדו יהוה כל טבעם לרפאות כל מכאוב וחולים</note>

> *And Adam was led through all the paths of paradise, he saw every wood, trees, plants, and stones, and the Lord taught him their entire nature for the healing of every pain and infirmity.*

<margin>Ham first taught the Egyptians the art of medicine, and thereafter Trismegistus.</margin>
Furthermore, Ham <note>referred to here as Cham</note>, being more curious among the other sons of Noah, was the first to bring the knowledge handed down to him into Egypt, which Mercury Trismegistus <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure Hermes Trismegistus, whom Kircher identifies as a real historical sage who codified Egyptian wisdom.</note> finally perfected in all its details. For as Clement of Alexandria rightly reports in the 6th book of the *Stromata* <note>"Miscellanies," a major work of early Christian philosophy.</note>, Mercury wrote forty-two very necessary books, of which thirty-six contain the entire philosophy of the Egyptians; the remaining six, however, which are learned by the "shrine-bearers" whom they call <term>pastophoroi</term> <note>original: παστοφόρους — a class of Egyptian priests who carried the sacred shrines or "pastoi" in processions and were often associated with medical duties.</note>, pertain to medicine: namely, on the construction of the body, on diseases, on instruments, and on medications. Indeed, these books were read only by those who were of the priestly order; hence, being veiled in various hieroglyphs, they were applied to the health of those oppressed by disease in such a way that the underlying reason for them remained hidden from the common people, as we shall discuss in the following sections. Moreover, Hermes himself testifies to the method of Egyptian Medicine in his *Asclepius* <note>A famous dialogue in the Hermetic corpus where Hermes instructs his disciple Asclepius.</note> with these words:

<margin>Clem. Alex. Books of Trismegistus regarding medicine.</margin>

<margin>Trismegistus. The Egyptian method of healing from Trismegistus and Proclus.</margin>
> *“Since our ancestors wandered much in error, being unbelieving toward the logic of the Gods and not paying attention to divine worship and religion, they discovered an art by which they could create Gods. To this discovery, they added a virtue fitting to the nature of the World, mixing it in; and since they could not create souls, they called forth the souls of Demons or Angels and placed them into their statues and divine mysteries, through which alone the idols could have the power of doing good or harm. Your grandfather, O Asclepius, was the first inventor of Medicine, to whom a temple is consecrated on the mountain of Libya, near the shore of the Crocodiles, in which his mundane man lies—that is, his body. For the rest, or rather the whole man (if a whole man exists in a better sense of life), has returned to heaven, even now providing all helps to infirm men by his divine power, which he formerly used to provide through the art of medicine. Hermes, whose name is my ancestral name, remaining in his father’s surname, assists and equally preserves all mortals coming from everywhere.” And a little later: “It is established, O Asclepius, concerning herbs, stones, and aromatics, that they possess the natural power of divinity within themselves; and for this cause the Gods are delighted by frequent sacrifices, also by hymns and praises, and by the sweetest sounds in the manner of celestial harmony; so that the celestial element, by the use and frequenting of these things in the idols, might endure for long periods of time, happily tolerating humanity. Thus is man the author of Gods. And lest you think these things are accidental, they are the gods of the earth inhabited by the heavenly Gods...”*

# THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS’S HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

### CHAPTER I (Continued)

...they sustain the highest celestial things, each one in the order they received, fulfilling and guarding it. But these spirits of ours, caring for certain things individually, foreseeing some, and predicting others by lot and divination, assist human affairs in this manner as if by a friendly kinship. These things are certainly consistent with what <margin>Proclus.</margin> Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher whose hierarchy of being influenced Kircher’s view of the spiritual world.</note> brings to this matter: For the intellect emerges from itself as a God, and the most ancient part of souls exists as intellectual; therefore the supreme genus of <term>Demons</term> <note>In this context, "Demons" refers to *daimones*—intermediary spirits or guiding geniuses—rather than evil entities.</note> as well, being closest to the Gods, is Uniform and divine.

The second order after these are the Spirits already endowed with intellectual property, presiding over ascents and descents, and declaring and handing down the works of the Gods to all. The third are the Spirits who distribute the effects of divine souls into subsequent things, and complete the bond of those receiving the flow from them. The fourth transmit the effective powers of universal natures into things capable of being generated, and they inspire life, order, and reason into particular natures and the entire realm of mortals. The fifth are corporeal in a way, and they bind the extremes of bodies. For in what way can eternal bodies agree with perishable ones? How can the causes agree with the effects, unless a medium of this kind binds them together? For a nature of this kind, acting as a medium, rules over corporeal goods and provides for all natural abundances. Most of their number are occupied with matter; they contain and weave together the powers descending from above from celestial matter into physical matter, guarding it thereafter and preserving the variety and "painting" of forms within it.

<margin>The Egyptians made idols presiding over individual diseases.</margin>
Therefore, they constructed idols for individual Deities who presided over various diseases, to which they added material appropriate from the nature of the World—namely from stones, herbs, and woods—looking toward the Gods according to a planned analogy. Then followed a suitable harmony of praises, hymns, and sounds, by which the Deities were enticed and solicited to grant health (as they falsely believed). Some of these spirits took up the care of individual limbs, as they likewise believed; some were attracted by lots and divination; some showed medicines to be applied to diseases through dreams <note>This refers to "incubation," a practice where the sick slept in temples to receive healing visions from a god.</note>; finally, others, transformed into animals, taught the method of applying medicines. For example, Mercury <note>original: "Mercurius"—Kircher identifies the Roman Mercury with the Egyptian Thoth.</note> in the form of an <term>Ibis</term> <note>The Egyptians observed the Ibis using its long beak to wash its bowels, which they believed taught humans the use of the clyster or enema.</note> taught the use of the clyster, and Typhon <note>Associated here with the hippopotamus; Kircher often links Typhon to destructive or raw natural forces.</note> in the figure of a Hippopotamus taught the cutting of a vein <note>original: "venæ ſectionem"—phlebotomy or bloodletting.</note>; all of these things will be treated more extensively and exactly in the following pages.
