# CLASS IX. HIEROGLYPHIC MEDICINE. CHAPTER II.

<margin>
The Egyptians scrutinized the virtues of plants born in their own soil.
</margin>

...least of all were they content with the knowledge handed down to them by their predecessors; they left nothing undone in their efforts to penetrate the innermost natures of things. Hence, when they were about to examine the individual properties of stones, plants, and herbs, they did not investigate Indian, Assyrian, or European plants, but rather those that had been born and raised in their native soil. They placed great emphasis on the disposition of the climates. For since these local plants had been allotted the same <term>temperament</term> <note>In historical medicine, "temperament" refers to the specific balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—which was believed to be influenced by the local environment and stars.</note> by the liberality of a benign nature as the Egyptians themselves possessed, they cared for no others besides them; indeed, they looked down upon foreign plants as being of a degenerate character. They did indeed possess many traditions regarding the "characters" <note>Originally "characteribus," referring to the "signatures" or physical signs on a plant that reveal its hidden purpose.</note> impressed upon individual things by nature, but access to the practical application of this art was not easy for everyone. Therefore, through industry and continuous exercise, and taught by experience, they finally arrived at what they desired through a constant investigation of the mind. Let us, therefore, explain the method through several established principles.

### CHAPTER II.

<margin>
The Egyptians scrutinized the chains of worldly things.
</margin>

It must first be noted that the Egyptians were entirely occupied with investigating the "chains" of worldly things, by which the fourfold World—the Archetypal, the Angelic, the Sidereal, and the Elemental—were tightly connected. Their entire study seems to have been placed in this: to know which stars and which presiding <term>Geniuses</term> <note>Guardian spirits or governing intelligences of specific parts of the universe.</note> each elemental thing was subject to. Elluchasen <note>Ibn Butlan (died c. 1066), an Arab Christian physician in Baghdad known for his "Tables of Health."</note> recounts all these things, which are in agreement with his own calculations, in clear words in his book on the rites of the Egyptians.

<margin>
Elluchasâm.
</margin>

-><note>original: "والفلسفه مصر..." (Arabic)</note> The philosophers of Egypt, as I found in their histories, sought with the greatest zeal that great chain by which the upper world is bound to the lower.<-
->That is, they endeavored to explore the bond by which the Angelic World is joined to the Sidereal World—<-
->that is, to the twelve signs of the Zodiac and the seven planets—and how this World is connected to the Elemental world.<-
->And from all things that are subject to it—from minerals, stones, herbs, plants, animals, and their properties and all their operations—<-
->they finally learned, through long use and experience, and through long reasoning, that all the forms and likenesses of the lower things are joined to the forms and likenesses of the higher things.<-
->And in this way, they performed great wonders in the use of Medicine. But let us explain each part a little more fully.<-

<margin>
What the "Chains of Sympathy" were among the Egyptians.
</margin>

"Chains of Sympathy" was the name given by the Egyptians to certain series of natural things that continued from the incomprehensible center of the supreme Divinity, through the linked substances of the intermediate Worlds, down to the final boundary of the last World. These series were divided according to the diversity of the levels of the lower nature, and were so ordered by the hidden counsel of God, the Best and Greatest, that individual things contained under one "chain" would regard each other with a certain sympathetic friendship and a fated necessity. Consequently, they proclaimed that person blessed who understood the order of natural things...

Kircher explains that Egyptian medicine relied on understanding these links and preferred local plants because they shared a "temperament" with the Egyptian people.</summary>

### CHAPTER II.

...had found the order encompassed under a single chain. For once these things were composed into one, they promised themselves marvelous effects in Medicine. But I shall exhibit the matter to the curious Reader with a specific example. 

<margin>An example of the Chain of Sympathy.</margin> 

The Supreme Deity of Deities, folding all things that are seen in the Universe into one simple essence, unfolded the individual grades of natural things—as they believed—into the **Genial World** <note>The "Genial World" (Mundus Genialis) refers to the realm of "genii" or guiding spirits/intelligences that bridge the gap between the divine and the physical.</note> instructed by nineteen presiding assemblies of Intelligences. Of these, twelve presided over the twelve signs of the Zodiac, and seven over the same number of planetary spheres. And these flowed into the **Elemental World**, which is distinguished by as many grades of beings, each flowing into its own analogous grade of things; finally, they flowed into the **microcosm** of man, whose body they distributed into as many members. According to a certain sympathy they held toward those things, they flowed into him <term>analogously</term> <note>original: "ἀναλόγως" (analogōs) — meaning in a proportional or corresponding manner.</note>, such that a specific limb had its own proper herb; the limb and herb had their own proper star and sign; and the limb, herb, star, and sign had their own proper Angel. All things, finally, were subject to the Supreme Deity, in whom all things are folded together. 

Therefore, when the Supreme Deity was petitioned through a prior disposition to obtain the health of some ill-disposed limb, they believed that the nod of the divine will was immediately unfolded into that Intelligence of the Angelic World which presided over the said limb. The Angel, struck by the divine nod, immediately stirred the influential power of the star analogous to the limb; the star struck the plant, stone, or animal subjected to it with its astral ray; this object, thus struck and imbued with **sympathetic virtue**, finally restored the limb (or the disease implanted in it) to perfect health through a certain mutual and harmonic correspondence of all the orders. 

Listen to Iamblichus in his *On the Mysteries*: 

<margin>Iamblichus</margin> 

*The world,* he says, *is one living being, in which the parts, though distant in place, are nevertheless drawn toward one another because of their single nature. Yet the reconciling force of the World itself, and the common cause of the mixing of all things, draws the parts toward one another by its very nature; however, such a drawing and appetite can be increased beforehand by some means beyond the ordinary. This reconciling force is a good thing innate to all, and is everywhere the cause of fulfillment, communion, harmony, mutual love, and the worldly union which exists and happens by the command of the containing power. In the parts, however—due to their distance from each other and from the whole, and because of their weak and needy nature—it effects a mutual meeting through compassion. From this, a sharper appetite is inborn in many things. Thus Art, detecting this "power of the curdling agent"* <note>original: "vis coaguli" — a metaphor for the force that binds different elements together into a single substance, like rennet curdling milk.</note> *scattered everywhere in nature, contracts it from every side, collects it together, and derives it into one. In this way, Art renders the naturally moderated appetite for necessary union into an unbridled one through its own devices, while it both applies the matter especially conducive to generation and mixes together different natural forces from all sides into one; by this mixture, it rules at will and completes the meetings for generation. Accordingly, since there are in herbs and stones forces both dissipative and congregative, and since these are much greater in larger things or natures, a striving for union can certainly be found when such things are applied; and from these very things, without the labor of art, love can be kindled and a drawing together can occur.* 

<margin>Proclus</margin> 

See also what Proclus wrote in his booklet *On Magic and Sacrifice*, where you will find almost the same words cited. How they actually arrived at the knowledge of the medicinal virtues which nature had sown into individual things was mentioned above from the cited works of Eluchasen <note>Eluchasen refers to Ibn Butlan (11th century), a Christian Arab physician from Baghdad, famous for his "Tacuinum Sanitatis."</note>...

CLASS IX. HIEROGLYPHIC MEDICINE. CHAPTER III.

...is clear from the words, namely from the similarity of plants and things to the members of the human body. As these must be explained more extensively, they also deserve a specific chapter.

# CHAPTER III.

### On the method and reasoning by which the Egyptians arrived at knowledge of the powers of things; that is, how the Egyptians recognized the powers of each natural thing through the characters and similarities impressed upon them.

<margin>The Ancients explored the powers of natural things in three ways.</margin>
It is certain from the Cabala <note>Here referring to a tradition of ancient, mystical knowledge passed down from the biblical patriarchs.</note> of the world's earliest patriarchs that they learned this art by tradition, which they later advanced with great zeal through long use and experience. Therefore, when they were about to investigate the virtues of things, they employed a triple method: the first was through the manifest qualities inherent in the things themselves; the second was through the signs or characters impressed upon each thing by sagacious nature; the third was through the similarities of things to other things; each of which will be treated in order.

## § I.

### On recognizing the powers of herbs through elemental qualities, which is the first method used by the Egyptians.

<margin>The Egyptians used only native herbs in healing diseases.</margin>
It must be known that the Egyptians used no herbs except those which their native soil supplied to them—having rejected foreign and strange plants as being of a degenerate nature. For only Egyptian plants were held in prize and esteem, as if they were a gift from the immortal Genii <note>original: "Geniorum" — guardian spirits or divine intelligences believed to oversee specific regions or species.</note> granted to the inhabitants. This was also the case with animals and stones; for they deemed no animal worthy of either divine honors or a place in the catalog of hieroglyphics except the Egyptian animal which, produced by the bounty of the native soil, had grown up in that same place; the cause of which matter we discuss more fully elsewhere. It has also been proved extensively in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* <note>Kircher refers to his own 1650 work, *Obeliscus Pamphilius*, where he interprets the hieroglyphs of the obelisk now standing in Rome's Piazza Navona.</note> that they used no stone for the construction of an Obelisk or other sacred images except a child of the Nilotic earth <note>i.e., stone quarried specifically from the banks of the Nile.</note>. Therefore, they held that the same should be established regarding plants; they sought these out with the greatest zeal, and in the manner of an anatomy, they resolved them into roots, flowers, fruits, and leaves—just as they were of a heterogeneous nature, so too were they of different uses in medicine. <margin>The Egyptians learned the virtues of herbs through the service of the five senses.</margin> However, they learned the virtues inherent in individual plants through the service of the five senses. **Sight** they dared to use to recognize [virtues] from the colors white, yellow, red, crimson, flame-colored, purple, green, blue, pale, ashen, and black or dark—all of which revealed the various proportions of the temperaments <term>temperamentum</term> <note>In ancient medicine, the "temperament" was the specific balance of the four primary qualities (heat, cold, moisture, and dryness) within a living thing.</note> hidden in plants. **Hearing**, from the sound with which they were struck—whether sharp, deep, tinkling, dull, harsh, or smooth...

<summary>Kircher explains that the Egyptians identified medicinal properties through three methods: physical qualities, natural "characters" (signatures), and symbolic similarities, while strictly preferring native Egyptian species as divine gifts. The text begins detailing how the sense of sight and hearing were used to diagnose a plant's elemental balance or "temperament."</summary>

<keywords>Egyptian medicine, signatures of nature, native flora, Obeliscus Pamphilius, five senses, temperament, botanical anatomy, Cabala of patriarchs</keywords>

--- Page 349 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Egyptian medicinal philosophy from Chapter III. Having established that the Egyptians relied on a triple method of investigation, Kircher here details the first method: the use of the five senses and physical properties to determine the elemental balance (heat, cold, moisture, dryness) of plants. He concludes this section by transitioning to the second method: the study of "signatures" or natural characters.</meta>

...with a gentle touch, they learned the temperament of the plant's structure. Taste, from their flavors—sharp, harsh, sour, bitter, sweet, salty, oily, or astringent—judged the powers of the plants. Smell also, from their odors—troubling, pleasing, disagreeable, dull, sweet, biting, or pungent—revealed their latent qualities. Finally, Touch perceived hidden virtues from lightness, roughness, softness, hardness, scabbiness, and hairiness. From these manifest qualities perceived by the senses, they judged the <term>caliditas</term> <note>heat</note>, <term>frigiditas</term> <note>coldness</note>, <term>siccitas</term> <note>dryness</note>, and <term>humiditas</term> <note>moisture</note>.

Indeed, from a white and pale color, they took a sign of a weak, moist temperament; yellow was an indicator of heat; red and saffron-yellow provided signs of excessive dryness and moisture; on the contrary, herbs of a green and leek-like color were established as symbols of excessive moisture. Again, a sharp taste showed that a sign of intense heat lay hidden; a harsh taste revealed to them a mark of a cold, dry, and earthy nature; a sour taste was a sign of a nature more moist than cold, for it occurs when more moisture is mixed with astringency. From bitterness, they noted a sign of parching heat and dryness—namely, the earthy dryness latent in herbs; in oily tastes, they noted an airy power; and finally, in the tasteless, an excess of cold and moist quality. Finally, a good odor uncovered good qualities, while a foul one uncovered bad qualities and those of "excremental" moisture. <margin>Abensina <note>The Latinized name of Avicenna (Ibn Sina), the famous 11th-century Persian physician and philosopher.</note></margin> All these things are confirmed by Avicenna in the *Canon of Medicine*, Book 2, Chapter 3.

Furthermore, through the thickness of the parts, Touch discovered an abundance of earthy, moist, and cold-frozen parts; through thinness, it found fiery and airy parts. And just as hardness was held by them to be the companion of earthy dryness, so softness was the companion of moisture, to which weight and lightness correspond. <margin>Other ways in which the Egyptians came to the knowledge of the virtues of herbs.</margin> Beyond these things, they recognized the qualities of things from their disposition or mutability, and their easy or difficult way of receiving [external effects]. Thus, a thing of faster freezing was deemed cold; of faster inflammation, hot. From age, they said the younger would be moister, and the old drier. From location, they also considered marsh plants moist and cold; river and sea plants cold and dry; but those which have their birth in sterile soil, or in the mountains, or in sandy places, they regarded as hot and dry. Finally, from their <term>operations</term> <note>The medical or physical effects a plant produces when applied or consumed.</note>, they called that "hot" which would make things thin, or would dissolve, cleanse, open, soften, ripen, digest, cut, attract, redden, or burn. "Cold" was that which would repel, thicken, or make raw. "Dry" was that which would constrict or squeeze out. "Moist" was that which would inflame, wash away, lubricate, or smooth. And this was the first method by which the Egyptians reached the knowledge of the secret qualities latent in herbs.

### CLASS IX. HIEROGLYPHIC MEDICINE. CHAPTER IV. ###

<margin>
The method of learning the virtues of natural things through the "seals of resemblance" impressed upon them; how ancient it is, and in what it consists. Cornelius Agrippa. Quercetanus.
</margin>

...only, we shall now review by what method the Egyptians arrived at a knowledge of the virtues of natural things through the occult <term>seals of resemblance</term> <note>original: "sigilla similitudinum," the physical markings on plants that resemble human organs</note> impressed upon individual things. For this science was not, as many think, invented by more recent authors, but was resuscitated anew from the monuments of the Orientals. This is beautifully taught by <term>Cornelius Agrippa</term> <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535), a famous Renaissance occultist and polymath</note>, and <term>Quercetanus</term> <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a French physician and chemist</note> subscribes to the same in his book *On Ancient Medicine*. It is a part of the <term>Cabala</term> <note>Here referring to received mystical tradition rather than just Jewish mysticism</note>, handed down orally by the Sages of Egypt or their descendants, or proposed to men of their own order through the "envelopes" of hieroglyphics. It consisted, moreover, in a certain hidden analogy of the members of the human body to various <term>characterisms</term> <note>distinctive physical shapes or marks</note> of herbs, which represented those said members. But let us show the matter by examples. The Egyptians, therefore,

<margin>
Plants having a resemblance to the head heal the head.
</margin>

wishing to heal diseases of the head, sought out a herb whose fruit or <term>calyx</term> <note>the protective outer layer of a flower bud</note> represented the shape of a human head. This, they said, was the appropriate medicine for the head; such was the flower of the **Peony** <note>original: "Paeonia"</note> while still enclosed in its calyx, which they used most especially for the disease of epilepsy, prepared in various ways. In this category, the **poppy**, **walnut**, **nutmeg**, **squill root**, **agaric**, **lily of the valley**, and similar things were also included. These, indeed, they did not use raw, but applied them for medicinal use after they were variously corrected and prepared.

<margin>
For the eyes, things resembling eyes.
</margin>

In this same way, since they found in the flowers of **eyebright** <note>original: "euphrasia"</note>, **marigold**, **hawkweed**, and **scabious** some sort of "ocular rudiment" <note>a shape resembling an eye</note>, they similarly persuaded themselves that these, once rightly prepared, would benefit the eyes. Those things which resembled teeth—such as **henbane** <note>original: "hioscyamus"</note>,

<margin>
For the teeth, things resembling teeth.
</margin>

**pomegranate seeds**, **pine nuts**, **toothwort**, and the root of the **lesser celandine**—they believed would heal toothaches. Likewise, the leaves of **asarum** <note>wild ginger</note>, and the "snail-like" leaves

<margin>
For the ears, things resembling ears. For the rest of the organs, their corresponding resemblances.
</margin>

of **water mint** (where the latter resemble the nose and the former the ears), they intended to benefit those specific members through a hidden <term>sympathy</term> <note>the natural attraction or "liking" between two things of similar form</note>. In a like manner, they applied the following for diseases of the throat: **wintergreen**, **stinking goosefoot**, **throatwort**, and **cassia fistula**. For the lungs: **lungwort** (both the stony and spotted varieties), or that which has its "cradle" in oak trees <note>referring to "oak lungs" or *Lobaria pulmonaria*, a lichen</note>. For the heart: the **citron fruit**, the root of **anthora** <note>yellow monkshood</note>, the fruit of the **cashew** <note>original: "anacardium"</note>, and the **persea**. For evils of the liver: **lichen**, **birch fungus**, **oak**, and **liverwort**. For the spleen: **hart’s-tongue fern** <note>original: "scolopendrion"</note>, **deer’s tongue**, **spleenwort** <note>original: "asplenium"</note>, and **ceterach**. For the stomach: the leaves of **cyclamen**, **ginger**, and **galangal**. For the intestines: **bindweed**, **aromatic calamus**, **cassia fistula**, and **vine tendrils**. For the bladder: **winter cherry** <note>original: "alcakengi"</note>, **bladdernut** <note>original: "staphylodendron"</note>, **vesicaria**, and **nightshade**. For the private parts: **arum** and **beans**. For the genitals: all **orchids** and types of **satyrium**. For the uterus: **round birthwort** <note>original: "aristolochia rotunda"</note>, whose leaves and root both display the shape of a uterus. For the kidneys: **purslane** and **cyclamen root**. For the joints: **hermodactyl**. For the hands: the **palm of Christ** <note>original: "palma Christi," the castor oil plant</note>, **ribwort plantain**, and so on. But contemplate a synopsis of all those reviewed so far, expressed in their own figures, in the following diagram. If anyone truly desires to know what Egyptian nomenclature these herbs are allotted, and what virtue they obtain for "drawing the chains of the Gods" <note>original: "Deorum catenas trahendas," a Hermetic concept where physical objects act as magnets for divine or celestial influences</note>, let him consult Volume III, Chapter 8, where he will find everything handed down at length, so that it is therefore superfluous to deal with them more extensively in this place.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of "Hieroglyphic Medicine" from page 354. # CLASS IX. HIEROGLYPHIC MEDICINE. CHAPTER III. #

<margin>
The juices of herbs heal the humors of the human body when they reflect their likeness.
</margin>

In a similar fashion, they used the juices of herbs that resembled the juices or **humors** <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that were believed to determine a person's health and temperament</note> of the human body in color to purge that particular offending humor. For this reason, the yellow juices of plants—such as **cumin**, **saffron**, **aloes**, **senna**, **wormwood**, **colocynth**, **castor**, and **rhubarb**—which resembled **yellow bile** <note>original: "bilem flauam"</note>, were also held to cure it. To purge **black bile** <note>original: "Bili atræ," or melancholy</note>, all those herbs are useful which have flowers, leaves, or juice that turn black or purple, or are of a dark blue color, such as **beans**, **bindweed**, **blite**, and **borage**. Plants with white flowers, **pumpkins**, **white mushrooms**, **lettuce**, and **agaric** <note>a type of tree-fungus</note> evacuate **phlegm** <note>original: "Pituitam," the cold, moist humor</note>, because they resemble the phlegmatic humor in their moisture. Furthermore, plants with a red color and juice—whether the red shines in the flowers, the stem, or the juice itself—are said to purify the **blood**; such plants include **red sandalwood**, **fern root**, and the stalks of **orach** and **red beet**. They believe that plants of mixed colors, such as the **iris**, cure mixed humors. Finally, **lettuce**, **sow-thistle**, **beitalzar** <note>likely an Arabic plant name borrowed by Kircher</note>, **spurge** <note>original: "tithimallus"</note>, and all species of milk-bearing herbs are used for milk and semen. Indeed, they did not use these juices raw, but applied them for medical use only after they had been prepared and preserved with the highest art.

<margin>
Those things which represent a certain disease, heal it.
</margin>

The Egyptians did not stop here, but reasoning further, they searched with all zeal for the **signatures** and characteristics of diseases. It happened through continuous use and experience that they discovered that whatever seemed to represent a certain disease contributed to the curing of that disease and its morbid condition. Thus, they found by experience that those things which mimicked **calculi** <note>stones, such as kidney or gallstones</note> and rocks were beneficial to those suffering from the stone. They asserted that **fish eyes**, stones found in the bodies of animals, **Gromwell** <note>original: "milium Solis"</note> among herbs, and others that dwell in stony places, were appropriate means for crushing stones hidden in the bladder and kidneys. Thus they believed that herbs naturally "perforated," such as **St. John’s Wort** <note>original: "hypericon," whose leaves appear to have tiny holes</note>, healed wounds—that is, perforations of the body. Likewise, spotted herbs healed skin spotted by **impetigo** <note>a skin infection or rash</note>; scaly plants healed scales; and they said that swollen plants and animals were beneficial for swollen limbs. In the same way, they extracted medicine from venomous animals, such as **serpents**, **scorpions**, **spiders**, and **toads** <note>original: "rubetis," specifically the bramble-toad</note>, which destroyed any kind of poison whether swallowed in a drink or drawn from a bite. Thus sterile herbs, such as **lettuce**, **willow**, **savin**, and **willow-herb**, were thought to bring sterility to man. On the other hand, deceptive <note>perhaps "stimulating"</note> and fertile things were judged to bring fertility, such as **satyr-orchid**, **sparrows**, and the **skink** <note>a type of lizard believed to have aphrodisiac properties</note>. Long-lived and ever-green plants were said to procure vigor for man. Voracious herbs and animals, such as the **Wolf** and the **Pike** <note>original: "Lucius," the northern pike fish</note>, were thought to provide men with the faculty of digestion. In this way, they persuaded themselves that animals endowed with wit and docility produced intelligence and memory; sad animals made men sad; sleepy ones made them sleepy; watchful ones made them vigilant; fierce ones made them fierce; and angry ones made them prone to wrath. Thus, those about to fight against enemies became most fierce by drinking the warm blood of animals previously driven into a rage; and so it was with other traits. Nor was this without reason: for these were men of great and subtle genius, and they knew how to apply the **analogy of things** <note>the perceived symbolic or physical correspondence between different parts of nature</note> fitly and elegantly to various matters; thus they also scrutinized the reasons and causes of each individual thing. For they knew that every single thing moves and turns toward its own likeness. Therefore, when they were about to work toward some particular—

<margin>
The use of herbs and animals in healing.
</margin>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 355 regarding the Egyptian "Doctrine of Signatures." While the previous page focused on plant humors and colors, this page extends the principle of "likeness" to animal organs and explains the Egyptian system of medical specialization based on this philosophy.</meta>

...property or virtue; they sought those things and animals in which such a property or action was most excellently present. Now, they called "action" a certain manner of being born, flowering, generating, growing, proliferating, bearing fruit, ripening, and giving birth, by which individual things—as if by an implanted weight and natural stimulus of desire—pursue, cling to, and are attracted to one another. But configuration, or <term>characterism</term> <note>original: "characterismus," a distinctive physical mark or signature indicating a plant's or animal's purpose</note>, is the resemblance of a signature or mark shining forth in both one thing and another. Indeed, a similar effect presupposes a similarity of the internal agent or cause in both; and this is all the more evident as that signature is more distinct. Thus, they would identify <term>Alexipharmics</term> <note>original: "Alexipharmaca," substances used as antidotes or to ward off poisons</note>—things that imitate a stag's horn or represent snakes, and so on—based on the principle that something which bears the shape of a stag's horn was produced by an internal principle similar to that of the horn itself. Therefore, the similarity of the principle suggests a similarity of powers.

The Egyptian philosophers best understood this secret of nature. <margin>The limbs of animals heal the afflicted limbs of men.</margin> They treated an afflicted limb by taking a similar limb from animals and giving it as food. Thus, those with liver disease were treated with the livers of goats, pigeons, and other animals possessing a liver-like nature. <term>Consumptives</term> <note>original: "Phthisici," those suffering from a wasting disease of the lungs, like tuberculosis</note> were healed with the lungs of pulmonary animals; the sacrificial animal having been fed for some time beforehand on decoctions and preparations of herbs that also resemble the lung. Those with heart ailments—<term>cardiacs</term> <note>original: "Cordiaci"</note>—claimed strength for themselves from the hearts of animals that reflect the nature of the heart. For infirmities of the head, they used the brains of appropriate birds. And so they established the care of various members for each individual case.

To prevent doctors from being overwhelmed by the sheer mass of such knowledge, it was long ago provided that no single physician should undertake the treatment of all human bodily infirmities; instead, each should focus on the care of individual organs, with the burden distributed among many. Hence, <term>Ophthalmologists</term> <note>original: "Ophtalmici"</note> sought suitable means for healing only diseases of the eyes. <term>Cephalic doctors</term> <note>original: "Cephalici"</note> examined diseases of the head and sought fit remedies for them. Just as <term>cardiac doctors</term> treated the heart; <term>splenetic doctors</term> <note>original: "Splenetici"</note> the spleen; <term>hepatic doctors</term> <note>original: "Hepatici"</note> the liver; <term>stomach doctors</term> <note>original: "Stomachici"</note> the stomach; <term>pectoral doctors</term> <note>original: "Pectorales"</note> the chest; and <term>pulmonary doctors</term> <note>original: "Pulmonares"</note> the lungs. Thus it happened that they progressed most successfully in their intended care. This method, passed down from the earliest ages to the present day, still survives in Egypt, <margin>Prosper Alpinus</margin> <note>A 16th-century Italian physician and botanist famous for his work on Egyptian medicine.</note> as Prosper Alpinus relates in his book *On the Medicine of the Egyptians*.

It consisted of the arrangement of the "worldly chains"—which we have explained above. The dogma...

### CLASS IX. HIEROGLYPHIC MEDICINE. 557 CHAPTER III.

<margin>
The astral philosophy of the Egyptians consisted in the arrangement of the Worldly Chains.

The Egyptian dogma concerning the agreement of the higher things with the lower.
</margin>

Indeed, it was a dogma, not only of the Hebrews but especially of the Egyptians, that no part of the human body exists that does not have its own herb, plant, or stone as a protector of its health. These are considered "friendly" or "sympathetic" because, by a natural inclination, they contribute to the preservation of that specific limb if it should ever fail. Again, there is no species in the lower economy of the sublunary world—among herbs, plants, stones, or animals—that does not have its own specific star. By the influence of this star, the species performs its natural functions of gifts and powers. Nor is there any star that does not have its own assigned <term>Genius</term> <note>original: "Genium," a guardian spirit or guiding intelligence believed to direct the "influences" of a celestial body</note>, by whose protection it is supported, and by whose command it communicates the gifts of its influences to the species committed to its care. These spirits rest in that abyssal center of divinity from which all things flow, ready to execute the will of the supreme Deity, who provides sufficient means for the preservation of every single thing. This dogma was held at such high value by the priests as a holy secret that they deemed it necessary to hide it behind <term>hieroglyphic symbols</term> <note>original: "hieroglyphicis symbolis"</note>, as will be shown later. But lest we seem to have invented anything, I will provide here the authority of <term>Abenephhim</term> <note>Aben Wahshiyya, a 9th/10th-century scholar whose works on "Nabataean Agriculture" and Egyptian scripts were primary sources for Kircher’s understanding of ancient wisdom</note>, son of the excellent elder Elmorgum, an Arabic philosopher. In this passage, he provides the doctrine in depth in the work he calls <note>Arabic text: تعليم حكماء مصر (Ta'lim Hukama Misr - The Teaching of the Sages of Egypt)</note> *The Teaching of the Sages of Egypt*. He speaks thus:

<margin>
Abenephhim.
</margin>

-> It is characteristic of the sages of Egypt to employ medicines from all seven types of nature, <-
-> and from every level of existence, all those things that have a likeness and property with the seven planets. <-
-> As you would say, all those that have a likeness to the Sun, and from its sphere and what belongs to it from the days, <-
-> from the earth, minerals, and its stones, and its wild and sea animals, and from its plants and its influences, <-
-> and its properties, and from all its actions—all for the use of medicine for the heart, which is like the Sun in the order <-
-> of the world, and other things. And thus they worked with all types of pain and diseases of the head, liver, stomach, <-
-> lungs, and others. <-

***

It was characteristic of the Egyptians to select, for medicinal use from all species of nature and all levels of beings, those things that possessed some similarity and property with the seven planets. For example, they selected all species having some likeness to the Sun from minerals, metals, stones, and animals (both wild and aquatic), from plants and herbs, and from those things concerning their influence and properties. Finally, they adapted all the operations of "Solar" things for the use of medicine for the heart, because the heart is like a Sun of the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>original: "minoris Mundi," literally the "lesser world," referring to the human being as a reflection of the vast universe</note>. And in this way they worked in every kind of infirmity, such as in the cures of the head, liver, stomach, lungs, and other members. Then he proceeds to details: to select from all the listed things and adapt "Solar" things to Solar diseases, "Lunar" things to Lunar ones, Saturnine to Saturnine, Martial to Martial, Venereal to Venereal, Jovial to Jovial, and Mercurial to Mercurial, demonstrating the power, composition, and strengths of the medicines. Since we have shown these things in the preceding pages, I have thought it superfluous to repeat them here. Therefore, since he subjects the individual members of the human body to one of the planets and signs of the Zodiac, and from the individual levels of nature—

### CHAPTER III. OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS, HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM. 338
### Yyy

...and accommodates those things into the Classes of Worldly Chains which correspond in similarity to such and such a planet and sign, he sets forth this declaration:

<note>The following Arabic text is preceded by a small sunburst or star symbol in the original manuscript.</note>

-> كل وحده من انواع للحيوانات والنبات ومعدنات الذين لهم المثل وصفة مع الكواكب مذكورين وهو باستعمال الدوا ينفع من عضا الذين لهم مثل مع النجوم الذين نكرناه <-

*Each of the species among animals, plants, and minerals possesses some similarity to the aforementioned planets; and these, in the practice of medicine, benefit those limbs which share a similarity with the stars we have mentioned.*

<margin>Marsilio Ficino.</margin> All of these things Marsilio Ficino <note>A 15th-century Italian scholar who was central to the revival of Hermetic and Neoplatonic thought</note> confirms from the tradition of the Ancients with these words: *By applying those things that pertain to a particular star, one undergoes the proper influence of that star and its <term>Spirit</term> <note>original: "Demonisque"; in the Neoplatonic sense, a "daimon" is a guiding spirit or intermediary being, not an evil entity</note>, just as wood prepared with sulfur is ignited by a flame present everywhere. And this happens not only through the rays of the star and Spirit themselves, but also through the Soul of the World, present everywhere, in which the rational principle of every star and Spirit flourishes—partly as a "seminal" power for generating, and partly as an "exemplary" form for knowing. For according to the older Platonists, this Soul, by its own rational principles, built beyond the stars in the Heavens such figures and parts of figures that they themselves are certain forms; and it impressed properties upon all of them. In the stars, however—in their figures, parts, and properties—all the species of lower things and their properties are contained. Indeed, it established 48 universal figures: namely twelve in the Zodiac, and thirty-six outside of it. Likewise, in the Zodiac, it established thirty-six according to the number of <term>faces</term> <note>original: "facierum"; also known as decans, ten-degree segments of the zodiac</note>. Again, in the same place, three hundred and sixty according to the number of degrees; for in every degree there are several stars, from which images are there composed. Similarly, it divided the images outside the Zodiac into many figures according to the number of their faces and degrees. Finally, it established from these universal images certain relationships and proportions to universal images, which images themselves also exist there. Furthermore, things have their own continuity of the same figure from the rays of their own stars cast upon one another by a certain peculiar property, upon which most orderly forms the forms of lower things depend—being, of course, ordered from that source. But even those Celestial forms, as if separated among themselves, proceed from the rational principles of the Soul joined together, and are in a way changeable by the stable ones. But insofar as these do not comprehend themselves, they are referred back to the forms in the Mind, whether animal or more eminent, comprehending themselves, which, as if multiple, are reduced to the simplest One and Good, just as the Celestial figures are reduced to the pole.*

Just as the individual species of things on earth were not subjected to the same Spirits, but to different ones according to the nature of the Nations over which they presided; so too the particular species of Egyptian things were thought to have been assigned their own proper <term>Egyptian Genii</term> <note>original: "Aegypti proprios Genios"; guardian spirits specific to the Egyptian landscape</note>; for the domains of the Spirits were, as they themselves hand down, diverse, just as there are diverse legal jurisdictions. Hence, they judged that foreign plants, as if living under a foreign jurisdiction, were never to be adopted for use—whether medical or for the mystical Sacred Rites—as was hinted at above; indeed, they had individual species distributed among the individual <term>prefectures</term> <note>original: "praefecturis"; referring to the Nomes or administrative districts of ancient Egypt</note> under their appropriated Spirits, as <term>Iamblichus</term> <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote extensively on Egyptian mysteries and theurgy</note> teaches in his book *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians*, with these words: *Therefore, having contemplated this wisdom of the Sacred Rites, and thus according to the harmony of fitness, for each of the Gods the appropriate receptacles [are] dili-*

Celestial figures established by the Ancients.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of "Hieroglyphic Medicine" within Kircher’s *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*. It develops the Neoplatonic theory of "chains" (catenas)—the idea that certain plants, animals, and minerals are physically and spiritually linked to specific celestial bodies and divine hierarchies. This page serves as a transition from the philosophical justification for these links to a visual "Typus" or diagram intended to help physicians use these correspondences for healing.</meta>

# CLASS IX. HIEROGLYPHIC MEDICINE. CHAPTER III.

...carefully finding them, he often combines into one: stones, herbs, animals, spices, and other similar things—sacred, perfect, and God-like—and thereafter fashions from all these a <note>The author is describing the creation of a "receptacle" or talisman designed to hold divine influence.</note> pure and whole receptacle. For it is not right to loathe all matter, but only that which is alien to the Gods. But one ought to choose matter proper to them, seeing as it can harmonize with and contribute to the dwellings of the Gods, the foundations of statues, and the works of sacrifice.

For in no other way can any possession or portion of the divine reach earthly places and the men living here, unless such a foundation has first been laid. One must believe the secret discourses, which testify through blessed spectacles that a certain matter was handed down from the Gods. This matter is therefore kindred to those who gave it. Thus, a sacrifice of such matter awakens the Gods so that they reveal themselves; it immediately calls them to be understood, takes hold of them while present, and demonstrates them perfectly.

One can perceive these same things from the very distribution effected by the divine according to places, and from the governance itself which is divided among individual things—whichever things, according to various orders, whether greater or lesser, have obtained such lots here and there. For it is certain that for the Gods who are the rulers of certain places, a sacrifice from those same things which grow in that same place will be most harmonious; the governed things will please the governors, and those things belonging to them will be pleasing. 

To creators, their own works are always most pleasing, and those who first bring things forth find such things especially acceptable. Whether they be certain animals, plants, or other things seen to be distributed by the powers above, they have both obtained a governorship under them and procure for us an indivisible communion with the higher powers. Some of these, as far as they are preserved and held, increase the familiar property of those holding them toward the Gods—namely, those which, by remaining whole, preserve the power of communion between men and Gods. 

Such are certain animals among the Egyptians, and everywhere the sacred man; some, however, when slaughtered and burned, make this familiarity clearer—namely, those which, through their dissolution into the principle of the first elements, effect a kinship with the causes of the higher powers, and are altogether more sacred. For everywhere, the more the property and familiarity are perfected, the more perfect are the goods that descend to us from there. 

Nor are these merely human inventions, nor did they gain authority from human customs; rather, God Himself, when duly called among the sacred rites, is the Author of such laws. Around Him, the soothed Gods and Angels occupy themselves, under whom a certain <term>Divinity</term> <note>original: "Numen"; a local deity or divine power</note> has obtained a <term>Governance</term> <note>original: "Præfecturam"; an administrative or protective role over a specific area</note> and a common Province through whatever nations are on earth. From there, a proper Divinity is also assigned to each temple. Likewise, over the sacred rites performed for the Gods, some God is the observer and governor; for those to the Angels, an Angel; for those to the <term>Demons</term> <note>original: "Dæmones"; in this context, the word refers to intermediary spirits or "daimons," not necessarily evil beings</note>, a Demon; and in others, in the same manner according to their own kind, a perfect being has obtained a kindred Governance. 

And although in the *Egyptian Astrology* we have exhibited the <term>chains</term> <note>original: "catenas"; the Hermetic concept that all levels of reality are linked by "sympathy" or shared qualities, like a chain hanging from heaven to earth</note> of herbs with the planets, the twelve signs of the Zodiac, as well as their <term>Decans</term> <note>original: "Decanis"; 10-degree subdivisions of the zodiac signs, each ruled by a specific spirit or deity</note>, together with the presiding <term>Spirits</term> <note>original: "Genijs"; protective or guiding spirits associated with specific places or times</note> through extensive tables, here nonetheless, as if by profession, it seemed best to exhibit the same more fully and specifically, lest we should seem to have omitted anything useful to our Physicians in this work. I place here a figure of the things said and to be said, from which the mind shines forth more clearly than at midday.

# The characteristics of plants compared to the Characteristics of the twelve signs, and the members of the human body, according to the method of both the Hebrews and modern Physicians; the latter of whom received everything from the Hebrews, and the former from the Egyptians by tradition.

<margin>Characteristics of plants compared to the Characteristics of the 12 Signs of the Zodiac, and the members of man.</margin>
Since, in truth, not all herbs that are referred to a specific sign possess the same degree of quality, nor do they obtain their full medicinal value at just any time; we shall therefore present the individual plants belonging to each sign, distinguished into four degrees. We shall declare in what place and at what time they are to be gathered so that they may serve the specific limb they correspond to, and furthermore, what antipathies <note>In this context, "antipathies" refers to medicinal contradictions or astrological conflicts.</note> they have toward other signs. In this way, this botanical argument may come forth in a form perfect in every detail. We have extracted these details partly from Avenar the Hebrew <note>original: "Auenar Hebræo"; referring to the scholar Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167).</note> and partly from the *Astral Botany* of Carrichter the German <note>original: "Carichteri Germani"; referring to Bartholomaeus Carrichter (c. 1507–1567), a physician to Emperors Ferdinand I and Maximilian II.</note>. We shall, therefore, make the beginning of our discussion with Aries.

---

->I. Aries <note>The Ram. Astrological symbol: ♈</note><-

<margin>Plants related to Aries (♈).</margin>
**A**ries is a masculine sign, fiery, hot and dry, and sympathetic to the head. The plants of the first degree are hot and dry.

<margin>Degrees of hot and dry things.</margin>
**Degree I.** Red Mugwort, Betony, Chicory, Larkspur, Dwarf Elder, Mint, Coltsfoot, and Speedwell. These are to be gathered at the end of the Dog Days <note>The "Canicular days," the hottest period of summer, usually from July 3 to August 11.</note> after the full moon.
**Degree II.** These plants are hot and dry in the second degree: Asparagus, St. John’s Wort, Yarrow, Plantain, and Peony. They are to be gathered while the Sun and Moon are positioned in Cancer.
**Degree III.** Agaric, Caper Spurge, Spurge Laurel, Bitter Apple, Coltsfoot, Gentian, Privet, Castor Oil plant, and Elderberry. They are to be gathered at the end of July and the beginning of August.
**Degree IV.** Southernwood, White Hellebore, Marjoram, Horehound, Wild Nasturtium, and Rosemary. They are to be gathered partly in the month of April and partly in September.

# CHAPTER III.

<margin>Degrees of hot-dry plants.</margin>

**Degree I.** <term>Basil</term> (Basilicon), <term>Saffron</term> (Crocus), <term>Cypress</term>, <term>Clove</term> (Caryophyllum), <term>Hyssop</term>, <term>Lavender</term>, <term>Water Plantain</term>, <term>Sundew</term> (Ros Solis), <term>Thyme</term>.
**Degree II.** <term>Wild Angelica</term>, <term>Twayblade</term> (Bifolium), <term>Centaury</term>, <term>Galangal</term>, <term>Gentian</term>, <term>Devil's-bit</term> (Morsus Diaboli).
**Degree III.** <term>Stinking Mayweed</term> (Cotula foetida), <term>Parsnip</term>, <term>Mint</term>, <term>Garden Cress</term>, <term>Pennyroyal</term>, <term>Buttercup</term> (Ranunculus), <term>Nettle</term>.
**Degree IV.** <term>Birch</term>, <term>Broom</term> (Genista), <term>Boxwood</term>, <term>Laurel</term>.
Herbs of the first degree are to be gathered when the <term>Sun is in Pisces</term> and the <term>Moon is in Cancer</term>. Species of the second degree are gathered at the beginning of May before sunrise, or toward the end of August; or with the Sun in Taurus and the Moon in Gemini, before sunrise. Species of the third degree are gathered with the Sun in Leo and the Moon in Virgo at the last quarter, or for the purpose of cooling, with the Sun in Taurus and the Moon in Gemini, before sunrise. Species of the fourth degree are gathered with the Sun in Pisces and the Moon in Aquarius; for by such an influence they are reduced to a temperate state. But let us hear <term>Avenar</term> <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a renowned Jewish scholar whose astrological works were highly influential in the Renaissance.</note> discussing these matters according to the mind of the Egyptians:

> <note>original Hebrew: ותולדתו חמה ויבשה וחמרה האדמה ומטעמו מחדריף ממראה העינים המבורכה והצהוב ומן החיות האריות והנמרים והצפעונים וחרובים וזואבים ומכלי המתכות הזהב והכסף והאבנים היקרות והאבן הנוקבת האבנים הנקראות אלמאס והאבן מלקטות החפץ חנפ" אזלרי וכל מלאכת האש:</note>
> *That is: In temperament, hot and dry; among the humors, it possesses <term>red bile</term> (cholera rubea); among tastes, the bitter and the sharp; among colors, saffron and red tending toward the sight; among animals, it has Lions, Leopards, Basilisks, Vipers, and Wolves; among metals, Gold and Silver. Also precious stones: the Diamond (Adamantem), <term>Chrysoprase</term>, and that which is called <term>El-sari</term>, and every work of fire.*

---

## <note>Astrological symbol: ♍ (Virgo)</note> Virgo

<margin>Plants related to Virgo.</margin>

**Virgo** is a feminine sign, earthy, and cold-dry; it possesses a <term>sympathy</term> <note>In Hermetic medicine, a "sympathy" is a natural resonance between a celestial sign and a specific organ.</note> with the liver, the intestines, and the belly, the species of which follow:

**Degree I.** <term>Sorrel</term> (Acetosa), <term>Barberry</term>, <term>Chicory</term>, <term>Ribwort Plantain</term> (Plantago acuta), <term>Pear</term>, <term>Wood Sage</term>; these are cold-dry by nature.
**Degree II.** <term>White Beet</term>, <term>Rosehip</term> (Cynosbatos), <term>Medlar</term>, <term>Solomon’s Seal</term>; cold-dry in the second degree.
**Degree III.** <term>Birthwort</term> (Aristolochia), <term>Bugle</term> (Consolida media), <term>Fleabane</term> (Coniza), <term>Self-heal</term> (Prunella), <term>Oak</term>; cold-dry in the third degree.
**Degree IV.** <term>Blessed Thistle</term> (Carduus benedictus), <term>Lesser Centaury</term>, <term>Adder's-tongue</term> (Ophioglossum), <term>Wild Plum</term> (Sloe) with all its parts, <term>Serpentaria</term>, <term>Tormentil</term>.

<summary>This page categorizes plants by their "degrees" of heat and dryness, providing specific astrological timings for their harvest. It also introduces the sign of Virgo, listing its medicinal sympathies and associated cold-dry botanical species.</summary>

# CLASS IX. HIEROGLYPHIC MEDICINE. CHAPTER III.

The first [class] has sympathies with the species of <term>Taurus</term> <note>the Bull</note>; its antipathies are with <term>Aries</term> <note>the Ram</note> and <term>Leo</term> <note>the Lion</note>; concerning which <term>Avenar</term> <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a 12th-century scholar whose astrological works Kircher frequently cites</note> says the following in the *Astrology of the Egyptians*:

> <note>The following is translated from the original Hebrew text provided in the manuscript:</note>
> Its nature is cold and dry, and it generates <term>black bile</term> <note>original: "choleram nigram," the humor associated with melancholy</note>; of tastes, it has the astringent; of the sight of the eyes, it has white and purple, and an ashy color; among living things, it rules man and birds; and among plants, every small plant that lacks a stalk, such as wheat, barley, and beans, and all kinds of manna and seeds.

---

-> VII  **Libra** <note>The Scales. Astrological symbol: ♎</note> <-

<margin>Plants related to ♎.</margin>
**L**ibra is a masculine, airy, warm, and moist sign; it is sympathetic to the kidneys and the bladder. Its species follow.

**Degree I.** All kinds of <term>Daisies</term> (Bellis), <term>Bugle</term> (Consolida media), <term>Feverfew</term> (Parthenium), <term>Self-heal</term> or Primrose (Prunella veris), <term>Spignel</term> (Meum), <term>Goat's-beard</term> (Tragopogon).
**Degree II.** <term>Garlic</term> (Allium), <term>Marshmallow</term> (Althaea), <term>Chamomile</term> (Chamaemilla), <term>Martagon Lily</term> (Martagon), <term>Mallow</term> (Malva), <term>Vervain</term> (Verbena), <term>Mistletoe</term> (Viscus), <term>Linden</term> (Tilia).
**Degree III.** <term>Snapdragon</term> (Antirrhinum), <term>Mugwort</term> (Artemisia), <term>Greater Celandine</term> (Chelidonium maius), <term>Black Mint</term> (Mentha nigra), <term>Scabious</term> (Scabiosa), <term>Figwort</term> (Scrophularia).
**Degree IV.** <term>Madwort</term> (Alyssum), <term>Chickweed</term> (Alsine), <term>Hazel</term> (Corylus), <term>Wall-rue</term> (Ruta muraria). But Avenar refers to the following species:

> <note>The following is translated from the original Hebrew text provided in the manuscript:</note>
> Its nature is warm and moist; it possesses man and every bird with a large head; and among plants, the tall trees; of tastes, the sweet; and of the sight of the eyes, green and an ashy color.

---

-> VIII  **Scorpius** <note>The Scorpion. Astrological symbol: ♏</note> <-

<margin>Plants related to ♏.</margin>
**S**corpius is a feminine, watery, cold, and moist sign; sympathetic to the genital parts. Its species follow.

**Degree I.** <term>Crosswort</term> (Cruciata), <term>Hawthorn</term> (Oxyacantha), <term>Wild Service-tree</term> (Sorbus sylvestris).
**Degree II.** <term>Ash</term> (Fraxinus), all kinds of <term>Roses</term> <note>original: "Roma," likely a variant of "Rosa"</note>, <term>Plum</term> (Prunus), <term>Shells</term> (Conchae), <term>Oysters</term> (Ostrea); to this category belong all the <term>remedies</term> <note>original: "supplicia," which usually means punishments, but in this medical context likely refers to "suppetia" or harsh medicinal applications</note> of the first degree from the <term>Canary Islands</term> (Canari), if they have been collected in the month of October.

-> Degree <-
